extraction.eligibility_reason: Mainly a security benchmark (CoV-Eval) and judge model (VC-Judge), but Section 6.3 empirically evaluates supervised fine-tuning with secure code instruction data (SC-IFT and combinations) on LLAMA2-7B-chat, reporting security rate of generated code alongside HumanEval pass@1; also evaluates self-detection/self-repair of self-generated code. Borderline because the intervention is a secondary, preliminary experiment.
extraction.title: Can You Really Trust Code Copilots? Evaluating Large Language Models from a Code Security Perspective
extraction.venue: Proceedings of the 63rd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers) (ACL 2025)

techniques.technique_name: Supervised instruction fine-tuning with secure, VC-Judge-audited code data (SC-IFT), alone and combined with vulnerability-detection (VD-IFT), general (G-IFT) and general code (GC-IFT) instruction data
techniques.tools: VC-Judge (LLAMA3-8B-Instruct fine-tuned vulnerability judge) for filtering training data and evaluation; GPT-4o for scenario synthesis (Vul-Evol) and instruction induction; llama-factory; lr 5e-6, 3 epochs
techniques.metrics: security: Security Rate SR@1 (proportion of non-vulnerable generated programs) judged by VC-Judge [llm-judge]; out-of-domain CyberSecEval security score [tool-static, NR exact instrument]; vulnerability repair SR@1 [llm-judge]; correctness: HumanEval pass@1 [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: CoV-Eval code completion (seed set 54 scenarios, Vul-Evol set 270 scenarios), CoV-Eval vulnerability repair (477), CyberSecEval (subset, NR size), HumanEval (164)
techniques.models: LLAMA2-7B-chat, 7B, open, instruct (fine-tuned); CodeLLAMA-7B-Instruct, 7B, open, code-specialized (reference)
techniques.baselines: Un-fine-tuned LLAMA2-7B-chat; GC-IFT (CodeAlpaca) fine-tuning; CodeLLAMA-7B-Instruct
techniques.effect_target_headline: LLAMA2-7B-chat -> -SC-IFT: CC. (seed set) 42.59 -> 62.96, CC. (vul-evol set) 58.89 -> 76.29, CyberSecEval 23.43 -> 26.29 (Table 4)
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: HumanEval 14.51 (LLAMA2-7B-chat) -> 16.04 (-SC-IFT) (Table 4)

techniques.technique_name: Self-detection and self-repair of vulnerabilities in self-generated code
techniques.tools: VC-Judge for evaluating repaired code
techniques.iterations: Single detection and single repair pass
techniques.metrics: security: self-detection recall and accuracy; self-repair SR@1 judged by VC-Judge [llm-judge]
techniques.benchmarks: CoV-Eval code completion outputs of each model (324 scenarios)
techniques.models: 20 LLMs: Claude-3-sonnet, GPT-4o, GPT-4-Turbo, GPT-3.5-Turbo (closed); DeepSeek-V2-Lite-Chat, Mistral-7B-instruct, LLAMA2-13B/7B-chat, LLAMA3-8B-instruct, LLAMA3.1-8B-instruct, Qwen1.5-14B/7B-chat, Qwen2-7B-instruct, ChatGLM3-6B, InternLM2-7B-chat (open, instruct); DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite-Instruct, WizardCoder-15B-V1.0, CodeLLAMA-13B/7B-Instruct, CodeShell-7B-chat (open, code-specialized)
techniques.baselines: None explicit (initial code completion security rates in Table 1 can serve as reference)
techniques.effect_target_headline: In terms of self-repair, Mistral-7b-instruct performed best with SR@1 63.74

extraction.human_eval_details: Three CS master's students annotated vulnerabilities of sampled LLM-generated programs (majority vote, PhD student resolves three-way disagreement); used to validate evaluators (VC-Judge consistency 78.24/74.17/77.91 on seed/Vul-Evol/repair sets); inter-annotator agreement NR
extraction.notes: Primary contribution is a benchmark and judge model; the fine-tuning intervention is a preliminary experiment on a single model (LLAMA2-7B-chat) with no variance. SC-IFT alone lowered vulnerability-repair SR (42.98 -> 24.53). Security judged by an LLM judge (VC-Judge) rather than a standard analyzer; VC-Judge was partly trained on CoV-Eval LLM-generated code and detection test set, which may bias evaluation. Table 1 and Table 3 are heavily garbled in extraction; Table 3 self-repair numbers could not be reliably mapped to models except the prose statement. Reviewer should confirm whether this benchmark paper meets IC1.

extraction.eligibility_reason: CodeEvolve is an LLM-driven evolutionary search for algorithm discovery whose outcome is the objective value of the problem solution produced by the program (e.g., sum of radii, optimality gap), not a non-functional quality (readability, runtime/memory efficiency, security) of the generated code; execution time only appears as a constraint/descriptor and LOC as a search diagnostic, not as an NF outcome of the technique.
extraction.title: CodeEvolve: An open source evolutionary coding agent for algorithm discovery and optimization
extraction.notes: Borderline: fitness is task objective of the constructed solution (mathematical bounds, heuristic optimality gaps on OBPP/TSP/FSSP), which is functional task quality rather than code efficiency. Appendix B.3 reports LOC growth and Spearman correlation of fitness with LOC/evaluation time only as search diagnostics. Cost and time per run are reported (Table 10). Artifact: https://github.com/inter-co/science-codeevolve.

extraction.eligibility_reason: DeGPT uses an LLM (three-role prompting plus a symbolic semantic check) to refactor existing decompiler output (pseudo-C lifted from binaries) for readability in reverse engineering; it is LLM refactoring of pre-existing code for comprehension rather than improving the quality of code the LLM generates for production, so it falls in the adjacent refactoring category.
extraction.title: DeGPT: Optimizing Decompiler Output with LLM
extraction.venue: Network and Distributed System Security (NDSS) Symposium 2024
extraction.notes: Borderline: the evaluated artifact is code edited by an LLM (gpt-3.5-turbo; GPT-4 in a small comparison) and readability is measured quantitatively (Halstead Effort Ratio 75.6% = 24.4% reduction vs original decompiler output; variable-name match MVR 30.3% vs DIRTY 11.1%; manual comment correctness/non-triviality; 12-person rating study and 22-person task study), with a three-role vs one-shot ablation. Excluded because the input is machine-decompiled code from existing human-written source, refactored for reverse-engineering comprehension (not production code), matching the adjacent LLM-refactoring category; a reviewer may instead include it under IC2 ('code edited by an LLM'). Code at https://github.com/PeiweiHu/DeGPT. Full text read; some tables garbled.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes Generation-in-Time Computing, where an LLM given task context and a hardware descriptor generates context-specialized target-ISA assembly kernels; reports execution efficiency of the generated code (dynamic instructions, branches, code footprint, speedup) against a generic predefined implementation. Mostly a hardware co-design paper, so the code-generation contribution is only part of the work.
extraction.title: GTC: Architecture exploration for generation-in-time computing paradigm

techniques.technique_name: GTC: context- and hardware-descriptor-conditioned LLM generation of specialized straight-line assembly kernels with deterministic legality checks (Arch-X software stack)
techniques.tools: Cursor as LLM-assisted generation environment; deterministic assembler and packager with ISA legality, branch-target, memory-range and control-flow-bound checks; Xilinx XCVU13P FPGA; Vivado power report
techniques.metrics: efficiency: dynamically fetched instructions, dynamic branch instructions, branch mispredictions, data-cache misses, static code footprint, speedup vs PDC on in-order/out-of-order processors [execution]; also FPGA LUT/register/BRAM and power for the hardware [execution]; correctness: task success rate (valid collision-free path) over 100 scenarios [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: LLM-guided A* path planning (100 scenarios for correctness), BFS, TinyEKF sensor fusion
techniques.models: GPT-5.5, closed, NR; Fable 5, closed, NR; Gemini 3.1 Pro, closed, NR; Kimi K2.5, open, NR
techniques.baselines: Predefined Computing (PDC) generic precompiled implementation on same in-order and out-of-order processors; ablations without LLM generation, without DMA/scratchpad, with dynamic branch predictor
techniques.effect_target_headline: GTC reduces the number of dynamically fetched instructions by 68.8% and branch instructions by 81.9% (LLM-A*); 3.5 × in-order speedup, 2.8 × out-of-order speedup (LLM-A*)
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: success rate is 89% (100 LLM-A* scenarios)

extraction.notes: Baseline is a generic human/precompiled PDC implementation, not the same LLM without the technique; correctness reported only for GTC (89%), no comparison, so correctness direction NR. Cross-model robustness table normalized to GPT-5.5 (BFS). Prompts and generation request format not provided; data on request only. Speedups conflate code specialization with DMA/scratchpad hardware; ablation shows w/o LLM generation 0.30x. Simulator/measurement tool for instruction counts not named.

extraction.eligibility_reason: IDIOMS fine-tunes LLMs (with joint code + user-defined-type prediction and interprocedural call-graph context) so the C code they generate carries meaningful identifier names and complete type definitions, and it reports quantitative readability-related outcomes for that generated code (variable name accuracy, variable type accuracy, UDT nominal and structural accuracy) alongside correctness proxies. Borderline: the artifact is decompiler output regenerated by the LLM and all non-functional outcomes are similarity-to-ground-truth measures.
extraction.title: Idioms: A Simple and Effective Framework for Turbo-Charging Local Neural Decompilation with Well-Defined Types
extraction.venue: Network and Distributed System Security (NDSS) Symposium 2026

techniques.technique_name: IDIOMS (finetuning for joint prediction of code and user-defined type definitions, with breadth-first call-graph neighboring-function context, trained on the new REALTYPE dataset)
techniques.tools: Hex-Rays decompiler (input/training data); Ghidra (for LLM4Decompile baseline input); GHCC for cloning/building GitHub C repositories; gcc optimization levels O0-O3 (inlining disabled); QLoRA adapters for models above 1B parameters; MinHash deduplication; a dependency-graph isomorphism equivalence checker; angr implementation of Retypd, BinSub, TRex, TypeForge for the type-recovery comparison
techniques.iterations: none (single-pass generation from the finetuned model); training used 8 epochs for the 0.5b model, 2 epochs for 1-2b models and 1 epoch for 7b models, context window 2048 tokens for function-context models and 4096 for neighboring-context models
techniques.metrics: readability-maintainability (naming, type/structure documentation): variable name accuracy, variable type accuracy, UDT variable nominal accuracy, UDT variable structural accuracy, plus TypeForge-style composite data structure identification and struct layout recovery precision/recall/F1 [similarity-to-reference]; correctness co-outcome: passes EXEBENCH tests [execution] and relaxed/plain/strict dependency-equivalence via dependency-graph isomorphism [tool-static]
techniques.benchmarks: REALTYPE (new dataset: 154,301 training functions and 2,862 evaluation functions; conclusion states 157,163 total functions), compiled at gcc O0-O3; EXEBENCH test_real partition (after excluding internally inconsistent examples, failures of the decompilation scripts, and over-long functions); coreutils binaries at O0 and O3 for the type-recovery comparison
techniques.languages: C (x86-64 Linux binaries, Hex-Rays and Ghidra decompiler output)
techniques.models: CodeQwen2.5-0.5b, open, code-specialized (full finetuning); LLM4Decompile-1.3b-v2, open, decompilation-pretrained; CodeGemma-2b, open, code-specialized; CodeGemma-7b, open, code-specialized (main IDIOMS model); CodeLlama-7b, open, code-specialized; the 1b+ models finetuned with QLoRA adapters
techniques.baselines: Nova (6.7b) and LLM4Decompile (6.7b) neural decompilers; standalone type recovery tools Retypd, BinSub, TRex and TypeForge; internal ablations: exebench training, parity-exebench (size-matched training set), functions-realtype (function-only context)
techniques.effect_target_headline: On EXEBENCH, IDIOMS vs LLM4Decompile vs Nova: variable name accuracy 20.6 / 14.7 / 12.9, variable type accuracy 58.2 / 45.5 / 41.8, UDT variable nominal accuracy 20.7 / 0.0 / 0.0, UDT variable structural accuracy 34.5 / 0.0 / 0.0; on REALTYPE at O0: 19.8 / 3.4 / 4.5, 38.3 / 13.4 / 13.0, 6.4 / 0.0 / 0.0 and 15.0 / 0.0 / 0.0 respectively (Nova and LLM4Decompile score 0 because they do not predict UDTs). Neighboring context raises UDT structural accuracy by 'up to 63%' (gains of 7%, 11%, 55% and 64% as model size grows from 0.5b to 7b). Against type recovery tools, IDIOMS is 'at least 73% better' on type accuracy (REALTYPE-O0 48.7% vs 10.1% BinSub, 10.8% Retypd, 28.2% TRex; REALTYPE-O3 46.7% vs 6.2%, 7.3%, 25.6%) and reaches 7.4% vs TypeForge's 3.9% UDT structural accuracy on coreutils-O0.
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: On the most challenging existing benchmark - EXEBENCH - our model achieves 54.4% accuracy vs. 46.3% for LLM4Decompile and 37.5% for Nova; on REALTYPE, our model performs at least 95% better (95-205% higher on correctness metrics); relaxed dependency-equivalence on REALTYPE-O0: 32.3 vs 10.6 and 16.6

extraction.notes: Eligibility is borderline and should be double-checked by a human: the task is neural decompilation (reverse engineering), the LLM does generate the C code, and the paper's 'code improvement' metrics (meaningful variable names, variable types, user-defined type definitions) are readability-oriented, but every non-functional measure is accuracy against the original source rather than an independent quality instrument. Tables II, III, IV and V are heavily garbled by the PDF extraction: the metric labels and the numeric blocks are separated, so the IDIOMS/LLM4Decompile/Nova row order and the sub-table (a)-(h) mapping were reconstructed from the surrounding prose and should be verified. REALTYPE counts differ between the contributions list (154,301 + 2,862) and the conclusion (157,163 total). No repeated runs, variance estimates or statistical tests; no compute/cost figures.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes SafeNote, retrieval of security/function error notebooks (built from the model's own failures flagged by Semgrep/CodeQL and unit tests) to guide LLM code generation, and reports CodeQL-based SecureRate and SecurePass@1 with Pass@1 across five LLMs.
extraction.title: Learning from Failures: Error Notebook-guided Secure Code Generation
extraction.venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: ACL 2026

techniques.technique_name: SafeNote: Security Error Notebook + Function Error Notebook retrieval (with hierarchical security knowledge base) for contrastive guidance, with online notebook evolution
techniques.tools: Semgrep (offline vulnerability summaries); CodeQL (online security validation and evaluation); BAAI/bge-base-en-v1.5 embeddings; Reciprocal Rank Fusion; vLLM
techniques.iterations: single generation per task with k=1 retrieved error note (k varied 0-5); notebooks updated online after each generation
techniques.metrics: security: SecureRate (share passing CodeQL checks) [tool-static]; SecurePass@1 (passes unit tests and CodeQL) [tool-static + execution]; correctness: Pass@1 unit tests on CodeGuard+ and LiveCodeBench
techniques.benchmarks: CodeGuard+ (94 security scenarios, 10 generations each; seen/unseen CWE split); LiveCodeBench (functional correctness only)
techniques.models: GPT-4o-mini (closed, instruct); Llama-3-8B (open, base per citation); Kimi-K2-Instruct-0905 (open, instruct); Qwen3-8B (open, instruct/reasoning); DeepSeek-V3.2 (open, instruct)
techniques.baselines: LLM alone; RESCUE (RAG secure code generation); ablations without Security EN / Function EN
techniques.effect_target_headline: SP@1 GPT-4o-mini improving from 60.21% to 66.70% on CodeGuard+; average SR 67.56 (LLM alone) vs 78.38 (SafeNote)
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: Average CodeGuard+ Pass@1 83.34 (LLM alone) vs 77.45 (SafeNote); average LCB Pass@1 30.30 vs 33.61

extraction.notes: CodeQL is both the online validation signal and the evaluation instrument, so the method may overfit the evaluator. Security gains come with a Pass@1 drop on CodeGuard+ for most models (e.g. Llama-3-8B 86.28 to 69.68). LiveCodeBench used as contamination-free functional check only. Table 2 (seen/unseen) partly garbled in extraction. Prompt templates in appendix figures (not in text). No code URL; no variance reporting.

extraction.eligibility_reason: LiveCANNBench is a benchmark for SWE-level AI coding in the Huawei Ascend CANN stack; it evaluates agent frameworks and LLMs only with edit-similarity of predicted execution logs (ES-C, ES-L) and patch format validity, which are correctness/similarity measures. No non-functional quality dimension (readability-maintainability, efficiency, security) of the generated code is quantitatively reported.
extraction.title: LiveCANNBench: Benchmark SWE AI Coding for Ascend CANN
extraction.venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: ACL 2026
extraction.notes: Benchmark/resource paper rather than a technique paper. Tables 2-5 are garbled by PDF extraction (column values appear detached from row labels), but the metric definitions (Section 3.2, Appendix S2) are clear: only edit similarity of execution logs and patch-format validity. Live benchmarking is used to mitigate data leakage, and token/LLM-call usage is reported (Table 4), but no NF code-quality outcome exists.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes QiMeng-MuPa, mutual-supervised fine-tuning of LLM Translator/Tester models for C-to-CUDA translation; besides correctness it reports the runtime speedup of the LLM-translated CUDA code across training rounds (Appendix C.3, Figure 10, Table 5), a quantitative efficiency outcome. Borderline because efficiency is not targeted and only appears in an appendix.
extraction.title: QiMeng-MuPa: Mutual-Supervised Learning for Sequential-to-Parallel Code Translation
extraction.venue: 39th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2025)

techniques.technique_name: QiMeng-MuPa mutual-supervised learning (Translator and Tester co-verify via executed unit tests, co-evolve via back-translation SFT)
techniques.tools: g++ 9.3.0, nvcc 12.1, Intel i9-14900KF CPU, RTX 4090 GPU, 60 s execution timeout; vLLM inference; LlamaFactory-style SFT hyperparameters; gcov for coverage
techniques.iterations: Iterative co-verify/co-evolve rounds until convergence; saturation at the 4th iteration (rounds 0-4 reported)
techniques.metrics: efficiency: speedup = runtime ratio of translated CUDA vs sequential C, input sizes 32 to 16,384 (Figure 10) and three hand-picked kernels with matrix sizes 32-8192 (Table 5) [execution]; correctness: Pass@1/5/10 with 5 unit tests per pair, Compile Pass [execution]; BLEU, CodeBLEU [similarity-to-reference]; Tester: Valid Input (VT) [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: BabelTower test/validation pairs filtered to 233 C-CUDA pairs with 5 GPT-4-generated unit tests each; training on 14,687 C and 28,756 CUDA functions from BabelTower unpaired set
techniques.models: Qwen2.5-Coder-7B, 7B, open, code-specialized; Llama3-8B-Instruct, 8B, open, instruct; Qwen3-0.6B, 0.6B, open, base/instruct (non-think mode, trained on the resulting dataset); comparison only: GPT-4o, closed, instruct; GPT-4.1, closed, instruct; DeepSeek-V3, 671B, open, instruct; DeepSeek-R1, 671B, open, reasoning; TransCoder 0.6B; CodeRosetta 0.8B
techniques.baselines: Untrained base models (round 0); CodeRosetta (prior SOTA); TransCoder; GPT-4o, GPT-4.1, DeepSeek-V3, DeepSeek-R1 with one-shot prompts; ablations: non-filtered and compile-filtered back-translation, freezing Translator or Tester
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: improves Pass@1 by up to 28.91% (Qwen2.5-Coder; 56.24 -> 85.15) and 29.44% for Llama3 (56.12 -> 85.56) on C-to-CUDA; outperforms CodeRosetta by 1.56 BLEU and 6.92 CodeBLEU

extraction.notes: Borderline eligibility: the technique targets functional equivalence; efficiency appears only in Appendix C.3 (speedup of translated CUDA vs sequential C, "later-round models achieve more stable and consistent acceleration", Figure 10 garbled) and Table 5 ("maximum speedup of 15,259.22", QiMeng-MuPa-r3 Llama3-8B gemm at 2048, vs sequential C with no LLM baseline). Efficiency direction '+' is a qualitative claim from a garbled figure. Inputs for speedup designed with Claude 4-Sonnet templates. Limitations in Appendix H only. Test unit tests generated by GPT-4; no contamination discussion though BabelTower is public.

extraction.eligibility_reason: ParaStudent fine-tunes LLMs to simulate realistic (often buggy, style-violating) novice student code revisions for AI tutor evaluation; PEP 8 violations, LOC and AST metrics are reported only as fidelity distances to real student code (Wasserstein/MAE), not as non-functional quality outcomes the technique aims to improve.
extraction.title: ParaStudent: Generating and Evaluating Realistic Student Code by Teaching LLMs to Struggle
extraction.notes: Borderline on IC3: style metrics (pycodestyle PEP 8 violations, LOC, AST depth/width) are measured on LLM-generated code, but the objective is matching the student distribution (prompted baselines produce fewer PEP 8 violations, i.e. 'better' style is treated as lower fidelity). arXiv v3 title differs: 'ParaStudent: Closing the Sim2Real Gap in User Simulators for AI Tutor Evaluation'. Code: https://github.com/rosensh/parastudent.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Empirical study of LLM code translation bugs with an iterative error-feedback prompting technique whose effect is measured only as translation success (compile/run/tests). The only NF remark (unsafe Rust blocks, C2Rust vs GPT-4) is a qualitative comparison of LLM vs transpiler, not an outcome of the proposed technique.
extraction.title: Lost in Translation: A Study of Bugs Introduced by Large Language Models while Translating Code
extraction.venue: ICSE '24 (IEEE/ACM 46th International Conference on Software Engineering)
extraction.notes: Metadata title differs ('Understanding the Effectiveness of Large Language Models in Code Translation', arXiv 2023); full text is the ICSE 2024 version 'Lost in Translation'. Finding 8 counts unsafe code (all C2Rust outputs vs three GPT-4 outputs) but this compares an LLM against a transpiler, not a technique applied to an LLM.

extraction.eligibility_reason: The model is a small 3-layer Transformer encoder-decoder (512-dim) trained from scratch on x86-64 assembly for superoptimization (SILO vs REINFORCE), not a large language model; this is a pre-LLM neural code model.
extraction.title: Learning to Superoptimize Real-world Programs
extraction.venue: Deep Learning For Code workshop at ICLR 2022 (arXiv preprint)
extraction.notes: Otherwise relevant to efficiency (static latency cost of generated assembly vs gcc -O3; SILO superoptimizes 5.9% of test set); a reviewer applying a looser LLM definition might reconsider, but the model is a 3-layer seq2seq transformer, clearly pre-LLM.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes Conditional DPG fine-tuning of a pretrained language model (GPT-Neo) for Python function generation under a PEP8-compliance constraint and reports the PEP8 violation count (pycodestyle) of the generated code, a style/readability outcome. Borderline: the code model is a small (125M) GPT-3-style LM and results are shown only in plots.
extraction.title: Controlling Conditional Language Models without Catastrophic Forgetting
extraction.venue: Proceedings of the 39th International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2022), PMLR 162

techniques.technique_name: Conditional Distributional Policy Gradients (CDPG) fine-tuning toward a conditional EBM with a PEP8-compliance constraint (binary scorer: zero pycodestyle violations)
techniques.tools: pycodestyle (PEP8 linter); codeop.compile_command (Python standard library) for compilability; ast module for AST node count
techniques.iterations: 1000 training epochs (constant LR with 100-epoch warmup)
techniques.metrics: readability-maintainability: average PEP8 error count via pycodestyle [tool-static]; also compilability (syntactic only) [tool-static], number of characters and AST node count, KL divergences to target and original model, token frequency/rank diversity
techniques.benchmarks: Python function signatures extracted from Python150 (GitHub code): 5k signatures for training, 5k held-out for evaluation
techniques.models: GPT-Neo 125M (EleutherAI/gpt-neo-125M), open, base
techniques.baselines: Original pretrained model a; DPG-like ablation (constant partition function); Reinforce; Ziegler (RL with KL penalty)

extraction.notes: PEP8 outcome reported only in plots (Fig. 4b, Fig. 5b); text states baseline GPT-Neo functions 'will contain on average 4 violations of PEP8' and CDPG 'decrease[s] the average number of PEP8 violations', with no exact post-fine-tuning number, so no headline copied. Only compilability (syntactic, not functional correctness) is measured; PEP8 objective incidentally increased compilability (separate compilability-constraint experiment: ~40% to ~65%). Check EC7: GPT-Neo 125M is a small pre-Codex GPT-3-style LM; reviewer should decide whether it counts as an LLM. Other tasks (translation, summarization with T5) are out of scope. Year: metadata says 2021 (arXiv), paper printed as ICML 2022. Code link stated as 'will be available'. Each training run ~5 days on 2 V100 GPUs. No variance/repeated runs, no threats section.

extraction.eligibility_reason: The study prompts LLMs (Codex variants, CodeGen) to repair hardware security bugs injected into or present in existing human-written Verilog designs (MITRE CWE examples, OpenTitan, Hack@DAC-21, CirFix benchmarks); it is LLM repair of human-written code rather than improving the NF quality of LLM-generated code.
extraction.title: On Hardware Security Bug Code Fixes by Prompting Large Language Models
extraction.venue: IEEE Transactions on Information Forensics and Security
extraction.notes: Full text is the arXiv v1 preprint titled 'Fixing Hardware Security Bugs with Large Language Models' (2302.01215). Security outcome (successful secure+functional repairs, e.g., 6376 of 20,000 correct, 31.9%) is reported for LLM-edited code, with prompt-instruction variations as the technique, so a reviewer may consider it under IC2 'edited by an LLM'; classified as adjacent (vulnerability repair of existing human-written code). Artifacts at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7540216.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Two-page workshop position paper with a single illustrative example (Codex prompted to make hand-written inefficient Fibonacci code time/memory efficient); it is under 4 pages and reports no quantitative NF outcome (efficiency gains shown only qualitatively via code listings).
extraction.title: Towards Objective-Tailored Genetic Improvement Through Large Language Models
extraction.notes: Also fails IC3: no measured runtime/memory numbers, only complexity arguments for two hand-written Fibonacci examples. Input code is human-written (LLM as GI mutation operator), so topically adjacent.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes a prompt-manager plus output-manager (simulator feedback, human correction, PPA-based enumerative selection) framework around ChatGPT for Verilog generation and reports power/area/latency of the generated designs versus plain ChatGPT. Borderline because the efficiency outcome is hardware PPA rather than software runtime/memory/energy.
extraction.title: ChipGPT: How far are we from natural language hardware design

techniques.technique_name: ChipGPT (specification split + template prompt manager with interface/post-addition/composition principles + output manager with machine/human correction + PPA cost manager and enumerative search)
techniques.tools: Synopsys Design Compiler with 65nm technology (power, area); ModelSim simulation with hand-written testbenches (latency, correctness); cloc (lines of code)
techniques.iterations: Several generations per prompt (number of correct candidates typically less than 10); enumerative search selects best program by target PPA metric
techniques.metrics: efficiency: power (mW), area (um^2), latency (cycles) of synthesized Verilog [execution/tool-static via Design Compiler and simulation]; correctness/programmability: lines needing human correction and custom LOC-subtraction 'quality' metric [human]
techniques.benchmarks: 8 custom hardware workloads (matmul, mux4x1, 3-8 decoder, button count, vector-matrix, adder-multiplier tree, accumulator, simple CPU)
techniques.models: ChatGPT (GPT-3.5), size unknown, closed, instruct
techniques.baselines: Original ChatGPT with module description only; Chisel and Vivado HLS implementations written by a graduate student
techniques.effect_target_headline: reduced average area by 47% (0.53x) and overall average area by 35% (0.65x) compared to the original ChatGPT model (complex CSM/CM workloads; overall)
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: a 2.01× average increase in code quality (LOC-subtraction quality metric incl. human-corrected lines)

extraction.notes: Eligibility borderline: NF outcome is hardware PPA (power/area/latency) of LLM-generated Verilog, mapped to efficiency. Area optimization comes mainly from selecting among multiple samples by PPA (best-of-n selection) plus prompt engineering. Correctness is assessed via simulation and human correction lines, not a pass rate. Single model, small custom benchmark, no repeated runs. Tables and figures heavily garbled in extraction (Table VII values readable). No threats-to-validity section.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Fine-tunes LLMs on HPC code (HPC-Coder) and evaluates generated C/C++ OpenMP/MPI code; besides pass@k it reports execution speedups of the generated parallel code over sequential baselines, a quantitative efficiency outcome. Borderline: efficiency is not the target and the speedup is not compared against the base model.
extraction.title: HPC-Coder: Modeling Parallel Programs using Large Language Models

techniques.technique_name: HPC-Coder: domain fine-tuning of PolyCoder on a curated HPC/scientific C/C++ source dataset
techniques.tools: g++ -O2 -std=c++17 -fopenmp; OpenMPI mpicxx; HuggingFace Trainer with DeepSpeed ZeRO
techniques.metrics: efficiency: speedup of generated parallel code over hand-written sequential baselines [execution]; correctness: average pass@k (k=1,10,100) and build rate [execution]; OpenMP pragma accuracy (textual and functional) [similarity-to-reference]
techniques.benchmarks: custom HPC code generation benchmark of 25 C/C++ problems (sequential, OpenMP, MPI variants); OpenMP pragma dataset (13,900 samples); relative performance prediction datasets (Kripke/Laghos 830 commits; CodeContests C++ pairs)
techniques.models: PolyCoder 2.7B, open, code-specialized base; GPT-Neo 2.7B, open, base; GPT-2 1.5B, open, base (all fine-tuned on HPC data)
techniques.baselines: PolyCoder (not fine-tuned); GPT-Neo+HPC; GPT-2+HPC
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: can pass these at up to 53% higher rate than the other models (HPC code generation tests)

extraction.notes: Efficiency evidence is only Fig. 10: speedups of PolyCoder+HPC generated code over sequential baselines (values in garbled figure roughly 1.5-2.8 for axpy/average/reduce/matmul/fft/cholesky), with no comparison against the base model, so direction for the technique is NR. Main outcomes are correctness (pass@k, build rate). Paper also has non-generation tasks (relative performance classification). Inclusion is borderline under IC3/EC5; reviewer should decide. Figures garbled.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes the self-planning prompting technique for LLM Verilog RTL generation and, alongside syntax/functional correctness, reports post-synthesis power, timing and area (efficiency-type design quality) of the LLM-generated RTL with and without the technique.
extraction.title: RTLLM: An Open-Source Benchmark for Design RTL Generation with Large Language Model

techniques.technique_name: Self-planning (two-step prompting: LLM first produces reasoning steps and syntax-error-avoidance advice, then generates RTL conditioned on them)
techniques.tools: Synopsys Design Compiler (compile_ultra) for synthesis and PPA; Synopsys VCS for RTL simulation
techniques.iterations: two queries per generation (plan, then code); five independent samples per design; no repair
techniques.metrics: efficiency (hardware design quality): area (um^2), power (uW), timing as worst negative slack (ns) of post-synthesis netlist, summarized as count of designs where a method achieves best PPA among correct candidates [tool-static, synthesis]; correctness: syntax (synthesizable, out of 5 samples) and functionality (passes testbench, success if any of 5 passes) [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: RTLLM (30 designs: 11 arithmetic, 19 logic), introduced in this paper
techniques.models: GPT-3.5, closed, instruct; GPT-4, closed, instruct; Thakur et al. fine-tuned CodeGen 16B, open, code-specialized; StarCoder 15B, open, code-specialized
techniques.baselines: Same model without self-planning (GPT-3.5, GPT-4); Thakur et al. fine-tuned model; StarCoder; human designer reference RTL for PPA
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: GPT-3.5 alone degrades to 55% correct syntax and 10/30 correct functionalities. After using our self-planning together with GPT-3.5, the performance rise back to 73% and 14/30 (GPT-4.0 + SP: 90%, 19/30 vs GPT-4 81%, 15/30)

extraction.notes: Primary contribution is a benchmark; self-planning targets correctness, PPA is a measured co-outcome (treated as efficiency for hardware). PPA headline: Best Quality Num (area, power, timing) GPT-3.5 = 2, 2, 5 vs GPT-3.5 + self-planning = 5, 7, 5 ('GPT-3.5 + self-planning ranks second, with 5, 7, 5 designs achieving the best area, power, and timing'); GPT-4 = 8, 5, 6; GPT-4 + SP PPA not reported in Table IV. The best-count comparison is confounded by functional correctness (only correct designs eligible) and authors call it 'less rigorous'. Tables III/IV heavily garbled in extraction. Venue per metadata ASP-DAC (not stated in the text, arXiv v3). Reviewer should decide whether hardware PPA counts as an NF efficiency outcome.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes an LLM framework (modular HLS template, demo-augmented prompting, evolutionary search driven by synthesis performance feedback) that generates HLS accelerator code and reports the latency/resource efficiency of the generated designs. Borderline because the artifact is hardware (HLS) code and efficiency is compared mainly against non-LLM baselines.
extraction.title: GPT4AIGChip: Towards Next-Generation AI Accelerator Design Automation via Large Language Models
extraction.venue: 2023 IEEE/ACM International Conference on Computer Aided Design (ICCAD)

techniques.technique_name: GPT4AIGChip: LLM-friendly decoupled HLS template + demo-augmented prompt generator (LLM-selected similar demonstrations) + evolutionary design search with synthesis/performance feedback and code correction
techniques.tools: Vivado/Vitis HLS (synthesis, performance and resource estimation); custom error parser; ZCU104 FPGA (XCZU7EV MPSoC) with PYNQ for on-board measurement
techniques.iterations: Evolutionary tournament-selection search until a maximum number of cycles; best-performing design chosen
techniques.metrics: efficiency: on-board latency of generated accelerators, latency-DSP Pareto frontier [execution]; correctness: Pass@k (successful compilation) and testbench output check [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: GEMM-based accelerator design space; six networks (e.g., VGG-16, ResNet-18, W-ResNet-32, ResNet-50) at two resolutions (32x32 CIFAR, 224x224 ImageNet); inner-product HLS task for Pass@100; output-stationary computing unit for Pass@10 ablations
techniques.models: GPT-4, size undisclosed, closed, instruct; CodeGen (size not stated), open, code-specialized (base and fine-tuned on HLS)
techniques.baselines: CHaiDNN (industry design automation tool); manual expert-optimized designs; random search; prompt ablations (No Demo, High-Level Description, Random/Dissimilar demos, 0-3 demos); CodeGen with/without fine-tuning
techniques.effect_target_headline: a 2.0%∼16.0% latency reduction across six networks and two resolution settings (vs CHaiDNN)
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: demo-augmented prompt Pass@10 60% vs 10% (No Demo) and 30% (High-Level Description)

extraction.notes: Efficiency results are in figures (Fig. 6, 7) and compared to a non-LLM tool and human experts; no LLM no-technique efficiency baseline (prompt ablations are on Pass@10 only). Human intervention still required to fix module interfaces and assemble the accelerator. Pass@k defined as successful compilations. Limitations section present; no explicit threats-to-validity section. Eligibility borderline (HLS hardware code).

extraction.eligibility_reason: Evaluates GPT-3.5 Turbo as a mutation operator inside Genetic Improvement (Gin) to edit JCodec code, reporting runtime improvements (efficiency) of the LLM-edited patches alongside compile and unit-test pass rates.
extraction.title: Enhancing Genetic Improvement Mutations Using Large Language Models

techniques.technique_name: LLM-based mutation operator for Genetic Improvement (Gin) with Simple/Medium/Detailed prompts, used in random sampling and local search
techniques.tools: Gin GI toolkit (llm branch, commit 9fe9bdf); Gin profiler (20 repeats for hot methods); JavaParser; Langchain4J; JCodec unit tests with 10000 ms timeout
techniques.iterations: Random sampling: 1000 edits per type; local search: 10 runs (one per top-10 hot method) of 100 evaluations each (99 edits); LLM asked for 5 variants per request
techniques.metrics: efficiency: number of runtime-improving patches, best and median runtime improvement in ms [execution]; correctness: patches parsed (valid), compiled, passed all unit tests [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: JCodec (Java), top-10 profiled hot methods
techniques.models: GPT-3.5 Turbo, size NR, closed, instruct (temperature 0.7)
techniques.baselines: Standard GI Statement edits (copy/delete/replace/swap) and Insert edits (break/continue/return)
techniques.effect_target_headline: Medium and Detailed, we found 164 and 196 improvements, respectively, while we only found 136 with Insert and 71 with Statement. The best improvement could be found with 508 ms with the Statement edit. The best improvement found using LLMs (using the Medium prompt) was only able to improve the runtime by 395 ms. (Local Search)
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: the number of patches passing unit tests is up to 75% higher for LLM-based edits than GI Insert edits (Random Sampling, Medium prompt: 292 vs 166 passed)

extraction.notes: Short paper (~6 pages); metadata venue is International Symposium on Search Based Software Engineering (SSBSE), not stated in the arXiv text. Budget expressed as evaluations (1000 per arm) rather than tokens/cost. Simple prompt yielded 0 passing patches in random sampling. No repeated runs or statistical tests. Also at github.com/gintool/gin llm branch.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes VeriPPA, an LLM Verilog-generation framework with simulator error feedback and a second PPA-constraint feedback loop (synthesis reports + in-context optimization strategies), reporting quantitative power/performance/area of the LLM-generated Verilog alongside syntax/functional correctness.
extraction.title: Advanced Large Language Model (LLM)-Driven Verilog Development: Enhancing Power, Performance, and Area Optimization in Code Synthesis

techniques.technique_name: VeriPPA: two-stage refinement (VeriRectify simulator error feedback for syntax/functionality, then PPA-constraint prompt with synthesis report feedback and in-context optimization strategy examples)
techniques.tools: ICARUS Verilog (iverilog) simulator; Synopsys Design Compiler (compile_ultra) with ASAP 7nm Predictive PDK; Python timing-constraint sweep
techniques.iterations: VeriRectify up to K=4 correction attempts, stop when no errors; PPA loop feeds synthesis report back to VeriRectify until PPA goal met (max not stated); 5 generations per design
techniques.metrics: efficiency: clock period (ps), power (uW), area (um2) from logic synthesis [tool-static synthesis reports]; correctness: syntax and functionality pass rates via testbench simulation [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: RTLLM (29 designs); VerilogEval-Human (156); VerilogEval-Machine (108); PPA optimization shown on 5 selected RTLLM designs
techniques.models: GPT-3.5 (closed, instruct); GPT-4 and GPT-4-0314 (closed, instruct); GPT-4 4-shot
techniques.baselines: RTLLM (self-planning prompt), VerilogEval, plain GPT-3.5/GPT-4 without correction; non-optimized PPA results as before-state
techniques.effect_target_headline: adder 32bit operates at an improved 180ps clock (from 500ps; Power 14.72 uW -> 587.31 uW, Area 213.21 um -> 1005.67 um)
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: Our framework achieves 62.0% (+16%) for functional accuracy and 81.37% (+8.3%) for syntactic correctness in Verilog code generation, compared to SOTAs

extraction.notes: Scope borderline: NF outcome is hardware PPA of synthesized LLM-generated Verilog, treated as efficiency. PPA optimization results are anecdotal (Table 2: 5 hand-selected designs, only optimized values; before-values shown only for adder_32bit); no systematic PPA comparison with baselines. Claimed 'open-source' but no URL given. Tables 1 and 2 garbled in extraction. No threats/limitations section.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes Module-of-Thought instruction tuning of a code LLM to produce modular code, and reports maintainability index (radon) and runtime/memory of the generated code alongside pass@k correctness.
extraction.title: MoTCoder: Elevating Large Language Models with Modular of Thought for Challenging Programming Tasks

techniques.technique_name: Module-of-Thought (MoT) instruction tuning (GPT-4o-transformed modular solutions with sub-module headers/docstrings, plus 'clean' renamed/commented code, filtered by tests)
techniques.tools: radon (maintainability index); GPT-4o for data transformation; DeepSpeed ZeRO stage 3
techniques.metrics: readability-maintainability: Maintainability Index (Halstead volume, cyclomatic complexity, LOC, comment density) via radon on passing code [tool-static]; efficiency: average execution time (s) and memory usage (MB) on passing samples [execution]; correctness: pass@1 [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: APPS test set (introductory/interview/competition); CodeContests test and validation; training data from APPS and CodeContests train (183K clean + 174K MoT samples)
techniques.models: Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct, 7B, open, code-specialized instruct (base for MoTCoder-7B); Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct, 32B, open, code-specialized instruct (base for MoTCoder-32B)
techniques.baselines: Base Qwen2.5-Coder-Instruct; normal fine-tuning on original training solutions; many prior code LLMs (CodeLlama, DeepSeek-Coder, WizardCoder, StarCoder, GPT-4o) and code-revision methods (Self-edit, CodeRL, Self-repair, CodeChain)
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: APPS pass@1 All: MoTCoder-7B 34.67 vs Qwen2.5-Coder-Instruct-7B 32.21 (normal finetuning 27.70); MoTCoder-32B 45.95 vs 40.13; CodeContests All: MoTCoder-7B 19.09, MoTCoder-32B 23.85

extraction.notes: Maintainability index and time/memory results are only shown in Figure 4 (b,c) with no printed numbers, so no exact NF headline can be copied; text states MoT code has 'significantly higher maintainability' than normal finetuning and baseline, and 'significantly lower memory consumption' with comparable time. NF metrics computed only on passing code (selection bias). Efficiency effect: memory lower, time comparable. Abstract pass@1 gains (5.8% APPS, 5.9% CodeContests) are relative to prior SOTA. Deduplication between CodeContests train and APPS test reported. No variance, no threats section, no compute reported. Text claims 'MoTCoder-6.7B outperformed GPT-4 by 12.61%' appears inconsistent with the current tables (stale from earlier version).

extraction.eligibility_reason: ReEvo evolves LLM-generated heuristic code for combinatorial optimization, but outcomes are the optimization objective/optimality gap of the solvers using the heuristics (task performance), not readability, efficiency or security of the generated code. Solver runtimes are reported only incidentally (e.g. identical per-instance times for KGLS vs KGLS-ReEvo), not as an efficiency outcome of the generated code.
extraction.title: ReEvo: Large Language Models as Hyper-Heuristics with Reflective Evolution
extraction.venue: 38th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2024)
extraction.notes: Borderline only in that the artifact is LLM-generated code and some solver execution times are tabulated (Table 1, NCO CVRP1000 50.0 s vs 49.8 s); the optimization target is heuristic solution quality, which is functional performance rather than an NF code-quality dimension. Figures 2 and 4 heavily garbled in extraction.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes BetterV, domain instruct-tuning plus generative-discriminator-guided decoding for Verilog generation, and reports quantitative non-functional outcomes of the generated HDL (synthesized AIG netlist node count and SAT formal-verification runtime) alongside functional correctness. Borderline in that the NF outcomes are hardware/EDA properties of the generated code rather than software runtime.
extraction.title: BetterV: Controlled Verilog Generation with Discriminative Guidance

techniques.technique_name: BetterV: domain-specific instruct-tuning (Verilog-C alignment, autocompletion, data augmentation) + task-specific generative discriminator guiding decoding via Bayes-rule weighted decoding
techniques.tools: Yosys (proc; aigmap; stat for AIG node counts; sat -verify -seq 100 -tempinduct -prove-asserts for SAT runtime; eqy equivalence checking; prep for syntax); V2C Verilog-to-C translator; DeepSpeed ZeRO, LoRA, DeepSpeed-Chat
techniques.metrics: efficiency: synthesized And-Inverter-Graph netlist node count (area proxy) [tool-static]; SAT formal-verification solving time [execution]; correctness: pass@k functional correctness via simulation, syntactic correctness via Yosys compilation [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: VerilogEval (machine and human subsets); 18 VerilogEval-human problems for node reduction; 5 designs from ANSI-C hardware verification benchmarks for SAT runtime
techniques.models: CodeLlama-7B-Instruct, open, code-specialized; DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B-Instruct, open, code-specialized; CodeQwen1.5-7B-Chat, open, code-specialized; discriminators: TinyLlama, open, base; DeepSeek-Coder-1.3B-Instruct, open, code-specialized
techniques.baselines: BetterV-base (instruct-tuned without discriminator); reference Verilog; GPT-3.5, GPT-4, CodeLlama, DeepSeek-Coder, CodeQwen, ChipNeMo, Thakur et al., VerilogEval, RTLCoder (correctness)
techniques.effect_target_headline: on average, the Verilog generated by BetterV have 46.52% fewer nodes than the reference model and 31.68% less nodes than BetterV-base; can save 22.45% in verification time compared with the reference Verilog, and 13.99% in time compared with BetterV-base
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: BetterV-CodeQwen ... pass@1 on VerilogEval-machine and VerilogEval-human outperforms GPT-4 by 8.1 and 2.6, respectively

extraction.notes: NF dimension mapping is a judgement call: AIG node count (circuit area/PPA) and SAT verification runtime coded as efficiency. NF experiments use only BetterV-CodeLlama on a small selection of problems (18 and 5); correctness of the node-reduced rewrites is not reported for those tasks. Rewrite task (from a reference module) for NF experiments rather than generation from scratch. Hyperparameters lambda, w, rho, tau are task-sensitive and not given. Limitations section brief; no threats to validity; no code URL.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes an MCTS-guided LLM decoding algorithm with synthesis-based reward for Verilog generation and reports area-delay product (hardware PPA efficiency) of the generated code against greedy and beam-search decoding, plus functional correctness.
extraction.title: Make Every Move Count: LLM-based High-Quality RTL Code Generation Using MCTS

techniques.technique_name: VeriGen+MCTS (Monte Carlo tree-search decoding with compile/function/PPA reward, comment-token pruning, modular reuse of submodules)
techniques.tools: Icarus Verilog 10.3 (compilability/functional check); custom Yosys scripts for synthesis to obtain area and delay
techniques.iterations: MCTS iterations per module (up to ~300 shown); reward alpha_NC=-1, alpha_NF=-0.1, alpha_B=0.5; no explicit stopping rule beyond iteration budget
techniques.metrics: efficiency: area-delay product (ADP), area (um2), delay (ps) from Yosys synthesis (tool-static/synthesis); correctness: functional correctness per module via simulation testbench (execution)
techniques.benchmarks: Custom set of 15 Verilog problems (adders, multipliers, MAC units at 4/8/16/32/64 bits)
techniques.models: VeriGen-2B (CodeGen fine-tuned on Verilog), open, code-specialized
techniques.baselines: Vanilla VeriGen greedy decoding; VeriGen + beam search
techniques.effect_target_headline: For the largest design generated by the state-of-the-art LLM (16-bit adder), our technique can achieve a 31.8% improvement in the area-delay product.
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: VeriGen+MCTS produces functionally correct codes for all tested modules (15/15), whereas VeriGen and VeriGen+Beam Search fail for 14 and 11 of the 15 tested modules

extraction.notes: NF outcome is hardware PPA (ADP) of LLM-generated Verilog, mapped to efficiency. ADP comparison possible only for few modules (4-bit, 16-bit, 32-bit adders, 16-bit multiplier) since baselines rarely produce functional code; average ADP improvement 5.69% over VeriGen and 14.27% over beam search. Single model (VeriGen-2B chosen for runtime). Compute reported as MCTS iteration rate per minute. Table 3 garbled.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Mainly an evaluation of LLM coding ability under prompt strategies (correctness), but it also applies an efficiency-optimization prompt to GPT-4's own code and reports running-time and memory percentiles (LeetCode) before and after, a quantitative NF outcome of an intervention. Borderline: the NF part is a small side analysis reported only in a figure.
extraction.title: Comparing Large Language Models and Human Programmers for Generating Programming Code

techniques.technique_name: Efficiency-optimization prompt: ask GPT-4 to 'Improve the memory usage and running time' of its previously generated (feedback CI) Python3 code
techniques.tools: LeetCode online judge (reports runtime and memory percentiles vs human submissions)
techniques.iterations: single optimization round
techniques.metrics: efficiency: running-time percentile and memory-usage percentile relative to all human LeetCode submissions [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: LeetCode tasks from contests after Sept 2021 (84 of 100 compiled tasks; 21 easy, 36 medium, 27 hard); GeeksforGeeks 15 tasks used only for contest ranking
techniques.languages: Python3 (optimization); Java, JavaScript, C++ for generation/translation
techniques.models: GPT-4 (gpt-4-0613, closed, instruct) for optimization; generation comparison also includes GPT-3.5-turbo-0613, Gemini Ultra 1.0, Gemini Pro, Claude 2, Llama 2 70B, Code Llama 34B
techniques.baselines: GPT-4 code before optimization prompt; human LeetCode submissions

extraction.notes: Efficiency result stated only qualitatively ('Both running time and memory usage improve slightly'; Figure 5c, Supplementary Table 5) with no numbers in the text, so no headline. Correctness of the optimized code is not reported. Main contribution is a correctness/human-comparison evaluation of prompt strategies (feedback CI prompt etc.); a reviewer may prefer exclusion as context. Contamination handled for GPT-4/GPT-3.5 by restricting to post-cutoff tasks. Data in supplementary tables; no code URL. Figures garbled.

extraction.eligibility_reason: The LLM predicts LLVM optimization pass lists for existing (non-LLM) IR, and the evaluated code-size outcome is measured on IR produced by the compiler running those passes, so the evaluated artifact is not code generated or edited by the LLM; it is LLM-guided compiler optimization of existing code.
extraction.title: Compiler generated feedback for Large Language Models
extraction.notes: Borderline: the model also emits optimized IR and the technique (compiler feedback + fine-tuned 7B Llama 2) is relevant to efficiency (code size, instruction count improvement over -Oz: +0.53% with Fast Feedback). If the review treats LLM-selected compiler passes on existing IR as LLM-edited code, this should be reconsidered as include (efficiency, feedback-loop + training).

extraction.eligibility_reason: Characterises flaws (memory leaks, integer overflows, out-of-bounds accesses, compiler-optimization instability) in SHA-1 C function rewrites produced by three open LLMs with RAG context; it proposes no technique to improve NF quality, and the prompt/temperature/model comparisons are reported only on compilability and correctness metrics, with security flaws counted only in aggregate.
extraction.title: Automated Creation of Source Code Variants of a Cryptographic Hash Function Implementation Using Generative Pre-Trained Transformer Models
extraction.notes: Borderline: the paper varies 10 prompts, 11 temperatures and 3 models (Llama-2-70b-chat-hf, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.1, zephyr-7b-alpha) and uses localGPT RAG, but these are factors for producing diverse rewrites, not interventions to improve NF quality; comparisons across prompts/temperatures/models (Figs 1-3) use only Metrics 1, 3, 7 (compilable, output-verified, correct-and-different). Valgrind/ASan security-flaw counts (Metrics 25-38) are aggregated across all settings in Table 1 (garbled extraction). Code is rewritten from an existing human implementation, so it is also close to the 'adjacent' category.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes VERT, an LLM transpilation-to-Rust loop with compiler-error repair, re-prompting with verification counterexamples, and equivalence checking. It reports quantitative readability/idiomaticity outcomes for the LLM-generated Rust (Clippy warnings per function, lines of code) besides correctness. The NF comparison is only against rule-based transpilers on 14 programs.
extraction.title: VERT: Verified Equivalent Rust Transpilation with Large Language Models as Few-Shot Learners

techniques.technique_name: VERT (LLM transpilation to safe Rust + rustc error-guided rule-based repair + few-shot re-prompting with equivalence-check counterexamples against an rWasm oracle)
techniques.tools: rustc (error-message-guided repair); WebAssembly compilers + rWasm (oracle); bolero (property-based testing); Kani bounded model checker; Verus (manual verification); Clippy (linter, evaluation); rustfmt (formatting before LoC count)
techniques.iterations: Re-prompt the LLM up to 20 times; rustc helper-message repairs applied first; stop when equivalence check (PBT, then bounded, then full verification, 120 s limit each) succeeds
techniques.metrics: readability-maintainability: Clippy warnings per function [tool-static]; lines of code after rustfmt [tool-static]; correctness: compiled, property-based testing pass, bounded verification pass, full verification pass [execution / formal verification]
techniques.benchmarks: TransCoder-IR benchmark subset: 569 C++, 520 C (506 stated elsewhere), 341 Go programs; 14 pointer-manipulating C programs from C2Rust/Laertes/CROWN projects (used for safe-Rust and readability/idiomaticity evaluation)
techniques.models: TransCoder-IR (open, translation-specialized, baseline); CodeLlama-2 13B (open, code-specialized); StarCoder 15.5B fine-tuned with adapter layers on 94 LeetCode solutions (open, code-specialized); Anthropic Claude-2 ~130B (closed, instruct)
techniques.baselines: TransCoder-IR single-shot; LLM single-shot; few-shot repair without counterexamples (ablation); for readability/idiomaticity: rule-based CROWN and rWasm transpilers
techniques.effect_target_headline: On average, Clippy produces 10.9 warnings per function for CROWN, and 372 warnings per function for rWasm. Clippy does not produce any warnings on VERT's transpilations (14 C pointer programs); VERT produces 5X less LoC than CROWN, 10x less LoC than rWasm
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: Combining Anthropic's Claude-2 and VERT increases Rust transpilations passing property-based testing from 31% to 54% and bounded model-checking from 1% to 42% compared to using Claude alone.

extraction.notes: Main goal is verified correctness; readability/idiomaticity (Clippy, LoC) is reported only for Claude-2 VERT outputs on the 14 C programs and compared with rule-based transpilers, not with the LLM alone, so the NF gain attributable to the loop itself is not isolated. The prompt asks for safe Rust and outputs are filtered for safe Rust (memory safety), but no quantitative security comparison is given. Wilcoxon signed-rank test reported for correctness only (p 1e-5 to 4e-5). Table 1 is flattened in the extraction but readable. C benchmark count inconsistent (506 vs 520). Claude-2 cost $0.0465 per thousand tokens stated; per-component runtimes in Table 2.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Besides an empirical StackOverflow study, RQ3 evaluates prompting interventions on ChatGPT-generated Java encryption code (asking for a 'secure' solution, then pinpointing the violating line) and reports the number of answers freed of security violations (CWE-mapped crypto-misuse rules), a quantitative security outcome on LLM-generated code.
extraction.title: Time to Separate from StackOverflow and Match with ChatGPT for Encryption

techniques.technique_name: Security-explicit prompting (ask ChatGPT to provide a 'secure' solution/code example)
techniques.metrics: security: number of answers free of violations of 13 symmetric-encryption crypto-misuse rules mapped to CWE-327/798/330/326/259, judged manually by two raters with a third as tie-breaker (Cohen's k = 0.82) [human]
techniques.benchmarks: 100 StackOverflow JCA symmetric-encryption questions with accepted answers, each containing at least one security violation (sampled from 400 manually inspected posts; Stack Exchange dump of March 8, 2023)
techniques.models: ChatGPT (GPT-3.5), closed, instruct
techniques.baselines: Exact StackOverflow question prompt ('answer this StackOverflow question and provide a code example'): only 3 of 100 responses free of violations
techniques.effect_target_headline: When we explicitly prompted to provide a “secure solution”, it cleared violations in 42 questions.

techniques.technique_name: Line-pinpointed follow-up prompting (asking ChatGPT to evaluate the security of the specific line containing a remaining violation)
techniques.iterations: one follow-up per remaining violation after the 'secure' prompt
techniques.metrics: security: number of answers free of crypto-misuse rule violations, manual two-rater inspection (Cohen's k = 0.82) [human]
techniques.benchmarks: the 58 of 100 StackOverflow questions still insecure after the 'secure' prompt
techniques.models: ChatGPT (GPT-3.5), closed, instruct
techniques.baselines: 'Secure solution' prompt alone; generic self-check prompts (e.g., 'examine your code example line by line and make sure that each line is secure') reported as not helping
techniques.effect_target_headline: We could clear violations in 26 more questions when we pinpointed the exact line where a violation existed.

extraction.human_eval_details: Two authors (A1, A2) independently inspected ChatGPT answers against 13 security rules; third rater (A3) for persistent disagreements; Cohen's k = 0.82
extraction.notes: Borderline eligibility: the paper is mainly an empirical study of StackOverflow posts (RQ1, RQ2); the LLM part (RQ3) is a small evaluation of prompting strategies on 100 questions with a single model. Correctness/completeness was judged only for answers to the exact-question prompt (67 of 100 as good as accepted answers), not for the secure-prompt outputs. Remaining 32 posts insecure mainly due to CBC mode. Additional prompt variants (security guidelines in prompt, 'secure example for production') reported qualitatively. No repeated runs; ChatGPT answers noted to change over time.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes LLM-Vectorizer, a GPT-4 multi-agent FSM with compiler dependence-analysis input and checksum-test feedback that generates AVX2-vectorized C code from scalar loops; reports runtime speedup (efficiency) of the LLM-generated code alongside correctness. Borderline because the input is existing scalar code (source-to-source optimization) and the speedup is compared to compilers rather than to a no-technique LLM baseline.
extraction.title: LLM-Vectorizer: LLM-Based Verified Loop Vectorizer
extraction.venue: IEEE/ACM International Symposium on Code Generation and Optimization (CGO) (per metadata; text is arXiv:2406.04693v1)

techniques.technique_name: LLM-Vectorizer (multi-agent finite-state-machine with Clang dependence-analysis input, checksum-based test feedback, and Alive2 bounded translation validation)
techniques.tools: Clang dependence analysis (Clang-19.0.0); checksum-based testing; Alive2 with Z3 (plus C-level unrolling and spatial case splitting); GCC-10.5.0, Clang-19.0.0, ICC-2021.10.0 for performance comparison
techniques.iterations: up to ten attempts or until a plausible (checksum-equivalent) solution is found; max observed 7
techniques.metrics: efficiency: runtime speedup vs GCC/Clang/ICC auto-vectorized code [execution]; correctness: checksum-based plausibility, pass@k, Alive2 formal equivalence (bounded) [execution / formal verification]
techniques.benchmarks: TSVC (Test Suite for Vectorizing Compilers), 149 integer for-loops
techniques.models: GPT-4 (API 2023-08-01-preview), closed, general instruct
techniques.baselines: GCC-10.5.0, Clang-19.0.0, ICC-2021.10.0 auto-vectorization (efficiency); GPT-4 single/multiple code completions without agents (correctness)
techniques.effect_target_headline: run-time speedup ranging from 1.1x to 9.4x as compared to the state-of-the-art compilers such as Intel Compiler, GCC, and Clang (57 formally verified TSVC tests)
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: the total number of plausible tests increased to 96 when considering just one LLM invocation, compared to the initial 72 tests; formally verify ... 57 (38.2%) of the test programs

extraction.notes: Speedup figure (Figure 6) not extractable; text notes slowdowns vs compilers in several categories (naively vectorizable, reduction), so efficiency effect is positive overall but not uniform. Efficiency is compared to compilers, not to GPT-4 without the agent loop; the agent FSM itself is evaluated only on correctness/LLM invocations. Input is existing scalar code (source-to-source optimization), so a reviewer may consider it adjacent. Only one model (GPT-4), no repeated runs or threats section.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes Code-Optimise, fine-tuning code LLMs (SFT/DPO) on self-generated preference data labelled by correctness and runtime; reports measured runtime (efficiency) of generated code alongside pass@k.
extraction.title: Code-Optimise: Self-Generated Preference Data for Correctness and Efficiency
extraction.venue: North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (metadata); full text is arXiv 2406.12502v2

techniques.technique_name: Code-Optimise (self-generated preference data; DPO QvS/PvF/All and SFT top-N% with Dynamic Solution Selection)
techniques.tools: Python interpreter + custom timing module (each solution executed 50 times, repeated until CoV <= 0.1, up to 1K times; averaged over 5 runs)
techniques.metrics: efficiency: median runtime (ns) of working solutions on the common solved subset [execution]; also Best@100 runtime [execution]; code length in characters (inference cost) [tool-static]; correctness: pass@1/10/100
techniques.benchmarks: MBPP (train/validation for training, test split in-domain); HumanEval (164 problems, out-of-domain)
techniques.models: StarCoder-1B (open, code-specialized base); StarCoder-3B (open, code-specialized base); CodeLlama-7B (open, code-specialized base); CodeLlama-13B (open, code-specialized base)
techniques.baselines: Base pretrained CLM (no fine-tuning); SFT25 and SFT100; static vs dynamic solution selection ablation
techniques.effect_target_headline: decreasing the competitive baseline runtimes by an additional 6% for in-domain data and up to 3% for out-of-domain data (DPO QvS / DPO All, averaged across model sizes)
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: CodeLlama-13B MBPP pass@1: Base 23.70 vs DPO QvS 33.50 vs DPO PvF 34.10

extraction.notes: Runtime effects are modest and inconsistent across models (e.g. DPO All slower on StarCoder-1B HumanEval; HumanEval runtimes less predictable); SFT generally increases runtime. Code length reductions (up to 48% MBPP / 23% HumanEval) framed as inference-cost savings, not readability. Variance reported as CoV of runtime only; no significance tests. Limitations section is brief. Tables extracted cleanly in appendix.

extraction.eligibility_reason: The paper empirically compares two prompting strategies (descriptive natural-language versus structured pseudo-code prompts) across seven LLMs generating Solidity smart contracts, and reports a quantitative efficiency outcome (execution time in seconds) for the generated code alongside test-pass accuracy and qualitative code-quality and security observations. Borderline: the efficiency numbers are extremely coarse and the quality/security assessment is qualitative only.
extraction.title: Efficacy of Various Large Language Models in Generating Smart Contracts
extraction.venue: FICC (Future of Information and Communication Conference) per record metadata; the PDF itself names no venue and carries an arXiv source (2407.11019)

techniques.technique_name: Structured (pseudo-code style) prompting versus descriptive natural-language prompting for smart contract generation
techniques.tools: HardHat (Web3/Ethereum development environment) for compilation and test execution; TypeScript test files written by the authors; Solidity 0.8.20; no versions given for HardHat or the Solidity compiler; no static analyzer or security scanner was used
techniques.iterations: None; single-shot generation per model per prompt per contract, no refinement loop
techniques.metrics: efficiency: 'execution efficiency' reported as whole-second execution time for the contract's test run [execution]. readability-maintainability: 'quality/verboseness' reported as free-text qualitative labels such as 'Excellent', 'Unnecessary variable check', 'No SPDX license identifier (warning flag)', 'Extra unspecified parameter', 'Majority code is excellent but few syntax errors' [human, single unblinded rater, no agreement reported]. security: qualitative observations only, e.g. a missing check that unlockTime must exceed the initialization time [human]. Correctness: accuracy as the percentage of author-written test cases passed [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: No standard benchmark; three author-constructed Solidity tasks of increasing complexity: (1) Storage, read/write a variable (5 test cases), (2) Lock, time-locked ether withdrawal based on the HardHat initialization example (9 test cases), (3) Create a New Token, a customized ERC-20/ERC-721 token (5 test cases)
techniques.models: GPT 4; GPT 4-o; GPT 3.5; Cohere (Coral); Mistral; Claude; Gemini (Gemini Pro) - all closed or hosted instruct models; exact versions, dates and decoding settings not reported. 'Bard' also appears in the per-case observations but is not a column in any results table
techniques.baselines: The two prompting strategies serve as each other's comparison; manually written / human-written contracts are referred to in the research questions and conclusions but no human-written baseline data is reported
techniques.effect_target_headline: Execution efficiency was essentially flat across both strategies: Storage was 2s for all seven models under both text-based (Table 2) and structured (Table 5) prompting; for Lock, GPT 4 went from 2s (text-based) to 3s (structured), Cohere was 3s under both, Claude 3s (text-based) and N/A (structured), Gemini 2s (text-based) and N/A (structured). All 'Create a New Token' efficiency cells are N/A under both strategies. Qualitatively: 'The efficiency of the programs is noticeably slow currently' and 'Code was also rather inefficient compared to human-written equivalent contracts', neither quantified
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: Structured prompting lowered test-pass accuracy on the Lock task for several models: Claude 100% (text-based, Table 1) versus 0% (structured, Table 4); Gemini 89% versus N/A; Cohere 78% versus 89%; GPT 4 89% under both; GPT 4-o 100% under both; GPT 3.5 0% under both. All seven models scored 100% on Storage under both strategies and N/A on Create a New Token under both. 'foundational models generally performed better using descriptive prompting as opposed to structured prompting'

extraction.human_eval_details: The code-quality column (Tables 3 and 6) is an unstructured qualitative judgement by the authors; the number of raters is not stated and no inter-rater agreement is reported
extraction.notes: Substantial quality concerns a human reviewer should weigh. (1) ELIGIBILITY IS BORDERLINE: the paper is mostly a cross-model benchmarking study (which would be the 'context' side list), and only Section 4.3 plus the paired result tables make it a prompting-technique comparison; the only quantitative non-functional outcome is a whole-second execution time that is identical (2s) for nearly every model and task, so a reviewer could reasonably exclude under EC5 or route it to 'context'. Gas cost, the natural efficiency metric for smart contracts, is discussed in the conclusion but never measured. (2) Only three tasks with one generation per model per prompt; no repeats, no variance, no statistical test. (3) Every 'Create a New Token' cell in all six tables is N/A, so the most complex task yields no data at all. (4) Internal inconsistencies: the descriptive prompt in Section 3.3 asks for an ERC-20 token while the structured prompt specifies ERC 721 and the conclusion refers to ERC-721; the Overall Findings cite 'Table 2 & Table 5' (the efficiency tables) when discussing accuracy, which should almost certainly be Tables 1 and 4; 'Bard' appears in the per-case observations and in finding 5 but is not a column in any table, while 'Gemini' is; finding 5 attributes the unlockTime vulnerability to 'Bard and GPT 4-o' whereas Section 3.2 attributes it to 'GPT-4 and Bard'; the Future Work section claims 'moving to more structured prompts significantly improves the quality and efficiency', directly contradicting the paper's own Section 4.3 and results. (5) Mistral's Lock result is N/A in the accuracy table but Table 3 records 'Did not compile', so N/A conflates several failure modes. (6) No security tooling (no Slither, Mythril, or similar) was used despite security being a headline claim; security findings are anecdotal. (7) No artifact, no code or test files released, no model versions or decoding parameters, no threats-to-validity section, no contamination discussion (notably relevant since the Lock contract is HardHat's own tutorial example and is near-certainly in the training data). (8) The extracted text is full of soft-hyphen/control characters and the six tables are heavily garbled, with headers separated from values; the mappings above were reconstructed from the column order and cross-checked against the running text, but should be verified against the original PDF.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Evaluates prompting strategies (zero/one/two-shot ICL, NL annotation, ISA spec) for GPT-4-turbo translation of C++ kernels to the Gemmini accelerator ISA, but the only systematic quantitative outcome is translation correctness (pass@k); the optimization phase is reported qualitatively plus one anecdotal GFLOPS transcript, with no systematic efficiency measurement.
extraction.title: LLM-Aided Compilation for Tensor Accelerators
extraction.notes: Short workshop position-style paper. Appendix B shows a single LLM autoscheduling transcript for the PolyBench doitgen kernel in Exo (5.64 to 43.33 GFLOPS), which is an illustrative example, not an evaluated efficiency outcome. Code optimization section says LLM output was 'similar in structure and performance' to hand-tuned code without numbers.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes an LLM pipeline (domain-knowledge prompting, self-prompting summaries, compile/execute error self-correction) for translating parallel codes between OpenMP and CUDA, and reports runtime of the LLM-generated code relative to reference implementations; borderline because efficiency is measured but not compared against a no-technique LLM baseline.
extraction.title: LASSI: An LLM-Based Automated Self-Correcting Pipeline for Translating Parallel Scientific Codes
extraction.venue: 2024 IEEE International Conference on Cluster Computing Workshops (CLUSTER Workshops)

techniques.technique_name: LASSI: domain-knowledge context (CUDA guide / OpenMP reference card) + LLM self-prompting summaries + compile and execution error self-correction loop for code translation
techniques.tools: local compilers for CUDA and OpenMP target offload (same commands as HeCBench originals); NVIDIA A100 GPU; Ollama for open models
techniques.iterations: Repeat compile-error and execution-error correction prompts until code compiles and executes without error (no fixed cap stated; up to 34 self-corrections observed)
techniques.metrics: efficiency: runtime ratio of reference target-language code to generated code, averaged over 3 executions (execution); code similarity Sim-T and Sim-L (similarity-to-reference); correctness: successful execution with output matching source (execution, manual output comparison); self-correction count
techniques.benchmarks: HeCBench, 10 applications across 9 categories, bidirectional OpenMP<->CUDA (80 translation scenarios over 4 LLMs)
techniques.languages: CUDA; C++ with OpenMP target offload
techniques.models: GPT-4 (API), closed, instruct; Codestral 22B 8-bit, open, code-specialized; WizardCoder 33B 8-bit, open, code-specialized; DeepSeek-Coder-V2 16B F16, open, code-specialized
techniques.baselines: original HeCBench implementations in the target language (human-written reference runtimes); no no-technique LLM baseline
techniques.effect_target_headline: approximately 78% of OpenMP to CUDA translations and 62% of CUDA to OpenMP translations execute within 10% of or at a faster runtime than the original benchmark code in the same language
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: 80% of OpenMP to CUDA translations and 85% of CUDA to OpenMP translations producing the expected output

extraction.notes: Technique aims at executable translations, not explicitly at efficiency (prompts include some performance hints, e.g., static scheduling); efficiency is reported only against human-written HeCBench reference code, with no ablation or no-technique LLM baseline, so the effect of the technique on efficiency is not identifiable. Correctness checked by manual output comparison. Runtimes averaged over 3 runs, std not reported. Tables garbled (panel columns interleaved). Workshop paper. Calls reported only as self-correction counts.

extraction.eligibility_reason: PEFT 'hotfixing' of CodeGen is evaluated mainly on generating fixed vs buggy single-statement code (exact-match correctness) plus HumanEval pass@k; the only other outcome is training-data email (PII) leakage counted by a PII detector, a model memorization/privacy property rather than a security vulnerability metric of generated code. Borderline: a reviewer may treat the email-leakage case study as a security outcome.
extraction.title: Hotfixing Large Language Models for Code: How Far Can Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning Go?

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes RTLRewriter, an LLM framework (partitioning, multimodal analysis, retrieval, cost-aware MCTS with synthesis feedback, fast verification) that rewrites RTL code, and reports quantitative efficiency outcomes (wires/cells, area/delay) of the LLM-rewritten code versus LLM and compiler baselines.
extraction.title: RTLRewriter: Methodologies for Large Models aided RTL Code Optimization
extraction.venue: International Conference on Computer Aided Design (ICCAD) (arXiv preprint version)

techniques.technique_name: RTLRewriter (circuit partition + multimodal CoT program analysis + RAG search engine + Cost-aware MCTS rewriting with synthesis feedback + fuzz/equivalence fast verification)
techniques.tools: Yosys; Vivado (PPA/synthesis); ABC (area/delay, SAT solver); egg (e-graph solver); iVerilog; ViT, LLama3 and DeepSeek embeddings for retrieval; XGBoost synthesis-time predictor
techniques.iterations: C-MCTS over 7 retrieval-combination root branches and 4 prompt actions (rewrite, optimization analysis, continue optimization, reflection); stops when no obvious improvement or a defined number of selections is reached
techniques.metrics: efficiency: wires and cells after Yosys synthesis (tool-static/synthesis), area and delay via ABC/Vivado (tool-static/synthesis), geo-mean ratio vs Yosys; overall running time (synthesis + verification); correctness only as a filter via fuzz testing and equivalence checking
techniques.benchmarks: Small Rewriter Benchmark (14 of 55 cases reported); Large Rewriter Benchmark (5 cases: CPU, CNN, FFT, Huffman, VMachine)
techniques.models: GPT-4V / GPT-4 Turbo, size NR, closed, multimodal instruct (RTLRewriter); GPT-4, size NR, closed (baseline); Claude3-Opus, size NR, closed (baseline); VeriGen, open, code-specialized (baseline); RTLCoder, open, code-specialized (baseline)
techniques.baselines: Yosys; Yosys+Egg; GPT-4; Claude3-Opus; VeriGen; RTLCoder (identical prompts); C-MCTS ablation vs GPT4, GPT4-DFS, GPT4-MCTS; w/o partition
techniques.effect_target_headline: Short benchmark GeoMean Ratio vs Yosys: Wires 0.69, Cells 0.77 (GPT4 0.85/0.87, Claude3 0.88/0.89); long benchmark Area 0.81, Delay 0.96; C-MCTS PPA-ratio 0.81 vs GPT4 1.0

extraction.notes: Borderline scope: artifact is LLM-rewritten Verilog of existing (human-written) RTL; NF outcome is hardware PPA (wires/cells/area/delay), mapped to efficiency. Also borderline EC4/adjacent since the LLM optimizes existing code. Tables 4 and 5 are garbled column-wise; headline ratios read from GeoMean rows. Long benchmark delay worsened on some cases. Database construction details omitted. Only benchmarks released, not framework code. Running time shown only in a bar chart. Venue from metadata (ICCAD), text is arXiv version.

extraction.eligibility_reason: OMPar uses small fine-tuned code models (OMPify classifier + MonoCoder-OMP) to insert OpenMP pragmas into existing serial loops from HeCBench/ParEval, i.e., LLM-based parallelization (performance refactoring) of existing code, compared only against rule-based tools (AutoPar, ICPC).
