Borderline: runtime speedups of the LLM-edited programs are reported, but only as categorical figures versus non-LLM tools and no LLM no-technique baseline on efficiency.
extraction.title: OMPar: Automatic Parallelization with AI-Driven Source-to-Source Compilation
extraction.notes: Borderline EC4/adjacent vs include. Efficiency outcome is speedup categories (1x-2x ... >10x improvement/degradation) over baseline HeCBench runs (Figure 3, garbled) and speedup vs 1 thread on ParEval (Figure 5); accuracy/compile-and-run results (86% accuracy with compile and run check; ~92% of 770 loops pass C&R). ParEval inputs were GPT-3.5-generated programs with pragmas removed. Contamination check: HeCBench ensured not in MonoCoder pre-training/fine-tuning. Repository mentioned but no URL in text.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes an LLM generative-optimization loop (Trace with GPT-4o) that writes and iteratively refines Legion mapper code in a DSL using execution feedback enriched by AutoGuide, and reports measured application throughput (efficiency) of the generated mappers versus expert, random and OpenTuner baselines, plus code generation success rates.
extraction.title: Improving Parallel Program Performance with LLM Optimizers via Agent-System Interfaces
extraction.venue: Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2025), PMLR 267

techniques.technique_name: Agent-System Interface: mapper DSL (compiled to Legion C++) plus AutoGuide execution-feedback explanation/suggestion, with generative optimization via Trace (also OPRO)
techniques.tools: DSL-to-C++ mapper compiler; Legion runtime execution (throughput/execution time); AutoGuide keyword matching over raw execution output; Trace framework; DSPy for the DSL-vs-C++ ablation
techniques.iterations: 10 optimization iterations per application, repeated 5 times; DSL-vs-C++ ablation allows up to 10 refinement iterations with compiler feedback
techniques.metrics: efficiency: end-to-end throughput normalized to expert-written mappers (failed mappers scored 0), relative throughput vs OpenTuner [execution]; correctness: generation success rate (compiles and passes predefined tests) on 10 natural-language mapping strategies [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: 9 Legion benchmarks: Circuit, Stencil, Pennant, and six parallel matrix multiplication algorithms (Cannon's, SUMMA, PUMMA, Johnson's, Solomonik's, COSMA); 10 mapping strategies for DSL vs C++ generation ablation
techniques.languages: Mapper DSL (compiled to C++ Legion mapper API); C++ for ablation
techniques.models: gpt-4o-2024-08-06, closed, instruct
techniques.baselines: Expert-written mappers; random mappers (10 seeds); OpenTuner (RL autotuning with scalar feedback, 10 and 1000 iterations); OPRO; feedback ablations (0-shot, 5-shot, execution only, execution+explain); C++ code generation instead of DSL
techniques.effect_target_headline: Our approach finds mappers that surpass expert-written mappers by up to 1.34× speedup across nine benchmarks; With just 10 iterations, it outperforms OpenTuner even after 1000 iterations, achieving 3.8× faster performance
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: Success rate: C++ (single trial) 0%, DSL (single trial) 80%, C++ (iterative refine) 0%, DSL (iterative refine) 100%

extraction.notes: Headline 1.34x is the best mapper across 5 runs; mean normalized throughput over 5 runs is lower for several benchmarks (e.g. SUMMA 0.86x, PUMMA 0.57x, Solomonik 0.52x vs expert; Appendix A.4). Generated artifact is mapper code in a custom DSL compiled to C++. Single model (GPT-4o) without justification. Compute reported as iteration counts and ~10 minutes per application; no token/cost. No code URL and no threats-to-validity section. Year set to 2024 per record metadata; paper printed as ICML 2025 proceedings (arXiv v4 May 2025).

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes MPLSandbox, a multi-language sandbox whose compiler feedback and code-smell analysis are fed back to GPT-4o for self-correction and self-refinement of its generated code; reports a quantitative NF outcome (average number of comment lines) alongside Pass@1. Borderline because the NF evidence is thin (comment-line counts plus a single-instance maintainability case study).
extraction.title: Multi-Programming Language Sandbox for LLMs

techniques.technique_name: MPLSandbox-driven self-correction (compiler feedback) and self-refinement (code smell analysis feedback)
techniques.tools: MPLSandbox code analysis module: Pylint & Radon (Python), Pmd (Java), CPPCheck (C++), StyleCop.Analyzers (C#), ShellCheck (Bash), golangci-lint (Go), ESLint (JS), ESLint & TSLint (TS); compilers/interpreters in isolated per-language sub-sandboxes
techniques.metrics: readability-maintainability: average number of comment lines (tool-static, Radon raw analysis); cyclomatic complexity, Halstead volume, Maintainability Index shown only for one case-study instance (tool-static); correctness: Pass@1 (execution)
techniques.benchmarks: TACO (APPS+ and CodeContests portions plus newly crawled contest data); 12,000/1,000/1,000 train/validation/test problems; evaluated in 8 languages via system-prompt templates
techniques.languages: Python, Java, C++ (C), C#, Go, Bash, JavaScript, TypeScript
techniques.models: GPT-4o, closed, general instruct
techniques.baselines: GPT-4o initial generated code before self-correction/self-refinement
techniques.effect_target_headline: Avg num of comment lines +8.9 (Python), +7.0 (Java), +7.2 (C++), +5.2 (C#), +5.6 (Go), +4.3 (Bash), +7.9 (JavaScript), +6.3 (TypeScript); GPT-4o after self-refinement (Table 3)
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: Pass@1 +3.7% (Python), +4.9% (Java), +2.7% (C++), +6.5% (C#), +5.0% (Go), +4.8% (Bash), +4.1% (JavaScript), +3.1% (TypeScript); GPT-4o after self-correction (Table 3)

extraction.notes: Primarily a tool paper. Metadata venue is ACL; the PDF itself says 'Preprint. Publication date: November 2024'. Other applications (Best-of-N verification, PPO with compiler-feedback reward on DeepSeek-Coder-Instruct-6.7B, unit test generation, code translation, vulnerability localization) are correctness-only or case demos and not extracted as NF techniques. Claims of lower complexity and better specification compliance after refinement are supported only by a single-instance example (Fig. 11: MI 59.24 -> 59.68, CC 7 -> 6); no aggregate complexity numbers. Number of refinement rounds not stated. Table 3 is a delta-only table with no absolute values; PPO results shown only in a figure without numbers. No threats-to-validity section.

extraction.eligibility_reason: DesignRepair uses retrieval-augmented GPT-4 to repair LLM-generated (Vercel V0) and GitHub frontend code, but the outcomes are UI design-guideline compliance (accessibility/usability violations detected and repaired, precision/recall vs manual annotation) and user-rated visual attractiveness, none of which fall in the review's NF dimensions (readability-maintainability, efficiency, security).
extraction.title: DesignRepair: Dual-Stream Design Guideline-Aware Frontend Repair with Large Language Models
extraction.notes: Borderline: the technique is an LLM post-generation repair of LLM-generated UI code, but quality is Material Design 3 guideline adherence (UI/UX, accessibility such as contrast and alt-text), not code readability, efficiency or security. A reviewer who treats UI accessibility as an NF code-quality dimension might include it. Metadata venue ICSE; PDF is arXiv v2 (Dec 2024). Code at https://github.com/UGAIForge/DesignRepair.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes a multi-stage LLM prompting framework (CoP) for geospatial code generation with retrieval, shared memory, user feedback debugging and a code-commenting stage; reports expert-rated readability of the generated code alongside executability/accuracy.
extraction.title: Chain-of-Programming (CoP) : Empowering Large Language Models for Geospatial Code Generation

techniques.technique_name: Chain of Programming (CoP): requirement analysis, algorithm design, code implementation, debugging with user feedback, and code annotation, with shared information pool and knowledge-base retrieval
techniques.iterations: Debugging loop up to 3 iterations by default (hyperparameter; 0/1/3/5 studied), stops on user feedback executable=Y and correct=Y or at the iteration limit; then a commenting stage
techniques.metrics: readability-maintainability: Readability rated 1-10 by five experts, trimmed mean of middle three, converted to percentage [human]; correctness: Executability and Accuracy judged by experts on execution, Matchability (entity match rate)
techniques.benchmarks: GeoCode-Eval, 500 code generation tasks (8 subcategories)
techniques.models: GPT-4, closed; GPT-4-turbo, closed; Claude-3-Opus, closed; ERNIE-4.0, closed; LLaMA3-70B, open; PaLM-540B, closed; BLOOM-176B, open; CodeGemma-7B, open, code-specialized; StarCoder 2-15B, open, code-specialized; CodeQwen-14B, open, code-specialized; WizardCoder-15B, open, code-specialized; Code Llama-13B, open, code-specialized; OctoCoder-15.5B, open, code-specialized; CodeGeeX2-6B, open, code-specialized; CodeT5+-16B, open, code-specialized; CodeGen-16.1B, open, code-specialized; CodeX-12B, closed, code-specialized
techniques.baselines: Zero-shot; Few-Shot, CoT, Self-Edit, Self-Debugging, INTERVENOR, Self-Planning, CodeCoT, ReAct, Reflexion, RAP, ToT, CodeAgent, AgentCoder, ChatDev, AgentVerse, MetaGPT, Self-Collaboration (on GPT-4, PaLM-540B, Code Llama-13B); ablations of pool/retrieval/feedback
techniques.effect_target_headline: GPT-4 readability 85.6 (zero-shot) to 93.4 with CoP; "due to CoP's unique code-commenting mechanism, readability improved by 7.8 points"
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: GPT-4 executability 52.8 to 92.4 (Table 6) and accuracy 42.6 to 86.8 with CoP

extraction.human_eval_details: Five experts rated readability 1-10; highest and lowest dropped, mean of remaining three; no agreement statistic reported
extraction.notes: Tables 5-8 are heavily garbled in extraction; the Table 5 column alignment is unclear (abstract says improvements 3.0% to 48.8%). Readability is the only NF dimension and is expert-rated without agreement; the commenting stage directly targets readability. The debugging loop relies on human expert feedback. Executability numbers for GPT-4 CoP differ between text (92.3 in Table 5, 92.4 in Table 6). Data available only on request. Limitations are mentioned only briefly in the conclusion.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes an automated LLM framework (compile/test/HLS double feedback loop plus a pragma-insertion step targeting area or latency) that rewrites C into HLS-synthesizable C, and reports quantitative area and latency of the LLM-produced designs alongside success rates. Borderline: the task is LLM refactoring of existing C code for hardware synthesis, and efficiency is hardware area/latency rather than software runtime.
extraction.title: C2HLSC: Leveraging Large Language Models to Bridge the Software-to-Hardware Design Gap
extraction.venue: ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems

techniques.technique_name: C2HLSC: hierarchical preprocessing + double feedback loop (g++/unit tests and Catapult HLS) refactoring with in-context examples, followed by LLM pragma insertion targeting area or latency, with GPT-4o-mini to GPT-4o model escalation
techniques.tools: g++; Catapult HLS (nangate45 library, 50 MHz, synchronous active high reset); gdb for unit-test input extraction; pycparser; Modelsim (case study)
techniques.iterations: Loop until code compiles, passes tests and synthesizes; switch from GPT-4o-mini to GPT-4o after 3 failing iterations; pragma step is single-shot with respect to synthesis results (no synthesis-result feedback); max rounds not stated
techniques.metrics: efficiency: synthesized hardware area (um2) and latency (cycles) from Catapult HLS [execution/tool-static synthesis report]; correctness: success rate (compiles, passes reference tests, synthesizable) and streaming-interface success [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: 10 benchmarks: AES, DES, PRESENT, SHA256, QuickSort, NIST 800-22 Cumulative Sums, Monobit, Monobit Block, Overlapping Template Matching, Runs; each run 10 times per model and target (area/latency)
techniques.models: GPT-4o-mini, closed, instruct; GPT-4o, closed, instruct; Claude 3.5 Sonnet, closed, instruct; Gemini (case study only), closed, instruct
techniques.baselines: Manual implementations by a graduate student; engineer-in-the-loop LLM-assisted case study; area vs latency targets; Xu et al. 2024 HLS repair framework (AES success rate only)
techniques.effect_target_headline: GPT ensemble AES: latency 853 (area target) vs 231 (latency target) cycles avg, area 2975.90 vs 17812.60 avg; authors: "the optimization step was not very effective on the single runs, but we noticed improvements on the best across the 10 performed runs"
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: In AES we performed generally better 60% vs. 80% (vs. Xu et al.)

extraction.notes: Borderline eligibility: LLM refactors existing human-written C into HLS-compatible C (could be seen as adjacent); NF outcome is hardware area/latency of synthesized designs. Tables 3-6 and 8-12 are garbled in extraction (column alignment uncertain; area/latency mapping inferred). No no-technique baseline for the pragma step; comparison vs manual designs shows manual is better on area/latency. Code said to be available at 'C2HLSC' but no URL in extracted text. extraction.title: Assessing ChatGPT’s Code Generation Capabilities with Short vs Long Context Programming Problems
extraction.venue: 11th International Conference on Networking, Systems, and Security (NSysS '24), ACM

techniques.tools: LeetCode and Codeforces online judges; GNU G++ 17 7.3.0; Python 3.8.10
techniques.iterations: one additional round (two-round interaction)
techniques.metrics: efficiency: average execution time (ms) reported by the online judge before vs after the targeted prompt [execution]; correctness: acceptance rate and AC/WA/TLE/RTE/MLE/CE status rates

Correctness changes in second run mix the efficiency prompt (accepted problems) with error-feedback re-prompting (rejected problems). Single model; no variance; exact prompts not provided. Main contribution is a correctness evaluation; reviewer may prefer exclusion as context.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes an LLM-based pipeline (static-analysis-driven decomposition, context slicing, LLM translation, compile/test feedback repair) that rewrites C2Rust-transpiled unsafe Rust into safer, idiomatic Rust, and quantitatively measures memory-safety/idiomaticity of the LLM-produced code (raw pointers, unsafe lines, unsafe casts/calls).
extraction.title: C2SaferRust: Transforming C Projects Into Safer Rust With NeuroSymbolic Techniques

techniques.technique_name: C2SaferRust (C2Rust transpilation + static-analysis-based decomposition into translation units with call-site/dataflow context + LLM translation to safe Rust + compiler/test feedback repair)
techniques.tools: C2Rust transpiler; custom Rust compiler passes on HIR/MIR (call graph, program slicing, live-variable dataflow) on Rust nightly-2022-08-08; GNU coreutils end-to-end test scripts
techniques.iterations: up to N=5 feedback attempts per translation unit; stop when it compiles and passes all end-to-end tests, otherwise revert unit to original unsafe Rust; chunk size L=150 lines
techniques.metrics: security/idiomaticity: raw pointer declarations, raw pointer dereferences, lines of unsafe code, unsafe call expressions, unsafe type casts (tool-static, counts via compiler analysis; metrics from Laertes prior work); correctness: end-to-end test pass, translation success rate (execution)
techniques.benchmarks: 7 GNU coreutils programs (split, pwd, cat, truncate, uniq, tail, head) with end-to-end tests (new benchmark); 10 of 17 Laertes benchmarks (no tests)
techniques.languages: C to Rust (rewriting C2Rust unsafe Rust into safer Rust)
techniques.models: gpt-4o-mini, closed, instruct
techniques.baselines: C2Rust output (no technique); Laertes; CROWN (CROWN ran on 4 of 10 programs); ablations: No Chunking, Random Order; variant with direct C-to-Rust translation
techniques.effect_target_headline: we are able to reduce the number of raw pointers by up to 38%, and reduce the amount of unsafe code by up to 28% (coreutils benchmark); C2SaferRust outperforms other approaches with a 39/2/9 aggregate win/tie/loss record over all 5 metrics (Laertes benchmark)
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: The resulting programs still pass all test cases.

extraction.notes: Venue taken from metadata (IEEE TSE); full text is arXiv v2 and does not state the venue. Input to the LLM is machine-transpiled (C2Rust) code from human-written C, so it is LLM translation/editing rather than pure refactoring of human code; reviewer may check EC4 borderline. Safety metrics are custom static counts of unsafe constructs, framed as both safety and idiomaticity; mapping to 'security' is approximate (no CWE/vulnerability scan). Tables 2-5 are heavily garbled in extraction. Correctness is maintained by construction (failed units reverted); per-baseline correctness not reported. Single model (gpt4o-mini), no repeated runs.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes an adaptive self-improvement LLM agentic system that generates ML library code in an emerging ASPL (STeP); main outcome is correctness (pass@k), but the appendix reports a quantitative maintainability outcome (Maintainability Index) for the generated code, so IC3 is technically met; borderline because NF quality is reported only descriptively without a baseline comparison.
extraction.title: Adaptive Self-improvement LLM Agentic System for ML Library Development
extraction.venue: Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2025), PMLR 267

techniques.technique_name: Adaptive self-improvement learning (filtered, difficulty-stratified self-generated demonstrations) with an agentic system (proposer + guardian agents, structural IR, code generator, verifiers)
techniques.tools: Python functional simulator of STeP with pytest-style unit tests against PyTorch reference; affine-type static check via Python ast module

techniques.metrics: readability-maintainability: Maintainability Index with and without comments (MI, MIwoc) [tool-static]; complexity counts (lines of code, shape transformations, specialized instructions) [tool-static]; correctness: pass@1 and pass@n via simulator unit tests and affine-type checker
techniques.benchmarks: Custom STeP ML-library benchmark, 26 tasks in 8 operator groups (attention, gemm, bmm, norm, rope, MoE index/expert/end-to-end)
techniques.languages: STeP (Streaming Tensor Programs, ASPL embedded in Python)
techniques.models: Claude 3.5 Sonnet (claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022), closed, instruct; GPT-4o (gpt-4o-2024-11-20), closed, instruct; DeepSeek-V3, open, instruct; Llama 3.1-405B-Instruct, 405B, open, instruct; Qwen2.5-Coder-32B, 32B, open, code-specialized; OpenAI-o1, closed, reasoning (baseline only)

extraction.notes: Borderline eligibility: technique targets correctness only; maintainability (MI) is reported in the appendix descriptively for the best configuration's correct programs, with no baseline or no-technique comparison, so no NF effect of the technique can be inferred. Reviewer should decide whether this descriptive NF report satisfies IC3 or whether the paper belongs on the correctness-only side list. Contamination is avoided by construction (STeP has no public code). Only 'example code' is released. Results report best over three temperatures; no variance or statistical tests; no threats-to-validity section.

extraction.eligibility_reason: CodeQUEST uses GPT-4o to iteratively evaluate and refactor existing human-written code (42 snippets from open-source libraries, some manually degraded); no LLM code generation from a specification is evaluated, so this is LLM refactoring of human-written code.
extraction.title: On Iterative Evaluation and Enhancement of Code Quality Using GPT-4o
extraction.notes: Borderline: the improved code is LLM-edited (LLM-judge feedback loop with Pylint/Radon/Bandit proxy validation; mean RPI 52.6%), so it could be read as IC2 'code edited by an LLM'. Excluded because inputs are human-written open-source snippets (adjacent: LLM refactoring). Reviewer should confirm the review's stance on LLM refactoring of human code.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Introduces KernelBench and empirically evaluates test-time techniques (repeated sampling, iterative refinement with execution/profiler feedback, hardware-aware few-shot examples, hardware specification in context) on LLM-generated GPU kernels, reporting wall-clock speedup (efficiency) alongside correctness.
extraction.title: KernelBench: Can LLMs Write Efficient GPU Kernels?

techniques.effect_target_headline: Providing hardware information does not significantly impact the outputs of Llama 3.1 70B or DeepSeek-V3

extraction.notes: Primarily a benchmark paper; included because it evaluates several test-time techniques with an efficiency (speedup) outcome. Venue metadata says ICML, but the full text is arXiv v1 with no venue stated, so venue recorded as preprint; reviewer should decide whether to record ICML 2025. Tables garbled but readable (Table 2, 9, 10, 15). Timing CV <3% over 100 trials reported, but no repeated generation runs or statistical tests. Open-source framework claimed, no URL in text. No threats-to-validity section; one limitation (temperature 0 in refinement) noted. Hardware-info effect direction for R1/o1 is mixed (some hardware-specific outliers); headline reflects the paper's summary.

extraction.eligibility_reason: AutoTEE uses LLMs (few-shot plus ReAct with compiler and differential-test feedback) to translate sensitive Java/Python functions into Rust for TEEs, but the evaluated outcomes of the LLM-generated code are compilability and functional equivalence (transformation success rate); security is the motivation of porting rather than a measured property of the generated code, and the TEE runtime overhead case study characterizes porting cost rather than comparing code quality across techniques.
extraction.title: Automated TEE Adaptation With LLMs: Identifying, Transforming, and Porting Sensitive Functions in Programs
extraction.notes: Headline: 91.8% Java and 84.3% Python transformation success with GPT-4o; ablation vs zero-shot, few-shot and compile-check-only (Table VIII); 4 models; token/cost reported (Table X). Table XI reports TEE runtime overhead for 8 transformed functions (e.g., 12.1x to 1255x) vs original code, which is an efficiency number but reflects TEE communication/attestation overhead, not a technique effect; a reviewer could argue for inclusion on efficiency/security grounds. Full text is arXiv v3 with 'Journal of LaTeX class files' header; TSE venue from metadata. No artifact URL in text.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes an LLM agent (retrieval + CoT modular synthesis + execution-feedback debugging and iterative algorithm refinement) that generates AIoT programs, and reports SonarQube counts of bugs, security issues and code smells of the generated code across improvement iterations, plus inference time/GPU memory of generated programs and a user rating of code readability. Borderline because the technique targets task accuracy and the NF outcomes are secondary and only shown in figures.
extraction.title: AutoIOT: LLM-Driven Automated Natural Language Programming for AIoT Applications
extraction.venue: ACM MobiCom '25 (31st Annual International Conference on Mobile Computing and Networking)

techniques.technique_name: AutoIOT (background knowledge retrieval + CoT modularized program synthesis + automated debugging and iterative algorithm-modification code improvement)
techniques.tools: LangChain; Tavily web search; OpenAI text embeddings; Faiss vector DB; sandboxed Python code executor; SonarQube (evaluation only); psutil (network traffic)
techniques.iterations: Debugging repeated until the code executes; algorithm-modification optimization loop run for five iterations (empirically chosen; varied 0-10), then LLM selects the best-performing program
techniques.metrics: security: SonarQube security issues per iteration [tool-static]; readability-maintainability: SonarQube code smells per iteration [tool-static], Code & Documentation Readability rating 1-6 by users [human]; efficiency: inference time per sample and GPU memory of generated programs [execution]; correctness: task accuracy, MAE, execution success rate, average iteration rounds, SonarQube bugs [execution/tool-static]
techniques.benchmarks: Four AIoT applications: heartbeat detection (MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database), IMU HAR (WISDM), mmWave HAR (XRF55), multimodal HAR (Harmony); user study on RFID HAR (XRF55) with 20 users
techniques.models: GPT-4 (closed, main); GPT-3.5 (closed); Cohere (closed); Claude 2 (closed); Llama2-7b (open); Gemma-7b (open)
techniques.baselines: Hand-written domain algorithms/repos (Hamilton, Christov, Engzee, Pan-Tompkins, SWT; LSTM-RNN, 1D-CNN, Conv-LSTM, BiLSTM, NN; ResNet-18..152; Harmony baseline); Penetrative AI direct LLM inference; ablations without retrieval/CoT steps/code improvement; initial iteration for SonarQube counts

extraction.human_eval_details: 20 participants (5 experts, 15 non-experts) rated System Utility, Requirement Coverage, Code & Documentation Readability, Generation Efficiency on a 1-6 scale; no agreement reported
extraction.notes: Eligibility borderline: NF outcomes are secondary (SonarQube Fig. 15b: 'several bugs and one security issue present initially are ultimately fixed by AutoIOT', code smells not all addressed). Figures 10-15 are garbled in the extracted text, so no exact NF numbers can be copied. Efficiency of generated programs varies by prompt requirement (A2 memory-constrained uses less memory and less inference time; A3 more). Network traffic 8MB vs >50MB and 25 minutes wall-clock compare against Penetrative AI, not code quality. No dedicated threats-to-validity section. XRF55 noted as unseen by LLMs (newly published).

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes an LLM framework (prompt-template generator, LoRA fine-tuning, RAG, synthesis-based validation loop) that generates Verilog TPU designs and reports power/area/latency (PPA) of the generated hardware, an efficiency outcome; borderline because efficiency is hardware PPA driven by chosen design parameters and is compared only to manual designs.
extraction.title: TPU-Gen: LLM-Driven Custom Tensor Processing Unit Generator
extraction.venue: 2025 IEEE International Conference on LLM-Aided Design (ICLAD)

techniques.technique_name: TPU-Gen (prompt-template generator + LoRA fine-tuned LLM + RAG module retrieval + YOSYS/OpenROAD validation loop)
techniques.tools: YOSYS synthesis; OpenROAD (PPA); Pyverilog; 45nm technology library; Design Compiler/Vivado for dataset
techniques.iterations: Invalid designs trigger a feedback loop for error analysis and retraining until predefined performance criteria are met; no max rounds stated
techniques.metrics: efficiency: power consumption, area, latency of synthesized designs vs PPA reference budget [execution/tool-static synthesis]; correctness: pass@k, pass/fail rates with testbench/manual verification [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: TPU-Gen dataset (25,000 TPU designs; v1 of 5,000 Verilog headers, 80:20 split); 30 designs for prompt-generator and RAG experiments; 4 DNN workloads (LeNet, ResNet18, VGG16, ResNet56) for PPA comparison
techniques.models: CodeLlama-7B-hf, open, code-specialized; CodeQwen1.5-7B, open, code-specialized; Mistral-7B, open, base; StarCoder2-7B, open, code-specialized; CodeLlama-13B (Q4), open, code-specialized; Claude 3.5 Sonnet, closed, instruct; ChatGPT-4o, closed, instruct; Gemini Advanced, closed, instruct
techniques.baselines: Manual optimization by an expert hardware designer (PPA); human input without prompt generator; fine-tuned models without RAG
techniques.effect_target_headline: average reduction in area and power of 92% and 96% from the manual optimization reference values
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: Models using RAG consistently achieved pass rates exceeding 95%, with Mistral-7B and CodeLlama-7B-hf attaining 100% success. In contrast, all models failed entirely without RAG

extraction.notes: Hardware (Verilog) generation; NF outcome is PPA of synthesized TPU designs, compared only against manual expert designs (Fig. 9, plotted, no per-workload numbers in text), not against a no-technique LLM baseline. The 92%/96% headline is stated in abstract/conclusion only. PPA largely depends on design parameters the LLM selects. Tables III-V garbled but readable. Dataset/models promised but link omitted.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes LMST, a GPT-4 prompt-engineering pipeline (with compile/deploy error feedback and stepwise gas-optimization prompts) that translates PyTorch MLPs into Solidity, and measures gas consumption (efficiency) of the LLM-generated contracts across optimization steps.
extraction.title: Generation of Optimized Solidity Code for Machine Learning Models using LLMs

techniques.technique_name: LMST: LLM-based PyTorch-to-Solidity translation with compile/deploy error feedback and stepwise gas-optimization prompts (A-D)
techniques.tools: Solidity compiler; local Ganache network (gas limit raised to 6.75 x 10^10); Ethereum Sepolia test network; PRBMath fixed-point library
techniques.iterations: Regenerate on compile or deployment failure until the contract deploys (no max stated); then four sequential optimization prompts A->B->C->D (remove unnecessary fixed-point conversions and redundant memory allocations; in-line calculations; avoid repeated loop calculations and use memory temporaries)
techniques.metrics: efficiency: gas consumed for contract deployment and weight upload, ETH/USD cost estimate [execution]; correctness: on-chain vs off-chain classification accuracy on MNIST test images [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: MNIST MLP models (784-input, one hidden layer of varying neurons, 10 outputs); accuracy on 1,000 test images; precision study on 40 images
techniques.models: GPT-4, size NR, closed, instruct
techniques.baselines: Initial LLM translation (step A) vs optimized steps B-D; off-chain PyTorch accuracy; ML2SC discussed but not compared quantitatively
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: Off-chain PyTorch 86.00% vs On-chain Solidity 81.10% accuracy (1000 test images)

extraction.notes: Gas reduction from A to D is shown only in Figure 3 (no numbers printed in text; text says 'The overall gas cost progressively decreases from A to D'). Final deployment gas 1,339,833 (Table 4) has no pre-optimization comparison number in text. Metadata venue is International Conference on Blockchain; PDF is the arXiv version with no venue stated. Accuracy inconsistency: text says 'three images incorrectly classified off-chain' vs 86% on 1,000 images. Prompts not reproduced.

extraction.eligibility_reason: EditLord learns LM-induced code transformation rules to fine-tune/prompt LLMs that edit existing human-written (or machine-decompiled) code: optimizing slow human C++ submissions (PIE HQ), improving readability of Ghidra-decompiled code, and hardening vulnerable code (SVEN/CWEval); the edited inputs are not LLM-generated, so it falls under LLM refactoring/repair of human-written code.
extraction.title: EditLord: Learning Code Transformation Rules for Code Editing
extraction.venue: Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2025), PMLR 267
extraction.notes: BORDERLINE: the evaluated artifact is LLM-edited code with quantitative NF outcomes for all three dimensions (efficiency: OPT@k/Speedup@k via gem5 on PIE HQ 978 test programs; readability: char/token/embedding similarity to original source on HumanEval-Decompile 131 samples; security: Security@k and Correct&Sec@k on CWEval), with correctness co-reported, so it would satisfy IC1-IC3 if LLM editing of human-written code counts under IC2. Excluded only because the side-list definition of 'adjacent' covers LLM refactoring/repair of human-written code. If included: technique = rule-augmented fine-tuning (also zero-shot prompting and iterative refinement with execution feedback); models DeepSeek-Coder 1.3B/6.7B, GPT-4o mini (rules generated by GPT-4o mini); baselines prompt, CoT, finetuned (Shypula et al. 2024, Tan et al. 2024, Fu et al. 2022); headline: outperforms SOTA by 23.3%, 12.7%, and 27.6% on performance optimization, decompilation, and security hardening; e.g., DeepSeek-Coder 1.3B OPT@1 16.4 vs 12.5 finetuned. No code URL given; no variance reported; human-expert rule augmentation uses two authors.

extraction.eligibility_reason: VecTrans uses an LLM with compiler, unit-test and formal-verification feedback to rewrite existing human-written TSVC/Skia loops into vectorizable forms (speedup measured), i.e. LLM performance refactoring of human-written code rather than improving the quality of code the LLM generates for a task. Borderline: the transformed code is LLM-edited and runtime speedup is measured, so a reviewer may treat it as an efficiency-of-LLM-edited-code inclusion.
extraction.title: VecTrans: Enhancing Compiler Auto-Vectorization through LLM-Assisted Code Transformations
extraction.notes: Borderline EC4/adjacent vs include. If included: feedback-loop (self + compiler -Rpass remarks + LLM-generated unit tests + Alive2), max 20 iterations; DeepSeek-V3, Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct; TSVC_2 (50-51 unvectorizable functions) + Skia; efficiency headline 'achieves an geomean speedup of 1.77x and successfully vectorizes 24 of 51 test cases'; baselines LLM-Vectorizer and no-feedback base model; cost $0.012 per function and tokens reported; no artifact URL; single run, no variance.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes RobGen, a decoding-time intervention (learned line-level checker + 'if'-token logit boosting) that changes LLM-generated Java code to add defensive checks, and quantitatively measures robustness (input validation/error handling) of the generated code alongside Pass@1.
extraction.title: A Preliminary Study on the Robustness of Code Generation by Large Language Models

techniques.technique_name: RobGen (line-level intervention checker + token-level conditional logit adjustment of the 'if' token)
techniques.tools: Checker: Qwen3-0.6B fine-tuned with LoRA (SFT, lr 2e-5, 5 epochs) on 12,000 line-start samples from 3 Java GitHub repos; HuggingFace Transformers LogitsProcessor; Tree-sitter for AvgABE; GPT-4o as robustness judge
techniques.iterations: per-line intervention at first non-whitespace token; logit += delta*(rank-1) applied only if 'if' is in top-3; delta = 1.60/1.70/1.29/1.78 per model (1.0 for unseen models)
techniques.metrics: robustness (defensive programming: input validation, boundary checks, error/exception handling): pairwise GPT-4o robustness comparison vs human reference, 1-5 scale, 3 repeats (llm-judge, validated against manual labels on 100 pairs, Cohen's kappa 0.81); AvgABE average atomic Boolean expressions (tool-static, Tree-sitter); EHAR exception-handling adoption rate (tool-static); correctness: Pass@1, Compile@1 (execution)
techniques.benchmarks: CoderEval Java, 230 repository-level tasks
techniques.models: DeepSeekCoder-1.3B-Instruct, open, code-specialized; DeepSeekCoder-6.7B-Instruct, open, code-specialized; Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B-Instruct, open, code-specialized; Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct, open, code-specialized; StarCoder2-7B, open, code-specialized
techniques.baselines: Greedy sampling (no technique); RobustCoder Prompt (robustness-instructing prompt); Post-Generation Insertion (FIM re-insertion of first-line 'if'); RobGen without checker (ablation)
techniques.effect_target_headline: RobGen reduces the proportion of less robust code by 10% (across five models); e.g., DeepSeekCoder-1.3B generated code underperforming human drops from 42.2% to 28.7%; average AvgABE 2.42 vs 1.65 greedy
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: achieves the highest average Pass@1 (43.57) vs 42.09 for greedy sampling

extraction.notes: Borderline on NF dimension: the target is 'robustness' (defensive programming: missing null/range/value checks, error handling), not explicitly security (no CWE/vulnerability scanner); mapped to security as input-validation-related; reviewer should decide whether robustness counts as an eligible NF dimension. The LLM judge was validated against manual comparison on 100 pairs (kappa 0.81) in the empirical part, and the open-coding of robustness patterns had kappa 0.71 between two authors. Judge scores averaged over 3 runs; runtime averaged over 3 runs on 20 tasks (RobGen +33.4% for DSC-1.3B, up to +197.9% for QWC-1.5B). Table 3 extraction is garbled but recoverable. Higher AvgABE is not monotonically better (StarCoder2-7B w/o checker 7.76 = redundant ifs).

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes MaintainCoder, a multi-agent LLM code-generation pipeline (waterfall model + design patterns) and evaluates the maintainability of the generated code with static (MI, CC) and dynamic maintenance-effort metrics alongside correctness.
extraction.title: MaintainCoder: Maintainable Code Generation Under Dynamic Requirements
extraction.venue: 39th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2025)

techniques.technique_name: MaintainCoder (multi-agent pipeline: requirements analysis, design pattern selection, framework design + framework evaluation loop, code generation, code optimization with execution feedback)
techniques.tools: AutoGen framework; Python interpreter for execution feedback; MI/CC computed by formula; difflib for AST similarity and code diff
techniques.iterations: Framework evaluation max 3 rounds (stops when evaluator outputs TERMINATE); code optimization max 5 rounds (until code passes tests)
techniques.metrics: readability-maintainability: Maintainability Index and Cyclomatic Complexity [tool-static]; dynamic maintainability via post-modification Pass@k [execution], AST similarity and code-diff (relative/absolute modified lines) between original and modified code [similarity-to-reference]; correctness: Pass@5 on original problems [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: MaintainBench (new): HumanEval-Dyn and MBPP-Dyn (30 problems each extended to 120 new problems), APPS-Dyn (50 problems extended to 200+), CodeContests-Dyn and xCodeEval-Dyn (30 each extended to 120+); 500+ problems total; plus original APPS, CodeContests, xCodeEval
techniques.models: GPT-4o-mini, closed, instruct; DeepSeek-V3, open, instruct; o3-mini, closed, reasoning (backbones); baselines also GPT-4o, Qwen-Plus, Gemini-2.5-Flash-Preview, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, Claude-3.7-Sonnet, GPT-4.1-mini (MetaGPT), all closed
techniques.baselines: Plain LLMs (GPT-4o-mini, DeepSeek-V3, GPT-4o, Qwen-Plus, Gemini-2.5-Flash-Preview, Claude-3.5/3.7-Sonnet, o3-mini); CoT and Self-Planning prompting; AgentCoder, MapCoder, EvoMAC, MetaGPT; human competitive programmers
techniques.effect_target_headline: MaintainCoder(DeepSeek-V3) attains 36.7% Pass@5 accuracy (outperforming the second-best by +60%), 0.785 AST similarity, and the lowest relative code changes 33.0% (xCodeEval-Dyn); APPS-Dyn: MaintainCoder (GPT-4o-mini) MI 69.5 vs 63.3, CC 2.75 vs 5.10 for GPT-4o-mini
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: MaintainCoder (GPT-4o-mini) achieves an 11% increase on xCodeEval (from 46% to 57%), which is over double the improvement seen on APPS (44% to 48%)

extraction.notes: Tables 1, 2, 7, 8 garbled in extraction (columns split); headline numbers taken from running text and reconstructed rows. On entry-level sets static MI is not consistently better (e.g. MBPP-Dyn MaintainCoder DeepSeek-V3 MI appears lower than baselines), so static gains are strongest on mixture/competition levels; authors argue static metrics are inconsistent. Dynamic metrics are newly proposed and use a fixed Phase II generator (GPT-4o-mini; Gemini robustness check). Results averaged over five rounds but no variance or significance tests. No dedicated limitations/threats section. Human programmers used as a baseline, not as raters.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Fine-tunes LLaMA2-7B (LoRA, P-Tuning v2) on an annotation-based instruction dataset whose output code is filtered by an AST-LSTM+Transformer defect detector trained on security-tool labels, and measures the security of the generated Solidity smart contracts with VaaS, Mythril and SmartCheck against the non-fine-tuned model and a prior approach.
extraction.title: Smart contract generation model based on code annotation and AST-LSTM tuning
extraction.venue: Research Square preprint (rs-3995739/v1); metadata lists Journal of Supercomputing

techniques.technique_name: Annotation-prompted instruction dataset with AST-LSTM+Transformer defect filtering and clustering, used for LoRA / P-Tuning v2 fine-tuning of LLaMA2-7B (FTmodel1 / FTmodel2)
techniques.tools: VaaS, Mythril, SmartCheck (labels for defect detector and evaluation of generated code); Sentence-BERT; K-means; Python 3.10, PyTorch 2.0, CUDA 11.8
techniques.metrics: security: pass rate ('accuracy') of generated contracts under VaaS, Mythril and SmartCheck, counting incomplete/repeated code and failed detection as errors [tool-static]; BLEU-1..4 against reference code [similarity-to-reference]
techniques.benchmarks: Self-crawled Ethereum (Etherscan) verified contracts: 6,739 samples split into function/contract/interface/library layers; 50 generated contracts per layer evaluated; ERC20 contract generation comparison
techniques.models: LLaMA2-7B (open, base) fine-tuned with LoRA (FTmodel1) and P-Tuning v2 (FTmodel2); comparison on ERC20 BLEU only: ChatGPT 3.5 (closed), Code Llama (open, code-specialized), Gemini (closed)
techniques.baselines: Non-fine-tuned LLaMA2-7B; an existing LSTM-based smart contract generation experiment (SmartCheck, contract layer only); ChatGPT 3.5, Code Llama, Gemini for BLEU on ERC20
techniques.effect_target_headline: The data accuracy of the two models in the contract layer increased by 9.3% and 8.2% respectively (SmartCheck, vs existing experiment); improvement of 6% and 7% over the non-fine-tuned model (71.2%); abstract: code security is improved by about 9%

extraction.notes: Full text is the Research Square preprint (March 2024), while metadata gives Journal of Supercomputing 2025; reviewer should check for differences with the published version. Correctness only proxied by BLEU (similarity to reference), so correctness_measured set false. 'Accuracy' of security tools is loosely defined and mixes completeness with vulnerability detection; only 50 samples per layer; comparison with 'existing experiment' uses a different setting. Security results are mixed across layers/tools (e.g., FTmodel2 interface layer VaaS 73.2% vs non-fine-tuned 69.6%; gains generally positive). No variance, compute, or artifacts (data on request).

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes a meta-prompt mechanism with performance-guided auto-tuning search that makes LLMs generate high-performance GEMM code, and reports quantitative efficiency (GFLOPS/TFLOPS) of the generated code versus vanilla and CoT prompts.
extraction.title: QiMeng-GEMM: Automatically Generating High-Performance Matrix Multiplication Code by Exploiting Large Language Models
extraction.venue: The Thirty-Ninth AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence (AAAI-25)

techniques.technique_name: QiMeng-GEMM: meta-prompts (platform-agnostic optimization-primitive descriptions plus platform-specific hints from a hint repository) with iterative beam-search auto-tuning over primitive permutations
techniques.tools: OpenBLAS 0.3.27 and cuBLAS 12.1 as references; XuanTie C910 RISC-V CPU, NVIDIA RTX 4070 and A100 GPUs
techniques.iterations: Beam search over optimization primitives (tiling, reordering, vectorization, layout, pipeline) with beam width k and max iterations T; incorrect code pruned; stops when no further performance improvement or T reached (values of k and T not stated)
techniques.metrics: efficiency: GFLOPS (CPU) / TFLOPS (GPU) throughput (execution); development time vs human coders; correctness: functional correctness of generated code (execution), reported as share of correct search trails and in hint ablation
techniques.benchmarks: GEMM on square matrix dimensions typical of deep learning (256-4096 on C910 CPU; 512-16384 on RTX 4070 and A100), 7 sizes per platform, 3 platforms
techniques.languages: C with RISC-V vector intrinsics; CUDA C
techniques.models: GPT-4o, closed, instruct; Claude 3.5 Sonnet, closed, instruct; DeepSeek-Coder-V2 236B, open, code-specialized; Codestral-22B, open, code-specialized
techniques.baselines: vanilla prompt; Chain-of-Thought prompt; hand-optimized libraries OpenBLAS 0.3.27 and cuBLAS 12.1; junior and senior human coders (development cost)
techniques.effect_target_headline: Compared to vanilla prompts, our method achieves a performance enhancement of up to 113× (GPT-4o, C910 CPU, 113.67×); up to 9.65× on RTX 4070 and 3.92× on A100; 211% of OpenBLAS on RISC-V CPUs and 115% of cuBLAS on NVIDIA GPUs

extraction.notes: Tables garbled in extraction. Correctness is used as a pruning gate; only partial correctness reporting (19-of-25-style '76%' of search trails correct; hint ablation says without hints LLMs fail to generate correct warp/thread tiling and float4 code). Codestral-22B shows near-zero or slightly negative gains on GPUs (0.97-1.15x), so effect is not uniform across models. Beam width and max iterations not given; meta-prompt full text not provided (appendix referenced but absent). No variance or repeated runs. Development time comparison with human coders reported.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes PR2, an LLM technique (decision-tree prompting plus compiler/test-feedback repair with code-change analysis) that rewrites C2Rust-translated Rust code, and reports a quantitative memory-safety outcome (number/percentage of raw pointers eliminated) for the LLM-edited code.
extraction.title: Raw Pointer Rewriting with LLMs for Translating C to Safer Rust
extraction.venue: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL) (arXiv v3)

techniques.technique_name: PR2: decision-tree-based prompting for raw pointer lifting and statement refactoring, with code-change-analysis-guided compilation and test-case error repair
techniques.tools: C2Rust (initial transpilation); tree-sitter (raw pointer extraction); cargo check (type and borrow checking); project test suites
techniques.iterations: Up to 5 repair attempts per pointer (N=5), then give up on that pointer; temperature 0.0
techniques.metrics: security (memory safety): number and percentage of eliminated local raw pointers and affected functions (tool-static, tree-sitter counting); correctness: compilation + project test pass as gate, human user study of semantic equivalence (human), LLM-synthesized tests on uncovered functions (execution)
techniques.benchmarks: 28 real-world C projects with test cases from the NOPCRAT evaluation set (437 to 136k LOC, 17 to 2,731 raw pointers)
techniques.models: gpt-4o-mini, size NR, closed, instruct (main); Claude-3.5-Sonnet, size NR, closed (top 10 projects); Deepseek-v3.2, open, instruct (top 10 projects)
techniques.baselines: LAERTES (rule-based raw pointer to reference rewriting); C2Rust output; ablations NT (no decision tree) and NCC (no code change analysis)
techniques.effect_target_headline: PR2 removes 2,255 raw pointers, compared to 506 by LAERTES (3.46× more); on average removes 18.57% of raw pointers and transforms 13.05% of functions into safer code
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: all volunteers confirmed the rewritten code preserved original semantics (200 sampled eliminations); in 59 total cases we found only 2 incorrect pointer rewrites, corresponding to a 96.61% correctness rate among inspected cases

extraction.human_eval_details: 10 Rust-experienced volunteers, each reviewed 20 randomly selected raw pointer eliminations for semantic equivalence; all confirmed preservation; no agreement statistic reported
extraction.notes: Input code is C2Rust-transpiled Rust (machine-generated, not human-written), edited by the LLM; NF outcome is memory safety measured as raw-pointer elimination counts (a proxy, not a vulnerability scanner). Borderline adjacent/EC4 if reviewers treat this as LLM refactoring of existing code. Limitations note rewritten code may have low readability (not measured). Tables 1-2 are column-garbled but totals are stated in text. Single deterministic run (temperature 0).

extraction.eligibility_reason: LLM-DSE is a multi-agent LLM design-space-exploration framework that selects HLS directive parameter values (pragmas) for existing human-written HLSyn/Rosetta kernels to minimize accelerator latency; it is LLM-driven tuning/optimization of existing code rather than improving the quality of code generated by an LLM. Borderline because a direct-generation LLM baseline (GPT-4o, o1) is compared on latency.
extraction.title: LLM-DSE: Searching Accelerator Parameters with LLM Agents
extraction.notes: Borderline EC4/adjacent vs include (multi-agent feedback loop with compiler/synthesis feedback, efficiency = clock cycles of synthesized accelerator). Headline: 2.55x speedup over AutoDSE-8 (average), geomean 1.87x vs AutoDSE-8 baseline; direct generation GPT-4o geomean 0.16, o1 0.17 vs DSE. Two runs with std reported; token costs reported (1-7 USD per program with GPT-4o). Output is directive parameter values rather than free-form code; hardware latency rather than software runtime. Code said to be open-sourced but no URL in extracted text.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Empirical study of prompting (base/ICL/RAG/CoT) and PEFT (LoRA, QLoRA, prefix/prompt tuning) for small open-source LMs generating logging statements in Java methods; all outcomes are agreement with the ground-truth log (position/level accuracy, variable match, BLEU/ROUGE, LLM-judge alignment to ground truth), not a non-functional quality dimension (readability, efficiency, security) of the generated code.
extraction.title: Larger Is Not Always Better: Exploring Small Open-Source Language Models in Logging Statement Generation
extraction.venue: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
extraction.notes: Borderline on scope: logging statements are inserted into production code and the paper frames log quality as aiding maintenance, but every metric is similarity/accuracy versus the removed developer log (PA, LA, AOD, PMR, F1, BLEU-4, ROUGE-L) plus an LLM-judge score that also rates alignment with ground truth; no readability/maintainability, efficiency or security metric of the code. Tables are garbled in extraction. Replication package: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Logging_Empirical_Study-9E54/

extraction.eligibility_reason: LIBRARIAN is a sample-and-rerank method in which LLMs/agents refactor existing (mostly human-written) code (CodeContests solutions, HuggingFace Transformers/Diffusers files) into shared libraries, scored by MDL, tokens, cyclomatic complexity and maintainability index; this is LLM refactoring of human-written code rather than improving the quality of newly generated code.
extraction.title: Refactoring Codebases through Library Design
extraction.notes: Borderline: the output artifact is LLM-edited code with maintainability-type metrics (MDL, tokens, CC, MI; human pairwise study with 14 participants), and Logo/Date source programs were generated by gpt-3.5-turbo, but the task is refactoring existing code into a library (adjacent). A reviewer may consider including it under IC2 'code edited by an LLM'.

extraction.eligibility_reason: iDSE uses an LLM as a black-box optimizer that outputs HLS directive configuration vectors (pipeline/unroll/array-partition parameters) for fixed human-written benchmark kernels; a script turns them into Tcl directives, and the outcome is Pareto-front quality (ADRS) of synthesized hardware latency/resource usage, not the quality of LLM-generated or LLM-edited source code.
extraction.title: iDSE: Navigating Design Space Exploration in High-Level Synthesis Using LLMs
extraction.notes: Borderline: directives are effectively pragmas inserted into human-written HLS C/C++ (PolyBench, MachSuite, CHStone; 12 kernels), and latency/resource utilization could be read as an efficiency outcome of LLM-edited code. Excluded because the LLM generates parameter configurations in a DSE loop (no code generation; the original code is unchanged except for tool directives applied via Tcl) and the metric is ADRS of the explored Pareto front against baselines NSGA-II, ACO, MOEA/D, Lattice, HGBO-DSE (headline: 5.1x to 16.6x ADRS improvement). No correctness outcome since directives preserve function. Models: DeepSeek-R1 main; Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-4.1, Grok-3, o1-preview in appendix. Figures garbled in extraction. A reviewer who counts HLS pragma insertion as LLM code editing for efficiency may include it.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Primarily a code-retrieval benchmark, but it proposes quality-aware contrastive fine-tuning of retrievers and evaluates it downstream in retrieval-augmented code generation, measuring vulnerability rate (CodeQL) and deprecated-API usage of LLM-generated code. Borderline because the NF outcome for generated code is a secondary experiment reported only in a figure.
extraction.title: CoQuIR: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Code Quality-Aware Information Retrieval
extraction.venue: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL)

techniques.technique_name: Quality-aware retriever fine-tuning (Repllama-3b/8b-quality) for retrieval-augmented code generation
techniques.tools: CodeQL (vulnerability check of generated code); SVEN official implementation; LLM judge prompt for deprecated API usage
techniques.metrics: security: vulnerability rate of generated code via CodeQL [tool-static]; maintainability: modern vs deprecated API usage rate on DepreAPI [llm-judge per Table 9 prompt]; retriever-level: PPA, MRS, nDCG@10, MRR [similarity-to-reference]
techniques.benchmarks: SVEN/He and Vechev (2023) split, nine CWE scenarios (575 outputs checked); DepreAPI with 20 test cases per API mapping; CoQuIR (42,725 queries, 134,907 snippets) for retriever evaluation
techniques.languages: C, Python (SVEN CWE scenarios); Python (DepreAPI); retriever benchmark covers 11 languages
techniques.models: CodeGen 2B, open, code-specialized; InCoder 6B, open, code-specialized; SantaCoder 1.1B, open, code-specialized; retrievers Repllama-3b (LLaMA-3.2-3B) and Repllama-8b (LLaMA-3.1-8B), open
techniques.baselines: Same generators with standard (non-quality-aware) Repllama-8b retriever top-5; variant with paired secure/vulnerable demonstrations; 23 retrievers on the benchmark

extraction.human_eval_details: 3 co-authors rated 400 LLM-generated query summaries (not code) on 5-point Likert; Fleiss kappa 0.72
extraction.notes: Downstream generation results (vulnerability rate, modern API usage) are shown only in Figure 5 with no numbers in text; the textual headline is retriever-level 'improvements of 20-30%' in PPA. Efficiency targeted by the retriever training but not measured on generated code. Three runs at temperature 0.4 but no variance reported in text. Tables 2-3 garbled. Limitations section present; no explicit threats-to-validity section. Eligibility borderline: main contribution is a retrieval benchmark.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes IaCGen, an LLM iterative feedback loop (yamllint, cfn-lint, live AWS deployment errors, optional human feedback) for generating CloudFormation IaC templates, and reports a quantitative security outcome (Checkov policy pass and compliance rates) for the generated templates alongside deployability. Borderline: security is measured but not targeted and not compared against a no-technique baseline.
extraction.title: Deployability-Centric Infrastructure-as-Code Generation: Fail, Learn, Refine, and Succeed through LLM-Empowered DevOps Simulation

techniques.technique_name: IaCGen (iterative format/syntax/live-deployment feedback with full conversation history; optional human-in-the-loop feedback)
techniques.tools: yamllint; cfn-lint (AWS CloudFormation Linter); AWS SDK boto3 live deployment; Checkov (evaluation only)
techniques.iterations: Up to 6 iterations per validation stage (2 general + 4 detailed feedback), reported up to passItr@15; with human feedback 4 more per stage (max 10 per stage, passItr@25); stop when template passes all three stages or max attempts exceeded
techniques.metrics: security: Checkov policy pass rate, unfiltered and filtered template compliance rate [tool-static]; correctness: passItr@n deployment success rate (live AWS deployment) [execution]; user intent coverage of required resources/attributes via Checkov custom policies [tool-static, expert-specified]
techniques.benchmarks: DPIaC-Eval (new), 153 CloudFormation tasks across 58 AWS services, 5 difficulty levels; IaC-Eval (Terraform) for generalizability (syntax only); intent matching on 51 sampled tasks
techniques.models: GPT-4o, size NR, closed, instruct; GPT-o3-mini, size NR, closed, reasoning; Claude-3.5 Sonnet, size NR, closed, instruct; Claude-3.7 Sonnet, size NR, closed, instruct; DeepSeek-R1, 671B, open, reasoning; DeepSeek-V3, 671B, open, instruct
techniques.baselines: Single-shot generation (passItr@1, no feedback); ablation without full conversation history (system prompt + original prompt + error + incorrect template only) on Claude-3.5
techniques.effect_target_headline: Security at maximum iterations (no comparison to baseline): average Policy Pass 75.3%, Unfiltered Compl. 20.2%, Filtered Compl. 8.4%
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: IaCGen can make 54.6∼91.6% generated IaC templates from all evaluated models deployable in the first 10 iterations (vs 20.8∼30.2% deployment success rate on the first attempt); average passItr@1 24.6 vs passItr@15 74.8

extraction.notes: Borderline eligibility: the technique targets deployability (a correctness-type outcome); security (Checkov) is measured only on final generated templates without a no-feedback comparison, so the NF effect of the technique is not reported. Reviewer should check whether this belongs in 'context' rather than include. IaC templates treated as production code. Human feedback in RQ3 is part of the technique variant, not an evaluation. Temperature 0, single run; total cost reported ($230.75 API tokens, $35.21 AWS). Benchmark templates sourced from public GitHub/AWS samples; contamination not discussed. Venue is PACMSE (FSE); venue_type could alternatively be journal. Figures garbled in extraction.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes CompilerGPT, an iterative loop feeding compiler optimization reports, compile errors and test results to an LLM that rewrites C++ code for performance, and reports runtime speedups of the LLM-edited code.
extraction.title: CompilerGPT: Leveraging Large Language Models for Analyzing and Acting on Compiler Optimization Reports

techniques.technique_name: CompilerGPT: iterative compiler-optimization-report-guided rewriting with CoT-style prompts, negative prompting, conversation history, and compile/test-failure correction prompts
techniques.tools: Clang 18.1.8 and GCC 12.2.1 optimization reports (-Rpass-missed, -O3 -march=native -DNDEBUG=1); user-defined evaluation harness (unit/regression tests and timing, sum of 10 runs); Intel Xeon Gold 6248R
techniques.iterations: Six iterations per run (fixed); success prompt with new report after passing, fail prompt with compile/test errors otherwise; 5 runs per configuration
techniques.metrics: efficiency: max and average runtime speedup over original code compiled with the same compiler, and number of runs with any speedup (execution); correctness: compile and regression test pass (execution), reported qualitatively
techniques.benchmarks: 5 codes: naive matrix multiplication, OpenMP prefix sum, OpenMP Smith-Waterman, NAS-FT, NAS-BT (compute_rhs subset)
techniques.models: GPT-4o, closed, instruct; Claude Sonnet 3.7, closed, reasoning-capable instruct
techniques.baselines: original input code compiled with same compiler (-O3); no LLM-without-report ablation
techniques.effect_target_headline: Speedups of up to 6.5x were obtained, though not consistently in every test (Sonnet 3.7, prefix sum, GCC; avg 2.73)

extraction.notes: Input code is human-written; the LLM edits it for performance (code optimization, not repair/refactoring), so could be argued adjacent. Authors explicitly did not compare against a configuration without optimization reports. Many configurations show no speedup (e.g., GPT-4o prefix 1.0x, NAS ~1.0-1.1x); 5 runs per configuration with max/avg but no variance. Correctness enforced by harness but pass rates not tabulated. Cost and time reported for matmul and NAS BT only.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes Feature Search and Reinforcement (FSR), an iterative LLM loop using compilation, functional validation and GPU profiling feedback to generate faster CUDA kernels; reports measured execution speedups of LLM-generated kernels alongside correctness.
extraction.title: CUDA-LLM: LLMs Can Write Efficient CUDA Kernels

techniques.technique_name: Feature Search and Reinforcement (FSR): generate N candidate kernels, filter by compilation verifier and function validator, select fastest via GPU performance profiler, refine prompt with errors/history or performance hints, repeat to depth D
techniques.tools: CUDA compiler (nvcc implied); runtime latency measurement on NVIDIA GTX 1660 SUPER and RTX 3090 Ti
techniques.iterations: Max depth D rounds with N candidates per round (values not reported); correctness-repair rounds do not increment depth; returns fastest correct kernel
techniques.metrics: efficiency: kernel execution latency, speedup normalized to human-written CUDA baseline, 5 input sizes per task [execution]; correctness: compilation plus output within deviation of human-written CUDA results on test inputs [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: 20 CUDA kernel tasks from NVIDIA CUDA Samples, LeetGPU and KernelBench, each at 5 input sizes
techniques.models: DeepSeek-V3-0324 (open, general instruct)
techniques.baselines: Human-written CUDA kernels (speedup baseline); direct LLM generation pass@5 (correctness)
techniques.effect_target_headline: the automatically generated kernels can outperform general human-written code by a factor of up to 179× in execution speeds; average speedups of 104×, 102×, and 179× (Matrix Transpose, Dot Product, Monte Carlo Integration) on an RTX 3090 Ti GPU
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: under the CUDA-LLM FSR framework, the LLM successfully completed all predefined tasks on GTX 1660 SUPER GPU and RTX 3090 Ti GPU (20 tasks), whereas direct generation (pass@5) failed some tasks

extraction.notes: Figure 3 (per-task speedups) is heavily garbled in extraction; Table 1 correctness checkmarks garbled. Efficiency baseline is stated as human-written CUDA, but Sec 4.2.2 also says 'compared to directly generated CUDA kernels, FSR consistently improves execution efficiency' - ambiguity in what the baseline is; some tasks show speedups below 1x (e.g. 0.433x, 0.494x) at some sizes. N and D not reported; no repeated runs, cost, artifacts or threats. Single model (DeepSeek-V3-0324) with brief justification. KernelBench-derived tasks may raise contamination concerns, not discussed.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes AlphaEvolve, an LLM-driven evolutionary coding agent that edits code under automated evaluator feedback; for engineering applications it reports quantitative runtime improvements of the LLM-evolved code (Pallas matmul tiling heuristic, XLA FlashAttention IR). Borderline because most results are algorithm/math discovery objectives rather than NF quality of code.
extraction.title: AlphaEvolve: A coding agent for scientific and algorithmic discovery

techniques.technique_name: AlphaEvolve (LLM-guided evolutionary code superoptimization with evaluator feedback)
techniques.tools: User-provided evaluate function; evaluation cascade; real TPU runtime measurement; data-center simulator; XLA compiler IR; optional LLM-generated feedback
techniques.iterations: Evolutionary loop over a program database (MAP-elites + island model); runs until compute budget is exhausted; thousands of LLM samples; e.g. 15 mutations for the 4x4 matmul program
techniques.metrics: efficiency: kernel runtime speedup on real TPU accelerators, FlashAttention IR execution time speedup, fleet compute resources recovered (execution); math/algorithm tasks use task-specific objective scores (e.g. tensor rank)
techniques.benchmarks: Google internal applications: Gemini Pallas matmul kernel tiling heuristic (realistic input shapes, half train/half eval), XLA-generated FlashAttention IR for one transformer inference configuration, Borg scheduling heuristic, TPU Verilog circuit; plus 54 matrix multiplication tensor targets and 50+ math problems
techniques.models: Gemini 2.0 Flash, size NR, closed, instruct; Gemini 2.0 Pro, size NR, closed, instruct
techniques.baselines: Existing expert-designed tiling heuristic; unmodified compiler-generated IR; production Borg heuristic; prior best-known constructions; ablations (no evolution, no context in prompt, no meta prompt evolution, no full-file evolution, small base LLM only) on math tasks
techniques.effect_target_headline: an average 23% kernel speedup across all kernels over the existing expert-designed heuristic (Gemini kernel tiling); FlashAttention kernel sped up by 32%; 15% speed up in pre- and postprocessing

extraction.notes: White paper; efficiency results come from proprietary Google case studies (single configuration each, no variance). Correctness is enforced by construction or checked against reference on randomized inputs but not reported as a rate. Ablations (3 seeds, std shown) are only on math tasks, not on efficiency tasks. Only mathematical results released (Colab); system code not released. Compute only described loosely (thousands of samples, ~100 compute-hours per evaluation possible). Eligibility borderline: reviewer should decide whether evolved-heuristic runtime counts as NF code quality.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes an LLM-driven evolutionary framework (selector, experiment designer, kernel writer) that generates and iteratively modifies HIP GPU kernels using benchmark timing feedback, and reports execution time of the LLM-produced kernel.
extraction.title: GPU Kernel Scientist: An LLM-Driven Framework for Iterative Kernel Optimization
extraction.venue: ES-FoMo: Third Workshop on Efficient Systems for Foundation Models @ ICML 2025

techniques.technique_name: GPU Kernel Scientist (LLM evolutionary selector + experiment designer + kernel writer with timing feedback)
techniques.tools: AMD Developer Challenge 2025 competition platform (compile, correctness test, end-to-end timing over 18 seeds/sizes); no profiler
techniques.iterations: Open-ended evolutionary loop; each iteration selects base+reference, designs 5 experiments, runs 3 kernel writers; evaluation requests made sequentially; no fixed stopping rule reported
techniques.metrics: efficiency: geometric average execution time (microseconds) over 18 matrix sizes on AMD MI300 (execution)
techniques.benchmarks: AMD Developer Challenge 2025 FP8 GEMM kernel with scaling (1 task)
techniques.models: Gemini 2.5 Pro Preview 05-06, closed, reasoning; Gemini 2.5 Flash Preview 05-20, closed, reasoning
techniques.baselines: Naive HIP translation; PyTorch reference; human 1st place competition entry
techniques.effect_target_headline: This work ≈ 450 µs vs Naïve HIP ≈ 5000 µs and PyTorch reference ≈ 850 µs (Human 1st place 105 µs)

extraction.notes: Brief workshop paper (about 5 pages plus appendix). Single task, single result table with approximate numbers; seed kernels partly human/LLM co-created, so human involvement in bootstrapping. Correctness is a gate in the loop but not reported as an outcome. Supplementary URL appears garbled by PDF extraction (spaces in ID). Limitations discussed briefly.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes EvoVerilog, an LLM-driven evolutionary search (idea-tree initialization plus crossover/mutation prompts and non-dominated sorting over testbench mismatch and hardware resource use) that generates Verilog, and reports hardware resource efficiency (wires/cells) of the generated designs alongside pass@k. Hardware resource usage is treated here as an efficiency outcome, which is borderline.
extraction.title: EvoVerilog: Large Langugage Model Assisted Evolution of Verilog Code

techniques.technique_name: EvoVerilog (idea-tree multi-representation initialization + LLM evolutionary search with positive/negative crossover and mutation, multi-objective non-dominated sorting on testbench mismatch rate and wire/cell resource use)
techniques.tools: VerilogEval testbenches; wire and cell counts of the synthesized module (synthesis tool not named)
techniques.iterations: budget of 20 samples per problem (generation 0 plus 2 generations; up to 20 total attempts) or 100 samples in extended evaluation (generations 1-13); max 5 ideas per node, 2 parent nodes

extraction.notes: Hardware-design domain: the efficiency outcome is latency (cycles) of the synthesized hardware from HLS-C, an estimate from the synthesis tool rather than measured software runtime; reviewer should confirm this counts as code efficiency. HLSTuner edits existing benchmark kernels (directive insertion only, semantics claimed unchanged), so a check against EC4 is advisable; the full ChatHLS pipeline also generates HLS-C from NL/C. Venue: PDF is arXiv v4 (Apr 2026), metadata says ACL and the repo is named ChatHLS-ACL-26, but the paper text gives no venue. Failed optimizations were assigned speedup 1 (penalty) in the geo mean. Correctness of tuned designs is not reported separately. Train/test Rouge-L similarity analysis addresses fine-tuning leakage; pretraining contamination only discussed for DeepSeek-V3.2. Several figures (speedups per kernel, token use, scaling) are garbled in extraction; Table 3 is partly garbled. Generation pass rates averaged over 20 repetitions, but no variance or significance tests reported.

Borderline: the artifact is agent actions/shell commands during setup tasks rather than application code, and the paper is framed as agent safety.

extraction.notes: Eligibility borderline on EC3/EC6: artifact is agent actions (shell commands, credentials in scripts, chmod, curl|sh, config files) during environment setup, not application code; framed as agent safety. Mitigations evaluated offline/post-hoc per insecure step; effect on task success not measured. Remediation judged by the same LLM detector (recall 61.11%), so remediation may be overestimated. Prompts provided in appendices; no code/data URL. No variance or statistical tests.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes a multi-turn RL (GRPO) training recipe that fine-tunes an LLM to generate and iteratively refine CUDA kernels, and reports quantitative efficiency outcomes (mean speedup over PyTorch Eager, fast_p) for the generated code alongside correctness.
extraction.title: Kevin: Multi-Turn RL for Generating CUDA Kernels

techniques.technique_name: Kevin: multi-turn RL (GRPO) with per-turn training samples, CoT summarization, and discounted cross-turn reward aggregation
techniques.tools: KernelBench evaluation harness (modified: sandboxed evaluation, enlarged tensor dimensions, fixed output-tensor recycling bug, rule-based anti-reward-hacking format checks); torch.utils.cpp_extension.load_inline; OpenRLHF, vLLM, DeepSpeed ZeRO-3; NVIDIA H200 GPUs
techniques.iterations: Training: 16 parallel trajectories x 4 refinement turns per task, 8 tasks per batch, 40 steps (80 gradient steps), max response length 16K raised to 22K at step 30; inference: 16 parallel trajectories x 8 refinement turns (also compared 128x1 and 32x4 under a fixed 128-kernel budget)
techniques.metrics: efficiency: mean speedup of fastest correct kernel over PyTorch Eager reference runtime, fast_1 and fast_1.5 (fraction of tasks with a correct kernel at >= p speedup), reported as best@16 and avg@16 [execution]; correctness: randomized differential testing against the PyTorch reference [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: KernelBench (modified): 180 training tasks (90 Level 1 + 90 Level 2); evaluation set of 100 unseen tasks (80 newly constructed following KernelBench methodology + 20 remaining original tasks)
techniques.models: Qwen QwQ-32B, 32B, open, reasoning (base model trained into Kevin); comparison models OpenAI o4-mini and o3-mini, closed, reasoning; early failed runs on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and -14B, open
techniques.baselines: Base model QwQ-32B (untrained); single-turn RL (GRPO) trained counterpart; frontier models OpenAI o4-mini and o3-mini; PyTorch Eager as the speedup reference
techniques.effect_target_headline: mean speedup from 0.53x to 1.10x of baseline (PyTorch Eager), and surpassing frontier models like o4-mini (0.78x); single-turn RL reaches 0.85x (best@16, 16 trajectories x 8 turns)
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: improving correctness of generated kernels (in pure CUDA) from 56% to 82% (best@16 on 100 unseen KernelBench tasks)

extraction.notes: Efficiency is the target dimension (speedup of generated CUDA kernels); correctness is a co-outcome. Contamination is handled only as train/test separation: 80 new eval tasks were generated with Gemini 2.5-Flash and checked not to duplicate KernelBench Level 1/2 programs; pretraining contamination is not discussed. No artifact/code URL in the text. No statistical tests or repeated-seed variance; best@k/avg@k over 16 trajectories only. Limitations section notes only 80 gradient steps of training and that speedups are specific to the fixed KernelBench tensor sizes on H200. Code listings in the appendices are lightly garbled but readable.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes the AlgoTune benchmark plus the AlgoTuner agent, an iterative LLM loop with execution, profiling and linter feedback that rewrites numerical Python solvers to run faster; it reports runtime speedup (efficiency) of LLM-generated code across four frontier models.
extraction.title: AlgoTune: Can Language Models Speed Up General-Purpose Numerical Programs?
extraction.venue: 39th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2025) Track on Datasets and Benchmarks

techniques.technique_name: AlgoTuner (budgeted SWE-Agent-style code-optimization agent: edit, lint, compile, run, profile, verify, keep fastest valid version)
techniques.tools: linter run after each edit (edit reverted on linter errors); profile and profile_lines commands (line profiler); Cython compilation for .pyx files; Numba, Dask, JAX etc. available; timing via time.perf_counter_ns on AMD EPYC 9454 CPU; LiteLLM API
techniques.iterations: Continuous querying until a $1 per-task budget (input+output tokens) is exhausted; each edit evaluated on 100 dev instances; best-scoring code (by dev runtime) is snapshotted and submitted
techniques.metrics: efficiency: speedup = reference runtime / LM code runtime on held-out test inputs (min of 10 timed runs after warmup), aggregated as harmonic mean (AlgoTune score), invalid or <1x assigned 1x; percentage of tasks with >=1.1x speedup [execution]; correctness: solution verifier is_solution on all test instances, % invalid [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: AlgoTune (new), 154 tasks in 13 categories (plus 5-task development set); reference solvers from NumPy, SciPy, CVXPY, sklearn, NetworkX, OR-Tools etc.
techniques.models: o4-mini-high, closed, reasoning; Claude Opus 4 20250514, closed, reasoning (highest thinking setting); Gemini 2.5 Pro, closed, reasoning; DeepSeek R1 0528, open, reasoning
techniques.baselines: Expert-contributed reference solver implementations (library calls); comparison across LMs; first vs best agent evaluation (Table 9). No non-agentic single-shot LLM baseline.
techniques.effect_target_headline: AlgoTuner achieves an average 1.72× speedup against our reference solvers (o4-mini-high, $1 budget per task; R1 1.70×, Gemini 2.5 Pro 1.51×, Claude Opus 4 1.33×)
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: Invalid (%): Claude Opus 4 25.3, DeepSeek R1 6.5, Gemini 2.5 Pro 27.3, o4-mini 5.8 (Table 7)

extraction.notes: Primarily a benchmark paper; AlgoTuner is presented as a baseline agent. Baseline is the human/library reference solver, not a no-agent LLM; first-vs-best evaluation transitions (Table 9) give partial ablation of the loop. Single run per task per model (checklist states no error bars). Contamination discussed (no answers to leak; reference solvers shown in prompt) but not tested. Code said to be in supplementary material; no URL in text. Tables 5, 7, 9, 10 garbled in extraction (column-wise dumps). Agent found mostly surface-level optimizations, no algorithmic innovation.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Besides introducing a benchmark, the paper proposes and evaluates a category-aware one-shot prompting technique for LLM kernel generation, and reports a quantitative efficiency outcome (SpeedUp_alpha@k, runtime speedup over PyTorch eager) for the LLM-generated kernels alongside compilation and correctness.

extraction.notes: Important caveats for a human reviewer. (1) No denominators are ever reported: the number of firmware programs, tasks, vulnerabilities identified, or fuzzing runs is never stated, so the headline percentages cannot be traced to counts. (2) The security metrics VRR, SCI, TMCS and IEI are custom metrics defined by the authors, not established instruments; SCI's weights w1/w2/w3 are never given a value, and IEI's 'resources consumed' denominator is never operationalized. (3) 'Agent Detection Accuracy compared to ground truth' is reported (91.7% / 93.2%) but how ground truth was established is never described. (4) Tables I, II and III are heavily garbled by PDF extraction; Table III's column headers (LLM Only, Detection Agent, Optimization Agent, Verification Agent, All Agents) are split from the value block, but the mapping is recoverable and the LLM-Only and All-Agents values match those quoted in the running text. (5) Functional correctness of the firmware is not reported as a metric; only an error analysis of failed compilations (approximately 60% missing context, 40% LLM logical inconsistencies) is given. (6) The authors explicitly note in Limitations that traditional code quality, maintainability and readability metrics were NOT measured. (7) Only GPT-4 is used, acknowledged as a model-specific bias limitation. (8) Reproducibility is addressed via fixed random seeds for generated unit tests, but no repeated runs, confidence intervals or statistical tests are reported. (9) Research questions RQ1-RQ3 in Section II are not directly answered by the results section; the paper reads partly as a methodology/experimental-plan paper.
