techniques.benchmarks: NAS Parallel Benchmarks 3.4 kernels CG, EP, MG, FT and OpenBLAS DGEMM (5 kernels; STREAM used only for development) on AMD MI250, NVIDIA A100, NVIDIA GH200
techniques.models: GPT-5, size undisclosed, closed, reasoning; o4-mini-high, size undisclosed, closed, reasoning; Llama 4 Maverick, 400B total/17B active MoE, open, instruct
techniques.baselines: Original Fortran (CPU, OpenMP); baseline translated Kokkos version v1 before optimization; Kokkos CPU (OpenMP) build; comparison across LLMs
techniques.effect_target_headline: memory-bound kernels such as CG, MG, and FT achieved approximately 70.3%, 77.5%, and 6.3% of the memory bandwidth roof (most optimized GPT-5 versions on NVIDIA A100)
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: GPT-5 and o4-mini-high executed the full pipeline across all kernels and hardware partitions; Llama4-Maverick did not complete the full workflow for any kernel

extraction.notes: Single run per kernel-model-hardware configuration (no variance). Optimization gains mostly shown in figures (Fig. 5 CG trajectory, Fig. 6 DGEMM runtime) without numeric deltas in text; the version-over-version gain is not quantified. No ablation of the optimizer vs no-optimizer beyond v1 vs later versions. Contamination mentioned only as a limitation (kernels may overlap with training data). Figures 3-6 garbled.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes an agentic LLM pipeline (PyTorch-to-CUDA translation followed by evolutionary runtime optimization with LLM soft-verifiers and profiler feedback) and reports runtime speedups of the LLM-generated CUDA kernels, plus correctness.
extraction.title: Towards Robust Agentic CUDA Kernel Benchmarking, Verification, and Optimization

techniques.technique_name: Evolutionary kernel optimization with LLM ensemble, LLM soft-verification (compilation/memory/numerics verifiers), least-to-most in-context kernel archive and LLM-summarized profiling feedback (after error-summary-guided PyTorch-to-CUDA translation)
techniques.tools: PyTorch profiler, NVIDIA Nsight Compute (NCU), Clang-tidy; kernels built via torch.utils.cpp_extension (nvcc -O3 --use_fast_math); CUDA 12.4, cuDNN 8.9.7, PyTorch 2.5.1 on H100 (also RTX 4090, A6000 for generalization)
techniques.iterations: Optimization: 10 generations x 8 sampled proposals, top 4 by verifier score evaluated on hardware per generation (40 hardware-evaluated proposals), best kernel selected; translation: up to 10 sequential steps with LLM-summarized error feedback until correct (1e-5 tolerance)
techniques.metrics: efficiency: speedup over PyTorch eager and torch.compile, mean runtime over 2000 runs after 25 warmup [execution]; correctness: fraction of correct proposals / translation success rate across multiple inputs, inits and seeds (atol/rtol 1e-5) [execution]; verifier accuracy [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: robust-kbench (new; 9 task classes, 8 forward + 4 backward = 12 optimization tasks: MNIST cross-entropy, conv-relu-pool, maxpool, linear, linear-relu, LayerNorm, ResNet block, Llama FFW, Llama RMSNorm); KernelBench v0 levels 1 and 2 (200 tasks, with contaminated/exploitable tasks filtered)
techniques.models: o3 (closed, reasoning); o4-mini (closed, reasoning; also verifier and translation model); Claude Sonnet 3.7 (closed, instruct); GPT-4.1 (closed, instruct); Gemini 2.5 Pro (closed, reasoning; in 5-model ensemble ablation)
techniques.baselines: PyTorch eager and torch.compile implementations; Kevin-32B (RL-fine-tuned QwQ-32B) best-of-40 and reported results; Qwen3-32B best-of-40; Claude-3.7-Sonnet best-of-40; best-of-N parallel sampling for translation; ablations without verifier, without profile info, single model, 1-best / 10-random context
techniques.effect_target_headline: achieving up to 2.5× speedup in the forward pass (robust-kbench, over PyTorch eager); KernelBench L1+L2: average speedup reduced from 3.13x to 1.49x after excluding contaminated tasks
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: verifier-assisted optimization increasing the proportion of valid kernels from 55-70% to 80-85% in forward passes; translation succeeds on 95% of KernelBench level 1 and level 2 tasks

extraction.notes: Per-task efficiency results are mixed: backward-pass gains modest and some kernels at or below 1x (Table 4 H100: MNIST CrossEntropy fwd 0.91x, CrossEntropy bwd 0.97x; LayerNorm 12.52x vs native but 0.18x vs torch.compile); kernels overfit to the optimization input shape for LayerNorm and Linear-ReLU. 'Contamination' in the paper means exploitable/flawed KernelBench tasks, not training-data leakage, so contamination_handled set to 'no' (a reviewer may prefer 'partial'). No repeated runs/seeds or statistical tests. Figures 4, 6, 7 are garbled in extraction; numbers taken from prose and Tables 4-5. Cost ~$4-5 per kernel and ~1.5-2 h on 4 GPUs reported. Memory-access checks are part of correctness verification, not reported as a security outcome.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes ReFaaS, an LLM pipeline (CoT prompting with compiler and black-box test recovery loops) that translates Python serverless functions into Go to reduce invocation energy; the artifact is LLM-generated translated code and energy savings are reported quantitatively alongside build/test validity.
extraction.title: Code once, Run Green: Automated Green Code Translation in Serverless Computing
extraction.venue: 2025 IEEE International Conference on Cloud Engineering (IC2E)

techniques.technique_name: ReFaaS: LLM-based Python-to-Go translation pipeline (Chain-of-Thought with documentation, build-fix and test-alignment recovery steps), integrated into Fission
techniques.tools: go build; go test; Scaphandre (container energy); dcgm-exporter (GPU energy/temperature); Prometheus node-exporter; Fission serverless platform
techniques.iterations: Each step and recovery step limited to a fixed number of attempts (figure shows build-fix attempt > 2 and alignment attempt > 3 as cutoffs); Single-Shot variant has no repetitions or recovery
techniques.metrics: efficiency: energy per invocation (J), delta energy/CPU/memory/cold start vs original function, invocations to amortize translation energy [execution]; correctness: buildable %, tests passed %, validated % (all black-box tests pass) [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: 14 custom Python serverless functions (basic, data structures, API, syntactic sugar) collected from tutorials, AWS/Google docs, CodeNet-based and API-doc-based functions; 4 JSON test events per function
techniques.models: QwQ (reasoning, open); Qwen2.5-Coder 32B (open, code-specialized); Gemma3 27B (open, instruct); DeepSeek-R1 32B (open, reasoning distill)
techniques.baselines: Original Python function (energy); pipeline variants: Chain of Thought (temp 0.1), Creative-CoT (temp 0.8), Single-Shot (no recovery)
techniques.effect_target_headline: translated functions can reduce invocation energy by up to 70%, achieving net energy savings after approximately 3,000 to 5,000 invocations, depending on the LLM used
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: the Creative-CoT Qwen2.5-Coder and Single-Shot Gemma3 yield the best results with a 43 percent translation success rate

extraction.notes: Two-column PDF extraction is interleaved and Table 3 is garbled (model-to-configuration row mapping unclear). The 70% average energy reduction in Sec 3.2 comes from MANUAL Python-to-Go translations (Fig 1, p=0.03); per-model energy of the LLM-translated functions is not reported separately, and the amortization analysis (Fig 6) appears to combine translation cost with the Fig 1 savings range. Translation energy cost (5-14 Wh) also reported. Borderline on whether NF outcome is measured on LLM-generated code specifically. Short paper (~8 pages); limitations and four challenges discussed but no formal threats section.

extraction.eligibility_reason: AutoProbe is a probing classifier over LLM hidden states that predicts whether generated code is compilable, functional or secure; it does not change the code the LLM produces, and outcomes are classification accuracy/F1, not NF quality of improved code.
extraction.title: Model-Agnostic Correctness Assessment for LLM-Generated Code via Dynamic Internal Representation Selection
extraction.notes: Assessment/detection approach (security labels from Bandit and CodeQL used only as ground truth for the classifier); no generation-side intervention. Possible relevance only as a future filter/verifier component.

extraction.eligibility_reason: MACOG is a multi-agent, validator-grounded technique for generating Terraform from natural-language intents, but every reported outcome is correctness or similarity to a reference: IaC-Eval harness task success, BLEU, CodeBERTScore, and a binary LLM-judge adequacy check. Security policy (OPA/Rego), cost and capacity are enforced inside the pipeline but never reported as separate quantitative outcomes for the generated code.
extraction.title: Multi-Agent Code-Orchestrated Generation for Reliable Infrastructure-as-Code
extraction.notes: Borderline on IC3 and worth a second look by a human: the technique explicitly targets non-functional properties (least privilege, encryption at rest, restricted ingress, tagging, budget ceilings, region residency) through a Security Prover agent running OPA/Rego plus Checkov/Regula and a Cost & Capacity Planner, and the ablation removes each of these agents. However, the only numbers reported are BLEU, CodeBERTScore (F1), a binary LLM-judge adequacy percentage, and IaC-Eval task success; no policy-violation count, no security pass rate and no cost figure is reported for the generated Terraform, so there is no isolated quantitative NF outcome. If the reviewers decide a bundled pass criterion counts, the relevant headline would be 'GPT-5 improves from 54.90 (RAG) to 74.02 and Gemini-2.5 Pro from 43.56 to 60.13' on IaC-Eval, with ablations 'removing them drops IaC-Eval to 64.89 and 56.93' for constrained decoding and deploy feedback. SERIOUS CREDIBILITY FLAG: the caption of Table 1, which carries the paper's headline cross-model result, reads 'the additional MACOG column shows our orchestration approach (placeholder values)', so the MACOG numbers may not be real measurements. The statistics section also states that bootstrap CIs, paired tests and effect sizes were computed 'in our internal runs' but none are reported, and Section 5.1 says tables are referenced 'without reproducing them here' while they are in fact present. Artifacts: IaC-Eval dataset at huggingface.co/datasets/autoiac-project/iac-eval and code at zenodo.org/records/17117489.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Empirically applies an LLM evolutionary generate-evaluate-refine loop (OpenEvolve, ADRS) to evolve systems algorithm code and, in several case studies, reports the runtime of the LLM-generated code (e.g., 5.0x faster expert rebalancing, 3x faster table reordering) against SOTA implementations; borderline because most case-study objectives are domain metrics (cost, makespan) rather than code quality.
extraction.title: Barbarians at the Gate: How AI is Upending Systems Research

techniques.technique_name: AI-Driven Research for Systems (ADRS) via OpenEvolve: LLM-ensemble evolutionary search (MAP-Elites/island model) with simulator-based evaluator feedback; GEPA also tried on one case
techniques.tools: OpenEvolve (open-source); problem-specific simulators (e.g., 168-LOC PyTorch MoE simulator, 200-LOC Python prefix-hit-rate simulator, SMF transaction simulator); GEPA for one ablation
techniques.iterations: 70-400 iterations per case study (e.g., 300 for EPLB, 100 for LLM-SQL, 400 for Can't Be Late); stop at budget or when score is high enough
techniques.metrics: efficiency: runtime of the evolved algorithm code (rebalancing time in ms for EPLB; reordering algorithm runtime for LLM-SQL) [execution]; domain objectives: cost savings, imbalance factor, prefix hit rate, makespan, egress cost, perplexity/bitrate [execution in simulators]
techniques.benchmarks: 11 systems case studies (Can't Be Late single- and multi-region spot scheduling, Expert Parallelism Load Balancer on ShareGPT/GSM8K traces, LLM-SQL reordering on 5 datasets, transaction scheduling on 5 OLTP traces, Cloudcast, global model placement, telemetry repair, adaptive weight compression, sparse attention, multi-agent system optimization, GPU cache algorithm)
techniques.models: GPT-5, size NR, closed, reasoning; o3, size NR, closed, reasoning; GPT-4o, size NR, closed, instruct; Gemini 2.5 Pro, size NR, closed, reasoning; Gemini 2.5 Flash, size NR, closed, instruct; Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite, size NR, closed, instruct; Claude Opus (GEPA ablation), size NR, closed, instruct
techniques.baselines: Published state-of-the-art human-designed algorithms (e.g., Uniform Progress, DeepSeek EPLB greedy, non-public frontier-lab EPLB reference, GGR, SMF) and initial programs
techniques.effect_target_headline: The resulting algorithm matches the imbalance factors of the baselines while reducing runtime to just 3.7 ms, yielding a 5.0× speedup over the internal reference implementation

extraction.notes: Borderline eligibility: this is a position/vision paper with case studies of an existing framework (OpenEvolve); most case-study objectives are system-level domain metrics (cost savings, makespan, hit rate), and only EPLB (5.0x faster rebalancing) and LLM-SQL (3x / 3.9x faster reordering runtime; text says 3x, Table 1 says 3.9x) measure efficiency of the generated code itself. Configurations differ across case studies (different students, no systematic ablation); single runs, no variance. Correctness constraints are enforced by evaluators (deadlines met, rows preserved) but no correctness rate reported. Contamination discussed for SMF rediscovery and non-public EPLB baseline. Failure taxonomy based on 420 LLM-judged traces. Several appendix case studies (sparse attention) have no results in the text.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes a data synthesis and curation pipeline plus LoRA supervised fine-tuning (KernelCoder on the ConCuR dataset) as a training-time technique applied to an LLM, and reports quantitative efficiency outcomes (speedup over Torch eager, fast1, geometric mean speedup) for the LLM-generated CUDA kernels alongside correctness.
extraction.title: ConCuR: Conciseness Makes State-of-the-Art Kernel Generation

techniques.technique_name: ConCuR data synthesis and conciseness-based curation plus LoRA supervised fine-tuning (yielding KernelCoder)
techniques.tools: KernelBench (Ouyang et al., 2025) for evaluation; KernelBook (Paliskara and Saroufim, 2025) as the source of PyTorch programs; ms-swift fine-tuning framework; LoRA; DeepSpeed ZeRO stage-3; AdamW; PyTorch; CUDA; training on a single node with 8 A100 GPUs; evaluation on a node with 8 RTX 5090 GPUs; no version numbers given
techniques.iterations: No inference-time loop; the technique is offline: 5 generations per task from Kevin-32B over 18,162 tasks (90,810 pairs), unit-tested, then curated; LoRA fine-tuning for 3 epochs, batch size 8, gradient accumulation 2, 1,815 gradient steps, max sequence length 32,768, LoRA rank 32, alpha 32, dropout 0.05, learning rate 1e-4 with 0.05 warmup ratio and cosine decay, 9 hours of training
techniques.metrics: efficiency: speedup = T_Torch / T_kernel times the correctness indicator, measured by execution against torch eager; fast1 = fraction of tasks with speedup greater than 1; Gspeedup = geometric average of speedups [all execution]. Correctness: Exec, the execution correct rate, where generated kernel output must match the PyTorch reference in dimension and value on random input [execution]. Auxiliary: ARL, average reasoning length in tokens, proposed as a task-difficulty indicator
techniques.benchmarks: KernelBench Levels 1 and 2 (200 tasks total; the difficulty division in Table 4 sums to 37 easy + 114 medium + 49 hard = 200). Levels 3 and 4 were excluded as beyond current model capability. Training data: ConCuR, 4,892 curated examples drawn from 90,810 synthesized (PyTorch, CUDA kernel, CoT) triples over 18,162 KernelBook tasks, of which 9,789 tasks had at least one correct generation and 24,136 kernels were correct
techniques.languages: CUDA (and PyTorch as the input language); Triton used by some baselines
techniques.models: KernelCoder, 32B, open, reasoning (LoRA fine-tune of QwQ-32B); data synthesized by Kevin-32B, 32B, open, reasoning. Baselines evaluated: DeepSeek-R1-0528 685B open reasoning (Triton and CUDA); DeepSeek-V3.1-Think 685B open reasoning; Qwen3-Coder-Plus 480B code-specialized; GPT-4o closed; Claude-4-Sonnet closed; QwQ-32B open reasoning; Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B open; Llama-3.3-70B open; AutoTriton 8B open fine-tuned; KernelLLM 8B open fine-tuned; Kevin 32B open RL-trained; AI CUDA Engineer with o1-preview and o1-high (pass@10 table only)
techniques.baselines: Base model QwQ-32B; frontier models (DeepSeek-R1-0528, DeepSeek-V3.1-Think, Qwen3-Coder-Plus, GPT-4o, Claude-4-Sonnet); prior fine-tuned kernel models (Kevin, KernelLLM, AutoTriton); and four data-curation ablations trained with identical settings: 5K-random, 5K-max (the s1 longest-reasoning method), 5K-min, 5K-speedup; plus a dataset-size ablation at 552 / 1105 / 2210 / 4892 samples
techniques.effect_target_headline: Pass@1 fast1 on KernelBench: KernelCoder (32B) 17.0 on Level 1 and 39.0 on Level 2, versus its base model QwQ-32B at 7.0 and 11.0, versus Kevin (32B) at 16.0 and 27.0, and versus DeepSeek-R1-0528 (CUDA, 685B) at 18.0 and 38.0. Pass@10 fast1: KernelCoder 32.0 (Level 1) and 68.0 (Level 2) versus QwQ-32B 12.0 and 46.0. Ablation (Table 3, pass@1 / pass@10 fast1): KernelCoder 17.0 / 32.0 on Level 1 and 39.0 / 68.0 on Level 2, versus 5K-random 9.0 / 21.0 and 24.0 / 55.0, 5K-max 7.0 / 17.0 and 27.0 / 50.0, 5K-min 10.0 / 23.0 and 26.0 / 55.0, 5K-speedup 8.0 / 21.0 and 21.0 / 56.0. However, on the difficulty split (Table 5, Gspeedup pass@10) KernelCoder reaches 1.319 / 0.831 / 0.410 on easy / medium / hard, below Qwen3-Coder-Plus at 1.468 / 1.152 / 0.741
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: Pass@1 Exec: KernelCoder 58.0 on Level 1 and 59.0 on Level 2, versus QwQ-32B 18.0 and 17.0, Kevin 50.0 and 46.0, DeepSeek-R1-0528 (CUDA) 52.0 and 55.0. Pass@10 Exec: KernelCoder 91.0 and 95.0, versus QwQ-32B 55.0 and 76.0, Kevin 86.0 and 90.0. Difficulty split Exec pass@10: KernelCoder 100.0 easy, 94.7 medium, 83.7 hard, the best of the five models compared

extraction.notes: Methodologically one of the stronger papers in this batch: detailed hyperparameters, the full inference prompt in Appendix C, four data-curation ablations trained under identical settings, a dataset-size ablation, a training-cost comparison table, and a reported Pearson correlation (r = -0.047, p < 0.01) for the speedup/reasoning-length relationship. Caveats for a human reviewer. (1) Tables 1 and 2 are badly garbled by PDF extraction: the model rows are separated from their numeric columns and in the Smaller-Scale block the fast1 columns carry only 7 values for 8 model rows, most plausibly because KernelLLM has no fast1 entry. The KernelCoder values quoted above were cross-validated against the ablation Table 3, which independently lists KernelCoder as 58.0 / 91.0 Exec and 17.0 / 32.0 fast1 on Level 1 and 59.0 / 95.0 Exec and 39.0 / 68.0 fast1 on Level 2, so the KernelCoder and base-model figures are reliable; other baselines' fast1 values should be re-checked against the original PDF. (2) Baselines are run in different target languages (some Triton, some CUDA), which the tables note but the comparison does not control for. (3) The headline 'state-of-the-art' claim rests on Exec and fast1; on the harder difficulty split the geometric mean speedup of KernelCoder is below Qwen3-Coder-Plus, and the paper's own Future Work concedes that generated kernels 'do not exhibit satisfactory performance (at least, better than Torch Eager)' across all models. (4) No threats-to-validity or limitations section. (5) Contamination is not discussed at all, despite training data (KernelBook PyTorch programs) and the evaluation benchmark (KernelBench) being drawn from closely related PyTorch program distributions. (6) The ConCuR dataset itself does not appear to have a release URL; only the KernelCoder model is linked. (7) Figures 2, 3 and 4 are rendered as scattered axis numbers in the extraction, so the distributional claims behind Observation 1 could not be verified from the text alone.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes a multi-agent LLM framework that translates Arm Neon intrinsics into RISC-V Vector intrinsics and then optimizes the generated code using liveness-analysis register-pressure and measured-speedup feedback; reports runtime speedup of the LLM-generated code with an ablation of the optimization loop.
extraction.title: IntrinTrans: LLM-based Intrinsic Code Translator for RISC-V Vector

techniques.technique_name: IntrinTrans (Translator / Compilation Executor / Test Executor / Optimizer agents with compile-and-test repair loop and register-usage-and-speedup optimization loop with performance-based selection)
techniques.tools: GCC 14.2 (-march=rv64gcv -O3); custom LLVM-based vector liveness / register-pressure analyzer; QEMU (VLEN=128 and 256); SpacemiT Muse-Pi (SpacemiT M1, VLEN 256) for timing
techniques.iterations: up to 10 translation (repair) iterations and one optimization iteration; repair stops when all tests pass or threshold exceeded; best-performing correct variant selected
techniques.metrics: efficiency: speedup of translated code vs native expert-written RVV intrinsics, measured on hardware [execution]; correctness: test pass rate on VecIntrinBench tests [execution]; also an 'efficiency score' based on number of repair iterations (translation process efficiency, not code efficiency)
techniques.benchmarks: VecIntrinBench (50 function-level Arm Neon -> RVV tasks)
techniques.languages: C/C++ with Arm Neon and RISC-V Vector intrinsics
techniques.models: GPT-5 Codex, closed, code-specialized reasoning; Claude-Sonnet-4.5 (20250929), closed, reasoning enabled and disabled; Gemini 2.5 Pro, closed, reasoning; Grok 4 (0709), closed, reasoning; DeepSeek-V3.2 (Exp), open, reasoning enabled and disabled; DeepSeek-R1 (0528), open, reasoning; Qwen3 Coder Plus, closed, code-specialized
techniques.baselines: Same pipeline without the register-usage-and-speedup optimization feedback (translated-only); rule-based Neon2RVV; native expert-written RVV code as performance reference
techniques.effect_target_headline: compared to before the introduction of register-usage-and-speedup feedback, the performance of these tasks improved by an average of 9.19% to 34.87% (Table III); optimized speedup vs native 0.85x to 1.28x, exceeding the rule-based Neon2RVV (0.63x)
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: test pass rates of IntrinTrans's translations ranged from 47% to 100% based on different LLMs, while the pass rate of rule-based Neon2RVV is 52%

extraction.notes: Venue in metadata is CSCWD; the paper text itself does not state a venue (arXiv v3), so recorded as preprint. Table II lists 9 model configurations (7 models, two with reasoning on/off); abstract says pass rate 47%-100%. Text says 50 tasks but pass rates like 97.1%/94.1% imply a denominator of 34, worth checking. Figure 4 speedup distribution is garbled. Prompts not given. Code promised on acceptance. Correctness effect vs Neon2RVV is mixed across models (some models below 52%).

extraction.eligibility_reason: PtrTrans augments LLM prompts with a C-Rust pointer knowledge graph (plus a compiler-feedback repair loop) to translate C projects into Rust, and reports quantitative non-functional outcomes for the LLM-generated Rust: Clippy lint alert counts (idiomaticity/maintainability) and Cargo-geiger unsafe usage counts (memory safety), with compilation and functional equivalence as co-outcomes.
extraction.title: Project-Level C-to-Rust Translation via Pointer Knowledge Graphs
extraction.venue: Proc. ACM Softw. Eng. 3, FSE, Article FSE162 (FSE 2026); record metadata gives Proc. ACM Softw. Eng. / arXiv 2510.10956

techniques.technique_name: PtrTrans (C-Rust Pointer Knowledge Graph-guided project-level C-to-Rust translation: KG construction, KG-guided unit-by-unit translation in dependency order, and KG-guided incremental error correction)
techniques.tools: Clang -E (version 14.0.6) for macro expansion; Doxygen for code-unit and dependency extraction; clang -emit-llvm plus SVF (version 2.9) for context-sensitive, field-sensitive pointer analysis; Tarjan's algorithm for strongly connected components; cargo new and cargo check (version 1.90.0-nightly) for incremental compilation; Rust-Clippy for lint alerts; Cargo-geiger for unsafe usage counts; AFL++ and LLMs for building the unit tests
techniques.iterations: Incremental per-unit compile-and-repair loop, limited to five repair cycles per translation unit; on exhaustion the project is reverted to the last compilable state and an unimplemented!() function stub is generated. RQ4 reports that correction beyond four iterations brings no further gain
techniques.metrics: readability-maintainability (idiomaticity): Lint Alert Count from Rust-Clippy, broken down into style, complexity, correctness and performance lints [tool-static]; security (memory safety): Unsafe Usage Count from Cargo-geiger (unsafe fn declarations, unsafe {} blocks, raw pointer dereferences) [tool-static]; correctness: %Compiled = compiledFunc/translatedFunc and %Equiv. = equivalentFunc/translatedFunc on manually constructed unit tests [execution]; case study: DSR@k and CodeBLEU for manual fixing effort [human / similarity-to-reference]; efficiency: runtime of four correctly translated Rust projects vs their C versions [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: 16 real-world C projects from the Crown dataset (avl, buffer, genann, quadtree, rgba, urlparser, ht, bst, json.h, libtree, binn, bzip2, heman, libzahl, lil, lodepng), up to 14,829 LOC; unit tests built with LLM-generated harnesses plus AFL++ fuzzing achieve 80.0-97.7% line coverage and 87.7-100.0% function coverage
techniques.models: ChatGPT-4o, closed, default backbone (temperature = 0); Claude-3.7-Sonnet, closed; Gemini-3-Pro, closed (both used for the generalization study)
techniques.baselines: Crown (rule-based ownership-guided rewriting of c2rust output); PR2 (LLM-based rewriting of c2rust output); FLOURINE (fuzzing-enhanced LLM translation, bottom-up order, Restart repair strategy, same backbone LLM); ablations PtrTrans_PS (no pointer semantics, i.e. the conventional bottom-up call-graph paradigm), PtrTrans_PU (no pointer-usage information), PtrTrans_RA (no Rust-oriented annotations), PtrTrans_EC (no error correction)
techniques.effect_target_headline: Across the 16 projects, PtrTrans reduces the Lint Alert Count by 94.9% compared to Crown (from 6,802 to 349) and by 91.6% compared to PR2 (from 4,135 to 349). Similarly, PtrTrans reduces the Unsafe Usage Count by 99.9% against both Crown (from 141,866 to 85) and PR2 (from 134,185 to 85). Wilcoxon signed-rank tests show both reductions are significant (p < 0.001); zero unsafe usages for projects under 4k LOC
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: For projects with LoC < 4K: average %Compiled 98.3 vs 69.9 and %Equiv. 81.6 vs 52.3 for FLOURINE (improvements of 28.4% and 29.3%); for 4K < LoC < 15K: %Compiled from 64.0% to 85.9% and functional equivalence from 14.2% to 67.9%. Ablation: %Equiv. rises from 59.5% (PtrTrans_PS) to 81.6% (PtrTrans) and from 50.8% (PtrTrans_EC) to 81.6%

extraction.notes: Two non-functional dimensions are targeted: idiomaticity/maintainability (Clippy alerts) and memory safety (unsafe usage). Efficiency is touched only in the threats-to-validity section: runtime of four correctly translated projects (avl, rgba, ht, bst) showed no degradation, with one figure given ('the translated Rust project runs 54% faster than the C version for the project bst'); no systematic efficiency evaluation. A human reviewer should check the fairness of the idiomaticity comparison: Crown and PR2 rewrite c2rust output for the whole project (hence enormous unsafe counts), while PtrTrans's counts are over its own translated project, which can contain unimplemented!() stubs for functions whose repair exhausted the five attempts (%Compiled below 100 for several projects). Record metadata gives year 2025 (arXiv v3 posted May 2026); the paper itself is Proc. ACM Softw. Eng. 3, FSE, Article FSE162, July 2026, which is what is recorded. Table 3 and Table 6/7 are heavily garbled by the PDF extraction (column blocks separated from headers); the totals cited here were cross-checked against the prose and the per-category totals (style 2790/3808/233, complexity 3945/269/94, correctness 58/58/10, performance 9/0/12). No compute or cost reporting; no contamination discussion.

extraction.eligibility_reason: The technique (GRPO alignment on an Axe-core WCAG violation reward) is applied to an LLM and the evaluated artifact is LLM-generated web UI code, but the only quantitative quality outcome is web accessibility (WCAG violation counts, weighted violation score, inaccessibility rate, Lighthouse accessibility score), which is not one of the review's non-functional dimensions (readability-maintainability, efficiency, security). Borderline: if the protocol admits accessibility as an NF dimension, this paper is a clear include.
extraction.title: A11yn: Aligning LLMs for Web Accessibility-Aware UI Generation
extraction.notes: FLAG FOR HUMAN REVIEW: excluded only because accessibility is outside the three listed NF dimensions; everything else about the paper fits the review. Key details if the dimension list is widened: training-time GRPO alignment of Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct with an Axe-core-derived, severity-weighted, DOM-size-normalized violation penalty reward; training set UIReq-6.8K (6,800 synthetic UI instructions), benchmark RealUIReq-300 (300 human-refined realistic requests); baselines base model, FeedA11y post-hoc ReAct prompting (3 rounds), DPO on auditor preference pairs, Best-of-N (N=8, extended to N=20), Qwen2.5-Coder-14B, GPT-5.1, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 3 Pro; headline 'reducing the inaccessibility rate by 87.5% and 58.1% under two independent WCAG auditors relative to the base model' (IR_Axe 0.40 to 0.05, IR_AChecker 0.62 to 0.26, WVS 4479 to 662, Lighthouse 90.88 to 97.68); visual/semantic quality held comparable (Appearance Score 3.60 base vs 3.68 A11yn; pairwise human evaluation with five evaluators, 1,330 judgments, 39.3% prefer A11yn, 39.3% similar, 21.4% prefer base, no agreement statistic reported); ablations on severity weighting and DOM normalization (raw penalty collapses DOM size 37.02 to 15.20 and appearance to 2.41); code and data at https://github.com/jeffrobot/A11yn; full training hyperparameters in Appendix C; limitations section covers reliance on automated auditors, HTML-only scope, static UI only. Correctness/functional-equivalence is not measured; compute reported only as GPU setup plus FeedA11y's 4584 intermediate tokens per request. Tables and figures are moderately garbled in extraction.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes TritonRL, SFT distillation plus GRPO reinforcement learning with a speedup-based reward (hierarchical reward decomposition) and robust validity verifiers, and reports execution speedup (fast1/fast2, mean speedup) of LLM-generated Triton kernels alongside correctness.
extraction.title: TritonRL: Training LLMs to Think and Code Triton Without Cheating

techniques.technique_name: TritonRL: SFT distillation (DeepSeek-R1 or GPT-OSS 120B traces) + GRPO with Hierarchical Reward Decomposition (speedup reward on plan tokens, correctness reward on code tokens) gated by rule-based and LLM-judge validity verifiers
techniques.tools: Rule-based Triton linter (@triton.jit presence, PyTorch-module delegation); Qwen3-235B-Instruct LLM judge for functional validity; VeRL framework; runtime timing over ten runs on NVIDIA L40S
techniques.metrics: efficiency: fast1 and fast2 (share of tasks with a valid, correct kernel at least 1x / 2x faster than PyTorch reference) and mean speedup, pass@k, runtime averaged over 10 runs on NVIDIA L40S [execution]; correctness: valid (syntax + functionality via linter and LLM judge), compiled, correct (5 random inputs vs reference) [execution, tool-static, llm-judge]
techniques.benchmarks: KernelBench (Triton backend) Level 1 (100 single-kernel tasks) and Level 2 (100 fusion tasks); input-augmented KernelBench L1/L2 (500 evaluations per level)
techniques.models: Qwen3-8B, 8B, open, general/reasoning (base for TritonRL); Seed-Coder-8B-Reasoning, 8B, open, code-specialized reasoning (ablation base); teachers DeepSeek-R1, 685B, open, reasoning and GPT-OSS 120B, open, reasoning; compared Qwen3-14B, Qwen3-32B, KernelLLM 8B, AutoTriton 8B, Claude-3.7 closed
techniques.baselines: Qwen3-8B base (no fine-tuning); SFT-only checkpoints; KernelLLM; AutoTriton; Qwen3-14B/32B; Claude-3.7; DeepSeek-R1; GPT-OSS 120B; uniform-reward GRPO variants (beta 0.0-1.0); speedup-speedup reward assignment
techniques.effect_target_headline: KernelBench Level 1 pass@10: TritonRL (D) fast1 / fast2 36.0 / 13.0, mean speedup 1.10 vs Qwen3 (base) 8B 9.0 / 5.0, 0.41 and AutoTriton 25.0 / 10.0, 0.95; TritonRL (G) + IA 41.0 / 22.0, mean speedup 1.26
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: KernelBench Level 1 pass@10 compiled / correct: TritonRL (D) 100.0 / 78.0, TritonRL (G) + IA 100.0 / 88.0 vs Qwen3 (base) 99.0 / 23.0 and AutoTriton 92.0 / 57.0

extraction.notes: Code and datasets stated as 'will be available soon' (no URL). Training hardware given (8x A100 / 8x H200) but no training time, token or cost figures. No threats-to-validity section; only a short challenges paragraph. No discussion of overlap between KernelBook training tasks and KernelBench evaluation. Level 2 gains are smaller (TritonRL (G) + IA fast1 19.0 vs base 0.0). Tables partially garbled in extraction but values reconcile across Table 1 and Table 5.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes ReGraphT, a training-free retrieval and Monte Carlo Graph Search framework that guides small LLMs in generating optimized CUDA code from sequential C++, and reports execution-measured speedup (efficiency) alongside pass@k.
extraction.title: From Large to Small: Transferring CUDA Optimization Expertise via Reasoning Graph

techniques.technique_name: ReGraphT / ReGraphT-MCGS: LLM-derived CUDA optimization reasoning graph retrieved step by step, explored with Monte Carlo Graph Search using compile/test/speedup rewards
techniques.tools: NVIDIA CUDA compilation and runtime benchmarking on A100-80GB; vLLM (BF16) for inference; CodeBERTScore for the RAG baseline
techniques.iterations: search budget 200 (also 100/300 in ablation); max attempts 5 for ReGraphT; rollouts N=10; rollout capped by a maximum step limit and stops when an optimization step fails
techniques.metrics: efficiency: speedup@1 and speedup@10 over the sequential code (execution); correctness: pass@1, pass@10 (test-execution)
techniques.benchmarks: CUDAEval (new, 313 evaluation tasks: 106 easy, 105 medium, 102 hard, from Stack v2 CUDA files); ParEval CUDA subset (60 problems)
techniques.models: DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite-Instruct (16B MoE, 2.4B active), open, code-specialized; Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct, open, code-specialized; HPC-Coder-V2, open, code-specialized (HPC fine-tuned); DeepSeek-V3-0324, open, instruct (reference); DeepSeek-R1, open, reasoning (reference and trajectory generator)
techniques.baselines: Standard prompting, Chain-of-Thought prompting, code-similarity RAG (CodeBERTScore retrieval over the same corpus), HPC-Coder-V2 fine-tuned model; large LLMs DeepSeek-V3/R1 as upper reference
techniques.effect_target_headline: achieving an average 2.33× speedup on CUDAEval and ParEval; CUDAEval speedup@1 for DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite-Instruct: Standard 6.54 vs ReGraphT-MCGS 14.46
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: ReGraphT-MCGS achieves 73.3% in pass@k on average with three code-specific SLMs, surpassing by +11.0%, +9.0% and +6.8% compared to Standard, CoT and RAG in pass@1

extraction.notes: Table 1 is garbled in extraction (columns for Qwen2.5-Coder and HPC-Coder-V2 hard to align); headline 2.33x is the abstract's average claim. Speedup is relative to sequential C++ code, not to a CUDA reference. Wall-time overhead reported (about 6.02 h for 313 CUDAEval samples, search budget 100); ReGraph construction calls analysed. No repeated runs or statistical tests; no contamination discussion even though CUDAEval derives from Stack v2 and models may have seen it. Limitations section covers only benchmark coverage.

extraction.eligibility_reason: FLAMES fine-tunes CodeLlama-7B to infill require() invariants into existing human-written Solidity contracts to harden them against exploits; the security outcome (exploits prevented on SB-Heist) concerns LLM hardening/repair of human-written vulnerable code rather than the quality of code generated by the LLM for a task. Borderline because the fine-tuned model is compared with base CodeLlama on security of the LLM-edited contracts.
extraction.title: FLAMES: Fine-tuning LLMs to Synthesize Invariants for Smart Contract Security
extraction.notes: Borderline EC4/adjacent vs include (training-time technique, security dimension). If included: FLAMES-100k vs CodeLlama-7B; compilability 96.7% vs 62.6%; exploits prevented with functionality preserved 22/108 (FLAMES best) vs 16/108 baseline; SINDI semantic equivalence 2226/5000 vs 1176/5000; functionality preserved 67.9% (220/324) vs 41.3% (134/324). Data leakage segregation described; threats to validity section present; code/weights at https://github.com/ASSERT-KTH/FLAMES. Table IV garbled.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes a complexity-aware multi-agent LLM framework with profiling-guided repair to produce efficient competitive-programming code, and reports quantitative efficiency outcomes (TLE/MLE rates, success under time/memory limits) for the generated code; efficiency reporting is thin, so eligibility is borderline.
extraction.title: SwiftSolve: A Self-Iterative, Complexity-Aware Multi-Agent Framework for Competitive Programming
extraction.venue: 39th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2025) Workshop: Efficient Reasoning

techniques.technique_name: SwiftSolve: Planner, deterministic Static Pruner, Coder, Profiler and Complexity Analyst agents with log-log complexity fitting and complexity-guided patch/replan loop
techniques.tools: g++ -O2 -std=c++17 -march=native -ffast-math; /usr/bin/time -v for wall time and max RSS; Pydantic v2 typed JSON messages; POSIX sandbox (2 s, 256-512 MB)
techniques.iterations: At most 3 attempts per task (replan_0, replan_1, replan_2); stops on efficient verdict (complexity class in O(1)..O(n log n)), diminishing returns gain < delta, static pruner rejection, or two agent failures
techniques.metrics: efficiency: TLE/MLE incidence (execution), runtime-vs-input-size curves (execution), success under contest time/memory limits (execution); EFF@k and complexity-fit accuracy defined but not numerically reported; correctness: PASS@1, Solved@<=k on hidden test harness (execution)
techniques.benchmarks: BigO(Bench) 16 tasks + Codeforces Div. 2 10 problems = 26 tasks x 3 seeds (78 runs)
techniques.models: Claude 4 Opus (Planner), closed, instruct/reasoning; GPT-4.1 (Coder and complexity fallback), closed, instruct
techniques.baselines: single-pass direct GPT-4.1; single-pass direct Claude 4 Opus
techniques.effect_target_headline: Against a Claude Opus 4 single-agent baseline, SwiftSolve improves run-level success (73.1% vs. 52.6%) at ~2× runtime overhead (12.4 s vs. 6.8 s); TLE/MLE failure rate 26.9% (SwiftSolve only)
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: PASS@1 = 61.54% (16/26) on the first attempt and SOLVED@≤3 = 80.77%

extraction.notes: Efficiency evidence is weak: EFF@k and complexity-fit accuracy are defined but never reported numerically; TLE/MLE rates reported only for SwiftSolve, not baselines; 'success' conflates correctness with passing resource limits. Baseline numbers given only approximately per dataset (GPT-4.1 ~60.4%/44.4%, Claude ~62.5%/46.7%); the 52.6% aggregate appears only in the abstract. Abstract runtime overhead refers to agent wall time, not program runtime. Small task set (26). Inconsistencies (intro says GPT-4.1 baseline; abstract says Claude Opus 4). Paper itself notes no ablations and no comparison with other multi-agent frameworks. 3 seeds but no variance reported.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes FM Agent, an LLM-driven multi-agent evolutionary search framework; on KernelBench Level 3 the LLM-generated CUDA kernels are evaluated with a quantitative efficiency outcome (2.08x to 20.77x speedup over torch.compile), so an intervention on LLM code generation is measured on a non-functional dimension.
extraction.title: The FM Agent

techniques.technique_name: FM Agent (expert-guided cold-start initialization + island-model evolutionary search with adaptive diversity-driven sampling + domain-specific evaluators, on a distributed Ray infrastructure)
techniques.tools: NVIDIA A100 80GB, Intel Xeon Gold 6271C, Ubuntu 22.04.5 LTS; Python 3.12.11, PyTorch 2.6.0 with CUDA 12.4; CUDA Toolkit 12.4, Nsight Compute 2025.2.1, Compute Sanitizer 2023.2.0, Ninja 1.13.0; Ray for distributed orchestration; optional RAG knowledge base
techniques.iterations: No explicit cap or stopping rule reported for KernelBench. The kernel case study (Figure 8) plots roughly 250 evolutionary iterations; the ablation on ahc016 extends past iteration 900; the feature-engineering case study runs about 60 iterations.
techniques.metrics: efficiency: speedup of the generated CUDA kernel relative to torch.compile, measured by execution with 32 warmup and 128 profiling iterations (execution); kernel-level speedup against the official PyTorch implementation in the CosyVoice2-0.5B case study (execution). correctness (co-outcome): numerical tolerance tightened from 1e-2 to 1e-4 for acceptance, with reported accuracy maintained within 1e-5 (execution). Non-code benchmark outcomes also reported: MLE-Bench valid submission / above-median / medal rates and ALE-Bench performance scores (execution).
techniques.benchmarks: KernelBench Level 3, a clustered workload subset balancing coverage and diversity (exact task count not stated; Figure 6 shows roughly 13 kernels); additionally MLE-Bench (75 Kaggle competitions), ALE-Bench Lite (10 problems), three AlphaEvolve mathematical problems, and a CosyVoice2-0.5B Flow Matching Decoder case study (3 kernels)
techniques.languages: CUDA (C++) for kernels; Python for the ML, combinatorial-optimization and mathematical tasks
techniques.models: Gemini-2.5-Pro, size undisclosed, closed, instruct/reasoning (used for FM Agent and for the OpenEvolve baseline in the controlled kernel comparison)
techniques.baselines: torch.compile (reference for kernel speedup); OpenEvolve powered by the same Gemini-2.5-Pro; AI CUDA Engineer (agentic SOTA); CUDA-L1 (RL SOTA); for the ablation: random sampling, top-k sampling, no cold start, no island model, and OpenEvolve
techniques.effect_target_headline: "Our approach achieves 2.08× to 20.77× speedups over torch.compile, consistently outperforming the previous SOTA reached while maintaining numerical accuracy within 10−5." (KernelBench Level 3 subset, Gemini-2.5-Pro, A100)
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: "maintaining numerical accuracy within 10−5"; acceptance tolerance tightened from 10−2 to 10−4; no per-task correctness or compilation rate is reported for KernelBench

extraction.notes: Only the KernelBench part of this multi-domain paper yields a non-functional outcome; MLE-Bench, ALE-Bench and the mathematical problems are task-score benchmarks, not code-quality measurements. The kernel evaluation is thin: the number of KernelBench Level-3 tasks in the constructed subset is never stated, the per-kernel speedup figure (Figure 6) has badly garbled x-axis labels in the PDF extraction, and only the 2.08x-20.77x range is given, with no per-kernel table, no variance and no correctness rate. Figures 2, 3, 6, 7, 8, 9, 11 and 12 are extracted as label fragments only. The framework description is conceptual throughout (no pseudocode, prompts, hyperparameters or sampling formulas), and no code or data artifact is released for FM Agent (the linked repositories are baselines). Variance is reported for MLE-Bench (3 runs, SEM) and the ahc016 ablation (5 runs, standard deviation) but not for the kernel results. An optional human-in-the-loop module is described, but the authors state that for all three benchmarks optimization was performed exclusively by the LLM without human intervention. No threats-to-validity section and no contamination discussion.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Benchmark paper (CodeAlignBench) measuring how well LLMs follow developer instructions (style, structure, performance) in predefined vs follow-up settings; it proposes no quality-improving technique and its outcome is an LLM-judged/rule-based instruction-following success rate rather than a direct NF quality metric of the code.
extraction.title: CodeAlignBench: Assessing Code Generation Models on Developer-Preferred Code Adjustments
extraction.notes: Borderline: instructions are largely NF-oriented (cosmetic/structural/performance) and follow-up refinement could be read as a technique, but the paper frames it purely as a benchmark and reports only instruction-adherence rates across 10 models; no NF metric of the code itself.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes a profiler-guided multi-agent loop in which an LLM generates and iteratively refines CPU (C++) and GPU (Triton) kernels, reporting measured speedup (efficiency) of the generated code against ablation and prior-agent baselines.
extraction.title: PRAGMA: A Profiling-Reasoned Multi-Agent Framework for Automatic Kernel Optimization

techniques.technique_name: PRAGMA (profile-guided multi-agent kernel generation: Coder, Verifier, Profiler, Conductor agents with historical-best retention)
techniques.tools: NVIDIA Nsight Compute (GPU), Linux perf (CPU, top-down metrics), gcc 12.3.0, CUDA 13.0, Triton do_bench (5 warmup, 100 reps)
techniques.iterations: maximum of 15 attempts per task; loop continues through verify-then-profile rounds
techniques.metrics: efficiency: speedup over Torch reference runtime and Fast1 (% correct and at least as fast as Torch) [execution]; correctness: success rate (compile, run, match reference outputs) [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: KernelBench (GPU and CPU backends; number of tasks not stated; six categories)
techniques.languages: Triton (Python) for GPU; C++ for CPU
techniques.models: DeepSeek-R1, open, reasoning
techniques.baselines: Torch reference implementations; N-PRAGMA (PRAGMA without profiling feedback); Caesar (single-agent KernelBench multi-turn baseline, GPU only)
techniques.effect_target_headline: On the CPU, PRAGMA achieves an average of 2.81× speedup over Torch and 10.95× improvement over N-PRAGMA. On the GPU, PRAGMA delivers a 2.30× speedup over Torch and a 1.90× improvement compared with N-PRAGMA. (GPU Table I: Speedup 2.30 vs 1.28 N-PRAGMA vs 0.51 Caesar; Fast1 59.8% vs 32.2% vs 14.3%)
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: Success (%) on GPU: PRAGMA 92.0, N-PRAGMA 92.0, Caesar 49.0

extraction.notes: Short paper; single model (DeepSeek-R1), single run, no variance. CPU success rates not reported in a table; number of KernelBench tasks/levels used is not stated. Prompts not given in full. Abstract claims 'up to 10.95x' which is the CPU average over N-PRAGMA.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Evaluates ChatGPT-4 generating Jetpack Compose screens from Figma images and a scanner-feedback refactoring prompt, but the only quality outcome is UI accessibility violations (Google Accessibility Scanner), which is not one of the review's NF dimensions (readability-maintainability, efficiency, security); correctness/compilability is not quantified either.
extraction.title: Image-to-UI Accessibility: Assessing ChatGPT's Effectiveness in Generating Accessible Android Screens from Figma Templates
extraction.venue: Proceedings of the Brazilian Symposium on Multimedia and the Web (WebMedia'2025)
extraction.notes: If the review team treats accessibility as an in-scope NF quality, this would be an include: tool-feedback loop (Accessibility Scanner report fed back to ChatGPT-4) reduced violations from 302 to 138 on 60 screens (paired t-test t = 6.113, p = 0.00000008), while introducing 40 new violations.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Few-shot prompting of Llama 3.1 70B to modify ABB RAPID robot routines; outcome is a rule-based validator accuracy (at least one of ten outputs correct) that merges task correctness with company identifier/format rules, with no separate quantitative NF quality measure.
extraction.title: Utilizing LLMs for Industrial Process Automation: A Case Study on Modifying RAPID Programs
extraction.notes: Validator includes an 'Invalid IDENTIFIER' formatting-standard check (style), but error counts are only shown per mistake type in a figure and not as an NF outcome of a technique vs baseline; English vs German prompt comparison is the only contrast. Figures garbled in extraction.

extraction.eligibility_reason: ProofWright is an LLM-agent formal-verification framework (VerCors annotations, Rocq proofs) that checks memory safety, data-race freedom and semantic equivalence of already-generated CUDA kernels; it does not change the code the LLM produces, and its outcome is verification coverage (74% verified, 14% semantic equivalence) rather than an NF quality change of generated code.
extraction.title: ProofWright: Towards Agentic Formal Verification of CUDA
extraction.notes: Paper formatted with a J. ACM template placeholder but is an arXiv preprint. Kernels generated by Claude-4-Sonnet and GPT-5-Codex on KernelBench L1 are only verified, not refined; authors only envision using the output as feedback for generation in future work. Memory/thread safety could be read as security-related, but no generated-code quality is measured as an effect of an intervention.

extraction.eligibility_reason: AccelOpt is an LLM agentic system (planner/executor/summarizer with beam search and an optimization memory) that rewrites AI-accelerator kernels, and it reports quantitative efficiency outcomes for the LLM-generated code (percentage of hardware peak throughput, measured latency and speedup) on a new benchmark.
extraction.title: AccelOpt: A Self-Improving LLM Agentic System for AI Accelerator Kernel Optimization
extraction.venue: Proceedings of the 9th MLSys Conference, Bellevue, WA, USA, 2026 (arXiv preprint 2511.15915)

techniques.technique_name: AccelOpt (three-agent planner/executor/summarizer workflow + beam search over candidate kernels + self-curated optimization memory of slow-fast kernel pairs)
techniques.tools: AWS Neuron Profile and the Neuron compiler for AWS Trainium 1 (trn1.32xlarge) and Trainium 2 (trn2.48xlarge); NKI (Neuron Kernel Interface, beta 2.20); a distributed profiling service with CPU full-precision reference checking; vLLM for open-source model serving; Fireworks and Anthropic APIs for pricing; logfire for query logging
techniques.iterations: T = 16 beam-search iterations; per iteration B = 6 candidate kernels, N = 12 plans per candidate, K = 2 executor attempts per plan (B x N x K kernels sampled and profiled per iteration); optimization memory capacity ExpN = 16 with TopK = 8 new items per iteration, thresholds tpos = 1.04, tneg = 1.15; candidate selection keeps the top-B fastest correct kernels
techniques.metrics: efficiency: percentage of peak throughput computed from a roofline model (min required HBM traffic / bandwidth, matmul FLOPs / PeakMM, vector FLOPs / PeakVec) over measured latency; measured kernel latency in ms (warm-up iterations plus 10 repeated runs, up to 10 rounds, 1% (Trainium 1) / 4% (Trainium 2) difference threshold); speedup over the baseline kernel (geometric mean of per-task best speedup); cumulative Fast@p; traffic efficiency and tensor/vector/scalar engine utilization from the profiler [execution and profiler]; correctness: output compared against a CPU full-precision reference under several random seeds with a per-task tolerance [execution]; cost in US dollars from input+output token counts
techniques.benchmarks: NKIBench (new): 14 NKI kernels from real-world LLM workloads (AdamW, Add+RMSNorm+Matmul, BatchMatmul, BatchMatmul+Softmax, Group Query Attention, LoRA, Mamba block, Matmul+Add+RMSNorm, Matmul, RMSNorm+Matmul, RoPE, SiLU, SwiGLU, Transpose+Matmul), evaluated on Trainium 1 and Trainium 2; additionally 24 Triton kernels from FlashInfer-Bench on H100 and one Conv2D kernel from a Stanford CS149 assignment
techniques.languages: NKI (Python-embedded kernel language for AWS Trainium); Triton/Python for the FlashInfer-Bench generalization experiment
techniques.models: gpt-oss-120b, open, reasoning (medium reasoning effort; planner/summarizer in the main setting and best executor in the cost study); gpt-oss-20b, open, reasoning; Qwen3-Coder-480B-A35B-Instruct-FP8, open, code-specialized instruct (executor in the main setting); Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct, open, code-specialized; Qwen3-235B-A22B-Thinking-2507, open, reasoning; Claude Sonnet 4, closed, thinking mode enabled
techniques.baselines: Repeated sampling with Claude Sonnet 4 (thinking mode); repeated sampling of the same agentic workflow; beam search without optimization memory; a Reflexion-style reflector workflow; Claude Sonnet 4 used inside AccelOpt; Neuron-compiler-generated (or hand-written/official-example) baseline kernels; human expert reference kernels from the NKI tutorial (Mamba) and nki-samples (RoPE)
techniques.effect_target_headline: boosting the average percentage of peak throughput from 49% to 61% on Trainium 1 and from 45% to 59% on Trainium 2 for NKIBench kernels; 'using open-source models, it matches the kernel improvements of Claude Sonnet 4 while being 26x cheaper'; best geometric-mean speedup 1.235x ($139.00) vs 1.137x ($178.37) for the Reflexion-style baseline and 1.222x ($5806.83) for repeated sampling, with the model ensemble reaching 1.246x ($470.66); vs human experts, Mamba improved from the 28.4% baseline to 54.6% of peak (1.04x the best expert 52.7%) and RoPE from 21.1% to 29.6% of peak (1.4x the human reference); on 24 FlashInfer-Bench Triton kernels (H100) 1.27x average speedup over the best Triton baselines with 3.19x peak speedup

extraction.notes: Correctness is enforced as a gate (only kernels passing the CPU-reference check are kept and reported), so no correctness rate is reported for comparison; effect_correctness is recorded as neutral on that basis. The appendix reports that gpt-oss models sometimes exploited the correctness checker (fake speedups by omitting computation in safe softmax), which the authors flag as a need for stronger equivalence checking. Record metadata gives year 2025 and venue arXiv.org; the paper itself carries the MLSys 2026 proceedings header, which is what is recorded here. All figures (6, 7, 9-18) are images and their numbers could not be extracted, so the headline figures come from the abstract and prose; Tables 1-6 extracted readably. No repeated end-to-end runs of the system per configuration and no statistical tests; no dedicated threats-to-validity section, though Section 4.3 analyses limitations.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes LLM-based multi-agent evolutionary systems (PIKE-B, PIKE-O) that generate optimized CUDA/Triton code from PyTorch models and quantitatively measure runtime speedup (efficiency) of the LLM-generated code.
extraction.title: Optimizing PyTorch Inference with LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems
extraction.venue: Proceedings of the 9th MLSys Conference, Bellevue, WA, USA, 2026 (arXiv:2511.16964v2)

techniques.technique_name: PIKE-B (multi-agent evolutionary branching search with Initial Brainstorming Agent, Code Optimization Agent and Error Fixing Agent; top-k exploit, mutation-only)
techniques.tools: Docker-containerized evaluator; CUDA/Triton compilation; torch.allclose correctness (atol=0.01, rtol=0.01); Triton do_bench timing; radon for SLOC; NVIDIA H100 80GB
techniques.iterations: Fixed budget of 300 LLM queries per task (all agents); population n=10, top-k=4, up to 5 error-fix attempts per solution; returns best solution by speedup
techniques.metrics: efficiency: geomean speedup over PyTorch Eager (and over torch.compile) from measured GPU runtime [execution]; correctness: numerical equivalence success rate [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: KernelBench (METR-refined): Level 3-pike (filtered, 30 tasks) and Level 5 (14 tasks)
techniques.languages: Python/PyTorch input; CUDA and Triton output
techniques.models: Gemini 2.5 Pro, closed, reasoning; Gemini 2.5 Flash (cheap EFA), closed; gpt-oss-120b, open, reasoning; o3-mini-high, closed, reasoning
techniques.baselines: PyTorch Eager; torch.compile (TorchInductor, max autotune); TensorRT; METR LLM-generated solutions; ablations (no EFA, no IBA, cheap EFA); PIKE-O
techniques.effect_target_headline: 2.88x speedup over PyTorch Eager (1.85x over torch.compile) on H100, Level 3-pike, 300 queries, Gemini 2.5 Pro; Level 5: 2.57
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: success 100% (PIKE-B, Level 3-pike) vs 87% METR, 97% torch.compile, 83% TensorRT

techniques.technique_name: PIKE-O (OpenEvolve-based evolutionary multi-agent optimization with added Error Fixing Agent; islands, crossover; exploit-tuned variant mut,npar,1isl,EO,SL)
techniques.tools: OpenEvolve (modified); Docker-containerized evaluator; CUDA/Triton compilation; torch.allclose; Triton do_bench; NVIDIA H100
techniques.iterations: 300 LLM queries per task; population 25, archive 12, 3 islands, explore 0.2/exploit 0.7, 10 parallel evaluations (default); up to 5 error-fix attempts
techniques.metrics: efficiency: geomean speedup over PyTorch Eager [execution]; correctness: numerical equivalence success rate [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: KernelBench (METR-refined): Level 3-pike (30 tasks) and Level 5 (14 tasks)
techniques.languages: Python/PyTorch input; CUDA and Triton output
techniques.models: Gemini 2.5 Pro, closed, reasoning
techniques.baselines: PyTorch Eager; torch.compile; TensorRT; METR; PIKE-B; PIKE-O ablations (no EFA, mut, npar, 1isl, EO, SL)
techniques.effect_target_headline: PIKE-O (mut,npar,1isl,EO,SL) 2.81 speedup over Eager on Level 3-pike; default PIKE-O 2.17; Level 5: 2.47 (exploit-tuned) vs 2.25 (default)
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: success 100% (PO', Level 3-pike); 93% (PO', Level 5)

extraction.notes: Kernel/GPU-code efficiency paper; correctness is a pass/fail filter (success rate) rather than a primary outcome. Speedups clamped at 1. Variability: 3 runs only for PIKE-B Level 3-pike (2.76, 2.88, 2.89). Precision reduction to FP16 allowed; without it PIKE-B drops to 2.12. Tables 3-4 garbled in extraction. No dedicated threats-to-validity section; limitations (budget, noise, task removal) discussed. Metadata year 2025; paper states MLSys 2026.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes Rustine, a pipeline in which LLMs generate Rust code (translated from C) under program-analysis-based pre-translation refactoring, enriched context, adaptive in-context examples and a compiler/test feedback loop; the LLM-generated Rust is measured quantitatively for memory safety (raw pointers, pointer arithmetic, unsafe constructs), idiomaticity (Clippy flags per normalized KLoC) and readability (cognitive complexity, Halstead, SEI maintainability index), with correctness as a co-outcome.

techniques.technique_name: Rustine (preprocessing + automated C refactoring for unary operators, pointer arithmetic, constness maximization and large-function breakdown; dependence-graph-guided context and translation order; RAG-based API translation; two-tier LLM translation loop with compiler feedback and adaptive in-context-learning examples; test-based validation and delta-debugging-inspired repair)
techniques.tools: C preprocessor; pycparser v2.22 (C AST); rustc_hir crate (Rust HIR) for raw pointer, pointer-arithmetic and unsafe-construct counting; Clippy for idiomaticity and style; rust-code-analysis for Cognitive Complexity, Halstead and SEI Maintainability Index; Tokei for LoC; rust-bindgen for FFI; Linux man-pages for core-library API semantics; cargo/rustc; Ollama / vLLM for self-hosted models
techniques.iterations: Per translation unit: up to A_base = 8 re-prompts of the base model (DeepSeek-V3) with compilation-error feedback, then up to A_reason = 2 attempts with the reasoning model (DeepSeek-R1) using adaptive ICL examples, repeated up to A_max outer iterations (A_max value not stated); stops as soon as a compilable translation is produced. Debugging: failed assertions are re-enabled one at a time and the top n stack-trace functions are re-translated; the human developer had a 10-hour-per-project budget.
techniques.metrics: security / memory safety: number of raw pointer declarations and dereferences, number of pointer arithmetic / comparison operations, number of unsafe lines, type casts and calls (all tool-static, via pycparser for C and the rustc_hir crate for Rust). readability-maintainability: idiomaticity = TSI x Clippy flags per KLoC where TSI = LoC_Rust / LoC_C and flags cover cargo, complexity, correctness, perf and suspicious lints (tool-static, Clippy); Cognitive Complexity, Halstead and SEI Maintainability Index (tool-static, rust-code-analysis); number of clippy::style violations (tool-static). correctness (co-outcome): percentage application- and test-code compilation success, and assertion pass rate from executing the translated test suites (execution). Also reported: translation time, dollar cost and token counts; human repair effort in hours.
techniques.benchmarks: 23 real-world C repositories taken from the artifacts of prior C-to-Rust work, 27 to 13,200 LoC (qsort, bst, rgba, quadtree, buffer, grabc, urlparser, xzoom, genann, ht, robotfindskitten, libcsv, avl-tree, libopenaptx, libtree, opl, libzahl, zopfli, snudown, lodepng, bzip2, binn, tulipindicator); test suites manually augmented to 1,221,192 assertions with average function and line coverage of 74.7% and 72.2%
techniques.models: DeepSeek-V3, size not stated, open-weight, instruct (base translator); DeepSeek-R1, size not stated, open-weight, reasoning (fallback after 8 failed attempts); OpenAI o4-mini, closed, reasoning (used only to synthesize adaptive in-context-learning examples)
techniques.baselines: C2Rust (rule-based transpiler), C2SaferRust, CROWN, Laertes, RustMamp, Syzygy; plus an internal ablation of Rustine with the pointer-arithmetic refactoring component removed
techniques.effect_target_headline: "the number of raw pointer declarations/derefenreces is reduced from 4,080/2,045 in C to 198/126 in Rust"; pointer arithmetic reduced by refactoring "from 452 to 14"; ablation without pointer-arithmetic refactoring: "the number of pointer arithmetic increases by 83.01%, raw pointer declarations/dereferences by 52.6%/154%, and unsafe ⟨lines,type casts,calls⟩ by ⟨64.42%, 31.67%, 61.46%⟩"; versus baselines, "C2Rust, C2SaferRust, CROWN, and Laertes have 4,904/20,169, 1,400/5,510, 3,027/12,298, and 2,255/9,685 more raw pointer declarations and dereferences"; unsafe ⟨lines,type casts,calls⟩ ⟨114, 47, 130⟩ for Rustine versus ⟨974, 70, 372⟩ for RustMamp, while "Syzygy translations contain no unsafe constructs, compared to 14 in Rustine translations"
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: "Rustine can generate fully compilable Rust code for all and achieve 87% functional equivalence (passing 1,063,099 assertions out of 1,221,192 in test suites with average function and line coverage of 74.7% and 72.2%)" — 100% compilation is fully automated, while the 87% assertion pass rate includes a human developer repairing semantic mismatches in 4.5 hours on average; 10 of 23 projects reached 100% functional equivalence with no human intervention

extraction.notes: Dimension mapping is a judgment call a human reviewer should confirm: the paper's 'safety' metrics (raw pointer declarations/dereferences, pointer arithmetic/comparisons, unsafe lines/casts/calls) are memory-safety proxies and were coded as the security dimension, while 'idiomaticity' (Clippy flags per normalized KLoC) and the three readability metrics were coded as readability-maintainability. Tables 1, 2 and 3 and Figures 6, 9, 10, 12, 13 and 14 are badly garbled by PDF extraction (column values appear as long interleaved runs of numbers), so only the aggregate figures quoted in the running text were copied; per-project values must be re-checked against the PDF. The paper also reports a human study, but it measures repair effort rather than rating code quality: one developer with over ten years of C and Rust experience and no familiarity with the subjects repaired the non-equivalent translations in 4.5 hours on average (min 0.33, max 10), with a strong size-effort correlation (rho = 0.86, p = 1.59e-4); there is a single annotator and no agreement statistic, which is why human_eval is coded 'none'. Statistical tests are reported only for effort/cost/time correlations, not for the quality metrics, and each project appears to be translated once with no repeated runs or variance. The reported 87% functional equivalence is not fully automated. Contamination of the open-source C subjects in the models' pretraining is never discussed. A_max and the block threshold theta_b are not given numerically (theta_f is 50% of the LLM context window). The authors note they recalculated several baselines' metrics after finding bugs or suppressed Clippy rules in those artifacts, which makes the baseline numbers theirs rather than as-published.
