techniques.metrics: readability-maintainability: lines of code of final policy [tool-static] (cyclomatic complexity listed as a metric but no values reported); task performance: average episode reward and success rate (reward >= 200) [execution]; LLM API calls
techniques.benchmarks: Gymnasium LunarLander-v3, single control task, 10 evaluation episodes per policy, 5 seeds
techniques.models: GPT-4o, size NR, closed, instruct (temperature 0.7)
techniques.baselines: Random policy; PPO (1M steps, Stable-Baselines3, neural network policy); FunSearch and EoH LLM evolution strategies
techniques.effect_target_headline: EvoEngineer+ produces a 59-line Python function; LoC 20-35 (FunSearch), 25-40 (EoH), 30-50 (EvoEngineer), 59 (EvoEngineer+)
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: EvoEngineer achieves an average reward of 66.6 and 40% success rate, while FunSearch and EoH remain near zero (9.1 and 6.2 respectively); EvoEngineer+ attains a 70% success rate, exceeding PPO's 60%

extraction.notes: Borderline eligibility: the only NF outcome is lines of code framed as interpretability; interpretability comparison is against a neural network (not code). Inconsistency: Table I gives EvoEngineer LoC 30-50, while discussion says scaling from 45 to 200 calls reduced code length from 80 to 59 lines. Cyclomatic complexity named as a metric but not reported. Short paper (~4-5 pages).

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes SFT plus GRPO reinforcement learning with formal-verifier rewards (terraform validate/plan, OPA policies) for LLM generation and mutation of Terraform IaC, and reports quantitative non-functional outcomes of the generated code (Checkov security compliance, TFLint best-practice pass rate) alongside correctness.
extraction.title: TerraFormer: Automated Infrastructure-as-Code with LLMs Fine-Tuned via Policy-Guided Verifier Feedback
extraction.venue: ICSE-SEIP 2026 (IEEE/ACM 48th International Conference on Software Engineering, Software Engineering in Practice)

techniques.technique_name: TerraFormer: SFT on verifier-curated TF-Gen/TF-Mutn data followed by GRPO with fine-grained verifier reward (compilability, deployability, policy-rule pass fraction)
techniques.tools: Terraform v1.12.0 (terraform validate, terraform plan); Open Policy Agent (opa eval, Rego policies); evaluation: TFLint, Checkov; Huggingface trl; Python 3.12.10
techniques.iterations: Training-time RL; data curation used multi-turn verifier-feedback repair loops up to five turns
techniques.metrics: security: Checkov security compliance (% passed checks per instance, averaged) [tool-static]; readability-maintainability: TFLint best-practice linter pass rate [tool-static]; correctness: compilability, deployability, policy-based correctness via terraform validate/plan and OPA [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: IaC-Eval (458 tasks); TF-Gen (Test) (704 instances); TF-Mutn (Test) (740 instances)
techniques.models: TerraFormer fine-tuned from Qwen2.5-Coder-3B (open, code-specialized) and Qwen2.5-Coder-14B (open, code-specialized); baselines: Claude Sonnet 3.7 (closed); DeepSeek-R1 671B (open, reasoning); GPT-4.1 (closed); Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct; DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B; DeepSeek-Coder-33B-Instruct; Qwen3-14B; CodeLlama-13B-Instruct; Llama-3.2-11B-Instruct; Qwen3-8B; DeepSeek-R1-0528-Qwen3-8B; Llama-3.1-8B; DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B; Mistral-7B-Instruct; Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct
techniques.baselines: Base Qwen2.5-Coder-3B/14B few-shot; SFT-only ablation; 17 SoTA LLMs with 3-shot prompting
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: TerraFormer† (SFT+RL) Correctness on IaC-Eval 31.44 (+15.94); TF-Gen (Test) 18.04 (+11.65); TF-Mutn (Test) 55.14 (+19.60)

extraction.human_eval_details: Cloud-expert survey of dataset alignment (not of NF quality): 100 sampled instances each from TF-Gen and TF-Mutn, 20 raters in groups of 10; three raters overlapped on 25 instances each; Gwet's AC1 89.87%, 91.71%, 94.47%, 97.30%
extraction.notes: NF dimensions are measured but not explicitly targeted by the reward (reward = compilable/deployable/policy-rule fraction; policies encode prompt intent). NF results for TerraFormer† (SFT+RL) vs base Qwen2.5-Coder-14B: Security Compliance 69.34 (+10.45) on IaC-Eval, 66.98 (+18.74) on TF-Gen (Test), 67.89 (+8.17) on TF-Mutn (Test); Linter Pass Rate 100.00 (+3.06) IaC-Eval, 100.00 (+6.68) TF-Gen, 100.00 (+0.68) TF-Mutn; paper claims highest security compliance across all three benchmarks. Tables 2 and 3 are garbled in extraction; values aligned by reading order. Single pass@1 runs, no variance. Dataset curation cost ~$15,000; code 'shared upon request'. Contamination handled only via repository-disjoint test split. No threats-to-validity section.

extraction.eligibility_reason: The LLM pipeline (LSP context + self-consistency + clangd feedback loop) repairs implicit data loss compiler warnings in existing human-written SAP HANA C++ code; the code being improved is not LLM-generated, so this is LLM repair of human-written code.
extraction.title: LLM-Based Repair of C++ Implicit Data Loss Compiler Warnings: An Industrial Case Study
extraction.notes: Borderline: the patches are LLM-generated edits and an efficiency-related outcome is reported (fix patches adding extra instructions reduced by 39.09% vs a range-check-everywhere baseline; 92.73% developer acceptance). Excluded because the target is repair of human-written code (adjacent). Reviewer may reconsider if 'edited by an LLM' is read to cover repair patches.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes an LLM evolutionary search framework (IGR and MCTS with structured testbench feedback) for Verilog generation and PPA optimization, reporting quantitative area/latency/power improvements of LLM-optimized RTL relative to reference designs on IC-RTL. Borderline domain (hardware RTL PPA as efficiency).
extraction.title: EvolVE: Evolutionary Search for LLM-based Verilog Generation and Optimization

techniques.technique_name: EvolVE Idea-Guided Refinement (IGR): LLM idea generation (optionally RAG over papers) followed by diff-based sequential refinement chains scored by testbench pass and Area x Latency product
techniques.tools: Icarus Verilog and Yosys for fast simulation/synthesis in the loop; Synopsys VCS, Design Compiler (TSMC 180nm) and PrimeTime for final validation; Structured Testbench Generation (STG); Aider-style diff coder
techniques.iterations: Budget of 300 nodes; IGR k=60 ideas x m=5 refinement steps; for optimization runs until max node limit; best-scoring node returned
techniques.metrics: efficiency: area (um2), latency (cycles x clock period), power (mW), Area-Latency (AT) product and PPA product improvement ratio vs. human reference, swept over clock periods 3-7 ns [execution / commercial synthesis tool]; correctness: testbench pass rate, Pass@nodes on VerilogEval v2, Mod-VerilogEval v2, RTLLM v2 [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: IC-RTL (6 problems: LBP, GEMM, CONV, JAM, Huffman Coding, Distance Transform; from Taiwan National IC Design Contest and hand-crafted) for PPA; VerilogEval v2 spec-to-rtl (156), Mod-VerilogEval v2, RTLLM v2 (50) for correctness
techniques.models: DeepSeek-R1-FP4, 671B MoE, open, reasoning (used for PPA); GPT-OSS-120B, 120B, open, reasoning; Siliconmind-7B, 7B, open, code-specialized (SFT+GRPO); Gemini-2.0-Flash, size NR, closed, instruct
techniques.baselines: PPA: human-authored contest reference implementations (initial code); Dolphin's program on GEMM. Correctness: repeated sampling baselines per model, REvolution, VerilogCoder
techniques.effect_target_headline: reducing the Power, Performance, Area (PPA) product by up to 66% in Huffman Coding and 17% in the geometric mean across all problems (IC-RTL, IGR with DeepSeek-R1-FP4, Synopsys DC TSMC 180nm)
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: DeepSeek-R1-FP4-MCTS achieves peak pass rates of 98.1% on VerilogEval v2 and 92.0% on RTLLM v2 (300 nodes; baseline 95.5% and 86.0%)

extraction.notes: Domain is hardware RTL PPA; reviewer should confirm it counts as efficiency. MCTS variant evaluated for correctness only (not an NF technique). PPA results only for IGR with DeepSeek-R1-FP4 on 6 problems, compared to human reference designs (no LLM-baseline PPA comparison except Dolphin on GEMM); Q1 converged to baseline, Q3 had power regression (0.45 mW to 0.50 mW) neutralizing PPA gain. Prompt-steered Opt Area / Opt Cycle variants also reported. Single runs, no variance. STG token reduction (38,818 to 15,440 output tokens for DeepSeek-R1-FP4) reported. Only IC-RTL benchmark released; codebase 'will be released shortly'. Appendix D tables heavily garbled.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes AscendCraft, a DSL-guided two-stage prompting/transcompilation technique applied to an LLM to generate AscendC NPU kernels, and reports quantitative efficiency outcomes (Fast0.2/Fast0.8/Fast1.0 speedup ratios vs PyTorch eager) for the generated code alongside correctness.
extraction.title: AscendCraft: Automatic Ascend NPU Kernel Generation via DSL-Guided Transcompilation

techniques.technique_name: AscendCraft (DSL-guided generation + multi-pass LLM transcompilation with per-pass compiler-error feedback)
techniques.tools: Ascend CANN toolkit 8.1; default Ascend compiler toolchain; PyTorch 2.6; Ascend 910B2 NPU; Ubuntu 22.04
techniques.iterations: Four lowering passes (host-side, kernel init, kernel computation, optional alignment/padding refinement); after each pass the code is compiled and compiler errors are fed back to the LLM for revision; no explicit max retry count stated
techniques.metrics: efficiency: Fast0.2@1 / Fast0.8@1 / Fast1.0@1, percentage of correct kernels whose execution time is within x× of PyTorch eager reference, measured by on-device kernel execution [execution]; speedup over PyTorch eager for mHC case study [execution]. Correctness: Comp@1 compilation rate and Pass@1 numerical correctness vs reference [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: MultiKernelBench (Ascend backend), KernelBench Level 1 updated task shapes from KernelBench v0.1; seven operator categories, 52 kernels (MatMul and Convolution excluded); plus 2 real-world mHC kernels (mHC_post, mHC_post_grad)
techniques.languages: AscendC (C++-based), plus the proposed Ascend DSL; PyTorch reference
techniques.models: LLM used not clearly named in the text for AscendCraft itself; Claude Sonnet-4 cited as prior direct-generation baseline number from MultiKernelBench (closed, instruct)
techniques.baselines: Direct LLM-based AscendC generation as reported in MultiKernelBench (e.g., Claude Sonnet-4 13.0% correctness); PyTorch eager execution as the performance reference
techniques.effect_target_headline: 82.7% of kernels achieve at least 20% of PyTorch eager performance, 57.7% reach 80%, and 46.2% match or exceed the eager baseline (52 kernels, MultiKernelBench Ascend); mHC case study: 6.6× and 3.0× speedup over PyTorch eager single-pass, up to 15.9× and 7.2× after human+LLM optimization
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: 98.1% compilation success and 90.4% functional correctness across 52 kernels, vs Claude Sonnet-4 only 13.0% correctness on the same benchmark

extraction.notes: The generating LLM for AscendCraft is never explicitly named anywhere in the text, which is a significant reporting gap; only the baseline Claude Sonnet-4 number is quoted from a prior paper. No threats-to-validity section, no ablation, no artifact link, no repeated runs or variance, no cost/token reporting, and no contamination discussion. Tables 1 and 2 are garbled by PDF extraction (the category label column of Table 2 appears merged into Table 1's header region) but the per-category numbers and totals are legible and the totals match the abstract. Efficiency here is kernel runtime performance; no readability or security measurement. Baseline comparison is against a number carried over from the MultiKernelBench paper rather than a direct re-run, so QA2 is partial.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes and evaluates KernelCraft, a tool-using agentic feedback loop (syntax check, simulator-based functional check, latency measurement, doc search) in which LLMs generate and then optimize assembly kernels for novel accelerator ISAs; reports execution efficiency (cycle counts / speedup vs compiler baselines) of the generated kernels alongside correctness. Borderline because the paper is framed primarily as a benchmark.
extraction.title: KernelCraft: Benchmarking for Agentic Close-to-Metal Kernel Generation on Emerging Hardware
extraction.venue: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026), PMLR 306

techniques.technique_name: KernelCraft agentic tool-calling diagnosis-and-repair loop (two-phase: correctness then performance optimization) with ISA documentation, hardware-specific prompting and native tools
techniques.tools: write_code, check_syntax (compile), run_evaluation (simulator/hardware: PLENA transactional simulator, AMD NPU via Peano compiler on Ryzen AI Cloud hardware, Coral NPU Verilator RTL simulation, BOOM Verilator), view_output (memory diff vs PyTorch reference), get_instruction_size, grep_docs (ISA documentation search)
techniques.iterations: max 15 / 20 / 25 iterations for Level 1 / 2 / 3 ML tasks (10/10/15 for CPU tasks); stops when budget exhausted or agent finishes after correctness (match_rate 100%) and optimization phase
techniques.metrics: efficiency: execution cycles / latency and speedup vs platform compiler baseline (cycle-accurate or RTL simulation or on-device execution) [execution]; correctness: success rate = functional match vs PyTorch/C++ reference within tolerance [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: KernelCraft benchmark: 23 ML tasks (Level 1 primitives, Level 2 composite ops, Level 3 end-to-end blocks) x 5 configurations on PLENA, AMD NPU, Coral NPU; 10 CPU tasks on RISC-V BOOM; preliminary NVIDIA SASS extension
techniques.languages: Assembly (PLENA custom ISA, AMD NPU AIE ISA, RISC-V + RVV, RISC-V; NVIDIA SASS preliminary)
techniques.models: GPT-5.2 (closed, reasoning, medium effort); Gemini-3-Flash preview (closed, reasoning, medium thinking); Claude Sonnet 4 (closed, 10K thinking budget); DeepSeek-R1-0528 (open, reasoning); GPT-5.2 Chat, Qwen3-Coder-Flash, DeepSeek-V3.2 (tool-use analysis); Gemini-3-Pro-Preview (ISA co-design case study)
techniques.baselines: Platform compiler baselines (PLENA native template compiler, Peano C++ compiler for AMD NPU, RVV intrinsics -O2/-O3 for Coral NPU, RISC-V -O2 for BOOM); human expert hand-optimized Coral NPU kernels; KernelBench agentic pipeline adapted to C++; iterative LLM agent with KernelCraft docs+prompts writing C++; ablations: no thinking, zero-shot vs one-shot, documentation levels, tool removal, prompt removal
techniques.effect_target_headline: Coral NPU exhibits the largest gains, with speedups reaching 2–8× on GEMV, GEMM, and ConvBlock ... including the 7.93× speedup on ConvBlock (Gemini-3-Flash); AMD NPU results cluster tightly around the baseline (0.89–1.18×); slowdowns on many configs (e.g., Conv2D 0.22×)
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: GPT-5.2 performs best on PLENA, AMD NPU, and Coral NPU, with success rates of 56%, 17%, and 47%; Table 27 success rate KernelBench 0/6, Iterative Agent+Docs+Prompts 4/6, KernelCraft 5/6

extraction.notes: Primarily a benchmark paper; included because it proposes the KernelCraft agent harness (with explicit performance-optimization phase) and reports execution speedup of generated kernels versus compiler baselines and versus KernelBench/iterative-agent baselines (Table 27). Efficiency comparison is against compilers rather than a no-technique LLM baseline; speedup only reported for correct kernels. Main-text speedup figure (Fig. 3) and Tables 5, 19-21 are heavily garbled in extraction. Contamination: tasks target novel ISAs (unseen in pretraining); BOOM noted as well represented in pretraining. Variance: 5 configurations per task, 95% CI in scaling figures; no formal statistical tests. No explicit threats-to-validity section; tolerance robustness discussed. Conflict of interest disclosed (AMD author). Appendix K shows 11.3% latency reduction from the optimization phase on one SDPA kernel.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes an LLM feedback-driven framework that refactors PQC reference C into synthesizable HLS-C with an LLM DSE loop guided by synthesis area/latency feedback, and reports quantitative hardware efficiency (area, latency, LUT/FF) of the generated code plus success rate.
extraction.title: LLM4PQC - Accurate and Efficient Synthesis of PQC Cores by Feedback-Driven LLMs

techniques.technique_name: LLM4PQC: LLM-aided subroutine extraction, HLS preprocessing (static memory mapping, initialization removal), C2HLSC iterative refinement with structure-aware prompting, and LLM pragma-insertion DSE loop with synthesis PPA feedback
techniques.tools: Catapult HLS 2023.1; Design Compiler (Nangate 45nm); Vivado (Artix-7, XCZU7EV); ModelSim SE-64 2021.3; C2HLSC; KAT-based tests
techniques.iterations: iterate on compile/simulation/synthesis errors until KAT correctness verified, then DSE loop on area/latency feedback; observed avg 11.56-15.75 compile runs and 6.00-7.67 HLS runs per benchmark; 10 independent runs per benchmark
techniques.metrics: efficiency: ASIC area (um2), FPGA LUTs/FFs/DSPs/BRAMs, cycles, frequency, latency (us) from synthesis [execution/tool-static synthesis reports]; correctness: success rate (compile + KAT simulation + timing closure), RTL simulation on 1,000 KATs [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: 5 PQC subroutines from NIST reference code: Kyber-NTT, Dilithium-NTT, Falcon-NTT, Falcon-Sampler, Falcon-FFT
techniques.models: OpenAI o3-mini (closed, reasoning) for HLS generation; GPT-5.2 (closed) for subroutine extraction
techniques.baselines: Published manual RTL FPGA designs [15],[16],[17] and prior LLM-to-HLS sampler [18] (o4-mini); no in-study no-technique baseline
techniques.effect_target_headline: for Kyber, Dilithium, and Falcon NTT primitives, LLM4PQC achieves lower area utilization (LUTs and FFs) compared to prior art ... this compactness currently incurs a latency penalty compared to manual designs (e.g., Kyber-NTT 146 LUTs vs 4,834; latency 75.00 us vs 1.11 us); sampler latency 0.39 us vs 0.73 us for [18]
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: Success rate 100% (Kyber-NTT, Dilithium-NTT, Falcon-FFT), 70% (Falcon-NTT), 40% (Falcon-Sampler)

extraction.notes: Borderline scope: NF outcome is hardware PPA (area/latency) of synthesized HLS-C generated by the LLM, treated here as efficiency. Baselines are published external designs (different tools/frequency), not a controlled no-technique condition. Synthesis latency cycles reported as unreliable for ASIC. Compute reported as compile/HLS run counts. Tables partly garbled but readable. Discussion section touches limitations; no formal threats section.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes a multi-agent pipeline that generates Solidity smart contracts from natural-language specifications with an LLM auditor/refiner security loop; reports quantitative security outcomes (contracts with medium+ severity issues, critical vulnerabilities) before vs after refinement on 9,000 generated contracts.
extraction.title: An end-to-end agentic pipeline for smart contract translation and quality evaluation

techniques.technique_name: CrewAI-style agentic pipeline: requirement-schema parsing, rule-constrained Solidity generation, LLM security Auditor and Refiner reinforcement loop
techniques.tools: solcx Solidity 0.8.x compiler; CrewAI / IBM Agentics
techniques.iterations: max 2 refinement iterations; refine only while audit not approved and severity is medium, high or critical
techniques.metrics: security: contracts with medium+ severity issues, average security issues per contract, critical vulnerabilities as rated by the LLM Auditor agent [llm-judge]; readability-maintainability: Code Quality rubric dimension (placeholders, error messages, events, structure) [llm-judge]; correctness: compilation success rate [tool-static], functional completeness / variable fidelity / state machine / business logic rubric scores [llm-judge]
techniques.benchmarks: FSM-SCG dataset (Luo et al., 2025), 9,000 contracts from requirement_code.jsonl
techniques.models: GPT-4o-mini, closed, NR
techniques.baselines: same pipeline before refinement (before/after loop); expert ground-truth Solidity implementations for rubric comparison
techniques.effect_target_headline: The refinement loop reduced contracts with medium+ severity issues from 45.9% to 13.4%—a 70.9% reduction. Critical vulnerabilities plummeted from 287 to 34 (88.2% reduction)
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: Compilation Success Rate 81.2% before vs 86.5% after refinement

extraction.notes: Security is judged only by the same GPT-4o-mini Auditor agent that drives the loop (no Slither/Mythril run despite being cited), so the security improvement is self-assessed and unvalidated. Baseline is the pipeline's own pre-refinement output, not an independent no-technique run. Code Quality (readability) compared only with ground-truth human code (83.85 vs 75.19), not with a no-loop ablation, hence NR. Paper states code and data are released but gives no URL. Some table layout garbled but values recoverable.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes K-Search, an LLM-driven search over GPU kernel implementations guided by a co-evolving LLM world model (planning intents, local refinement, tree edit updates from execution feedback), and reports kernel performance (latency/speedup, efficiency) of the LLM-generated CUDA/Triton code versus evolutionary baselines.
extraction.title: K-Search: LLM Kernel Generation via Co-Evolving Intrinsic World Model

techniques.technique_name: K-Search (Search via Co-Evolving World Model: LLM world model maintains a search tree of optimization intents with priority scores; local refinement samples implementations until stagnation; Insert/Update/Prune tree edits from execution feedback)
techniques.tools: FlashInfer-Bench evaluator (compilation, correctness suite, benchmark harness); CUDA 12.8, FlashInfer 0.5.3, PyTorch 2.8.0; official GPUMODE TriMul evaluator
techniques.iterations: budget B = 120 evaluations per kernel (300 for TriMul: 150 GPT-5.2 + 150 Gemini-3-Pro); local refinement stops after K = 7 consecutive non-improving attempts (K = 5 for TriMul)
techniques.metrics: efficiency: score J = correctness-gated speedup relative to FlashInfer x 100 averaged over workloads, per-workload speedup, fast_p fraction of workloads above speedup thresholds, geometric-mean latency on GPUMODE TriMul [execution]; correctness only used as a gate (score 0 if incorrect)
techniques.benchmarks: FlashInfer-Bench kernels: GQA Paged Decode, MLA Paged Decode, MLA Paged Prefill (Hopper H100), FP8 MoE (Blackwell B200), 152 workload traces total; GPUMODE TriMul (H100)
techniques.models: gemini-3-pro-preview, closed, reasoning (main experiments); GPT-5.2, closed, + Gemini-3-Pro (TriMul); Qwen3-8B embedding model for ShinkaEvolve baseline only
techniques.baselines: OpenEvolve and ShinkaEvolve with the same LLM, initial program and evaluator; FlashInfer expert kernels as reference; GPUMODE leaderboard submissions (human CUDA/Triton, TTT-Discover)
techniques.effect_target_headline: overall average final score of 56.13, representing a 2.10x improvement over OpenEvolve (with score 26.68) and a 2.21x improvement over ShinkaEvolve (with score 25.37); MoE 14.3x over OpenEvolve; TriMul 1030 µs on H100

extraction.notes: Generated kernels rarely exceed FlashInfer expert kernels (scores below 100); K-Search underperforms baselines on small-batch GQA decode workloads. Correctness rates not reported (incorrect programs score zero). Main experiments use one LLM (Gemini-3-Pro); TriMul uses GPT-5.2 then Gemini-3-Pro and is compared to leaderboard entries evaluated locally after the competition closed. 3 runs with min-max bands; figure data garbled in extraction. World model prompts not provided (only baseline prompt template). No threats-to-validity section.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Empirically compares three prompt input modalities (natural-language description, sequential reference code, parallel pseudo code) for LLM generation of task-based parallel C++ code and reports complexity/comment metrics (scc) per prompt modality alongside correctness; scaling efficiency is also measured for the generated code.
extraction.title: From Prompts to Performance: Evaluating LLMs for Task-based Parallel Code Generation

techniques.technique_name: Prompt input modality: parallel pseudo code or sequential reference implementation added to the prompt vs natural-language problem description only
techniques.tools: scc (lines, comments, approximate cyclomatic complexity); GCC 13.3.0; OpenMP 4.5; HPX 1.11.0; dual-socket AMD EPYC 7742 up to 128 threads
techniques.metrics: readability-maintainability: lines of code, comment lines, scc complexity (approx. cyclomatic) [tool-static]; efficiency: strong and weak scaling efficiency and PCGQS (combines correctness fix level and scaling) [execution], reported by model/problem/framework but not by prompt modality; correctness: pass@1 and human-judged fix-effort levels [execution, human]
techniques.benchmarks: 4 author-selected problems (Monte Carlo pi, merge sort, matrix-matrix multiplication, conjugate gradient) x 3 frameworks (OpenMP tasking, C++ standard parallelism, HPX) x 3 prompt modalities
techniques.models: ChatGPT-5, closed; Gemini-3, closed; Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct, open, code-specialized
techniques.baselines: Natural-language problem-description prompt (Normal); comparison across the three models and frameworks
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: No statistically significant performance differences can be attributed to the prompt type. Prompts containing parallel pseudocode yield only marginal improvements.

extraction.human_eval_details: Fix-effort levels (no fix/easy/medium/hard/infeasible) assigned by the authors; number of raters and agreement not reported
extraction.notes: Borderline include vs context: mainly an LLM evaluation study, but prompt modality is an explicit input intervention. Table 1 by prompt level (Normal / Sequential / Pseudo): complexity 9.01 / 10.23 / 8.04; comments 10.35 / 8.86 / 6.87; lines 73.46 / 73.86 / 67.69 (pseudo code lowers complexity, sequential code raises it). Scaling results are not broken down by prompt modality. Number of samples per configuration not stated. Venue per metadata WAMTA (not stated in text). Figures are garbled in extraction.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes a decoding-time constrained-decoding technique that eliminates hallucinated package names in LLM-generated installation commands, framed and measured as a software supply-chain security outcome (package hallucination rate), with HumanEval correctness as co-outcome. Borderline because the artifact is pip install commands/dependency recommendations rather than application code and the security metric is not CWE-based.
extraction.title: PackMonitor: Towards Zero Package Hallucinations via Decoding-Time Monitoring
extraction.venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Software Engineering, Vol. 3, ISSTA (ISSTA027)

techniques.technique_name: PackMonitor (Context-Aware Parser + DFA-based Package-Name Intervenor with logits masking + DFA-Caching)
techniques.tools: PyPI index (706,618 package names) compiled into a DFA; token trie over tokenizer vocabulary; CFG-based context parser
techniques.metrics: security: Package Hallucination Rate (PHR), Response Hallucination Rate (RHR), number of unique hallucinated packages, checked against PyPI list [tool-static]; correctness: HumanEval Pass@1 [execution]; also generation latency
techniques.benchmarks: HFuzzer (one round of 1,000 iterations per model, DeepSeek-V3 tester); Package4U (Spracklen et al., ~40,000 coding tasks, subset); HumanEval (164)
techniques.models: DeepSeek-Coder-Instruct-6.7B, open, code-specialized instruct; CodeLlama-7b-Instruct, open, code-specialized instruct; Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct, open, code-specialized instruct; Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct, open, instruct; Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, open, instruct
techniques.baselines: vanilla; RAG; Self-Refinement (SR); RAG+SR; SFT (Spracklen et al. checkpoints)
techniques.effect_target_headline: on DeepSeek-Coder, the vanilla setting exhibits a PHR/RHR of 8.39%/11.60%, while PackMonitor achieves 0% PHR/RHR (HFuzzer); Package4U PHR 16.14% vanilla, 2.66% SFT, 0% PackMonitor (DeepSeek-Coder)
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: HumanEval Pass@1 unchanged, e.g. DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B 72.6% (↓ 0%), vs SFT 45.7% (↓ 26.9%)

extraction.notes: Eligibility borderline: artifact is package names in generated pip install commands (dependency recommendation), and security is supply-chain (package hallucination/slopsquatting) rather than CWE vulnerabilities in code. Latency overhead (x1.07-x1.28) refers to inference time, not generated-code efficiency. Single HFuzzer round per model; latency SD reported only. SFT baseline evaluated on Package4U with released checkpoints; SFT HumanEval numbers taken from prior work. Zero-hallucination guarantee is by construction relative to the PyPI list.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Evaluates an LLM-driven bounded iterative Detect-Repair-Verify loop with test feedback that edits web-application code, and reports security outcomes (security tests fixed, secure-and-correct yield) alongside functional regressions. Borderline: the vulnerable baseline projects were implemented by the author and their LLM provenance is not stated, so this could be read as LLM repair of human-written code (EC4/adjacent).
extraction.title: Detect-Repair-Verify for Securing LLM-Generated Code: A Multi-Language Empirical Study

techniques.technique_name: Bounded iterative Detect-Repair-Verify (W2) with test-grounded feedback, function-level prompts
techniques.tools: Project-specific functional test suites and targeted OWASP Top 10:2025-mapped security test suites (HTTP- and state-level verdicts)
techniques.iterations: Max K = 2 iterations per target; stops early when the target security test passes with no functional regression; second iteration adds file-level context requested or implied by the model
techniques.metrics: security: secure-and-correct yield (SCY), Fixed/FixRate of initially failing security-test targets [execution]; detection report actionability (PlanRate, Avg.#Files, Avg.#APIs, MissingRate, WrongLocRate) [execution/manual record]; correctness: functional regressions FuncReg on functional test suite [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: EduCollab benchmark (new): 3 web apps (PHP, JS/Express, Python/Flask), 37 functional tests and 26 initially failing security-test targets (Python 15/7, JS 8/13, PHP 14/6)
techniques.models: ChatGPT-5 (closed, general instruct); GLM-5 (size NR, general instruct)
techniques.baselines: W0 unrepaired project state; W1 single-pass detect-repair-verify
techniques.effect_target_headline: For ChatGPT-5, SCY increases from 0.00/0.54/0.17 in W1 to 0.57/0.77/0.50 in W2 for Python/JS/PHP, corresponding to improvements of +0.57, +0.23, and +0.33, respectively. For GLM-5, SCY rises from 0.43/0.23/0.33 in W1 to 0.86/0.69/0.83 in W2, with improvements of +0.43, +0.46, and +0.50.
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: No functional regressions are observed in Python for either model. In contrast, one regression is observed under W2 in JavaScript for both models, and one regression is observed under W2 in PHP for ChatGPT-5.

extraction.notes: Eligibility check needed: the paper frames the code as LLM-generated, but the three EduCollab projects are described as implemented to a shared spec with no stated LLM generation step; if they are human-written, this is LLM repair of human code (EC4, adjacent). Project- and requirement-level granularities are only used for detection-report analysis (RQ2); SCY is reported only at function level despite RQ1 asking about granularity. Table numbering inconsistent in text (Table 13 cited for Repair-Success-Rate but that is Table 12; PHP ChatGPT-5 W2 SCY 0.50 vs FixRate 0.67 differ because of one regression). Single run per setting; no variance. Model versions/sizes not specified. Small sample (26 targets).

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes an autonomous LLM coding-agent pipeline (staged synthesis, supervisor agent, profiling, expert knowledge, regression rollback) that generates workload-specific OLAP engines in C++ and reports quantitative runtime efficiency of the generated code against DuckDB/Umbra and across optimization-stage ablations.
extraction.title: Bespoke OLAP: Synthesizing Workload-Specific One-size-fits-one Database Engines
extraction.venue: Proceedings of the VLDB Endowment (PVLDB), Vol. 19, No. 11

techniques.technique_name: Bespoke OLAP synthesis pipeline: staged LLM agent loop (storage planning, basic implementation, four optimization rounds with cardinality info, self-tracing, expert knowledge, human-expert persona, then multi-threading) with supervisor agent, hotpatching, fuzzy correctness testing against DuckDB and external regression rollback
techniques.tools: C++ compiler with incremental compilation and hotpatching; benchmark tool comparing results against DuckDB 1.4.1 over parameter instantiations; agent-injected tracing/performance counters; DuckDB query plans with actual cardinalities; curated expert-knowledge file; Git-based snapshotting
techniques.iterations: Four optimization rounds plus a multi-threading stage, each looped until supervisor approves; external monitor rolls back any regression; about 15,000 agent turns for TPC-H
techniques.metrics: efficiency: total and per-query workload runtime (s) and speedup over DuckDB and Umbra, single- and multi-threaded, across scale factors [execution]; correctness: result equality vs DuckDB across random template instantiations (used as gate, not reported as a rate)
techniques.benchmarks: TPC-H v3.0.1 (22 query templates, SF 20 main, up to SF 100); CEB templated JOB on IMDB (SF 2 main, up to SF 10; query 8a excluded)
techniques.models: Claude Sonnet 4.7, closed, instruct (primary); GPT 5.4-Codex, Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it, MiniMax-M2.7, GLM-4.7-FP8, GLM-5.1-FP8 tested only qualitatively
techniques.baselines: DuckDB 1.4.1; Umbra 26.02; ablations: basic implementation without optimization stages, flat (struct-of-arrays) storage vs bespoke storage
techniques.effect_target_headline: On TPC-H (SF20), it achieves 11.17x over DuckDB v1.4.1 and 7.24x over Umbra; on CEB (SF2), it achieves 45.33x and 9.56x; stage ablation: basic implementation 2.34x vs final 12.35x over DuckDB on TPC-H

extraction.notes: Baselines are human-engineered DBMSs (DuckDB, Umbra) rather than a no-technique LLM; the within-pipeline stage ablation (Figure 8, Table 1) provides the technique-attributable comparison. Correctness is enforced as a gate (fuzzy testing vs DuckDB) but no correctness rate is reported. Other models mentioned without numbers. Single synthesis run per benchmark; no variance. API cost $276.44 (TPC-H) and $303.25 (CEB), 10-30 h wall clock. Figure 5/9 data garbled in extraction. Generated code also at https://github.com/DataManagementLab/BespokeOLAP_Artifacts.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes an LLM agentic framework (Claude Sonnet 4.5) that rewrites host-driven multi-GPU CUDA/NCCL programs into device-initiated co-designed kernels via a correctness-first fast path and an LLM-driven evolutionary slow path, and reports end-to-end latency/speedup (efficiency) of the generated kernels against baselines.
extraction.title: CUCo: An Agentic Framework for Compute and Communication Co-design

techniques.technique_name: CUCo (structured design-space directive + fast-path host-to-device transformation with LLM-judge loop + slow-path island-based LLM evolutionary search with cascade evaluation, MAP-Elites archive, novelty filter and meta-summarizer)
techniques.tools: Custom static analyzer for NCCL communication dependency graph; CUDA 13.1; NCCL 2.28.9; mpirun numerical verification; CUDA events latency benchmarking; Nsight Systems (case-study profiling); neural code encoder embeddings
techniques.iterations: Fast path 2-3 iterations (Stage A 1-2, Stage B 1-3 LLM-judge rounds until compile+correct); slow path 10-20 generations fixed budget, explore fraction 40% then exploit; best-scoring candidate returned
techniques.metrics: efficiency: end-to-end latency (median of five stable runs, CUDA events) and speedup vs host-driven NCCL baseline and DeepEP; per-phase latency breakdown; cascade score 10000/(1+t_ms) [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: Four author-constructed multi-GPU workloads: Flash Attention with context parallelism (4 configs), DeepSeek-V3 MoE dispatch/combine (4 skew ratios), KV-cache transfer (4 configs), GEMM+AllGather (4 matrix sizes)
techniques.languages: CUDA C++ with NCCL device API
techniques.models: Claude Sonnet 4.5, size undisclosed, closed, instruct
techniques.baselines: Host-driven NCCL baselines with multi-stream overlap; DeepEP sequential usage (MoE); naive iterative prompting; ablations: slow-path only, exploit-only
techniques.effect_target_headline: CUCo achieves up to 1.57× speedup over host-driven baselines (four multi-GPU workloads); latency reduced by 5.3%–36.2%; 12–14% per-layer advantage over standard DeepEP on intranode MoE

extraction.notes: Correctness is enforced as a gate (compile + mpirun numerical verification) but no correctness rate is reported as an outcome; ablation reports failed candidates in early generations. Single LLM (Claude Sonnet 4.5) without justification. Evolution hyperparameters (island count, migration interval) claimed in appendix but not actually given; prompts not fully reproduced. Search is stochastic but only best-found solution reported (median of 5 runs for latency). Workloads author-constructed (no public benchmark). Search cost $4.98-$10.96 per workload, 0.8-1.8 h. Figures/tables garbled in extraction.

extraction.eligibility_reason: GenDB is an LLM-powered multi-agent technique that synthesizes per-query C++ execution code and iteratively refines it from runtime feedback; quantitative efficiency outcomes (query execution time in ms, speedups over DuckDB/Umbra/ClickHouse) are reported for the LLM-generated code.
extraction.title: GenDB: The Next Generation of Query Processing - Synthesized, Not Engineered
extraction.venue: preprint (arXiv; formatted for PVLDB, includes PVLDB Artifact Availability statement)

techniques.technique_name: GenDB (multi-agent LLM pipeline: Workload Analyzer, Storage/Index Designer, Query Planner, Code Generator, Query Optimizer, with iterative runtime-feedback refinement)
techniques.tools: Claude Agent (Claude Code Agent) as the agent framework; Claude Sonnet 4.6 as the LLM; DuckDB v1.4.4, ClickHouse v26.2.1, Umbra (February 2026 release), MonetDB v11.55.1, PostgreSQL v18.2 as comparison engines; SQLSmith for query generation; C++ compiler with OpenMP; hardware: 2x Intel Xeon Gold 5218, 384 GB RAM
techniques.iterations: Iterative optimization with user-configured budget (maximum number of optimization iterations) and early stopping on reaching user-specified targets; results shown for iterations 0-3 (one SEC-EDGAR query over four iterations); query-level timeout 300 seconds and agent-level timeout 30 minutes with rollback to best previous implementation
techniques.metrics: efficiency: per-query and total hot-run execution time in ms, and speedup factors versus baseline engines [execution]; generation cost in US dollars and generation time in minutes [execution/reported]. Correctness: validated by comparing generated query results against a traditional DBMS (e.g., DuckDB) ground truth, reported qualitatively only [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: TPC-H scale factor 10, representative subset Q1, Q3, Q6, Q9, Q18 (5 queries); SEC-EDGAR, a new manually constructed benchmark from SEC financial statement data 2022-2024 (5 GB), 1,000 SQLSmith-generated queries diversity-sampled down to six queries
techniques.languages: C++ (generated execution code); SQL input; GenDB itself implemented in JavaScript; Python mentioned for future AI operations
techniques.models: Claude Sonnet 4.6, closed, instruct/reasoning; selected to balance cost and performance
techniques.baselines: State-of-the-art query engines DuckDB, Umbra, MonetDB, ClickHouse, PostgreSQL (with default indexes, and with GenDB-generated additional indexes); ablation baselines: Single-Agent (Guided) and Single-Agent (High-Level)
techniques.effect_target_headline: On TPC-H, GenDB achieves a total execution time of 214 ms across five representative queries. This result is 2.8x faster than DuckDB (594 ms) and Umbra (590 ms), which are the two fastest baselines, and 11.2x faster than ClickHouse. On SEC-EDGAR, GenDB achieves 328 ms, which is 5.0x faster than DuckDB and 3.9x faster than Umbra. Ablation: multi-agent 236 ms on TPC-H, 1.2x faster than the best single-agent variant (guided, 281 ms); on SEC-EDGAR the gap widens to 2.3x over guided (752 ms) and 4.1x over high-level (1,325 ms)

extraction.notes: Short vision/proof-of-concept paper (about 8 pages) with an early prototype. Figures 2 and 3 are badly garbled by PDF extraction: the per-query bar values and axis labels are interleaved as loose numbers, so only the numbers stated in the running text are reliable; a human should re-check per-query values against the original figures. Correctness is validated against a reference DBMS but no quantitative correctness rate (e.g., pass rate) is reported anywhere, so QA4 is partial. Only one LLM (Claude Sonnet 4.6) is used, justified briefly on cost/performance grounds. No repeated runs, variance or statistical tests. Contamination is explicitly addressed by constructing the SEC-EDGAR benchmark to reduce TPC-H leakage from LLM training data. Limitations are discussed at length in the research-agenda section but there is no formal threats-to-validity section. Efficiency here is query execution runtime of the LLM-generated C++ code; no readability or security measurement.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes contrastive prompt tuning (soft prompts trained on efficient/inefficient program pairs with a frozen LLM) to make generated code more energy-efficient, and measures energy and execution time of the generated code alongside pass@1.
extraction.title: An Initial Exploration of Contrastive Prompt Tuning to Generate Energy-Efficient Code

techniques.technique_name: Contrastive Prompt Tuning (CPT): soft-prompt tuning with Triplet or InfoNCE loss on efficient vs inefficient solution pairs
techniques.tools: HuggingFace PEFT prompt tuning; PyTorch Metric Learning (Triplet loss); macOS powermetrics at 100 Hz; Apple Clang 14.0.0 -std=c++17 -O0; javac; python3.12
techniques.metrics: efficiency: energy consumption (J) and execution time (ms) as percentage of baseline-generated program, 10 runs, Mann-Whitney U alpha=0.005 [execution]; correctness: pass@1 [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: HumanEval-X (164 problems per language: C++, Java, Python); LeetCode hard set (52 problems per language) from Solovyeva et al.; training pairs from GEC (Python, 3,548) and CodeNet (C++, 3,921)
techniques.models: Phi-3 Mini 3.8B, open, instruct (general-purpose); CodeLlama-7B, open, code-specialized; DeepSeek Coder 7B instruct, open, code-specialized
techniques.baselines: Base model without CPT; base model with efficiency instruction in prompt
techniques.effect_target_headline: up to 66% for C++, up to 56% for Java) reductions in energy usage compared to baseline results; e.g. 58.5% energy for HumanEval-X C++ (code-first, best variant) vs 207.6% for LeetCode Java (general-purpose, trained)
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: general-purpose model 40.1% baseline to 47.4% best CPT variant; code-tuned 38.4% to 52.0%; code-first 21.6% baseline vs 21.3% best CPT variant (pass@1 over 648 tasks)

techniques.technique_name: Efficiency instruction prompt ('Write efficient code for the following problem:')
techniques.tools: macOS powermetrics at 100 Hz
techniques.metrics: efficiency: energy and execution time as percentage of baseline [execution]; correctness: pass@1 [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: HumanEval-X (164 per language) and LeetCode hard (52 per language)
techniques.models: Phi-3 Mini 3.8B, open, instruct; CodeLlama-7B, open, code-specialized; DeepSeek Coder 7B instruct, open, code-specialized
techniques.baselines: Base model with standard prompt
techniques.effect_target_headline: the first model shows an energy efficiency of 58.5% for HumanEval-X C++ in the best variant versus 174.5% with instruction; instruction 92.0% for LeetCode Java (general-purpose)
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: 21.6% to 23.1% (code-first), 40.1% to 45.7% (general), 38.4% to 43.2% (code-tuned) pass@1

extraction.notes: Table 5 is garbled; mapping of percentages to model/benchmark rows is uncertain. Only statistically significant comparisons reported, and energy compared only where both baseline and variant produced correct code, so denominators differ. Text reports instruction variant 45.5% for general model while Table 4 shows 45.7%. Exploratory workshop paper on a single 2016 MacBook. Hyperparameters partially given (lr 5e-5, init text) but soft prompt length and epochs per variant only partly reported.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes an LLM agentic framework that generates project-level Rust migrations of C projects and reports Unsafe Ratio (fraction of Rust lines inside unsafe constructs, a memory-safety/security measure) for the generated code, alongside compilation and test pass rate as correctness co-outcomes.
extraction.title: His2Trans: A Knowledge-Guided Agentic Framework for Project-Level C-to-Rust Migration

techniques.technique_name: His2Trans (historical C/Rust migration knowledge mining and retrieval at interface and fragment level, scaffold-constrained knowledge-guided function translation, then project-level agentic refinement with compilation, semantic and unsafe feedback)
techniques.tools: Clang 14.0.0; Rust 1.94.0-nightly; Python 3.13.5; jina-reranker-v3 style neural reranker for mining C/Rust pairs; project build systems (GN/Ninja for OpenHarmony); Ubuntu 22.04, dual Intel Xeon Gold 6430, 503 GiB RAM, 4x NVIDIA RTX 5880 Ada
techniques.iterations: Refinement agent iterates within a fixed budget (budget value not stated); per-function translation retries on validation failure; translation ordered by scaffold dependency graph
techniques.metrics: security/memory-safety: Unsafe Ratio = fraction of Rust source lines inside or directly associated with unsafe constructs [tool-static]; correctness: Incremental Compilation Pass Rate (per-function body replay under a common scaffold) and Test Pass Rate on the project's own tests [execution]; all averaged per project then across projects
techniques.benchmarks: Two datasets: 10 OpenHarmony modules (161-3,544 LOC each, 1-14 files, 7-160 functions, 4-135 tests) and 8 open-source C projects used in prior C-to-Rust studies (urlparser, avl, ht, qsort, buffer, rgba, quadtree, genann)
techniques.models: DeepSeek V4 Pro, size NR, open-weight, instruct (main translation and refinement); Qwen2.5-Coder-32B, 32B, open, code-specialized (offline knowledge extraction only); Claude Code (general coding agent, underlying model not stated) as a baseline
techniques.baselines: C2Rust (rule-based transpilation); C2SaferRust (unsafe-reduction pipeline); EvoC2Rust; Tymcrat; Claude Code-only (general SE agent); plus an ablation: knowledge-guided translation alone, + compiler-driven per-function repair, + project-level agentic refinement
techniques.effect_target_headline: On ten OpenHarmony modules, His2Trans reaches a 100.00% incremental compilation pass rate, a 94.92% Test Pass Rate, and a 16.35% Unsafe Ratio. On eight open-source C projects, it reaches 100.00% for both incremental compilation and Test Pass Rate, reducing Unsafe Ratio from 42.88% under C2Rust to 8.59%
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: OpenHarmony averages: Test Pass Rate 94.92% (His2Trans) vs 80.08% (Claude Code-only), 67.50% (C2Rust), 40.92% (C2SaferRust), 0.00% (EvoC2Rust and Tymcrat); incremental compilation 100.00% vs 99.58% for C2Rust

extraction.notes: Unsafe Ratio is treated here as the security/memory-safety dimension; a reviewer who reads 'security' strictly as vulnerabilities/CWE may disagree, and unsafe ratio is also partly a maintainability/idiomaticity proxy. The effect direction is not uniformly positive against every baseline: on the open-source dataset Claude Code-only reaches a lower Unsafe Ratio (4.04% vs 8.59%) at equal compilation and test pass rates, which the authors attribute to Claude Code being free to abandon the C-compatible interface boundary; on OpenHarmony His2Trans is clearly better (16.35% vs 33.67%). Ablation on OpenHarmony: knowledge-guided translation alone 95.82% / 39.29% / 15.95% unsafe; + compiler-driven per-function repair 100.00% / 94.92% / 22.52%; + project-level refinement 100.00% / 94.92% / 16.35%, i.e. the refinement stage buys back unsafe reduction without changing test pass rate. The Unsafe Ratio instrument (how lines 'directly associated with' unsafe are counted) is defined only in prose, no tool named. Single translation model, no repeated runs or statistical tests, no token/cost/time reporting. Contamination: evaluated target modules are excluded from the retrieval pool and a threats paragraph acknowledges residual leakage from public mirrors and pretraining data. Tables IV and V are heavily garbled in extraction (per-project columns interleaved); the quoted numbers are taken from the abstract, prose and average rows, which are unambiguous. Venue metadata is empty; arXiv v4 (cs.SE), formatted as an IEEE conference submission.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes fine-tuning LLMs (SFT/DPO on a performance-filtered Parlay-Instruct corpus) and an evolutionary coding agent driven by compiler, stress-test and runtime-profiling feedback to generate parallel code, and reports execution speedup (efficiency) of the LLM-generated code alongside build and pass rates.
extraction.title: ParEVO: Synthesizing Code for Irregular Data: High-Performance Parallelism through Agentic Evolution
extraction.venue: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), PMLR 306, 2026

techniques.technique_name: Domain fine-tuning on Parlay-Instruct (13,820 compiler/unit-test verified ParlayLib tasks plus DMOJ slow-fast performance pairs filtered for >=1.2x speedup); SFT with LoRA/QLoRA, plus DPO stage for Qwen (DeepSeek-Parlay, Gemini-2.5-Parlay, Qwen3-Parlay, Qwen3-Rust)
techniques.tools: Compiler + unit-test rejection sampling for data; OpenEvolve with Gemini-3-Pro for performance trajectories; ThreadSanitizer on corpus; evaluation on dual Intel Xeon Platinum 8562Y+ (64 cores), 32 threads
techniques.metrics: efficiency: Speedup@1 (arithmetic and geometric mean) over sequential baseline, strong scaling up to 64 cores, runtime vs expert code (execution); correctness: Build@1, Pass@1 (execution)
techniques.benchmarks: ParEval extended to ParlayLib and Rust/Rayon (59 problems, 12 categories); PBBSBench (C++) and RPB (Rust) expert baselines; held-out DMOJ problems
techniques.models: DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B-base, 6.7B, open, base (fine-tuned: DeepSeek-Parlay, DeepSeek-Syntax); Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct, 30B MoE, open, code-specialized (fine-tuned: Qwen3-Parlay, Qwen3-Rust); Gemini-2.5-Pro, size NR, closed, reasoning (fine-tuned: Gemini-2.5-Parlay); comparators Claude Opus 4.5, GPT-5 Thinking, Gemini-2.5-Flash, Gemini-3-Pro (closed), Qwen2.5-Coder-32B(-Instruct), DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite, StarCoder2-15B (open)
techniques.baselines: Corresponding base models without fine-tuning; commercial LLMs (Claude Opus 4.5, GPT-5 Thinking, Gemini-2.5/3); open code LLMs; token-matched OpenMP fine-tuning (DeepSeek-OMP)
techniques.effect_target_headline: Gemini-2.5-Parlay achieves an average 107× speedup over the baseline provided by ParEval (Speedup@1 AM 107.43 vs 85.34 for Gemini-2.5-Pro; DeepSeek-Parlay 126.16 vs 0.73 for DeepSeek-6.7B-Base)
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: Pass@1 0.58 (Gemini-2.5-Parlay) vs 0.54 (Gemini-2.5-Pro); 0.26 (DeepSeek-Parlay) vs 0.11 (DeepSeek-6.7B-Base); graph Pass@1 : 0.42 → 0.76

techniques.technique_name: Evolutionary Coding Agent (ECA): OpenEvolve-based population search with MAP-Elites diversity archive, fitness = 1/runtime if compiled and passing tests (0 otherwise), compiler logs and performance profiles fed back to the LLM
techniques.tools: OpenEvolve; C++/Rust compilers; human-written stress tests run five times on inputs of ~10 million vertices; runtime profiling on dual Intel Xeon Platinum 8562Y+
techniques.iterations: Up to 30 evolutionary iterations (5/10/15/30 in ablations); each generation keeps top k=3 by fitness and d=5 diverse via MAP-Elites (complexity x diversity grid); returns max-fitness candidate
techniques.metrics: efficiency: speedup over first valid solution, runtime in seconds on DMOJ problems, speedup vs expert PBBS/RPB code at 32 threads (execution); correctness: passing unit tests (execution)
techniques.benchmarks: Reserved DMOJ training problems (ablation, Table 3); 7 DMOJ problems (Table 8); 4 DMOJ problems (Table 9); PBBSBench and RPB problems (MIS, Maximal Matching, MSF, Spanning Forest, Histogram)
techniques.models: Gemini-3-Pro, size NR, closed, reasoning; Gemini-2.5-Pro and Gemini-2.5-Parlay, closed; Qwen3-Coder-30B-Instruct and Qwen-Parlay, 30B MoE, open, code-specialized
techniques.baselines: Single-shot generation (no ECA); Best-of-N; Best-of-N + CoT; Self-Refine; ECA without MAP-Elites diversity; ECA on base model; expert human PBBSBench/RPB implementations
techniques.effect_target_headline: 30 iterations of ECA yield a 2.2× performance multiplier over single-shot generation (Gemini-3-Pro + ECA (30 iter) 2.218×); for Maximal Independent Set, the generated Rust solution achieved a 4.1× speedup over the baseline
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: On coci19c1p3 every base-model configuration failed to generate a valid parallel solution; only ECA-Finetuned yielded a correct, optimized implementation (Table 9)

extraction.notes: Two techniques (fine-tuning and ECA) evaluated separately; ablations combine them. Fine-tuning has a correctness-speedup trade-off on graph problems (Speedup@1 21.76 -> 13.67 while Pass@1 0.42 -> 0.76); Qwen3-Rust Pass@1 0.46 vs 0.50 base (slight regression), so correctness effect is not uniformly positive. Arithmetic-mean speedups are heavy-tailed (authors also report GM). ECA-generated Rust uses unsafe code (unwrap_unchecked, raw pointers) to gain speed; security not measured. No variance/statistical tests or compute/cost figures; ECA DMOJ ablations are single runs on few problems. Tables and figures heavily garbled in extraction (Table 1/5, Figures 5-8). Conflict of interest disclosed (Google DeepMind authors, Gemini models).

extraction.eligibility_reason: Benchmark of LLM coding agents refactoring existing human-written open-source codebases; the outcome is alignment with the human developer's refactoring (static rule matching plus test pass), not a non-functional quality measurement of LLM-generated code from a generation task.
extraction.title: CodeTaste: Can LLMs Generate Human-Level Code Refactorings?
extraction.venue: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), PMLR 306
extraction.notes: Borderline: evaluates Plan and Oracle Multiplan propose-then-implement modes (alignment A rises e.g. 7.9% to 15.1% to 20.6% for GPT-5.2), and the targeted refactorings are maintainability-oriented, but the metric (instruction-following rate against mined human refactoring rules) measures agreement with a reference refactoring rather than an NF quality attribute, and the code edited is human-written. Reviewer may consider IC3 failing as well.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes KernelSkill, a memory-augmented multi-agent LLM framework that generates and iteratively optimizes CUDA kernels from PyTorch references using compiler, verifier and profiler feedback plus retrieved expert optimization skills; reports runtime speedup (efficiency) and correctness of the LLM-generated kernels.
extraction.title: KernelSkill: A Multi-Agent Framework for GPU Kernel Optimization

techniques.technique_name: KernelSkill (multi-agent Generator/Reviewer/Planner/Optimizer/Diagnoser/Repairer loop with long-term expert-skill memory and short-term trajectory memory)
techniques.tools: NVIDIA Nsight Compute (ncu), Nsight Systems (nsys); CUDA 12.4, PyTorch 2.6.0+cu124, cuDNN 9.1.0, cuBLAS 12.9; KernelBench timing framework (25 warmup, 100 timed iterations); rule-based + LLM static code feature extractor (18 feature types)
techniques.iterations: 3 seed kernels, best selected; up to 15 refinement rounds per task; base kernel promoted if relative speedup > 30% (rt=0.3) or absolute gain > 0.3 (at=0.3); returns best kernel
techniques.metrics: efficiency: average speedup vs Torch Eager, Fast1 (fraction at least as fast as Torch) [execution]; correctness: Success (compiles and matches PyTorch reference within tolerance) [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: KernelBench Levels 1-3 (100 + 100 + 50 = 250 tasks)
techniques.models: ChatGPT-5.1 (GPT-5.1), closed, general/reasoning
techniques.baselines: Kevin-32B, Astra, PRAGMA, CudaForge, QiMeng, STARK (STARK and QiMeng numbers taken from their papers; Astra and PRAGMA reimplemented); ablations w/o memory, w/o short-term memory, w/o long-term memory
techniques.effect_target_headline: average speedups of 5.44x, 2.82x, and 1.92x over Torch Eager on Levels 1, 2, and 3; vs STARK +79.5% on Level 1 (5.44 vs. 3.03), +4.8% on Level 2 (2.82 vs. 2.69), and +21.5% on Level 3 (1.92 vs. 1.58)
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: 100% success rate on KernelBench Levels 1-3 (w/o memory: 0.96, 0.98, 0.94)

extraction.notes: Only one LLM (GPT-5.1) used. Baseline numbers for STARK and QiMeng copied from original papers (different hardware/setup possible), Astra/PRAGMA reimplemented; comparability caveat. STARK has higher Fast1 on Levels 1 and 3 (0.71 vs 0.62; 0.87 vs 0.82). Compute reported only as refinement rounds (15 vs STARK 30), no tokens/cost. Tables extracted as flattened columns but values reconstructable. No threats-to-validity section; brief limitation in conclusion.

extraction.eligibility_reason: EvoKernel is a value-driven memory/agentic technique applied to LLMs that generate NPU (Ascend C) and CUDA kernels, and it reports a quantitative efficiency outcome (measured kernel latency and speedups) for the LLM-generated code, alongside correctness as a co-outcome.
extraction.title: Towards Cold-Start Drafting and Continual Refining: A Value-Driven Memory Approach with Application to NPU Kernel Synthesis

techniques.technique_name: EvoKernel (value-driven self-evolving memory agent: cold-start drafting + continual refining)
techniques.tools: Ascend C / CANN toolchain (CANN 8.5.0 for the mHC experiments); msprof profiler via torch_npu.profiler (3 warm-up runs, 3 profiling passes: PipeUtilization, Memory, ResourceConflict); PyTorch reference execution for correctness; rule-based AST anti-hacking checker plus an LLM auditor; Codex CLI (baseline)
techniques.iterations: Strict per-operator budget of T = 30 iterations covering drafting and refining; drafting repeats until a feasible kernel is found or the budget is exhausted, then refining continues on the remaining budget; baselines also capped at 30 iterations / 30 verification attempts
techniques.metrics: efficiency: on-device execution latency in ms from msprof step_trace_time.csv 'Computing' column, and speedup = Lref/Lopt (within-operator speedup of best candidate over first correct draft; also speedup vs Torch-NPU / PyTorch baseline and a Fast1 ratio) [execution]; correctness co-outcome: Correctness (Acc, % of operators with a functionally valid solution within budget, atol=rtol=1e-2) and Compilation Rate (CR) [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: An Ascend C (NPU) variant of KernelBench built by the authors, Level 1 and Level 2 operators (results reported as percentages per level; 159 operators had at least one valid optimization candidate beyond the initial correct draft); cross-level transfer on L2; held-out transfer subset of 50 operators (30 L1, 20 L2); scaling-out: Attention Set 70 operators on CUDA, Attention Set 70 operators on Ascend, KernelBench 250 operators on CUDA, 15 DeepSeek mHC kernels on Ascend

techniques.models: GPT-5.2, closed, frontier/reasoning (Codex baseline uses GPT-5.2 medium reasoning effort); DeepSeek-V3.2, open; Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct, open, code-specialized instruct
techniques.baselines: Pass@k (stateless, K = 30 independent candidates per operator with a single demonstration); Iterative Refinement (stateful agentic repair loop then latency hill-climbing, 30 iterations); Codex by OpenAI (autonomous GPT-5.2 agent with shell and file-system access, 30 verification attempts); ablations: heuristic-driven (similarity) retrieval vs value-driven retrieval, with/without Q-value, candidate pool multiplier lambda
techniques.effect_target_headline: achieves a median speedup of 3.60x over initial drafts through iterative refinement (abstract); 'This yields a median speedup of 3.60x, with an interquartile range of 1.38-10.05x' for within-operator refinement across 159 operators at budget T=30; 'top performers achieving more than 200x speedup over their first correct version'; on 15 Ascend mHC kernels 6 of 10 correct implementations outperform the PyTorch baseline, e.g. SinkhornKnopp 41.96x, OrthostochasticProject 2.94x, MhcPostBlock 2.88x
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: EvoKernel improves frontier models' correctness from 11.0% to 83.0% (abstract); with GPT-5.2, overall CR 98.5% and Acc 83.0% vs Codex (83.0% CR, 46.0% Acc) and Refinement (71.5% CR, 22.0% Acc), and Level 2 100.0% CR with 76.0% Acc

extraction.notes: Efficiency is the NF dimension; the paper's headline latency gain is relative to the model's own first correct draft rather than an expert/library baseline, and the text states many operators remain slower than Torch-NPU. Figures 2-8 are heavily garbled in the PDF extraction (axis labels, per-operator speedup values and the Attention Set figure are interleaved text), so per-operator numbers from figures should be re-checked against the PDF. Table 2 is garbled but the method/row mapping is recoverable from the prose. Number of benchmark operators per level is not stated explicitly (results given as percentages). No explicit threats-to-validity section; only a project page is given, no code repository link. Contamination handling covers memory leakage for the transfer experiment (test-operator traces excluded), not pretraining contamination. Some method details are described as an 'upgraded system' (hybrid API retrieval, profiler-derived bottleneck matching) with limited implementation detail.

techniques.iterations: 40 generations x population 8 (SYCL, robust-kbench) or 4 (AI CUDA Engineer comparison); meta-prompt update every 10 generations (max 3 mutations); then 2 iterations of parameter optimization (best@8); fixed budget, no early stop; 100-iteration runs in appendix
techniques.metrics: efficiency: speedup over PyTorch eager (average and geometric mean), fast_p (fraction of tasks with speedup > p, p=1,2), speedup vs oneDNN, hardware-speedup hws across GPUs [execution]; correctness: correct rate with relative tolerance (nu < 0.01 in 99% of outputs) [execution]

techniques.models: o3-mini, size NR, closed, reasoning; GPT-o3, size NR, closed, reasoning; o4-mini, size NR, closed, reasoning; GPT-4.1, size NR, closed, instruct; GPT-5-mini, size NR, closed, reasoning; Claude Sonnet 4.5, size NR, closed, instruct (first iteration only in SYCL runs); GPT-OSS 20B, 20B, open, reasoning (appendix)

extraction.notes: Single runs per configuration; no variance across runs or statistical tests reported (benchmarking procedure reduces timing variance). KernelBench tasks filtered for reward hacking (not a contamination analysis). Ablation (20 iters): avg speedup 2.539 full vs 2.505 w/o prompt evolution vs 2.178 w/o gradient guidance. Cost about $5.7 per kernel (11,102 input / 5,377 output tokens). Baseline comparisons use only a subset of the LLMs used by the baselines. No explicit threats-to-validity section. Tables partly garbled in extraction (abstract/intro text interleaved).

Baseline is human-authored specs, not a non-fine-tuned LLM, so the technique's effect versus a plain LLM is not isolated. Only one AI-generated artifact and one scenario. extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes an RL mid-training plus test-time scaling technique (SemRep) for LLM code transformation, and reports execution speedup of LLM-generated CUDA kernels on KernelBench (efficiency) alongside correctness.

techniques.metrics: efficiency: Speedup (best@16, avg@16) and fast_1 / fast_1.5 on KernelBench [execution]; SWE-Perf statistical performance gain and AlgoTune MST speedup in case studies [execution]; correctness: KernelBench correctness best@16/avg@16, EditBench Pass@1/Pass@16, robustness consistency [execution]

techniques.effect_target_headline: KernelBench Speedup best@16: SemRep 2.87 vs Kevin-32B 1.36 vs QwQ-32B 1.25; abstract: outperforms the extensively finetuned baselines with strictly the same training budget by 6.9% in correctness, 1.1× in performance
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: KernelBench Correctness best@16: 93 vs Kevin-32B 65; EditBench Pass@1 57.41 (SemRep QwQ-32B) vs 53.70 (Finetuned QwQ-32B)

extraction.notes: Efficiency is measured only on KernelBench (speedup) and in case studies; EditBench is correctness-only. Training budget is matched against baselines but inference compute is not quantified except the 25% less compute claim in the OpenEvolve case study. Single runs; no variance. Limitations section discusses test coverage and reward hacking but no formal threats-to-validity section. Tables partially garbled in extraction. No code URL given.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes an agent keep/revert loop for GPU kernel optimization, but the paper's own quantitative evaluation (Table 4, H100) measures the system's hand-provided Triton starter kernels, not kernels produced by the LLM loop; the only LLM-produced results are anecdotal community reports (a leaderboard entry and a community-reported FP4 matmul vs CUTLASS), with no LLM named and no controlled comparison.
extraction.title: AutoKernel: Autonomous GPU Kernel Optimization via Iterative Agent-Driven Search
extraction.notes: Borderline. If community-reported results count as evaluation of LLM-generated code, it could be included as feedback-loop (test-execution + profiler/roofline signals) targeting efficiency: Table 5 reports 'the Triton kernel achieves 1.63x to 2.15x speedup over CUTLASS fused kernels' and vectorsum_v2 B200 first place at 44.086us. The abstract's 5.29x/2.82x/2.21x numbers are for starter kernels (Table 4 caption: 'AutoKernel Triton starters'). No underlying LLM is named; loop dynamics (10-30% per tier) are described qualitatively. Code: https://github.com/RightNow-AI/autokernel. Header oddly carries a NeurIPS 2023 template footer.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Engram is an LLM agentic architecture that writes system heuristics, but outcomes are task-objective scores of the heuristics' decisions (multicast dollar cost, simulated LLM-serving mean response time, KV-cache prefix hit rate, ADRS task scores), not readability, security or the runtime/memory efficiency of the generated code itself.
extraction.title: Improving Coherence and Persistence in Agentic AI for System Optimization
extraction.notes: Borderline: response time in the LLM request-routing case is a property of the simulated serving system under the routing policy, not of the code's execution; the LLM-SQL combined score includes a 5% algorithm-runtime bonus but runtime is not reported separately. Reviewer may reconsider if 'algorithmic efficiency of discovered heuristics' is deemed in scope.

techniques.tools: Triton verifier (lint/compile, faithfulness, 5 test cases); execution-time benchmarking

techniques.benchmarks: Synthetic held-out benchmark (400 programs); KernelBench (250 tasks, Levels 1-3)
techniques.models: DRTriton-7B (Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct based, open, code-specialized); AutoTriton (open, specialized)

Only one model trained (7B; 1.5B used in reward ablation). Compute: 8xH100, SFT ~2h, RL ~10 days, test-time search hours in Table 5. Limitations only briefly in conclusion/checklist. extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes AscendOptimizer, an LLM agent that rewrites AscendC operator kernels and host-side tiling code using retrieved experience and hardware-in-the-loop search; the LLM-edited code is evaluated on measured latency (efficiency), with correctness checked as a co-outcome.

techniques.technique_name: AscendOptimizer (Optimization Rewind experience bootstrapping + retrieval-guided kernel refinement (Stage I) + hardware-in-the-loop evolutionary tiling search (Stage II))
techniques.tools: Ascend 910B2 NPUs with CANN 8.3; CANN compile/profiling toolchain; CPU-reference correctness harness with absolute/relative tolerance; text-embedding-3-small dense retriever
techniques.iterations: 230 hardware evaluations per operator total (20 for rewind-stage experience construction, 210 for online optimization); each evaluation is one compile-correctness-profiling attempt; failures/timeouts count toward budget; incumbent updated only on validated improvement
techniques.metrics: efficiency: measured latency on hardware, geometric-mean speedup over cann-ops baseline, fast_p (fraction of operators exceeding p x speedup for p in {1.2, 1.4, 1.8, 2.0}) [execution]; correctness: NPU vs CPU reference absolute/relative tolerance checks per official CANN example policies
techniques.benchmarks: Custom benchmark built from the official AscendC cann-ops repository: 101 operators after filtering, stratified by engineering complexity into Level 1 (25), Level 2 (63), Level 3 (13)

techniques.baselines: cann-ops open-source reference implementations (speedup denominator); Best-of-N sampling (BoN); OpenEvolve; ablations: Stage I only, Stage I w/o Experience, Stage II only

extraction.notes: Correctness is enforced as a hard filter (candidates failing compile/correctness are discarded) rather than reported as a separate rate, hence QA4=0.5. Only one LLM (DeepSeek-V3.2) is used with no justification given. Variance is handled via baseline-latency stability filtering and a noise threshold tau_noise, plus budget-sweep curves, but no repeated-run statistics or significance tests. Evaluation budget is reported in evaluations (~2 minutes each) rather than tokens/cost. Contamination is addressed only indirectly: the paper argues AscendC is under-represented in pretraining corpora and describes the setting as transductive system autotuning, not zero-shot generalization. Project website given (github.com/KernelHive) but no explicit code/data release statement. Tables 2-4 were somewhat garbled in extraction; numbers were reconstructed by column order and should be spot-checked. 53.47 % appears in the abstract only (fast_1.0 is not in the main tables).
