techniques.effect_target_headline: improving GPT-5-mini from 0.40× to 1.27× (3.2× improvement), GPT-5 from 0.86× to 1.69× (2.0× improvement), and GPT-5.2 from 2.04× to 2.85× (1.4× improvement)

techniques.technique_name: SOL-guided steering (MANTIS: Measure-Analyze-Nominate-Triage-Implement-Summarize) using roofline Speed-of-Light bounds plus profiler data, in-prompt or orchestrated, with cross-problem memory
techniques.tools: NVIDIA Nsight Compute (ncu); LLM-generated SOL report (cross-checked with SOLAR); OpenHands
techniques.iterations: 40 attempts per problem; orchestrated = 5 iterations x 2 hypotheses x 4 attempts; optional SOL-guided budget scheduling stops a problem when t_best <= (1+eps) t_SOL or no progress for w attempts
techniques.metrics: efficiency: geomean/median speedup over PyTorch (NCU kernel time), Fast-p curves, token savings and efficiency gain under scheduling [execution]; correctness: correctness check vs PyTorch reference [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: KernelBench (Levels 1-3), 59-problem LLM-relevant subset
techniques.languages: CUDA/CUTLASS C++ (raw or via uCUTLASS DSL)
techniques.models: GPT-5-mini, size NR, closed, reasoning; GPT-5, size NR, closed, reasoning; GPT-5.2, size NR, closed, reasoning
techniques.baselines: Flat MI agent; uCUTLASS + MI; component ablations (no Analyze, no Triage, no Summarize, no cross-problem memory); Sakana AI CUDA Engineer
techniques.effect_target_headline: Combined with µCUTLASS, SOL-guided steering reaches 1.56×, 2.07×, and 2.79× geomean speedup on GPT-5-mini, GPT-5, and GPT-5.2, respectively

extraction.notes: Efficiency here is runtime speedup of LLM-generated GPU kernels; the paper also frames 'efficiency' as iteration/token efficiency of the agent (scheduling saves 19-43% tokens), which is agent cost, not code quality. GPT-5.2 best SOL-guided variant uses in-prompt form; uCUTLASS+SOL on GPT-5.2 (2.79x) does not exceed uCUTLASS alone (2.85x). Correctness reported only as solved counts in text (e.g., MI GPT-5-mini solves 52 of 59), no clean correctness comparison. Results are after integrity filtering (LLM game detector). Stability: one independent repeat run for GPT-5-mini plus ablation envelope, CV reported. Figures not in extracted text; compiler code not released (grammar in appendix). No explicit threats-to-validity section.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Kernel-Smith proposes an evaluation-driven evolutionary agent plus an evolution-oriented SFT/RL post-training recipe applied to LLMs that generate Triton/MACA GPU kernels, and reports quantitative efficiency outcomes (speedup ratio, fast_p) for the generated code alongside correctness.
extraction.title: Kernel-Smith: A Unified Recipe for Evolutionary Kernel Optimization

techniques.technique_name: Kernel-Smith (evaluation-driven evolutionary kernel agent + step-centric evolution-oriented post-training: SFT cold start and GRPO RL on 'best evolution steps')
techniques.tools: OpenEvolve evolutionary coding agent (island model + MAP-Elites archive); custom distributed evaluation service with warm-up runs, repeated measurement with outlier removal and CUDAGraph timing (execution-time fluctuation constrained to within 1%); runtime hack-detection to prevent fallback to native PyTorch ops; Triton backend on NVIDIA GPUs and MACA backend on MetaX GPUs; HDBSCAN clustering for data curation; GRPO for RL. No version numbers given.
techniques.iterations: 40 rounds of iterative evolution per model under the unified protocol; input prompt and max output capped at 32K tokens per round; real-world application cases run up to 512 iterations. No early-stopping rule stated.
techniques.metrics: efficiency: Average Speedup Ratio (avg AMSR, mean speedup over PyTorch eager baseline with sub-1.0 speedups scored zero) and Fast Proportion (fast_1, fraction of kernels faster than the baseline) [execution]; end-to-end serving latency and throughput for the real-world cases [execution]. correctness: 'corr', numerical agreement with the PyTorch reference within tolerance after hack detection [execution].
techniques.benchmarks: KernelBench (Triton backend), Levels 1/2/3 reported separately plus an average; a MetaX MACA benchmark the authors construct of 45 common operators (Activation 15, Normalization 8, Reduction&Aggregation 17, Loss Function 5); three real-world cases (SGLang normal_decode_set_metadata, LMDeploy DeepSeek MoE routing, DeepSeek Engram). Task counts per KernelBench level not restated in the text.
techniques.languages: Triton (Python), MACA (MetaX GPU backend), PyTorch/CUDA as reference
techniques.models: Kernel-Smith-235B-SFT and Kernel-Smith-235B-RL (trained from Qwen3-235B-A22B, open-weights, reasoning); Kernel-Smith-MACA-30B and Kernel-Smith-MACA-235B (open-weights); baselines Qwen3-235B-A22B-2507-think; Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-think; MiniMax-M2.5; Kimi-K2.5; DeepSeek-v3.2-Speciale / DeepSeek-v3.2-think (all open-weights); Gemini-3.0-pro (closed); Claude-4.6-opus (closed); GPT-OSS-20B; Qwen3-30B-A3B. Teacher models for data synthesis: DeepSeek-V3.2-Speciale and Gemini-3.0-pro.
techniques.baselines: The same Kernel-Smith evolutionary agent framework driven by untrained open-weights and proprietary models (agent held constant); for the RL model, the Qwen3-235B-A22B base model and the SFT-only variant; for kernels, PyTorch eager mode (NVIDIA) and a correctness-verified LLM-generated CUDA implementation (MetaX).
techniques.effect_target_headline: "recording the highest avg amsr of 3.70 across all difficulty levels" (Kernel-Smith-235B-RL, KernelBench AVG Level-1/2/3, vs Claude-4.6-opus 3.33 and DeepSeek-v3.2-Speciale 3.44); "this distinct advantage is particularly pronounced in the Level 2 subset, where our model delivers a remarkable avg amsr of 7.77, substantially exceeding even Claude-4.6-opus (5.83)"; MACA backend AVG avg AMSR 13.27 (Kernel-Smith-MACA-30B) and 14.26 (Kernel-Smith-MACA-235B) vs 12.30 (Qwen3-235B-2507-think); real-world: "4.78x speedup" (SGLang kernel), "about 1.36x speedup" (LMDeploy routing kernel), "a reported 14.59x speedup" (DeepSeek Engram).
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: "achieving an average corr of 96.33 to effectively outperform all other advanced baselines, including Gemini-3.0-pro (94.33) and DeepSeek-v3.2-Speciale (94.67)"; Claude-4.6-opus remains higher at 99.33. Level 3 corr 94 for Kernel-Smith-235B-RL.

extraction.artifact_url: https://chat.intern-ai.org.cn/kernel-smith (project page / online demo); data access by e-mail request only; merged PRs https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/20778, https://github.com/InternLM/lmdeploy/pull/4345, https://github.com/DeepLink-org/DLBlas/pull/102; agent built on https://github.com/algorithmicsuperintelligence/openevolve
extraction.notes: Tables 1 and 2 are badly garbled by PDF extraction (column headers are detached from values); the numbers quoted above were cross-checked against the prose in Sections 5.2-5.3, which states them explicitly, except the MACA AVG column values (13.27/14.26 and the baseline 12.30) which were read off the reconstructed table and should be verified against the original PDF. The agent framework and the post-training recipe are presented as one unified recipe and are not separately ablated against a multi-turn-agent baseline, so they are recorded as a single hybrid technique; an SFT-only variant appears only in the Figure 1 curve, not in Table 1. KernelBench task counts per level are never restated. No threats-to-validity section. Compute is reported as a protocol budget (40 evolution rounds, 32K-token cap per round, 100 repeated unit-test executions) rather than measured cost, hence QA7 = 0.5. Contamination is addressed only indirectly, via the DeepSeek Engram case chosen as a fresh module.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes an agentic generate-test-profile-refine framework in which GPT-5 generates CuTe GPU kernels, and reports execution speedup (efficiency) of the LLM-generated kernels against PyTorch and the CudaForge agent baseline, with correctness as co-outcome.
extraction.title: CuTeGen: An LLM-Based Agentic Framework for Generation and Optimization of High-Performance GPU Kernels using CuTe

techniques.technique_name: CuTeGen (CuTe-targeted generate-test-refine agent with diagnosis/patch repair, category-aware structural optimization prompts and delayed Nsight Compute profiling feedback)
techniques.tools: NVIDIA Nsight Compute; PyTorch 2.8.0 CUDA extension interface; CUTLASS v4.3.0 (commit acb4593) / CuTe; CUDA 13.0; RTX 4090
techniques.iterations: Correctness loop (diagnosis then localized patch) until correct or max rounds; optimization loop applies one optimization per iteration until max round reached; profiling feedback withheld early for structurally complex kernels (e.g., matmul); exact max rounds not stated
techniques.metrics: efficiency: average speedup over PyTorch eager runtime, Fast1 (% tasks faster than PyTorch), speedup on Fast1, % best kernel, low-precision rate [execution]; correctness: % tasks with at least one correct kernel passing automated tests and manual inspection [execution + human audit]
techniques.benchmarks: KernelBench Level-1 and Level-2, 209 tasks
techniques.models: GPT-5, size undisclosed, closed, reasoning
techniques.baselines: PyTorch eager reference; CudaForge (agentic, GPT-5, 10 rounds); ablations: CuTeGen with raw CUDA, without profiling, profiling from start
techniques.effect_target_headline: CuTeGen achieves an average speedup of 1.71× over PyTorch vs CudaForge 0.89× (KernelBench L1+L2, 209 tasks, GPT-5)
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: Correct 87% (CuTeGen) vs 63% (CudaForge), KernelBench L1+L2

extraction.notes: Single model (GPT-5) justified only by compute budget in Limitations. Manual audit excluded reduced-precision kernels from speedups (CudaForge 24% low precision). Cost $1.69 vs $1.41 per task. Per-level tables: L1 1.32x vs 0.61x; L2 2.12x vs 1.19x. Ablation (L1 total speedup): CuTeGen 1.35x vs with cuda 1.12x. No repeated runs/variance. Max iteration counts not given. Tables garbled but recoverable.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Industrial case study using LLM agents (Gemini 2.5 Pro planner, Cursor executors) to generate unit tests and then refactor an existing human-written React/Next.js MVP codebase; the NF outcomes (coupling, cyclomatic complexity, LOC distribution) concern LLM refactoring of human-written code, with no comparison of a technique against a baseline.
extraction.title: AI-Assisted Unit Test Writing and Test-Driven Code Refactoring: A Case Study
extraction.notes: Venue per metadata MIPRO (not stated in text). Reported refactor metrics: routing-layer imports 893 -> 379 (57.5% reduction), average cyclomatic complexity 2.24 -> 2.13, LOC 18,619 -> 21,624. Test generation part is EC3 (tests only).

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes a training technique (error-driven CoT synthesis with an industrial code world model, SFT of a 32B thinking model) and reports quantitative efficiency outcomes of the generated code (Mercury Beyond@1, KernelBench fast_1 speedup, SuperCoder speedup). Borderline because efficiency is a side benchmark of a general foundation-model paper rather than the primary target.
extraction.title: InCoder-32B-Thinking: Industrial Code World Model for Thinking

techniques.technique_name: InCoder-32B-Thinking: training on Error-driven Chain-of-Thought (ECoT) traces synthesized with real toolchain feedback and an Industrial Code World Model (ICWM)
techniques.tools: Triton/CUDA backend, Renode/STM32, CadQuery, Yosys/Icarus/Verilator, ARM GCC (data synthesis); DeepSeek-V3.2 as trace generator
techniques.iterations: data synthesis: up to K=4 correction rounds, stop when code passes all checks; single-pass generation at inference
techniques.metrics: efficiency: Mercury Beyond@1 (execution), KernelBench fast_1 L1/L2/L3 (execution, correct and >=1x speedup), SuperCoder speedup (execution); correctness: pass@1 on EvalPlus, BigCodeBench, LiveCodeBench, SWE-bench Verified, VeriScope, RealBench, etc.
techniques.benchmarks: Mercury; KernelBench (250 tasks, L1-L3); SuperCoder (8,072 x86-64 programs); TritonBench-G/T; plus 14 general and 9 industrial benchmarks (HumanEval/MBPP EvalPlus, BigCodeBench, LiveCodeBench v5/v6, SWE-bench Verified, VeriScope 568, RealBench, ArchXBench 51, VeriRepair 300, EmbedCGen 500, CAD-Coder, etc.)
techniques.languages: Python, CUDA/Triton, Verilog, C (embedded), x86-64 assembly, CadQuery, SQL
techniques.models: InCoder-32B-Thinking, 32B, open, reasoning (fine-tuned from InCoder-32B)
techniques.baselines: InCoder-32B (non-thinking counterpart); Qwen2.5-Coder, Qwen3/Qwen3.5, Qwen3-Coder, DeepSeek-V3.2, Kimi-K2/K2.5, GLM-4.7/5, KAT-Dev, Seed-Coder, GPT-OSS, MiniMax-M2.5, Claude-Sonnet-4.6
techniques.effect_target_headline: 38.0% on KernelBench (abstract); text notes "a moderate trade-off appears on benchmarks that favor concise responses (e.g., Mercury, Text2SQL)"
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: Compared to its instruct counterpart, InCoder-32B-Thinking achieves comparable performance on SWE-bench Verified, while improving by 28.0% on LiveCodeBench

extraction.notes: General-purpose foundation model paper; NF (efficiency) is not the stated aim but GPU kernel optimization and assembly superoptimization tasks are efficiency tasks and profiling feedback is used in data synthesis. Tables 1-5 are badly garbled; my reading of Table 2 suggests Mercury Beyond@1 drops from 71.4 (InCoder-32B) to 62.4 (Thinking) and KernelBench L2 fast_1 36.0 -> 38.0, SuperCoder speedup possibly 1.3x -> 3.93x, but column alignment is uncertain; verify against PDF. Contamination only via LiveCodeBench time-stamped split mentioned in appendix. No variance, no compute cost, no threats-to-validity section. Training hyperparameters not given.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes PAFT, a preservation-aware fine-tuning recipe that changes LLM-generated program-repair patches, and reports quantitative maintainability/reviewability outcomes (average edit distance, code consistency rate, changed lines/tokens, validated against human preferences) alongside pass@k.
extraction.title: PAFT: Preservation-Aware Fine-Tuning for Minimal-Edit Program Repair

techniques.technique_name: PAFT: preservation-aware fine-tuning (token-level alignment-based upweighting of copy-worthy target tokens, full-sequence loss masking, edit-difficulty curriculum) with QLoRA
techniques.tools: Ratcliff/Obershelp (SequenceMatcher-style) token alignment between buggy and fixed code; QLoRA 4-bit NF4, rank 32, alpha 16, 3 epochs, w_align = 2.0; single RTX 4090
techniques.metrics: readability-maintainability (patch minimality / stable-context preservation on plausible patches): Average Edit Distance (character Levenshtein) [tool-static], Code Consistency Rate [tool-static], Average Total Changed Lines and Tokens [tool-static]; metrics validated by human preference study [human]; correctness: pass@1/5/10 via compilation and test suites [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: Defects4J (MORepair release, single-file Java bugs); HumanEval-Java; training on TutorLLMCode (1535 instances)
techniques.models: Qwen3-8B (open); OpenCoder-8B-Instruct (open, code-specialized instruct); DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B (open, code-specialized); Qwen3-Max (closed, zero-shot reference); DeepSeek-V3 (open, zero-shot reference)
techniques.baselines: Base models; standard SFT (assistant-only masking); minimal-change Prompting; RepairLLaMA; AdaPatcher (SFT + DPO)
techniques.effect_target_headline: reducing average edit distance (AED) by up to 32.6% over Sft; Defects4J DS-Coder-6.7B: reduces AED from 142.9 to 80.7, and increases CCR from 70.7 to 76.3; vs AdaPatcher median AED from 61.0 to 42.0
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: PAFT improves pass@1 by up to 65.6% over standard supervised fine-tuning (Sft); Defects4J DS-Coder-6.7B pass@1 from 5.8% to 10.1%; vs AdaPatcher pass@1 from 5.9% to 10.1%

extraction.human_eval_details: 3 annotators (CS PhDs), 50 Defects4J bugs, pairwise forced-choice in two rounds to validate metrics; Fleiss' kappa 0.710-0.733
extraction.notes: NF dimension is patch minimality/edit locality as a proxy for review and maintenance burden; authors explicitly say it is not maintainability in full. CCR not uniformly improved (HumanEval-Java DS-Coder-6.7B CCR 71.4 under SFT vs 67.2 under PAFT). Percentages in tables are relative to Base, headline 32.6% AED reduction is relative to SFT. Contamination checked via SHA-256 of normalized snippets. Single run, no variance reported. Artifacts mentioned as released scripts/results but no URL in text.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes ENCRUST, an LLM (GPT-4o) pipeline with compile-and-test feedback and a tool-using agent that translates C projects into safe Rust; the evaluated artifact is LLM-generated Rust code and it reports quantitative NF outcomes (unsafe-construct counts as a memory-safety measure, Clippy warnings for idiomaticity) alongside functional correctness.
extraction.title: ENCRUST: Encapsulated Substitution and Agentic Refinement on a Live Scaffold for Safe C-to-Rust Translation

techniques.technique_name: ENCRUST: ABI-preserving wrapper-pattern per-function translation with compile-test retry and rollback (Phase 1), type-directed wrapper elimination, and tool-equipped agentic refinement under a baseline-aware compile-and-test gate (Phase 2)
techniques.tools: C2Rust (initial unsafe transpilation); cargo build (debug/release); test-vector suites (Coreutils shell scripts; AFL++-generated inputs for Laertes); agent tools incl. find_static_mut_usages (signal-reachability analysis) and self_reflect (unsafe counts); cargo clippy for evaluation
techniques.iterations: Phase 1: up to five compile-test retries per function, then rollback to original unsafe body; Phase 2: up to 40 tool-call iterations per task (MAX_ITER = 40), task marked complete only after build + test gate passes, otherwise rollback; stall hints after five consecutive compile failures
techniques.metrics: security (memory safety): raw pointer declarations, raw pointer dereferences, unsafe lines of code, unsafe type casts, unsafe call expressions (tool-static counts, metrics from C2SaferRust); readability-maintainability (idiomaticity): Clippy warning count (tool-static); correctness: test-script / test-vector pass rate (execution) and function compilance pass rate (compiler)
techniques.benchmarks: 7 GNU Coreutils programs (C2SaferRust benchmark; 65,117 LoC, 1,210 functions, 63 test scripts) and 8 of 10 Laertes libraries (132,589 LoC, 1,156 functions, 1,000 AFL++ inputs each); 197,706 LoC and 2,366 functions in total
techniques.models: GPT-4o, closed, general instruct (temperature 0.0)
techniques.baselines: C2Rust (rule-based transpiler output); C2SaferRust (with GPT-4o, temperature 0.0); EvoC2Rust (with GPT-4o, temperature 0.0); ablation Phase 1 only
techniques.effect_target_headline: Encrust reduces unsafe lines of code by 37.8% over the C2Rust baseline while achieving 100% test-vector correctness on all programs (15 programs); on Coreutils, reduces raw pointer dereferences by 55% and unsafe type casts by 60% relative to the C2Rust baseline
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: Function compilance pass rate 96.4% (Encrust) vs 66.0% (C2SaferRust) on Coreutils; Encrust achieves 100% correctness on all seven Coreutils programs and all eight Laertes libraries (EvoC2Rust 0%)

extraction.notes: Code translation (C to Rust) task; security dimension is operationalized as counts of unsafe Rust constructs (memory-safety proxy), not CWE/vulnerability scans. Clippy totals improve vs C2Rust and C2SaferRust (Coreutils 2,951 / 2,087 / 1,495; Laertes 7,174 / 7,034 / 6,453) but are worse than C2Rust for some libraries (genann 32 -> 59, lil 583 -> 698, qsort 7 -> 16, urlparser 153 -> 196), so the readability effect is mixed at program level. EvoC2Rust has lower nominal unsafe counts but does not compile (0% correctness). Correctness is 100% by construction (test-gated); EvoC2Rust safety numbers computed after substituting C2Rust bodies for missing functions. Only GPT-4o used, single deterministic run (temperature 0). Compute reported only as loop iterations (avg 21.0 per completed Phase 2 task); no tokens/cost. Laertes test vectors promised upon publication; no code URL. ACM template with placeholder venue/dates (Proc. ACM Program. Lang. 2018) - treated as preprint (arXiv 2604.04527v1). Tables are extracted as column streams but values are interpretable.

extraction.eligibility_reason: The paper presents a JAX gyrokinetics physics solver; the agentic (vibecoding) workflow used to build it is only described as an experience report, and the reported speedups evaluate the solver against the Fortran GKW code, not an LLM technique against a controlled baseline.
extraction.title: gyaradax: Local Gyrokinetics JAX Code
extraction.notes: Borderline: Appendix D describes a multi-agent CUDA kernel optimization loop (reasoning-model proposer/reviewer, lightweight coding model implements, compile+benchmark harness vs JAX reference); Table 2 shows CUDA MP 10.53x vs JAX MP 5.37x speedup over GKW (adiabatic), i.e. roughly 2x from the LLM-generated kernels. A reviewer taking a lenient view of IC1 could include it as an efficiency-targeted feedback-loop/multi-agent case study (single case, no ablation, heavy human oversight). Repo given as gerkone/gyaradax. Figures garbled in extraction.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Babbling Suppression stops LLM generation early once a candidate passes tests; the outcomes are the energy, tokens and time of LLM inference plus pass@1, not any non-functional property (efficiency, readability, security) of the generated code itself.
extraction.title: Babbling Suppression: Making LLMs Greener One Token at a Time
extraction.notes: Borderline: 'efficiency' here is GPU energy of the generation process (up to 65% savings on Python, 62% on Java), not runtime/memory/energy of the produced code. If the review counts inference-cost reduction as efficiency, reconsider. Replication package on Zenodo (doi:10.5281/zenodo.19237762).

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes R3, an LLM-driven MAP-Elites evolutionary search over GPU kernel source rewrites combined with record-replay evaluation and Bayesian optimization of compiler passes and launch parameters, and reports measured kernel and application speedups of the LLM-rewritten kernels versus OpenEvolve and BO baselines.
extraction.title: Record-Remix-Replay: Hierarchical GPU Kernel Optimization using Evolutionary Search

techniques.technique_name: Record-Remix-Replay (R3): LLM-ensemble MAP-Elites evolution of kernel source with record-replay evaluation, inner Bayesian optimization (TPE) over compiler pass pipelines and launch parameters, prefix-cache-aware prompting and runtime-aware LLM selection
techniques.tools: Mneme record-replay engine built on Proteus LLVM-IR JIT; LLVM; parallel Tree Parzen Estimation (30 iterations per candidate); ROCm 7.0.2 on AMD MI300A; CUDA 12 on NVIDIA H100; vLLM for gpt-oss
techniques.iterations: 200 MAP-Elites iterations, 4 islands, population 20, migration every 20 iterations; stopping by max iterations, wall-clock time, or no-improvement window; kernels replayed K (e.g. 10) times
techniques.metrics: efficiency: kernel speedup over baseline implementation, absolute kernel time, end-to-end application speedup, compute-time reduction [execution]; search cost: time-to-solution, evaluations per hour, GPU utilization; correctness used only as a filter (bitwise or annotated-tolerance replay check), not reported as an outcome
techniques.benchmarks: HeCBench CUDA/HIP versions of Lulesh (15 kernels), MiniFE (7), S3D (54), miniWeather (7 on data path); QUDA CoarseDslash kernel case study
techniques.models: gpt-oss-120b, 120B, open, reasoning; gpt-5-mini, closed, reasoning; gpt-5, closed, reasoning (used as an ensemble)
techniques.baselines: OpenEvolve (same MAP-Elites settings and LLM ensemble); Record-Replay + Bayesian optimization over launch and compiler parameters (based on Parasyris et al. SC'23), 200 iterations; original kernel implementation
techniques.effect_target_headline: The final kernel speedup on an MI300A is 1.33×. When placed into the whole QUDA application we see a 28.4% reduction in time spent in compute

extraction.notes: Main comparative results are given as box plots (Figs 6-9) without numeric tables; headline numbers come from the QUDA case study. Correctness is a hard filter (bitwise replay check; final kernels manually verified) rather than a reported rate. Only one LLM ensemble configuration; no per-model ablation of optimization quality. Prompts not shown. Only the record-replay component (Mneme) is released; R3 'planned to be open-sourced'. No threats-to-validity section. Time-to-solution and throughput reported; no token or dollar cost.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Short workshop extended abstract (CoDAIM 2026, roughly two pages of content plus references) evaluating compiler optimization remarks as feedback for a Qwen2.5-Coder 7B agent refactoring TSVC loops to enable auto-vectorization; topically relevant (efficiency) but below the 4-page full-paper threshold.
extraction.title: AI Coding Agents Need Better Compiler Remarks
extraction.notes: Page count inferred from extracted text length (no page numbers visible); reviewer should verify. If counted as a full paper it would qualify: compiler-remark feedback (Clang 21.1.8, Intel 2025.3) raised vectorization success, e.g. 'At T = 0.8, providing remarks increases Clang's success rate from 0.80% to 2.68% (3.3× increase) and Intel's from 2.38% to 6.95% (2.9× increase)'; outcome is vectorization success (efficiency proxy, no runtime measured), semantics checked by differential testing; 100 trials per loop, 151 TSVC loops.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes Ave, an agentic framework in which LLMs generate and iteratively optimize GPU kernels guided by compile-time data-flow invariant checking, an ICRL planner and a knowledge base, and reports execution-measured throughput (efficiency) of the LLM-produced kernels alongside validity/correctness.
extraction.title: Ave: Guiding Agentic GPU Optimization Using Data-Flow Invariants
extraction.venue: SOSP '26 (ACM SIGOPS 32nd Symposium on Operating Systems Principles)

techniques.technique_name: Ave: tile-based DSL with tag functions/assertions checked by compile-time SMT-backed static analysis, ICRL (text-gradient) planner over an expert knowledge base, and a lowering agent, iterating with unit tests and runtime profiling
techniques.tools: Ave compiler (MLIR, LLVM 20 AMDGPU backend extensions, ROCm 7.2.2), Z3 SMT solver; Codex harness runtime; latency profiling (1 s warm-up, mean over at least 100 runs); CUDA 12.8 for H200
techniques.iterations: Up to ten optimization trials (rounds) per workload, keeping the fastest valid candidate; only a measured speedup replaces the current kernel; KernelBench generation stops at first test-passing candidate (pass@1/3)
techniques.metrics: efficiency: normalized effective throughput (geometric mean) vs hipBLASLt/AITER/PyTorch reference, effective TFLOPS, count of tasks above parity [execution]; correctness: compilation, invariant checks, unit tests, manual reward-hacking review, pass@1/3, optimization success [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: Production kernels on AMD MI300X: BF16 square GEMM, causal GQA flash attention, fused MoE (FP8), five configurations each; same on NVIDIA H200; KernelBench Level 1 (100 tasks) and Level 2 (100 tasks); 60 selected KernelBench GEMM/convolution tasks for invariant ablation
techniques.languages: Ave Pythonic tile-based DSL (GPU kernels; AMD CDNA3/CDNA4, NVIDIA Hopper)
techniques.models: GPT-5.6 Sol (closed); DeepSeek V4 Pro (open); DeepSeek V4 Flash (open)
techniques.baselines: Agentic frameworks KernelFalcon, KSearch, CUDAForge, Atrex; expert libraries hipBLASLt, AITER, HipKittens, ROCm Triton (cuBLASLt, FlashAttention-3 fork, DeepGEMM fork on H200); ablations without ICRL, without invariants, runtime feedback only
techniques.effect_target_headline: With GPT-5.6 Sol, its optimized kernels achieve 89–99% of the effective throughput of state-of-the-art hand-optimized libraries and improve geometric-mean throughput by 1.62–1176× over uncontaminated agentic baselines (AMD MI300X, GEMM/flash attention/MoE)
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: On 200 KernelBench tasks, with GPT-5.6 Sol and in-context DSL examples, Ave produces valid kernels within three attempts for 100% of Level 1 and 88% of Level 2 problems; invariants improve success in every dataset–model pair (Table 4)

extraction.notes: Tables 1, 3, 4 and Figure 2/3 are garbled in extraction (cost/turn/token columns misaligned). Contamination considered via 'uncontaminated agentic baselines' (Atrex copies AITER reference kernel) and a DSL absent from training corpora; manual reward-hacking review. Ablation (flash attention): full Ave 588 TFLOPS vs 190/255/194 for ablated harnesses. Best-of-trials reporting; no variance across agent runs; limitations discussed in Discussion but no formal threats section.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Dr. RTL is a multi-agent LLM framework that rewrites existing human-written RTL (Verilog) designs for better post-synthesis timing/area, i.e. LLM optimization/refactoring of human-written code rather than improving code the LLM generates for a task; the outcome is hardware PPA, not software NF quality. Borderline: the rewritten RTL is LLM-edited and a quantitative efficiency-like outcome is reported.
extraction.title: Dr. RTL: Autonomous Agentic RTL Optimization through Tool-Grounded Self-Improvement
extraction.notes: Borderline EC4/adjacent vs include (and whether hardware PPA counts as efficiency). If included: multi-agent feedback loop with Synopsys Design Compiler timing reports and Cadence Jasper SEC plus a learned skill library; 10 iterations x 5 parallel candidates; 20 human-written Verilog designs; Claude Opus main, also Sonnet, Haiku, GPT-5.3, Qwen Coder 8B; baselines single-shot LLMs, RTLRewriter, SymRTLo; headline 'average WNS/TNS improvements of 21%/17% with a 6% area reduction over the industry-leading commercial synthesis tool'; SEC pass rate 86%; cost about $50 and one week wall-clock reported; artifacts https://github.com/hkust-zhiyao/Dr_RTL; 4-fold cross-validation for skills.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes an LLM-driven multi-stage pipeline (CoVeR generate-verify-refine agent plus curated Intel GPU knowledge base) that rewrites LLM-generated (KernelFalcon) Triton kernels and reports execution speedup (efficiency) with correctness on KernelBench Level-2 and Flash Attention.
extraction.title: Xe-Forge: Multi-Stage LLM-Powered Kernel Optimization for Intel GPU

techniques.technique_name: Xe-Forge: LLM-planned multi-stage optimization pipeline with Chain-of-Verification-and-Refinement (CoVeR) agents and Intel GPU knowledge base
techniques.tools: Intel XPU Triton backend (SPIR-V/IGC); PyTorch 2 torch.xpu; AI Bench harness (hardware-event timing, torch.allclose rtol=1e-2 atol=1e-5); DSPy 3.x; YAML knowledge base (84 entries, 6 files, 9 full-code examples); GPU hardware query (torch.xpu.get_device_properties / xpu-smi)
techniques.iterations: Up to nine optimization stages ordered by an LLM planner with skip logic and re-analysis after each stage; CoVeR loop max T=5 iterations per stage, stops when compile_and_verify returns success sentinel (correct and faster), else ChainOfThought fallback and revert to original if verification fails; best-of-k with k=1
techniques.metrics: efficiency: speedup and TFLOPS vs PyTorch eager, torch.compile and unoptimized Triton; geometric mean speedup; fraction of kernels improving; roofline placement [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: KernelBench Level-2, 97 kernels in seven families (GEMM 19, MatMul 17, BMM 1, Conv2D 21, Conv3D 12, ConvTranspose2D 10, ConvTranspose3D 17); Flash Attention forward, 16 LLM-serving configurations
techniques.models: GPT-5.4, closed, reasoning (temperature 1.0)
techniques.baselines: PyTorch eager; torch.compile (TorchInductor); unoptimized KernelFalcon-generated Triton kernel (pipeline input)
techniques.effect_target_headline: 1.17× geometric mean speedup over PyTorch eager with 67% of kernels improving (97 Level-2 KernelBench kernels, Intel Arc Pro B70); 2–13.3× speedups on Flash Attention across all tested configurations without regression
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: Across all benchmarked kernels the pipeline maintains 100% correctness

extraction.notes: Input kernels are LLM-generated (KernelFalcon) correct Triton code, which the LLM pipeline then rewrites; treated as LLM generation/editing rather than refactoring human code. Single model (GPT-5.4); appendix claims 'comparable results' with Claude Sonnet 4.6 but no data shown. No ablation of knowledge base or stages, no repeated runs. Cost reported only as estimate (40-50 calls worst case, 10-20 typical, ~$0.50-$2.00 per kernel). Setup says full KernelBench suite across three levels but results reported only for 97 Level-2 kernels; Level-1 described as minimal gains without numbers. Text says largest speedup 82x but a figure label shows 134x (garbled figures). Per-family geomeans: GEMM 1.28x and MatMul 1.76x over best baseline; some kernels regress (0.5-0.8x). Appendix .env lists AGENT_MAX_ITERATIONS=3 vs T=5 in setup.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes an LLM agent framework (failure-driven skill memory plus diversity-preserving tree search with execution feedback) that generates Triton GPU kernels and reports runtime speedup (efficiency) alongside correctness.
extraction.title: AdaExplore: Failure-Driven Adaptation and Diversity-Preserving Search for Efficient Kernel Generation

techniques.technique_name: AdaExplore (Adapt: cross-task skill memory distilled from execution failures on synthesized tasks; Explore: UCT-style tree search alternating small-step patch refinement and large-step regeneration with working memory and representative kernel pool)
techniques.tools: Triton 3.1.0; CUDA events timing (10 warmup + 100 timed trials, 5% symmetric trimming); torch.allclose tolerance 1e-2; NVIDIA A6000 at fixed 1500 MHz (also L40S, A100, GB200, B200)
techniques.iterations: Search budget T steps (50 default; 100 and 200 also reported); returns best correct kernel; Adapt stage 25 steps per synthesized task over 200 tasks, rules kept if frequency >= 3
techniques.metrics: efficiency: speedup over PyTorch eager (clipped at 10), Fast@1.2, Fast@2 [execution]; correctness: accuracy (at least one correct kernel), Pass@1/Pass@25 [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: KernelBench Level-2 and Level-3 (Level-1 used for task synthesis); TritonBench-T (166 tasks); FlashInfer-Bench case study (3 kernels)
techniques.models: GPT-5-mini, closed, reasoning; GPT-5, closed, reasoning; Claude-4.6-Opus, closed, instruct; Qwen3-Coder-Next, open MoE 3B active, code-specialized; DeepSeek-R1, open, reasoning (memory transfer only); AutoTriton and DR. Kernel (open, RL-trained Triton models) as baselines
techniques.baselines: Single-pass GPT-5-mini, GPT-5, Claude-4.6-Opus, AutoTriton, DR. Kernel; Parallel Sampling and Iterative Refinement with and without skill memory; OpenEvolve w. SM; DR. Kernel 4x14 steps; static Triton documentation instead of skill memory; ablations (w/o small step, large step, skill memory, representative kernels, MCTS)
techniques.effect_target_headline: AdaExplore achieves 3.11× and 1.62× speedups on KernelBench Level-2 and Level-3, respectively, within 100 steps and using GPT-5-mini; at 50 steps 2.63× (L2) vs 2.59× IR w. SM and 1.69× PS
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: AdaExplore (50 Steps) 100% accuracy on KernelBench L2 vs 22% single-pass GPT-5-mini; skill memory raises GPT-5-mini Pass@1 from 22% to 54%

extraction.notes: Contamination: skill memory built on synthesized tasks from KernelBench Level-1 and evaluated on L2/L3 (train/test separation), but pretraining contamination not discussed. No repeated runs or statistical tests of the search results (only per-kernel timing statistics). No threats-to-validity section. Speedups clipped at 10. Appendix E.4 reports kernel size growth (tokens) for iterative refinement vs AdaExplore, not treated as a readability metric. Some tables garbled but values recoverable.

extraction.eligibility_reason: The prompt-representation conditions (semantic role labels, I/O specifications) are evaluated only on structural similarity to gold DMN decision models (shortest-path graph kernel) and outcome equivalence under execution, both of which are correctness/similarity-to-reference measures; no readability, efficiency or security outcome is reported for the generated artifacts.
extraction.title: From Legal Text to Executable Decision Models: Evaluating Structured Representations for Legal Decision Model Generation
extraction.venue: ICAIL 2026 (International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Law), Singapore
extraction.notes: Borderline on two counts a reviewer may want to check. (1) Artifact type: the generated output is an executable DMN decision model serialized as JSON, not general-purpose source code. (2) Complexity statistics (nodes, edges, rules, rules per node, inputs per rule, depth, max width, and the finding that generated models remove 83-100% of the gold models' identity/pass-through nodes, which are 54.7% of Outcome and 45% of Requirements nodes) look like structural-complexity measures, but they are reported as descriptive deviations from the gold standard rather than as a non-functional quality the technique improves; the paper's own framing is 'generation quality'. Headline numbers if a reviewer disagrees and includes it: I/O specifications improve shortest-path kernel similarity by +37% for Outcome (0.433 vs 0.315) and +54% for Requirements (0.549 vs 0.356), both p<0.001; srl alone helps only Requirements (+20.8%, 0.430 vs 0.356); outcome equivalence 51.3% (Text+io) / 53.1% (Text+srl+io) macro-averaged over 58 testable models and 13,080 test cases, with 33% of models reaching full equivalence and 50% reaching >=90% on their best of 5 runs. Single model (GPT-5.1, temperature 0.1, JSON mode, reasoning disabled), 1-shot, 1,900 generations (95 models x 4 conditions x 5 runs); Wilcoxon tests and 5-run variance reported; dataset and code released at https://github.com/opengov-lab/legal-text-to-decision-model.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Benchmark paper (PDB) evaluating LLM debugging of benchmark solutions with LLM-injected bugs; outcomes are unit-test pass rate plus edit-level precision (edit minimality/over-editing) and bug-level recall, none of which is a readability-maintainability, efficiency or security measure of the code. Prompting (minimal vs freeform) and iterative/agentic variants are compared only on these correctness/edit-minimality metrics.
extraction.title: Precise Debugging Benchmark: Is Your Model Debugging or Regenerating?
extraction.notes: Borderline: edit precision (penalizing over-editing/regeneration) could be argued as a maintainability/reviewability property, but it is not one of the review's NF dimensions (naming, structure, complexity, smells, idiomaticity, documentation, style). Minimal-edit prompting raised precision vs freeform (e.g. Gemini-2.5-Pro ~40% absolute drop under freeform). Human study: experts rated patches 1-5, Spearman rho = 0.72 with PDB precision. Dataset/code/leaderboard links present in header but URLs not extracted.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Quasi-experimental developer study evaluating a developer training package that teaches layer-based (MA-CoT) structured security prompting, applied when developers use a fixed LLM to generate a Spring Boot backend; the outcome is validated security weaknesses (CWE, severity) in the LLM-assisted code, pre vs post training.
extraction.title: A Quasi-Experimental Developer Study of Security Training in LLM-Assisted Web Application Development

techniques.technique_name: Developer training package with MA-CoT layer-based security model and structured security-constraint prompting scaffold
techniques.metrics: security: count of validated CWE-mapped weaknesses and severity-weighted score (4/3/2/1 for critical/high/medium/low) from independent manual review by two authors with adjudication [human]
techniques.benchmarks: Custom identity-centric Java Spring Boot user-management backend, two counterbalanced task sets (A, B); 24 repositories from 12 developers
techniques.models: gpt-5.2-2025-12-11, size unknown, closed, reasoning
techniques.baselines: Same developers before training using free-form prompting (within-subject pre-training condition)
techniques.effect_target_headline: validated weaknesses decreased from 162 to 111 (31.5%), the severity-weighted burden decreased from 432 to 267 (38.2%), and critical findings decreased from 24 to 5 (79.2%) (exact Wilcoxon p = 0.0059)

extraction.human_eval_details: Two authors (security-experienced) independently reviewed all 24 repositories with a predefined guide; disagreements adjudicated; no inter-rater agreement statistic reported. 12 developer participants (6 junior, 6 senior).
extraction.notes: Human-in-the-loop study: the intervention trains developers, who then write prompts; generated code is LLM-assisted and may include developer edits. Fixed pre-to-post order (no causal identification); bundled intervention not ablated. Acceptance tests used only as a completion aid, not an endpoint, so no correctness co-outcome. Artifact URL is the MA-CoT reference repository cited for the training model; study data release not stated. Reviewers are authors (possible bias).

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes an LLM framework that learns a rule library automatically from contrasting LLM-rewritten Verilog pairs and uses retrieval-augmented beam search to rewrite RTL for better power, performance and area (PPA), reporting area/delay/power improvements of the LLM-rewritten code against vanilla LLM sampling and prior methods.
extraction.title: AutoPPA: Automated Circuit PPA Optimization via Contrastive Code-based Rule Library Learning

techniques.technique_name: AutoPPA (Explore-Evaluate-Induce contrastive rule library learning + Adaptive Retrieval Augmented Optimization with rule-enhanced beam search)
techniques.tools: Yosys; SiliconCompiler (Yosys + OpenSTA) with FreePDK 45nm; commercial EDA tool at 12nm and 65nm; auto-generated testbenches for equivalence; gte_Qwen2-7B-instruct embeddings
techniques.iterations: Beam search with beam width k, expansions m, max steps s (configs 2-3-3, 3-5-4, 3-8-5, 5-10-5; 15 to 210 RTL samples)
techniques.metrics: efficiency: synthesized cell area (um2), cycle delay (ns), dynamic power (mW), Impr@k relative to original [tool-static synthesis]; functional equivalence enforced via testbench as a filter (non-equivalent counted as 0 improvement) [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: RTLRewriter benchmark, 60 designs (54 + 3 large designs split into 6 modules); 11 RTLRewriter circuits; 5 SymRTLO circuits
techniques.models: DeepSeek-V3-0324, 685B, open, instruct; Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, open, instruct; Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct, open, code-specialized; baselines CodeV-All-QC 7.62B, open, code-specialized; HaVen-DeepSeek 6.74B, open, code-specialized; DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, open, reasoning
techniques.baselines: Vanilla LLM sampling with identical sample budget (HaVen, CodeV, DS-R1-Dist, Qwen-Coder, DeepSeek-V3); RTLRewriter; SymRTLO (self-reported); manual optimization by Verilog engineer; manually constructed rule library
techniques.effect_target_headline: At the largest search budget, our method outperforms vanilla LLM by 4.11% for area-oriented optimization and 3.58% for delay-oriented optimization (area Impr@210: AutoPPA-DS 15.31% vs DeepSeek-V3 11.20%)

extraction.notes: Hardware RTL optimization of existing benchmark designs (LLM edits human-written Verilog); NF outcome is PPA. Correctness is a filter (testbench equivalence) and not reported as a separate rate. Delay can degrade in area-oriented mode (e.g., -4.85% delay vs RTLRewriter setting, -14.79% at 12nm). SymRTLO comparison uses self-reported numbers under different synthesis settings, acknowledged by authors. No code link. Tables partially garbled.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Trains reasoning world models that predict ThreadSanitizer and Caliper outcomes; the only code-producing evaluation is LLM repair of data races in human-written DataRaceBench programs, and the Caliper part is prediction/ranking, not generation. Race-freedom is also closer to correctness than an NF dimension.
extraction.title: Learning Reasoning World Models for Parallel Code
extraction.notes: Race-fixing loop with world-model feedback on DataRaceBench (human-written code) reports race-free percentages measured by ThreadSanitizer; a reviewer could argue data races map to CWE-362 (security), but the repaired code is human-written benchmark code, so EC4/adjacent. Caliper world model only ranks code pairs (prediction task).

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes FACT, a three-stage LLM agent workflow (pattern discovery with retrieval of CUTLASS examples, kernel synthesis with correctness/benchmark loop and auto-tuning, composition) that generates GPU kernels, and reports measured speedups of the generated code.
extraction.title: FACT: Compositional Kernel Synthesis with a Three-Stage Agentic Workflow

techniques.technique_name: FACT: agentic CUTLASS transpilation with retrieval of vetted CUTLASS examples, verify-and-benchmark refinement loop, agent-driven architecture-specific auto-tuning, dynamic pattern registry and multi-pattern composition
techniques.tools: CUTLASS 3.8.0 (commit ea46e277); NVCC via torch.utils.cpp_extension; CUDA 12.4/PyTorch 2.4.1 (A100), CUDA 12.8/PyTorch 2.8.0 (H100); Torch-TensorRT 2.4.0; torch.allclose rtol=1e-3 atol=1e-5
techniques.iterations: Loop until pattern passes correctness and achieves satisfactory performance (no max stated); auto-tuning sweeps 16-98 configurations per problem
techniques.metrics: efficiency: end-to-end latency and speedup vs PyTorch eager/cuBLAS, TFLOPS and percent of peak (5 warmup + 20 timed iterations, averaged over 20 trials) [execution]; correctness: element-wise allclose verification [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: KernelBench Level 1 problems 1, 3, 6 (GEMM); KernelBench Level 3 problem 44_MiniGPTBlock; Llama 3 8B decoder block from HuggingFace (5 workloads)
techniques.models: GLM 4.7, size not stated, open, instruct
techniques.baselines: PyTorch eager (cuBLAS TF32/FP16); PyTorch Inductor max-autotune; Torch-TensorRT
techniques.effect_target_headline: FACT achieves 2.03× speedup on MiniGPT (vs. Inductor: 1.89×, TensorRT: 1.85×) and 1.41× on Llama 3 8B (vs. Inductor: 1.17×, TensorRT: 1.18×); Level 1 GEMM 1.06×–1.18× on A100 and 0.84×–1.80× on H100 over cuBLAS

extraction.notes: No LLM-without-technique or raw-CUDA LLM agent baseline; comparisons are against libraries/compilers only. Only 5 workloads; correctness verification is a gate, no pass rate reported. LLM identity (GLM 4.7) appears only in the artifact statement. On H100 some kernels are slower than cuBLAS (0.92x, 0.84x). Part of the speedup comes from mixed precision (FP16 inputs) vs TF32 baseline. Variance stated as <1%. Limitations section present but short; no compute/token cost.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes an LLM-based lift-transfer-lower framework (executable IR, verification loops, reference-guided patching) that adapts expert CUDA attention kernels into new variants; the LLM-produced kernels are evaluated for runtime efficiency (TFLOPS, speedup) alongside correctness.
extraction.title: CuBridge: An LLM-Based Framework for Understanding and Reconstructing High-Performance Attention Kernels
extraction.venue: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (per metadata; full text is arXiv:2605.05023v1)

techniques.technique_name: CuBridge (lift-transfer-lower via executable CuIR with IR-level verification and reference-guided patch lowering)
techniques.tools: CuIR backend executor (numerical comparison vs PyTorch reference, tolerance e.g. 1e-2 for fp16); FlashAttention v2.8.0 as source expert kernel; NVIDIA A100/H100
techniques.iterations: Lifting and IR transfer: regenerate/refine until IR output matches reference or max_iterations (value not stated); lowering via ReAct line-level Edit_Line patching; best-of-k with k = 10, temperature 0
techniques.metrics: efficiency: throughput TFLOPS, latency (ms), speedup and geometric-mean normalized speedup [execution]; correctness: pass/fail vs PyTorch reference, Pass@1/3/5
techniques.benchmarks: Own suite: 8 attention variants not in FlashAttention (PrefixLM, Global Sliding Window, Share Question Mask, Causal Blockwise Mask, Relative Position, ReLU, Sigmoid, PrefixLM+Softcap+Sigmoid combo) x 3 model configs (Llama2-7B, Qwen2.5-72B, Llama3.1-405B) x seq len {1k,2k,4k,8k} on A100 and H100; ablation 96 test cases (8 variants x 12 sequence lengths) on H100; FlashInfer comparison incl. 4 native variants; GEMM+ReduceSum case study (5 shapes)
techniques.languages: CUDA C++ (IR in Python, specifications in PyTorch)
techniques.models: GPT-5, size NR, closed, reasoning; Claude-3.5-Sonnet, size NR, closed, instruct; DeepSeek-V3, 671B MoE (size not stated in paper), open, instruct; Qwen-3-235B, 235B, open, instruct; Qwen-3-32B, 32B, open, instruct
techniques.baselines: PyTorch operator composition; FlexAttention (template compiler); Qimeng-Attention (LLM-based, GPT-5); FlashInfer v0.6.0 (expert library); ablation: vanilla GPT-5 single-shot rewrite, GPT-5 + ReAct without CuIR
techniques.effect_target_headline: average speedups of 16.03× over general frameworks, 1.39× over template-based compilers, and 3.33× over prior LLM-based approaches (A100 and H100); ablation on H100: Norm. Speedup 4.19× (CuBridge) vs 1.23× (GPT-5 + ReAct) vs 1.00× (GPT-5)
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: Pass@5 = 1.00 for GPT-5 + CuBridge vs 0.38 for GPT-5 and 0.58 for GPT-5 + ReAct (Pass@1 0.70 vs 0.21 vs 0.41), 96 test cases on H100; "achieves 100% correctness" in end-to-end evaluation

extraction.notes: Venue taken from metadata (ACL); PDF itself is arXiv v1 with ACL-style Limitations section. LLM edits expert-written kernels (adaptation to new semantics), so artifact is LLM-edited code with new functionality, not pure refactoring. Headline efficiency comparisons to Qimeng-Attention use GPT-5 for both; best-of-k=10 reporting best performance, no variance or statistical tests. No token/call/cost reporting. Limitations section is short (2 items). Appendix tables 4 and 5 are garbled in extraction. Max refinement iterations not specified. No code URL given.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Empirically evaluates three prompting strategies and LoRA fine-tuning applied to five LLMs for generating code, and reports quantitative security outcomes (CodeQL-detected CWEs, severity-weighted reduction) for the generated code.
extraction.title: On Fixing Insecure AI-Generated Code through Model Fine-Tuning and Prompting Strategies

techniques.technique_name: Negative Example Prompting (NEP)
techniques.tools: CodeQL (evaluation only); custom regex script for Go
techniques.iterations: single regeneration: model's own raw insecure sample is included in the prompt with an instruction not to generate insecure code like it
techniques.metrics: security: CWE severity-weighted percentage reduction vs raw output (CodeQL severity = P75 of CVSS 3.1 of related CVEs) [tool-static]; percentage reduction in number of samples containing one or more CWEs [tool-static]; categories of fully/partially removed and introduced CWEs; Cramer's V between original and introduced CWEs; all detections manually checked by first author
techniques.benchmarks: 10 CWE scenarios (partial code snippets) from Majdinasab et al. Copilot replication study (Python), manually ported to JavaScript (Express.js), Java (Servlet) and Go (net/http); 10 samples per scenario per model per technique
techniques.models: GPT-4.1, size NR, closed, general-purpose; Gemini 2.0 Flash, size NR, closed, general-purpose; o4-mini, size NR, closed, reasoning; DeepSeek R1 Distill 32B, 32B, open, reasoning; GPT-5, size NR, closed, general-purpose with reasoning
techniques.baselines: raw model output (no technique); compared with CoT, MP and fine-tuning
techniques.effect_target_headline: 33.75% reduction in overall CWE severity (GPT-4.1 average); JavaScript showed a negative average reduction of -5.6% in the number of samples containing CWEs

techniques.technique_name: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) security prompting
techniques.tools: CodeQL (evaluation only); custom regex script for Go
techniques.metrics: security: CWE severity-weighted percentage reduction vs raw output (CodeQL severity) [tool-static]; percentage reduction in number of samples containing CWEs [tool-static]; introduced-CWE categories
techniques.benchmarks: 10 CWE scenarios (partial code snippets) from Majdinasab et al., ported to 4 languages; 10 samples per scenario per model
techniques.models: GPT-4.1, size NR, closed, general-purpose; Gemini 2.0 Flash, size NR, closed, general-purpose; o4-mini, size NR, closed, reasoning; DeepSeek R1 Distill 32B, 32B, open, reasoning; GPT-5, size NR, closed, general-purpose with reasoning
techniques.baselines: raw model output (no technique); compared with NEP, MP and fine-tuning
techniques.effect_target_headline: CoT reduced overall CWE severity by 39.8% for Gemini 2.0 Flash, 43.0% for o4-mini, 39.8% for DeepSeek R1 32B Distill, 49.8% for GPT-5, and 50.0% for GPT-4.1

techniques.technique_name: Meta Prompting (MP)
techniques.tools: CodeQL (evaluation only); custom regex script for Go
techniques.iterations: model first generates a security-oriented prompt, which is appended to each scenario prompt before generation
techniques.metrics: security: CWE severity-weighted percentage reduction vs raw output (CodeQL severity) [tool-static]; percentage reduction in number of samples containing CWEs [tool-static]; introduced-CWE categories
techniques.benchmarks: 10 CWE scenarios (partial code snippets) from Majdinasab et al., ported to 4 languages; 10 samples per scenario per model
techniques.models: GPT-4.1, size NR, closed, general-purpose; Gemini 2.0 Flash, size NR, closed, general-purpose; o4-mini, size NR, closed, reasoning; DeepSeek R1 Distill 32B, 32B, open, reasoning; GPT-5, size NR, closed, general-purpose with reasoning
techniques.baselines: raw model output (no technique); compared with NEP, CoT and fine-tuning
techniques.effect_target_headline: MP reduced overall CWE severity by 69.3% for GPT-4.1, 58.8% for Gemini 2.0 Flash, 56.0% for o4-mini, 52.8% for DeepSeek R1 32B Distill, and 65.3% for GPT-5

techniques.technique_name: LoRA fine-tuning on secure code samples
techniques.tools: CodeQL (to verify training samples free of CWEs, and for evaluation); OpenAI fine-tuning dashboard; Google Vertex AI
techniques.metrics: security: CWE severity-weighted percentage reduction vs raw output (CodeQL severity) [tool-static]; percentage reduction in number of samples containing CWEs [tool-static]; introduced-CWE categories
techniques.benchmarks: 10 CWE scenarios (partial code snippets) from Majdinasab et al., ported to 4 languages; 10 samples per scenario per model; fine-tuning data: manually created secure completions per scenario per language
techniques.models: GPT-4.1, size NR, closed, general-purpose; Gemini 2.0 Flash, size NR, closed, general-purpose; o4-mini, size NR, closed, reasoning; DeepSeek R1 Distill 32B, 32B, open, reasoning (GPT-5 not fine-tuned)
techniques.baselines: raw model output (no technique); compared with NEP, CoT and MP
techniques.effect_target_headline: Fine-Tuning reduced overall CWE severity by 80.5% for GPT-4.1, 80.8% for Gemini 2.0 Flash, 75.5% for o4-mini, and 82.8% for DeepSeek R1 32B Distill

extraction.notes: Fine-tuning evaluated on the scenarios whose secure completions formed the training data (possible train/test overlap, not discussed). Generation time and memory were said to be recorded but are not reported. Sample totals inconsistent (9,600 in 4.1.1 vs 9,300 in 4.2 and conclusion). No functional correctness check. Heatmap figure (Fig. 9) is garbled in the extraction. Fig. 12 caption duplicates Fig. 11 (says MP with DeepSeek though text describes CoT with o4-mini). Severity-based improvement reported; count-based improvement sometimes negative for NEP/CoT. Inference for closed models ran through GitHub Copilot in VS Code.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes VibeServe, a multi-agent coding-agent loop (planner + implementer/judge/profiler-backed evaluator) that generates entire LLM serving systems, and reports the runtime efficiency (throughput, latency, TTFT, goodput) of the LLM-generated code against vLLM/SGLang and ablations.
extraction.title: VibeServe: Can AI Agents Build Bespoke LLM Serving Systems?

techniques.technique_name: VibeServe (outer issue-tracker planning loop + inner Implementer / Accuracy Judge / Performance Evaluator agents with serving-systems skills library)
techniques.tools: Codex CLI v0.125 (GPT-5.5 Medium); Claude Code v2.1.122 (Opus 5, Scenario B); Nsight Systems and PyTorch profiler; user-provided accuracy checker and benchmark scripts; MCP server; git checkpoints
techniques.iterations: Outer loop rounds per scenario (e.g., 60 rounds/25.0 h in Scenario A, 15 in C/D, 16 in E, 7 in F, 20 in G); inner loop retries until accuracy checker passes or retry budget is exhausted; Orchestrator may revert to earlier checkpoints
techniques.metrics: efficiency: token throughput, goodput under SLO, TTFT, TPOT, p50 latency, speedup vs baseline serving system [execution]; correctness: accuracy gate vs Hugging Face reference implementation (greedy-output match, teacher-forced top-1 match, image MAE/PSNR/SSIM) [execution], used as acceptance gate rather than reported outcome

extraction.notes: Systems paper: the generated artifact is a whole LLM serving runtime written by coding agents; NF outcome is runtime efficiency of that generated code. Correctness acts only as an acceptance gate (accuracy checker), not reported as a separate outcome. Most results are single runs per scenario (B notes ~±10% node variation, paired same-node runs). Limitations only briefly noted in conclusion (maintainability of generated systems unmeasured, single node). Figures with speedup curves are garbled in extraction; Table 1 (calls/time per role) and Table 6 (ablations) partially garbled but readable.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Benchmark and evaluation-protocol paper (CUDABeaver, 213 broken CUDA kernels, 7 LLM fixers) that measures whether LLM repairs preserve performance; its varied axes (performance gate, iterative vs repeated sampling, feedback richness, history depth) are evaluation-protocol settings rather than techniques assessed for improving code quality, and efficiency is reported only as a combined correctness-plus-speedup pass@k gate and an iter-1 vs iter-N degeneration analysis.
extraction.title: CUDABeaver: Benchmarking LLM-Based Automated CUDA Debugging
extraction.notes: Borderline. A reviewer could instead include it as a technique-evaluation of an iterative execution-feedback CUDA repair loop (family feedback-loop, signal compiler + test-execution): it reports efficiency-relevant outcomes such as pass@5 vs performance-gate p (e.g. GPT-5.4 55.5% at p=0.0 to 15.5% at p=1.5), iter-1 vs iter-N median speedup and degeneration rate (9.1% to 56.2%), and feedback-richness effects (GPT-5.4 31.0% at L0 to 43.7% at L3*), but per-variant efficiency is never reported separately from the combined pass@k gate. Repaired code is LLM-generated (broken starts from LLM generation, 17 manually injected). Code/data: https://github.com/HaoyangChen23/CUDABeaver. Some tables garbled in extraction.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Benchmark paper that empirically evaluates iterative self-refinement (compile/execution feedback) and tool-augmented profiling-feedback loops against one-shot generation of LLM-written CUDA code, reporting expert-relative runtime speed (efficiency) alongside correctness.

Borderline: efficiency figures describe the synthesized hardware (largely from tool-driven grid-search DSE) with no no-technique efficiency baseline, and the code is LLM refactoring of existing application code.

extraction.notes: Short case-study paper (~6-7 pages). LLM edits existing human-written expert kernels (optimization of existing code), but the artifact is LLM-generated code, so included; borderline with EC4/adjacent. Underlying LLMs not named. Only one run reported, no variance. Text gives CKKS-Rot 4874->3754 us (1.31x) while Table I gives 4854->3714 us (1.3x); TFHE bootstrap 10->4 ms (2.5x). 'Security checks' are cryptographic parameter checks, not code vulnerability measurement. Evolved code is merged into jaxite PRs #88-#90; compute reported only as 24 hours on 100 TPUv5e chips. Lessons-learned section partly serves as limitations.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes CDC, a training-free constrained denoising framework for diffusion code LLMs; its MDFI instantiation injects static-analysis feedback during denoising to improve security of generated code, with quantitative security (sec@1, func-sec@k) outcomes on CWEval and LLMSecEval+.
extraction.title: Constrained Code Generation with Discrete Diffusion

techniques.metrics: security: sec@1 (security oracle pass rate) and joint func-sec@1/5/10 [execution, benchmark security oracles]; correctness: func@1 [execution]; edit locality (edited tokens, edit span, edit clusters) and token cost

techniques.effect_target_headline: On CWEval, CDC increases fs@1 from 12.04% to 34.26% ... (func@1 26.85% → 39.81%, sec@1 18.52% → 41.67%); On LLMSecEval+, CDC ... increasing sec@1 from 54.67% for vanilla diffusion and 58.67% with secure prompting to 80.67%
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: CWEval func@1 26.9 -> 39.8 (+13); LLMSecEval+ func@1 32.0 -> 30.7 (-1) (Dream-Coder 7B, Table 2)

extraction.notes: Only the MDFI instantiation targets an NF dimension (security). Security evaluated with a single diffusion backbone. 'Efficiency' in the paper refers to generation token cost and edit locality, not runtime efficiency of the code. AR re-prompting still obtains highest fs@1. LLMSecEval+ prompt count missing in text. Tables partly garbled but key numbers stated in prose. No code URL; no variance reported.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes a retrieval-augmented, compiler-in-the-loop agentic framework in which frozen LLMs refactor (edit) Lean 4 proofs, largely LLM-generated prover outputs, and reports quantitative NF outcomes on the LLM-edited code: proof-length compression, dependency reduction, compilation time/heartbeats and cross-version compatibility. extraction.notes: Eligibility borderline: artifact is Lean formal proofs (code) refactored by an LLM; competition inputs are LLM-generated proofs (ProofOptimizer releases, Seed-Prover), research inputs are human-written (could be read as adjacent/EC4). Proof length treated as readability-maintainability proxy; compile time/heartbeats as efficiency. Correctness enforced as a compile gate, not reported as an outcome. Length-only retrieval worsened relative compile time on miniF2F (-103.98%), so efficiency is mixed without reranking; heartbeat relative reduction negative for several non-reranked variants. Zero-shot version transfer: better than originals on miniF2F but worse on PutnamBench. Strategy bank decontaminated against eval set (exact + embedding + LLM judge); no contamination check of frontier LLMs. Dataset release claimed but no URL given; prompts partially elided. Std devs only across 5 compilations, not across agent runs. ~10,000 GPU-hours and ~$5,000 API cost total. Tables partly garbled but recoverable.
