techniques.effect_target_headline: speedups of 92.68× on Fused MoE, 1101.02× on DSA TopK Indexer, and 181.35× on DSA Sparse Attention relative to the PyTorch reference implementations (FlashInfer: 47.08×, 52.03×, 10.33×); official contest Fused MoE kernel 1.71× speedup over the FlashInfer baseline

extraction.notes: Human-in-the-loop orchestration (redirecting search, supplying references) is part of the technique, so results are not fully autonomous. Correctness is a gate, not a reported rate. Single model, single run per kernel, no ablation of workflow components; per-token-cost curves in figures not extractable. Discusses benchmark exploitation (reward hacking via output caching) and anti-hacking rules, but no formal threats section. Technical report (~7 pages + NCU appendices).

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes an LLM-driven C-to-Rust (Aya) eBPF translation pipeline whose post-generation loop uses compiler, kernel-verifier, a safe-Aya static analyzer and symbolic equivalence feedback; reports quantitative security outcomes of the LLM-generated Rust (safety-policy pass rates, unsafe-operation counts, verifier-accepted bugs fixed) plus bytecode-size and runtime overhead, alongside equivalence (correctness).
extraction.title: Heimdall: Formally Verified Automated Migration of Legacy eBPF Programs to Rust

techniques.technique_name: HEIMDALL (Deterministic): scripted six-stage pipeline (LLM translation, compile + kernel-verify repair, safe-Aya static safety check, angr symbolic execution, Z3 equivalence check, LLM bug triage with counterexample-guided repair)
techniques.tools: rustc 1.93.1 with lint guards (deny unused_unsafe, clippy::multiple_unsafe_ops_per_block, clippy::undocumented_unsafe_blocks, unused must_use); Linux kernel 6.8 eBPF verifier; custom pattern-based safe-Aya safety engine (11 rules); angr 9.2 with authors' eBPF backend; Z3 4.13; clang 14.0.0, bpftool v7.4.0, libbpf v1.4; tree-sitter-rust for unsafe-op counting
techniques.iterations: Stateless LLM re-prompted with stage feedback (compiler errors, verifier diagnostics, safety violations, Z3 counterexamples) until all of compile, kernel verify, safety and equivalence pass, or LLM triage returns Bug Found; maximum rounds not stated
techniques.metrics: security: safety-policy pass rate (tool-static, authors' safe-Aya analyzer), unsafe operations per program (tool-static, tree-sitter-rust), verifier-accepted bugs found/fixed and kernel-memory leaks closed (execution + upstream developer confirmation); efficiency: bytecode size overhead Rust/C (tool-static, .text/prog sections), runtime overhead Rust/C ns/invocation via kernel.bpf_stats_enabled (execution); correctness: compile, kernel-verifier acceptance, Z3 conditional semantic equivalence (formal), runtime output match over 1,000 paired trials (execution)
techniques.benchmarks: Authors' dataset of 115 Aya-supported eBPF programs from 11 sources (libbpf-tools, libbpf-bootstrap, KEN samples, DAE, Fluvia, Hercules, Suricata, CRAB, XDP-FW, BMC, cache_ext); 51-program comparison subset (44 libbpf-tools + 7 others); synthetic bug set of 34 programs (16 buggy, 18 correct)
techniques.models: Claude sonnet-4.6, closed, general/instruct; Claude opus-4.6, closed, general/instruct; gpt-5.4, closed, general/instruct
techniques.baselines: Unrestricted coding agents (Claude Code with sonnet-4.6 and opus-4.6, Codex with gpt-5.4, Gemini-CLI with gemini-3-flash-preview) iterating until a compilable translation they believe equivalent
techniques.effect_target_headline: Safety: 43/51 (84%) for HEIMDALL (Deterministic) opus-4.6 vs 18/51 (35%) for baseline opus-4.6 (Table 2)
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: KV ∩ Safety ∩ Equiv.: HEIMDALL (Deterministic) reaches 23-32/51 (45-63%) vs baseline agents 2-6/51 (4-12%)

techniques.technique_name: HEIMDALL (Agentic): coding agent following the same six stages via tool-mediated reasoning with access to compiler, kernel verifier, safety analyzer and equivalence-checker counterexamples
techniques.tools: Claude Code 2.1.112, Codex 0.116.0, Gemini-CLI 0.36.0 harnesses; rustc 1.93.1 lint guards; Linux kernel 6.8 eBPF verifier; safe-Aya safety engine (11 rules); angr 9.2 eBPF backend; Z3 4.13; llvm-objdump for binary inspection; tree-sitter-rust
techniques.iterations: Agent iterates (with subagents) until compile, kernel verify, safety and equivalence all pass for every entry point or a bug is reported; maximum rounds not stated
techniques.metrics: security: safety-policy pass rate (tool-static), unsafe operations per program (tool-static), bugs found/fixed incl. KASLR-breaking leaks (execution + upstream acknowledgement), bug triage TPR/FPR on synthetic set; efficiency: bytecode size overhead (tool-static), runtime overhead with 95% CI over N=100 paired trials on 10 programs (execution); correctness: compile, kernel verifier, Z3 equivalence, runtime output match
techniques.benchmarks: 51-program comparison subset; full 115-program dataset (opus-4.6); synthetic 34-program bug set
techniques.models: Claude sonnet-4.6, closed, general/instruct; Claude opus-4.6, closed, general/instruct; gpt-5.4, closed, general/instruct; gemini-3-flash-preview, closed, general/instruct
techniques.baselines: Same unrestricted coding agents without the HEIMDALL stages; HEIMDALL (Deterministic)
techniques.effect_target_headline: Safety: 50/51 (98%) for HEIMDALL (Agentic) opus-4.6 vs 18/51 (35%) for baseline opus-4.6 (Table 2); identifies and fixes nine verifier-accepted bugs, two of which leak randomized kernel addresses and break KASLR
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: KV ∩ Safety ∩ Equiv.: 50/51 (98%) agentic opus-4.6 vs 6/51 (12%) baseline opus-4.6; full scale 109/115 (94.8%) formally verified translations

extraction.notes: Code translation task (C to Rust), i.e. LLM-generated code. Main security metric is the authors' own pattern-based safe-Aya policy, which mixes security (unsafe escape hatches, discarded Results, over-reads) and idiomaticity (typed Aya APIs); readability-maintainability is targeted via 'idiomatic' but not measured separately. Unsafe-op counts are roughly unchanged between baseline and HEIMDALL (e.g. opus-4.6 19.7 vs 19.7 agentic, 29.5 deterministic); bytecode size overhead mostly slightly higher for agentic (opus 2.41x baseline vs 2.63x agentic, 2.12x deterministic), hence efficiency 'mixed'; runtime overhead only compared Rust vs C (1.14x-1.89x, one 0.44x), not vs baseline. Single run per setting in Table 2; CI only for runtime trials. The equivalence checker (formal) is mapped to 'static-analyzer' signal in the absence of a formal-verifier category. Bug triage on synthetic set: TPR 0.81, FPR 0.00, F1 0.90. No dedicated threats-to-validity section (Limitations only); no contamination discussion. Two-column PDF text heavily interleaved in code listings/appendices.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Evaluates feedback-conditioned planning configurations (tool feedback, summarization, strong-to-weak plan distillation) and proposes the CuGEdit controller for LLM agents that generate CUDA kernels, reporting execution-measured efficiency outcomes (fast rate vs baseline, speedup over torch.compile) alongside pass rates.
extraction.title: Towards Feedback-to-Plan Decisions for Self-Evolving LLM Agents in CUDA Kernel Generation
extraction.venue: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), PMLR 306

techniques.technique_name: Feedback-grounded explicit planning in a self-evolving agent (CUDAnalyst: debugger/analyzer/profiler feedback, SummaryAgent, PlanAgent, strong-to-weak plan injection)
techniques.tools: clang-tidy v18.0.0; Compute Sanitizer v2023.2.0 (CUDA Toolkit v12.2.91); Tree Sitter Language Pack v0.13.0 (tree-sitter v0.25.2); Nsight Compute v2025.2.1; OpenEvolve; LLM4AD; cProfile and line_profiler for Numba study
techniques.iterations: OpenEvolve single-island evolution, 200 iterations; generation-level re-evaluation of frozen trajectories (generations 0-7/0-10), k=5 code-generation attempts per sample (pass@5/fast@5)
techniques.metrics: efficiency: fast rate (fraction of samples outperforming the baseline implementation, relative speedup over official PolyBench-ACC/NPB/XSBench/robust-kbench baselines, minimum speedup across sizes) [execution]; Numba N-body speedup [execution]; correctness: compiled and pass rates (functional validation) [execution]; Banzhaf values and synergy terms for attribution
techniques.benchmarks: PolyBench-ACC full suite (empirical study); NPB-GPU CG/MG/FT, XSBench, robust-kbench (llama ffw, layernorm, mnist cross entropy (B), resnet block) for generalization; Numba N-body (CPU)
techniques.models: DeepSeek-V3.2 (thinking disabled), size NR, open, general; Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B, 30B MoE, open, code-specialized; DeepSeek-R1-0528, open, reasoning; Qwen3-235B-A22B, 235B MoE, open, reasoning; GLM-4.5-Air (backbone trajectory generator), open; Kimi-K2, MiniMax-M2.5, Gemini-2.5-Pro (alternative backbone trajectories)
techniques.baselines: implicit planning without feedback (NP+NF, OpenEvolve default full-rewrite loop); P+NF; NP+F; DummyPlan; randomized feedback (P+RF); NP+S; self-generated plans
techniques.effect_target_headline: reaching a 12.5× peak speedup for DeepSeek-R1guidance (Numba N-body, guided planning)

techniques.technique_name: CuGEdit (similarity-gated feedback/summarization controller with strong-to-weak plan distillation)
techniques.tools: GraKeL graph kernels (Weisfeiler-Lehman, Graphlet, Subgraph Matching, Propagation) on basic-block CFGs; CUDAnalyst tools (clang-tidy, Compute Sanitizer, Tree Sitter, Nsight Compute); OpenEvolve
techniques.iterations: evolutionary search within OpenEvolve; gating threshold tau_s = 0.42; iteration budget not stated for KernelBench runs
techniques.metrics: efficiency: speedup vs torch.compile [execution]; correctness: numerical tolerance 1e-4 validation [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: KernelBench Level 3, 50 workloads
techniques.models: DeepSeek-V3.2, open, general (code generation); DeepSeek-R1, open, reasoning (plans)
techniques.baselines: OpenEvolve without CuGEdit (Base); AI CUDA Engineer (agent, SOTA); CUDA-L1 (RL, SOTA)
techniques.effect_target_headline: CuGEdit achieves 2.08× to 10.32× speedup over torch.compile (KernelBench Level 3, 50 workloads)

extraction.notes: Primary contribution is an attribution/analysis layer (CUDAnalyst); planning-configuration effects are shown only in figures (no exact numeric headline in text for PolyBench-ACC fast/pass rates). Figure/table text heavily garbled (Banzhaf tables, Fig. 8, Fig. 29). CuGEdit compared against SOTA methods' reported best kernels, not re-run. Compute: inference-volume analysis and throughput (programs/hour) for the analysis pipeline; CuGEdit converges with approximately 40% fewer iterations. Only a short limitations paragraph; no contamination discussion for KernelBench. Model sizes partly not stated in the paper.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes Verilog-Evolve, an LLM feedback loop (simulation, Yosys synthesis, ABC timing proxy, GEMM downstream evaluator) with versioned candidate promotion and evolving skill memory; it reports quantitative synthesized-hardware efficiency metrics (cell count, ABC delay, area-delay proxy) of LLM-generated Verilog alongside functional correctness.
extraction.title: Verilog-Evolve: Feedback-Driven and Skill-Evolving Verilog Generation

techniques.technique_name: Verilog-Evolve: versioned major/minor candidate generation with multi-tool executable feedback, multi-objective scoring/promotion, and cross-session validation-gated skill evolution and retrieval
techniques.tools: iverilog/vvp (VerilogEval harness); Yosys synthesis; ABC (via Yosys) timing proxy; custom GEMM downstream evaluator over Yosys JSON netlists; optional DC/SEC adapter (not used in main results)
techniques.iterations: 3 major rounds x 5 minor candidates per round; promotion only if score strictly improves and gates pass; early stop on first functional pass in non-PPA runs
techniques.metrics: efficiency (hardware): Yosys cell count, DFF cells, multiplier cells [tool-static]; ABC delay proxy [tool-static]; area-delay-product proxy and aggregate GEMM downstream score [tool-static]; correctness: final success on public VerilogEval tests, best functional score, promotion pass, compile pass, GEMM held-out pass [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: VerilogEval-Machine and VerilogEval-Human (task counts not stated); 3 built-in mixed-precision GEMM tasks (int4_int8_mac_pe, mixed_precision_dot4, requantize_int32_to_int8)
techniques.models: BetterV-CodeQwen-7B (7B, open, code-specialized)
techniques.baselines: Direct LLM (no feedback); C-Bridge; Repair-only (iverilog feedback); Verilog-Evolve w/o skill evolution; evaluator-stack ablation (Correctness-only F, PPA-aware F+Y, Timing-aware F+Y+A, Downstream-aware F+Y+A+D); skill modes (no skills, static, evolved immediate, evolved validated)
techniques.effect_target_headline: GEMM tasks: Downstream-aware (F+Y+A+D) Cell Count 151.6, ABC Delay 5.48, ADP Proxy 332.5, Downstream Score 3.21 vs Correctness-only (F) 182.4, 6.81, 512.6, 4.92 (Table 2)
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: Final Success: Verilog-Evolve Full 85.3 (VerilogEval-Machine) and 72.8 (VerilogEval-Human) vs Direct LLM 76.8 and 61.5 (Table 1)

extraction.notes: NF dimension is hardware efficiency (synthesized area/cell count and timing-delay proxy of generated RTL) mapped to 'efficiency'; reviewer should confirm this counts as code efficiency. Efficiency metrics are only reported on 3 GEMM tasks, averaged; no efficiency results on VerilogEval. Single model (justified as isolating algorithmic contribution). Two-column extraction interleaves text; Table 2 DFF column shows downstream-aware worse (21.8 vs 18.3), and Timing-aware has lower Func. Pass (88.9). No variance, compute, artifacts, contamination or threats discussion. Short paper (~7 pages).

extraction.eligibility_reason: FT-Pilot uses a GNN plus an LLM analyzer/rewriter with RAG and auto-repair to rewrite existing human-written RTL (Verilog) designs for soft-error fault tolerance; the targeted and measured quality (SEU error rate under fault injection, plus hardware area and critical-path delay overhead of the added redundancy) is circuit reliability and hardware cost, not one of the review's code NF dimensions (readability-maintainability, efficiency, security).
extraction.title: FT-Pilot: Automated Fault-Tolerant RTL Rewriting via Vulnerability-Guided LLMs
extraction.notes: Borderline. If hardware area/delay overhead of LLM-rewritten RTL is accepted as an efficiency outcome, this could be included as a technique-proposal (hybrid: GNN vulnerability prediction + CoT analyzer + dual-KB RAG + compile/simulation auto-repair loop, max 3 rounds; Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5.3, GLM-5, Qwen-3.6 Plus; 14 RTL designs; baselines Unhardened, Full TMR, GNN+TMRG). Headlines: average area overhead +71% vs +112% (GNN+TMRG) vs +176% (Full TMR) on 11 designs at the same error rate; RAG ablation pass@1 74.29% -> 85.00%, pass@3 83.93% -> 95.60%. Inputs are pre-existing human-written designs being transformed, so it also resembles LLM refactoring of human code. No artifact URL given. Table V garbled in extraction.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes an agent skill system (phase skills, optimization/debug skills, independent evaluator) that drives a coding agent to generate NPU deployment code for LLMs, and reports quantitative runtime efficiency (TTFT, tokens/s, speedup, eta_scale) of the agent-produced implementations.
extraction.title: From Human Guidance to Autonomy: Agent Skill System for End-to-End LLM Deployment on Spatial NPUs
extraction.venue: Machine Learning for Architecture and Systems Workshop (MLArchSys), co-located with ISCA 2026

techniques.technique_name: Agent skill system for end-to-end LLM deployment on NPUs (eight-phase skill chain with numerical correctness gates, optimization and debug skills, independent evaluator agent)
techniques.tools: MLIR-AIR compiler stack; IRON baseline (commit 2b62dc7); CPU FP32 reference oracle; AMD XDNA 2 NPU in Ryzen AI 9 HX 370
techniques.iterations: Phases 0-6 each close with a numerical gate (absolute error, relative error, Pearson correlation thresholds) plus a human-in-the-loop checkpoint; Phases 4-5 require each optimization step to measurably improve performance; on gate failure a debug skill is invoked or the user is asked; Phase 7 independent evaluator re-runs all gates; no fixed max rounds
techniques.metrics: efficiency: prefill TTFT (s), decode tokens/s, speedup over hand-optimized IRON baseline, eta_scale sustained compute throughput / memory bandwidth normalized to reference [execution]; correctness: absolute/relative error and Pearson correlation vs CPU FP32 reference [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: End-to-end deployment of 9 decoder-only LLMs (Llama-3.2-1B reference; Llama-3.2-3B, SmolLM2-1.7B, Qwen2.5-0.5B/1.5B/3B, Qwen3-0.6B/1.7B/4B) on AMD XDNA 2 NPU, sequence length 2048
techniques.languages: MLIR-AIR / NPU kernels with host-side runtime code (language not specified)
techniques.models: Claude Opus 4.7 (1M context), size NR, closed, reasoning (max reasoning effort), via Claude Code
techniques.baselines: Hand-optimized IRON BF16 Llama-3.2-1B example (human-engineered); Llama-3.2-1B agent-assisted reference deployment for eta_scale normalization; no agent-without-skills ablation
techniques.effect_target_headline: speedup of 2.2× on prefill and 4.0× on decode over the hand-optimized baseline (Llama-3.2-1B, human-guided agent-assisted stage); autonomous deployments: ηscale ranges 0.24–1.07 on prefill and 0.28–1.27 on decode
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: All eight LLMs pass all correctness gates and are also manually verified.

extraction.notes: Short workshop paper (~5 pages + appendix). Headline speedups come from the human-guided stage, not the autonomous skill system; autonomous runs have no no-skill agent baseline, only eta_scale relative to the reference. Claims open-source deployments but no URL given. Table II garbled in extraction. Borderline eligibility: technique is a deployment workflow rather than a code-generation quality intervention per se.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes KLineage, a skill memory induced by deoptimizing expert GPU kernels and retrieved to guide LLM agents generating CUDA/AscendC kernels; reports kernel runtime speedups of the LLM-generated kernels against no-skill and memory-based agent baselines.
extraction.title: KLineage: Recovering the Missing When of Kernel Optimization by Deoptimizing Experts

techniques.technique_name: KLineage: conditioned SkillCards induced by validation-gated deoptimization of expert kernels, scope-conditioned retrieval, and LLM materialization under a compile/correctness/profile gate
techniques.tools: triton.testing.do_bench (warmup=25, rep=100); ncu; msprof; PyTorch 2.11.0+cu130; FlashInfer 0.6.11; TileLang 0.1.8; FLA 0.5.0; CANN 9.1.0; Torch-NPU 2.10.0; harnesses Claude Code and Codex
techniques.iterations: fixed budget: $10 per expert workload; 2-hour wall clock per transfer target; 30 minutes per KernelBench/MultiKernelBench problem
techniques.metrics: efficiency: kernel latency and speedup vs vendor reference / torch.compile / eager PyTorch, share of problems faster than reference [execution]; correctness: correctness check over three random seeds, % correct [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: 5 expert workloads (GEMM, Conv2d, FMHA, GDN, Top-K) on H100, RTX PRO 6000 and Ascend 910B; 5 transfer operators (KDA, Sparse Attention, Top-P, Fused Add-RMSNorm, GQA); KernelBench Level 2 (100 problems); MultiKernelBench Fusion (100 problems)
techniques.models: Claude Opus 4.6, closed, NR; DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, open, NR
techniques.baselines: AdaExplore; AccelOpt; expert-source prompting (agent given expert kernel sources); Codex agent without skills; vendor references (cuBLAS, cuDNN, FlashInfer, FLA, Torch-NPU), torch.compile, eager PyTorch
techniques.effect_target_headline: KLINEAGE raises mean speedup from 1.05× to 1.32× (KernelBench Level 2, NVIDIA vs torch.compile); mean speedup from 0.63× to 2.09× (MultiKernelBench Fusion, Ascend vs eager); KLINEAGE reaches 1.12× vs AdaExplore 0.25× and AccelOpt 0.54× (five expert workloads, vs vendor reference)
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: On Ascend, correctness rises from 68 to 100 problems; correct on all ten workload-platform pairs vs AdaExplore and AccelOpt failing on four and two

extraction.notes: Different backbones used per experiment (Claude Opus 4.6 for expert workloads; DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash for transfer and benchmarks), no same-experiment model comparison. 5 runs per workload with success-only geometric mean, no variance reported. Transfer targets excluded from skill induction (held-out), but LLM pretraining contamination of KernelBench not discussed. Baseline AdaExplore fallback-wrapper outputs excluded; post-hoc adapter audit marked. Several figures/tables (Tables 3, 8) garbled in extraction. No explicit threats-to-validity section; scope of comparison discussed in Appendix D.

extraction.eligibility_reason: AlphaEvolve evolves a compiler code-layout heuristic and the reported speedups (0.23% to 1.6%) are for third-party binaries (Clang, LevelDB, Redis, Search) laid out by that heuristic, i.e. the task objective of the discovered algorithm, not a non-functional quality measure of the LLM-generated heuristic code itself; build time/memory of the evolved heuristic is only stated qualitatively.
extraction.title: AI-PROPELLER: Warehouse-Scale Interprocedural Code Layout Optimization with AlphaEvolve
extraction.venue: AI Agents for Discovery in the Wild (AID-Wild) Workshop at ACM CAIS 2026
extraction.notes: Borderline: an LLM evolutionary loop with hardware cycle-count reward edits code_layout.cc; one could argue the evolved code's goal is runtime efficiency, but the efficiency measured belongs to the compiled target programs (algorithm-discovery objective), not the generated code. Reviewer should confirm scope decision for AlphaEvolve-style heuristic-discovery papers.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes HTAM, a hierarchical transition-attended memory that guides an LLM's multi-step evolution of CUDA kernels with execution feedback, and reports execution speedup (efficiency) alongside correctness on the full KernelBench suite against controlled baselines.
extraction.title: HTAM: Hierarchical Transition-Attended Memory for Operator Optimization

techniques.technique_name: HTAM (Hierarchical Transition Graph memory with transition-aware global direction selection, LLM local strategy selection, and execution-feedback evolution)
techniques.tools: KernelBench 0.2.0.dev0 (commit 423217d) evaluator; CUDA 12.8; PyTorch 2.9.1+cu128 (load_inline); NVIDIA A100-SXM4-80GB
techniques.iterations: T = 6 evolution steps per task (2 LLM calls per step: local selection + code generation, optional repair); best correct and fastest candidate returned
techniques.metrics: efficiency: geometric-mean speedup vs PyTorch eager (overall and per level L1-L3), Fast@1 (correct and faster than reference) [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: KernelBench full suite, 250 tasks (L1=100, L2=100, L3=50); 50-task stratified subset for backend study; 5 Robust-KBench tasks for transfer
techniques.models: DeepSeek-R1, 671B MoE, open, reasoning (main); DeepSeek-V4-Flash, open, instruct; GPT-4o, closed, instruct (backend study); DeepSeek-V3, Gemini-2.5-Flash-Thinking as direct-generation baselines
techniques.baselines: Direct generation (DeepSeek-R1, DeepSeek-V3, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, Gemini-2.5-Flash-Thinking; OpenAI-o3 reported); Best-of-N sampling (N=5); Feedback-only refinement; Flat memory retrieval; KernelBlaster and CudaForge (reported external results)
techniques.effect_target_headline: HTAM reaches 98.4% correctness, 84.0% Fast@1, and 1.978× geometric-mean speedup on the full 250-task KernelBench vs Flat Memory Retrieval 1.464× and DeepSeek-R1 direct generation 0.827× (same backbone)
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: 98.4% correctness vs 74.4% (DeepSeek-R1 direct generation) and 89.6% (Flat Memory Retrieval); improves correctness by 8.8 percentage points over the strongest reproduced baseline

extraction.notes: Single seed (42), no variance or significance tests. Ablations on full suite (e.g., w/o local memory 0.974×, randomized memory 0.812×). Cost: ~12 LLM calls, ~170k tokens, ~$0.21 per task under DeepSeek-R1 pricing, excluding one-time graph construction. Scoring weights w, epsilon, tau and lambda values not reported. Paper says task IDs, prompts, configs and supplementary are released but gives no URL. KernelBlaster/CudaForge/o3 rows are external reported numbers, not controlled. Robust-KBench transfer: GeoM 1.20× cold vs 1.58× with KernelBench memory (5 tasks; Cross Entropy regressed). Main table layout garbled but key numbers stated in text.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Besides a dataset/benchmark, the paper empirically evaluates an iterative agentic scaffold with performance-evaluator feedback and SFT distillation on ~4K trajectories for LLM-generated compiler passes, reporting execution speedup (efficiency) of the generated code jointly with correctness.
extraction.title: PassNet: Scaling Large Language Models for Graph Compiler Pass Generation

techniques.technique_name: PassAgent iterative agentic scaffold (file_editor + pass_evaluator giving matching/correctness/performance diagnostics and AS Score feedback, up to 50 iterations)
techniques.tools: PassBench evaluator (AST inspection, PoisonDispatchTensor dispatch interception, reverse evaluation); PyTorch 2.9.1 / Triton 3.5.1, CUDA 12.8 on NVIDIA A30; 20 warmup + 100 timed trials
techniques.iterations: Up to 50 iterations; agent refines until convergence; results reported at convergence (50 iterations)
techniques.metrics: efficiency: G-Mean speedup over eager on correct subgraphs, fast_1 (fraction of correct subgraphs with speedup >= 1.0) [execution]; combined: Error-aware Speedup Score ES_t and aggregated AS Score [execution]; correctness: sample and subgraph correctness ratios under numerical tolerance [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: PassBench fusible-subgraph tasks: 200 tasks, 2,060 subgraphs
techniques.languages: Python (PyTorch FX passes) with Triton/CUDA kernels
techniques.models: GPT-5.4 (closed); Claude-Opus-4.6 (closed); Claude-Sonnet-4.6 (closed); GLM-5.1 (open); MiniMax-M2.7 (open); Qwen3-4B (open); Qwen3-30B-A3B (open)
techniques.baselines: Single-shot (first-iteration) evaluation; Eager execution; TorchInductor (torch.compile default)
techniques.effect_target_headline: a single evaluation captures only 31%–51% of each agent's best AS score (mean 38%); at convergence best AS Claude-Sonnet-4.6 0.448 vs Inductor 0.706 (trails by 37%); all models G-Mean Speedup below 1.0

techniques.technique_name: SFT distillation of Claude-Sonnet-4.6 PassAgent trajectories (3,899 trajectories with AS > 0.1) into Qwen3 models
techniques.tools: PassBench evaluator used to filter trajectories (AS score > 0.1)
techniques.metrics: efficiency: G-Mean speedup over correct subgraphs, fast_1 [execution]; combined AS Score [execution]; correctness: Samp. CR, Sub. CR [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: PassBench fusible-subgraph tasks: 200 tasks, 2,060 subgraphs (training on 4,476 non-overlapping training samples)
techniques.languages: Python (PyTorch FX passes) with Triton/CUDA kernels
techniques.models: Qwen3-30B-A3B (open, MoE; Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507 student); Qwen3-4B (open); Claude-Sonnet-4.6 (closed, teacher)
techniques.baselines: Base Qwen3-30B-A3B and Qwen3-4B; frontier models
techniques.effect_target_headline: Qwen3-30B-A3B-SFT yields an AS of 0.371, a 2.67× gain over the base model (0.139); G-Mean Speedup 0.693 -> 0.809 (30B) but 0.953 -> 0.808 (4B); fast_1 0.6% -> 5.3% (30B), 0.2% -> 3.0% (4B)
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: Sub. CR and Samp. CR surge to 48.8% and 44.0% from 11.8% and 7.5% (Qwen3-30B-A3B-SFT)

extraction.notes: Primarily a dataset/benchmark paper; included because it evaluates an iterative feedback scaffold and SFT effects on speedup. G-Mean speedup is computed only over correct subgraphs, so it is confounded by which subgraphs pass (4B SFT G-Mean drops while correctness rises). AS Score is a composite of correctness and speedup defined by the authors. Iteration effect only reported as a share of best AS (Figure 3), not as a pure speedup. Timing uses 100 trials with stability re-runs; no variance across LLM runs. Memorization risk discussed; train/eval non-overlap stated.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes an agentic LLM framework (tree search with execution/profiling feedback and retrieval-augmented prompting) that generates Triton kernels, and reports quantitative runtime speedup (efficiency) of the LLM-generated code alongside correctness.
extraction.title: KernelEvolve: Scaling Agentic Kernel Coding for Heterogeneous AI Accelerators at Meta
extraction.venue: ISCA 2026 (International Symposium on Computer Architecture); arXiv:2512.23236v4 technical report

techniques.technique_name: KernelEvolve (graph-based tree search with universal operator, retrieval-augmented dynamic prompt synthesis, context-memory and deep-search sub-agents, hierarchical profiling feedback)
techniques.tools: TritonBench (correctness via torch.allclose + speedup), PyTorch/Torch Profiler, NVIDIA Nsight Compute (NCU v2025.3.1 cited), Triton Proton, Triton MPP (Multi-Pass Profiler), MTIA Insight, linter; torch.compile reference; hardware interpreters for NVIDIA/AMD/MTIA
techniques.iterations: Termination when wall-clock/artifact budget exhausted, progress stalls, or fitness threshold reached; ATen runs: 50 steps (10 draft steps without feedback + 40 tree-expansion steps); conv1d case: 300 search steps; selection policies greedy, MCTS (UCT) or evolutionary
techniques.metrics: efficiency: kernel latency (ms) and speedup over PyTorch (torch.compile) baselines, fitness = t_pytorch/t_triton or 1/latency [execution]; correctness: numerical equivalence via torch.allclose with tolerances / pass rate [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: KernelBench (250 problems, Levels 1-3); curated suite of 160 PyTorch ATen operators x 3 platforms (480 operator-platform configurations); Meta production case studies (conv1d in Convolutional Transformer, WuKong Optimized FM, InterFormer PFFN, MapIdTransform, MergeBucketizedDense Transform, Batch Event Truncate, plus others in Fig. 4 e.g. RMSNorm 2D backward, Llama-3.1-8B attention)
techniques.languages: Triton (Python DSL), Triton-TLX; MTIA Triton extensions / emitted C++ for debugging
techniques.models: Claude 4.5, size NR, closed, instruct; GPT-5, size NR, closed, reasoning; CWM (Meta Code World Model), size NR, open-weights, code-specialized; Llama, size NR, open, instruct (which backend produced which results is not stated)
techniques.baselines: PyTorch eager/compiled (torch.compile) reference implementations; optimized conv2d channels_last cuDNN path for conv1d; non-batched PyTorch loop for Batch Event Truncate; draft-phase (no feedback) sampling vs tree-expansion trajectory shown in Fig. 10
techniques.effect_target_headline: KernelEvolve achieves 1.25-17× speedups across Meta LLMs and production use cases (Figure 4); conv1d production shape on H100 FP16: 2.30× speedup over conv1d and 1.62× over the optimized conv2d baseline
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: 100% pass rate on all 250 problems across three difficulty levels (KernelBench); 100% correctness over all 480 operator-platform configurations (160 ATen operators x 3 platforms)

extraction.notes: Industrial system paper (Meta). Efficiency is measured by execution speedup vs PyTorch/compiler baselines, not vs an LLM without the technique; no ablation of components (retrieval, sub-agents, search strategy) and no per-LLM-backend results. Speedups are on production-targeted shapes; regressions on out-of-distribution shapes reported (e.g., 0.49-0.63x for conv1d, 0.78x / 0.80x for MapId edge cases) handled by fallback dispatch. KernelBench reports only pass rate, no speedups. No variance/repeated runs, no token/cost numbers (stated as future work), no threats-to-validity section. Inconsistencies: Fig. 13 caption says up to 6.22x while text/figure show 6.54x on MTIA v3; text says 2.54x on MI350 while figure shows 2.64; abstract says 'up to 17 times', contributions say '1.2 to 17 times'. Figures and tables are partially garbled in extraction (Figs 5, 9, 13, 15, 17). Appendix A provides one generated conv1d kernel source; system itself not released (internal URLs only).

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes an LLM agent harness (MCTS search with compile/validate/profile feedback) that generates and optimizes CUDA kernels, and reports quantitative runtime speedup (efficiency) of the LLM-generated kernels.

techniques.technique_name: Kernel Forge (MCTS-guided agentic CUDA kernel generation with compile/repair, numerical validation, benchmarking and guarded dispatch)
techniques.tools: nvcc 13.0 V13.0.88; CUDA 13.0; PyTorch 2.10.0+cu130; cuDNN 9.15.1; NVIDIA GB10 GPU (DGX Spark)
techniques.iterations: 50 optimization iterations per kernel variant (arms opt0, opt5, opt10, opt20, opt50); bounded repair loop for compile/runtime failures; MCTS with progressive widening and UCT (C = 1.0)
techniques.metrics: efficiency: operator-level latency speedup vs PyTorch eager (execution, 20 warmup + 100 timed runs); correctness used only as an admission filter (numerical match to captured eager outputs), no correctness rates reported

techniques.baselines: PyTorch eager execution (framework/vendor-backed kernels such as cuDNN, cuBLAS, ATen) for the same captured variant

extraction.notes: Baseline is human/vendor PyTorch eager kernels, not a no-search LLM baseline; opt0..opt50 arms reported only for cost, speedups shown at opt50. Code link referenced ('The code is available at: Kernel Forge') but URL lost in extraction. Figures garbled. No explicit threats-to-validity section, though limitations of validation are discussed. extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes TTT-RTL, per-design test-time reinforcement learning of an LLM with syntax/simulation/synthesis rewards, and reports the area-delay-power product of the LLM-generated Verilog (hardware efficiency) against published agent baselines and a frozen Best-of-N baseline. Borderline because efficiency is hardware PPA of synthesized RTL rather than software runtime, and the LLM is given the reference RTL as context.
extraction.title: Alpha-RTL: Test-Time Training for RTL Hardware Optimization

techniques.technique_name: TTT-RTL: per-design test-time RL (PUCT-indexed design-state pool, EDA-feedback prompting, entropic policy-gradient advantage, three-stage syntax/simulation/synthesis reward, adaptive KL-budget controller)
techniques.tools: iverilog/vvp (syntax and simulation), Yosys (logic synthesis), OpenSTA (timing/power), Nangate 45 nm typical corner (RTLLM v2.0), Sky130 HD (C910), verl training framework, vLLM
techniques.iterations: 100 gradient steps per design; B = 4 parent states, n = 4 rollouts/prompt (RTLLM v2.0) or n = 8 (C910; 3200-rollout budget); top-k = 2 children, pool cap 500; returns best-reward design
techniques.metrics: efficiency: reference-normalized PPA product (Area x Delay x Power) ratio, geometric/arithmetic mean, #Improved, #Best (RTLLM v2.0); area-delay product ADP (C910) [tool-static: Yosys + OpenSTA synthesis]; correctness: coverage = compilable and functionally correct designs vs reference testbench [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: RTLLM v2.0 (49 designs; common subset N = 44); XuanTie C910 ct_vfmau_lza_simd_half industrial unit (ablations); second C910 unit ct_vfdsu_fadd_close_s0_d (single-seed case study)
techniques.models: Qwen3-8B, 8B, open, reasoning/hybrid-thinking (RTLLM runs with lightweight SFT warm-up on 5,000 CodeV-R1 rows; C910 runs raw base); baseline systems use GPT-4o-mini, closed, instruct
techniques.baselines: EvolVE, VeriAgent, REvolution (frozen-policy agent baselines, numbers taken from Ping et al. 2026 with GPT-4o-mini); reference RTL implementations; frozen Best-of-N (N = 3200) and naive test-time RL; ablations of reuse (epsilon-greedy, none), advantage (expected reward/GRPO) and KL schedule (fixed ln 2, cosine)
techniques.effect_target_headline: On RTLLM v2.0 under Nangate 45 nm, TTT-RTL reduces the geometric-mean PPA product by 65.1% over the reference, outperforming the strongest published frozen-policy agent baseline under the same reference-normalized metric at 26.1% (GeoMean N=44: 0.349 vs 0.739 REvolution); C910 LZA: 59.4% ADP reduction over the original implementation
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: Coverage 48/49 designs vs 46/49 (EvolVE), 44/49 (VeriAgent), 45/49 (REvolution); on C910 the frozen Best-of-N never produces a functionally correct design within the 3200-rollout budget

extraction.notes: Paper body names the method TTT-RTL while the title says Alpha-RTL. Baseline numbers are copied from another paper (Ping et al. 2026) using GPT-4o-mini, so the main comparison is a systems comparison with different backbones (acknowledged by the authors). Main results single-seed (seed 42); 4-seed replication only for the KL controller, no significant difference (p >= 0.32). Compute: ~780 GPU-h for RTLLM sweep, ~320 GPU-h for C910 ablations. Artifact promised 'to be released on GitHub', no URL. Contamination: SFT corpus excludes RTLLM problems, memorization risk discussed. Efficiency here is hardware PPA (area/delay/power) from synthesis; reviewer should confirm this counts as code efficiency (prior HLS papers were included). Table 4 and Figure 2 partially garbled.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes Diff-SQL, a two-stage patch generation plus constraint alignment framework (inference-only Diff-ICL and RL-trained Diff-RL) in which LLMs rewrite slow SQL queries into faster equivalent ones, with execution-time efficiency (R-VES, speedup) and correctness (Delta EX) of the LLM-edited SQL reported.
extraction.title: Diff-SQL: SQL Efficiency Optimization via Patch Generation and Constraint Alignment

techniques.technique_name: Diff-ICL (inference-only two-stage: Patch Generator emits diagnosis + unified diff patch, Constraint Aligner revises patch for executability and semantic equivalence)
techniques.tools: Query execution plan (EXPLAIN ANALYZE for PostgreSQL) and column statistics supplied as context; rule-based unified-diff patch application
techniques.iterations: Fixed two stages (generate patch, then one alignment/revision pass); no execution feedback loop at inference
techniques.metrics: efficiency: R-VES (reward-based valid efficiency score; discretized gain g(tau) on execution speedup, credit only for result-equivalent queries) [execution]; speedup ratio vs expert (SR, harmonic mean) for direct generation only [execution]; correctness: Delta EX = 1 - EX (executable and result-multiset-equivalent) [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: Effi-SQL (new), PostgreSQL subset, 300 Slow-Fast pairs (90 Simple, 135 Moderate, 75 Challenging) on TPC-H SF3 and three 10x-scaled BIRD-Interact databases
techniques.models: Claude-Opus-4.5, closed, general; Claude-Opus-4.6, closed, general; Qwen3-Coder, open (size not stated), code-specialized
techniques.baselines: Direct full SQL generation with the same base model (same prompt context); R-Bot (LLM-selected rule-based rewrite); direct generation with GLM-4.7, DeepSeek-V3, MiniMax-M2, Kimi-K2-Thinking; ablation patch-only vs full Diff-SQL
techniques.effect_target_headline: Overall R-VES: Claude-Opus-4.5 71.33 -> 80.50 (+9.17); Claude-Opus-4.6 65.50 -> 77.92 (+12.42); Qwen3-Coder 55.17 -> 63.58 (+8.41) (PostgreSQL subset of Effi-SQL); abstract: improves R-VES by 10.0% on average
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: Overall Delta EX: Claude-Opus-4.5 6.00 -> 3.00 (-3.00); Claude-Opus-4.6 9.33 -> 5.00 (-4.33); Qwen3-Coder 25.67 -> 14.67 (-11.00); abstract: reducing execution accuracy degradation by 6.11% on average

techniques.technique_name: Diff-RL (two-stage Diff-SQL trained on a 7B model: SFT optimization-distillation of Patch Generator, SFT warmup + GRPO with execution-grounded reward for Constraint Aligner, LoRA)
techniques.tools: verl framework, LoRA (rank 64, alpha 128), vLLM, 4x A100 80G; GRPO group size 8, 300 steps; reward from executing patched SQL on PostgreSQL (TPC-H 0.1G and unscaled BIRD-Interact for RL feedback)
techniques.metrics: efficiency: R-VES [execution]; correctness: Delta EX [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: Effi-SQL PostgreSQL subset (300 pairs); also MySQL subset (multi-dialect check); training data 4,283 validated PostgreSQL instances from StackOverflow-mined Slow-Fast pairs
techniques.models: Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct, 7B, open, instruct (student); teacher model for distillation not named
techniques.baselines: Same base model with direct full SQL generation; ablations: patch-only SFT, SFT warmup without RL
techniques.effect_target_headline: Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct overall R-VES 33.42 -> 46.83 (+13.41) on Effi-SQL PostgreSQL subset; MySQL R-VES 19.88 -> 30.75 (+10.87)

extraction.notes: Artifact is SQL queries rewritten (edited) by the LLM from human-written slow SQL; included because the LLM generates the optimized code (cf. EC4/adjacent borderline). R-VES conflates correctness and speedup (only equivalent queries earn credit). Timing uses median of 3 runs and a 1.2x noise threshold justified from repeated runs; no repeated model sampling or significance tests. Training time reported (4.5 h SFT, 30 h GRPO); no token/call costs. Benchmark built from StackOverflow; contamination not discussed. Table 1 and Table 17 (SQL Server row missing) garbled in extraction. Human annotation (93.4% agreement) concerns benchmark construction, not evaluation of outputs. Limitations section brief, no threats-to-validity section.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes RTLScout, an agentic loop in which an LLM writes and refines RTL source (Spire/Verilog) under area/delay feedback from open-source synthesis and timing tools, reporting quantitative efficiency outcomes (area, delay, cell count) for the LLM-written code alongside functional correctness.
extraction.title: RTLScout: Joint Agentic Code and Synthesis Optimization for Efficient Digital Circuits

techniques.technique_name: RTLScout: four-phase pipeline combining ReAct agentic RTL rewriting, agent-guided synthesis optimization via source-local @abc_optimized decorators, arithmetic-architecture selection (sweep or @arithmetic_optimized decorator), and high-effort gate-level Deepsyn refinement, run inside a multi-run elite pool with z-score softmax seeding and lessons-learned feedback; Spire, a Python-embedded HDL, is introduced to carry source-local optimization intent
techniques.tools: Yosys (logic synthesis, post-synth cell and CMOS transistor count via stat -tech cmos); OpenROAD (static timing analysis); Verilator (lint + simulation); ABC with the &deepsyn engine; ASAP7 7 nm predictive FinFET PDK (7.5-track, RVT, TT corner, NLDM); Spire Python-embedded HDL
techniques.iterations: Phase 1 and 2: 6 runs per campaign (2 concurrent, 30 steps each, elite pool size 2, temperature 1.0, 3 fresh-first in Phase 1); RTLRewriter generalization uses 3 independent single-run repetitions per phase at 30 steps; Phase 3 sweep evaluates 180 synthesis runs per design (5 x 6 x 2 x 3); Phase 4 runs 50 distinctly seeded 20-minute Deepsyn trajectories per Pareto-optimal design (700 x 20 min total); agent stops at the step budget, best-design tracker snapshots every 100%-correct lower-cost evaluation
techniques.metrics: efficiency: post-mapping circuit area (um^2), delay (ps), area-delay product (10^3 um^2.ps), power, and Yosys post-synth cell count and CMOS transistor estimate [all tool-static / execution via Yosys + OpenROAD STA on ASAP7]; correctness: simulation pass rate against a golden self-checking testbench (exhaustive over all 2^32 input pairs for fpmul_f16; 16M/2M/>=10k vectors for the larger designs and RTLRewriter cases), Verilator lint, plus post-hoc combinational/sequential equivalence checking [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: fpmul_f16 (IEEE-754-compliant FP16 multiplier with subnormals, primary benchmark); fpadd_f32 (IEEE-754 binary32 adder); PDPU-16 posit dot-product unit, combinational and 5-stage pipelined tops; the 14 short-bench control-and-datapath cases of the RTLRewriter benchmark
techniques.languages: Spire (Python-embedded HDL introduced in this work), Verilog
techniques.models: GLM 5.2 (open-weights) as the underlying LLM for the agent campaigns
techniques.baselines: Starting (unoptimized) design; Deepsyn-only at matched compute (700x20 min and 700x40 min); phase-ablated configurations (Phase 3 only, Phases 1+2, Phases 1+3, Phases 1-3); commercial Cadence Genus reference FP16 multiplier from Larsson-Edefors on the same ASAP7 PDK; published RTLRewriter reference designs; an otherwise identical Verilog pipeline (for the Spire-vs-Verilog comparison)
techniques.effect_target_headline: On an IEEE-754-compliant 16-bit floating-point multiplier with subnormal support, RTLScout reduces area by 34% and delay by 38% relative to a starting design and outperforms a commercial-tool reference design on the ASAP7 technology. On 14 RTLRewriter benchmarks, the Spire-based pipeline achieves 16.3% lower mean per-case Yosys cell count than an otherwise identical Verilog pipeline. (fpmul_f16 best area 116 -> 77 um^2, best delay 1530 -> 949 ps; RTLRewriter mean per-case cell-count reduction vs the RTLRewriter reference: 10.9% Verilog, 25.8% Spire)
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: A best-design tracker snapshots every evaluation that achieves 100% correctness at lower cost; every Pareto-optimal fpmul_f16 design reported in this paper is furthermore verified exhaustively: all 2^32 input pairs are simulated at the gate level against a bit-exact golden model

extraction.notes: Domain is hardware RTL rather than general-purpose software; the NF dimension is circuit efficiency (area, delay, power, cell/transistor count) rather than program runtime, so a reviewer should confirm this fits the review's efficiency definition. Only one LLM (GLM 5.2) is evaluated, with no justification and no cross-model comparison. No threats-to-validity section and no contamination discussion, although the RTLRewriter benchmark is public. Tables 1, 4 and 5 are badly garbled in PDF extraction (column values run together); headline numbers were taken from the abstract, Section 5.3, Section 7 and the conclusion rather than from the garbled table cells. Cost reported precisely in Table 2 ($65.07 total for fpmul_f16, $0.04 per core-hour); context window growth reported as ~36k to ~69k tokens per run.

extraction.eligibility_reason: LLM agent (Llama 3-70B) generates PyTorch time-series architectures with a traceback-driven reflection loop that targets executability/shape validity; outcomes are forecasting/anomaly-detection accuracy of the trained models plus parameter count and inference latency of one generated architecture versus other architectures, not a non-functional quality measure of the generated code attributable to the technique. Borderline because inference latency of generated models is reported.
extraction.title: GenAutoML: An Agentic Framework for Dynamic Architecture Generation and Optimization in Time-Series Analysis
extraction.notes: arXiv 2606.05860v2. Reflection loop success reported as 100% validation within five iterations; latency (<0.01 ms per sample for WaveInterferenceNet vs 987.93 ms Chronos-T5-Mini) compares neural architectures, not code quality with/without the technique. Reviewer should confirm that ML-model inference latency is out of scope for IC3.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes and evaluates an LLM workflow (deoptimize, translate, reoptimize) for porting C++ to CUDA, measuring the performance (efficiency) of the LLM-generated CUDA code against direct translation, with feasibility (validation pass rate) as a co-outcome.
extraction.title: LLM-Based Porting of Optimized C++ to CUDA Through Deoptimization and Reoptimization

techniques.technique_name: Deopt-Reopt (Single-shot): LLM deoptimization of CPU C++, then CUDA translation, then reoptimization
techniques.tools: NVHPC 25.9 (nvc++), CUDA 12.6 (nvcc -O3 -arch=sm_90), cuDNN 9.5.1, NVPL 25.9, ArmPL 25.07.1; benchmark-specific validation drivers; CUDA events timing on H100 (GH200)
techniques.iterations: three sequential LLM calls (deopt, translate, reopt); trial fails if a required stage yields no passing code; last passing CUDA retained if reopt fails
techniques.metrics: efficiency: median kernel performance (GFlops or GB/s) over successful trials, min of 5 timed runs, Mann-Whitney U with BH-FDR [execution]; correctness/feasibility: success rate passing per-element relative-error validation [execution]; LOC of normalized code reported [tool-static]
techniques.benchmarks: 12 author-selected hand-optimized HPC kernels (Conv2D, BFFT, Softmax, BGEMM, DFSpMM, FFT, BTDMA, DDGEMM, Stencil, SpMM, GEMM, SpMV); 50 trials per mode and model
techniques.models: gpt-oss-120b (117B MoE, open, reasoning); qwen-3-235b-a22b-instruct-2507 (235B MoE, open, instruct)
techniques.baselines: Direct (translate then reoptimize, 2 calls); Direct-3 call-count-matched control (translate + 2 reoptimizations)
techniques.effect_target_headline: In Single-shot, among 18 testable cases Deopt-Reopt was significantly faster among successful trials (after BH-FDR correction) in five ... but Direct was faster in three
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: Deopt-Reopt sharply raises Q235 success on most kernels, ... whereas for O120 the effect is mixed and can even lower feasibility (e.g., O120 BTDMA Single-shot success 92% Direct vs 44% Deopt-Reopt; Q235 Conv2D 12% vs 96%)

techniques.technique_name: Deopt-Reopt (Iterative): PM/programmer multi-role loop with compile-run-validate repair and best-candidate selection over up to 3 generations per phase
techniques.tools: NVHPC 25.9 (nvc++), CUDA 12.6 (nvcc), cuDNN 9.5.1, NVPL 25.9, ArmPL 25.07.1; validation drivers; CUDA events timing on H100
techniques.iterations: up to 3 generations per phase; 1 PM call + 3 PG candidates per generation; one repair per PG on compile/run/validation error; deopt selects smallest-LOC valid code, reopt selects fastest valid code
techniques.metrics: efficiency: median kernel performance over successful trials, Mann-Whitney U with BH-FDR [execution]; correctness/feasibility: success rate [execution]; LOC progression [tool-static]
techniques.benchmarks: same 12 HPC kernels; 50 trials per kernel-mode-model (2400 Iterative trials)
techniques.models: gpt-oss-120b (117B MoE, open, reasoning); qwen-3-235b-a22b-instruct-2507 (235B MoE, open, instruct)
techniques.baselines: Direct Iterative (same loop without deoptimization phase)
techniques.effect_target_headline: after BH-FDR correction within Iterative seven were significant — five favored Deopt-Reopt (Q235 conv2d, ddgemm, and bgemm; O120 bfft and softmax) and two favored Direct (O120 and Q235 stencil)
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: Deopt-Reopt markedly raises Q235 Iterative feasibility, recovering several kernels (bgemm, spmm, gemm, dfspmm) that Direct rarely compiles (e.g., Q235 GEMM 2% vs 84%)

extraction.notes: Translation task (C++ to CUDA) rather than NL-to-code; LLM-generated CUDA is the evaluated artifact, so included. Exact prompts not printed in paper (in repo). Compute reported only as LLM call counts (D+R ~50% more calls). Performance conditioned on successful trials. Table II and figures garbled in extraction; headline numbers taken from prose. Limitations paragraph in conclusion serves as threats discussion.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes Arbor, a multi-agent tree-search framework in which LLM agents write and edit kernel, library and framework code across the LLM serving stack, and reports quantitative efficiency outcomes (throughput, throughput-interactivity Pareto) for the resulting system.
extraction.title: Arbor: Tree Search as a Cognition Layer for Autonomous Agents

techniques.technique_name: Arbor: heuristic-scored depth-first tree search over a dynamically expanding action space, with an Orchestrator agent delegating to dynamically-constructed Domain Specialists, a Critic agent (guardrails, root-cause analysis, introspection, stability monitoring), hard/soft skill decomposition, and a persistent cross-session knowledge base
techniques.tools: GPU profilers (bottleneck/GPU time share); vLLM and SGLang serving frameworks; ROCm/composable_kernel and ROCm/aiter libraries; Triton, HIP, ASM, CK kernel toolchains; RCCL; InferenceX benchmark harness; AMD Instinct MI355X and MI300X GPUs
techniques.iterations: Depth-first loop until action scores fall below a threshold or the wall-clock budget is exhausted; multi-day campaigns (ablation curves over 24 hours); automatic backtracking to last verified state after every revert or crash; example campaign on gpt-oss-120b used 30 actions (9 kept, 16 reverted, 3 crashed)
techniques.metrics: efficiency: output throughput (tokens/s/GPU) at concurrency 64, throughput-vs-interactivity (1/TPOT) Pareto frontier, TTFT, TPOT, request completion rate, per-kernel speedup [all execution]; correctness/accuracy: accuracy gate with <1% degradation, GSM8K accuracy used in the no-Critic ablation [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: InferenceX (SemiAnalysis) serving benchmark, concurrency 4-512, ISL = OSL = 1024; six production models on MI355X: gpt-oss-120b (MXFP4), DeepSeek-R1-0528 (FP8), MiniMax-M2.5 (FP8), GLM-5-FP8, Qwen3.5-397B-A17B (FP8), Kimi-K2.5 (MXFP4); three models re-run on MI300X
techniques.languages: Triton, HIP, GPU assembly, Composable Kernel (C++), Python (vLLM/SGLang framework and configuration code)
techniques.models: Agent backbones: frontier-tier reasoning LLMs at the capability level of Claude Opus 4.6 / 4.7 (closed, reasoning); per-agent assignment dynamic and configurable. Optimization targets (served models, not agents): gpt-oss-120b, DeepSeek-R1-0528, MiniMax-M2.5, GLM-5-FP8, Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, Kimi-K2.5
techniques.baselines: InferenceX vendor-optimized baseline configurations (manually optimized by engineering teams); ablations: single unstructured agent with the same tools (no tree search), Arbor without Domain Specialists, Arbor without the Critic
techniques.effect_target_headline: Arbor achieves up to 193% inference throughput-latency Pareto improvement over vendor-optimized baselines, while a single agent without the harness plateaus at +33% throughput improvement and crashes irrecoverably within hours; at concurrency 64: +48% gpt-oss-120b, +90% DeepSeek-R1-0528, +50% MiniMax-M2.5, +193% GLM-5-FP8, +40% Qwen3.5-397B, +60% Kimi-K2.5
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: each candidate is additionally gated on TTFT, TPOT, request completion rate, and accuracy (<1% degradation)

extraction.notes: Borderline on IC2 in scope terms: many kept actions are configuration/parameter changes (TP degree, max-seqs, block-size, tuning tables) rather than generated source code, though the paper also reports genuine LLM-written kernel and ROCm library rewrites (8-27% per-kernel speedup, +7% end-to-end). No code or data artifact URL is given; the open-source pull requests are mentioned but not linked. Agent prompts and scoring constants not published (constants acknowledged as hand-chosen, no sensitivity analysis). Ablation figure (Figure 4) is badly garbled in PDF extraction (encoding shifted); its numbers are recoverable only from the body text. Correctness is an accuracy gate rather than a reported co-outcome, except in the no-Critic ablation where accuracy fell to 0%.

extraction.eligibility_reason: The paper proposes an agentic LLM-judge data-curation pipeline used to select SFT trajectories, fine-tunes Qwen3-8B/14B/32B on the curated data, and reports a quantitative non-functional outcome for the resulting LLM-generated patches (the distribution of architectural-conformance verdicts, i.e. structural/maintainability quality) alongside SWE-bench resolved rate.
extraction.title: Beyond Correctness: Enhancing Architectural Reasoning in Code LLMs via Scalable Labeling with Agentic Judgment

techniques.technique_name: Agentic architectural judging pipeline for SFT data curation (Architecture Complexity Judge + Architecture Quality Judge with repository-specific generated rubrics), followed by supervised fine-tuning on the filtered trajectories
techniques.tools: OpenHands as the agent scaffold at inference (max 300 turns per instance); RepoForge environment-construction pipeline for the initial trajectory pool; MiniMax-M2.5 as the trajectory-generating teacher; both judges operate by static structural exploration of the repository with no code execution; 157 deterministic static architecture metrics (Chidamber-Kemerer suite, cyclomatic complexity, Maintainability Index, LCOM4, coupling/dependency-graph metrics, patch-specific metrics) implemented only as a comparison baseline, plus a random-forest predictor over them. The LLM backbone used for the judges themselves is never named.
techniques.iterations: Not a generation-time loop. Data selection is one pass per candidate example with thresholds ACJ >= Trivial and AQJ >= Acceptable; training is 3 epochs with loss masked to assistant trajectory tokens only. Inference uses OpenHands with max 300 turns per instance, pass@1.
techniques.metrics: readability-maintainability (architectural conformance / structural quality): distribution of AQJ four-tier verdicts over all generated patches - High, High-with-concerns (HWC), Acceptable, Low - produced by a repository- and issue-specific rubric with priority-ordered axes and prose anchors [llm-judge]; the ACJ five-level complexity verdict (Trivial/Low/Moderate/High/Expert over five axes) is used for data selection, not as an outcome [llm-judge]. correctness: SWE-bench resolved rate under pass@1 (all specified unit tests pass on first attempt) [execution]; patch precision = resolved issues / patches generated [execution]. Convergent validity: Spearman correlation of the judge verdicts against 157 static architecture metrics [tool-static].
techniques.benchmarks: SWE-bench Verified (500 verified bug-fixing instances) and SWE-bench Multilingual (300 bug-fixing instances across 9 non-Python languages). Training pool: 5,000 high-quality Python trajectories from RepoForge, filtered to 3,360 architecturally curated instances; the metric-based filtering baseline yields 1,548 instances. Stated to have no overlap between training and evaluation data.
techniques.languages: Python for training; evaluation additionally covers 9 non-Python languages via SWE-bench Multilingual (e.g., Ruby, Java)
techniques.models: Fine-tuned: Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-14B, Qwen3-32B (open-weights, instruct/reasoning). Teacher for trajectory generation: MiniMax-M2.5 (open-weights). Judge backbone: described only as 'a strong LLM' and never identified.
techniques.baselines: Original (base model, no fine-tuning); FullData (fine-tuned on the entire 5,000-trajectory pool, i.e. unfiltered SFT); Metrics (filtering by thresholded static architecture metrics, Qwen3-8B only); for the judge itself, random-forest prediction of ACJ/AQJ verdicts from 157 static metrics.
techniques.effect_target_headline: "our approach increases the proportion of architecturally conformant patches from 61-72% to 84-94% across model sizes" (abstract/introduction); per model, "For Qwen3-8B, the combined High+HWC proportion increases from 60.9% to 83.6%; for Qwen3-14B, from 64.0% to 87.1%; and for Qwen3-32B, from 72.1% to 93.5%." Versus the unfiltered FullData baseline the architectural quality is only comparable: "High+HWC proportions of 83.6% vs. 87.5% on Qwen3-8B, 87.1% vs. 83.9% on Qwen3-14B, and 93.5% vs. 93.3% on Qwen3-32B".
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: "Fine-tuning Qwen3-8B/14B/32B on 3,360 curated instances achieves resolved rates of up to 27.2% on SWE-bench Verified - up to 540% over the base model and 256% over unfiltered fine-tuning." Per model on SWE-bench Verified: 3.2% -> 17.4% (Qwen3-8B), 4.6% -> 17.8% (Qwen3-14B), 9.0% -> 27.2% (Qwen3-32B) versus Original; 6.8% -> 17.4%, 9.4% -> 17.8%, 15.6% -> 27.2% versus FullData. SWE-bench Multilingual: "our approach improves over the Original baseline by 286% - 420%" (1.4% -> 4.0%, 4.3% -> 9.7%, 3.3% -> 14%). Metric-based filtering baseline: 14.4% vs 17.4% on SWE-bench Verified and 4.7% vs 6.7% on Multilingual (Qwen3-8B).

extraction.notes: Main methodological concern for a reviewer: the architectural-quality outcome is measured by AQJ, the same author-built LLM judge that was used to select the training data, so the headline NF improvement is partly circular; the judge is never validated against human expert ratings (only against static metrics, where it deliberately does not correlate), and the LLM backbone powering the judges is nowhere identified. Against the unfiltered FullData baseline the architectural-conformance gain essentially disappears (83.6 vs 87.5, 87.1 vs 83.9, 93.5 vs 93.3), so the clear NF gain is only versus the untuned base model; the paper's distinctive claim versus FullData is about resolved rate and data efficiency, not conformance. Table 1 is hard to read because the AQJ columns are reported as relative changes to each model's own baseline while the baseline row is absolute, and the extraction garbles one cell ('17,1' for 17.1). Internal inconsistencies to check: the abstract says 286-424% cross-language improvement while Section 5.2 says 286-420%; Section 5.1 says 'improves the resolved rate by 174% - 256% compared to using the full dataset' where those figures are ratios rather than percentage improvements; Table 3's first row is labelled 'Original' with size 5,000 and value 6.8%, which is the FullData condition in Table 1, not the untuned base model; Table 3 lists SWE-Multi 5.0% for that row while Table 2 gives FullData Qwen3-8B as 3.0%. Tables 4 and 5 appear to have their captions swapped relative to their contents (the 'ACJ-style' table uses AQJ-correlated features). Results are single pass@1 runs with no variance, repeated runs or statistical tests, and no compute/cost figures despite the paper itself noting the token cost of agentic judging.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Studies a role-based agentic workflow (Planner, Analyzer with optional CodeQL, Fixer, Verifier) for detecting and patching real-world vulnerabilities in existing human-written C/C++ code (25 CVEs); this is LLM vulnerability analysis/repair of human-written code rather than improving the quality of LLM-generated code.
extraction.title: Security in a Workflow: Exploring Role-Based Agentic Architectures for Vulnerability Handling
extraction.notes: Outcomes are detection accuracy (44% Workflow 1) and fix accuracy (19%) judged by two authors with a rubric (Cohen's kappa 0.83) against developer patches; replication repo https://github.com/SriAbir/SecurityAgentWorkflow.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes a multi-agent RL training framework with an evolving, execution-verified skill library to make an LLM generate faster GPU (Triton/CUDA) kernels, and reports execution-time speedup of the generated kernels (KernelBench Fast_x) against strong baselines.
extraction.title: daVinci-kernel: Co-Evolving Skill Selection, Summarization, and Utilization via RL for GPU Kernel Optimization

techniques.technique_name: daVinci-kernel (SFT cold start on diversity-filtered data + joint multi-turn REINFORCE/TRLOO training of Skill Selection, Policy and Skill Summary agents sharing one backbone, with BM25+LLM skill retrieval injected at inference and execution-verified skill library updates)
techniques.tools: KernelBench execution environment (correctness + wall-clock speedup, profiling ratio of generated-kernel runtime); BM25 index; Qwen3-Embedding-8B + HDBSCAN for SFT diversity filtering; GPT-5.4 for SFT trajectory generation
techniques.iterations: multi-turn policy with execution feedback (5 turns in SFT data); RL with k=3 skill schemes + null scheme, n=4 rollouts each (16 per task), s=2 summary calls; skill admitted only if verified first-turn speedup >= max(beta, alpha*r1), alpha=beta=1.2; top-20 BM25 then up to 3 LLM-selected skills
techniques.metrics: efficiency: Fast_x = % of tasks with a functionally correct kernel achieving >= x speedup over the PyTorch reference, x in {1.0, 1.2, 1.5, 2.0}, last-turn and best-turn (execution)
techniques.benchmarks: KernelBench Level 1, Level 2, Level 3 (task counts not stated)
techniques.models: Qwen3-8B-Base fine-tuned (daVinci-kernel-8B), open, base; Qwen3-14B-Base fine-tuned (daVinci-kernel-14B), open, base
techniques.baselines: GPT-5, Claude-4.5-Sonnet, DeepSeek-V3.2-Thinking, GLM-4.7 (zero-shot, from Dr. Kernel paper); Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-32B, Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B, AutoTriton; Cold-Start-8B/14B; Dr. Kernel-8B/14B (reported and reproduced); 5 ablations (no skill injection at inference, unfiltered SFT, policy-RL only, BM25-only selection, no skills)
techniques.effect_target_headline: daVinci-kernel-14B achieves 37.2%, 70.6%, and 32.2% on Level 1, Level 2, and Level 3 under the Fast1 threshold, outperforming the strongest prior RL-trained model, Dr. Kernel-14B (reproduced: 30.4, 58.5, 22.1); Fast1.2 at 14B improves Level 2 from 18.1 to 27.1 and Level 3 from 2.8 to 7.3

extraction.notes: Correctness is folded into Fast_x (a task counts only if the kernel is correct and faster); no separate correctness rate except 8-sample case studies (Task B: 8/8 vs Dr. Kernel 5/8). Some ablations beat the full method on individual cells (e.g., Ablation 5 Level 2 Fast1 51.6 vs 44.8 at 8B), so effect is mixed across thresholds/levels but positive overall vs Dr. Kernel. Baseline frontier-model numbers copied from the Dr. Kernel paper, not rerun. Single run per configuration, no variance. Training cost only as seconds per step (1734s vs 1466s). The case study's 2.0x speedup comes from skipping computation when min_value==0.0, which reviewers may view as a benchmark shortcut. Learning rate and several RL hyperparameters not given in text. Tables garbled but recoverable; only a brief limitations section, no threats-to-validity section.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes SwiftTrans, an LLM code translation framework (fine-tuned multi-perspective ICL candidate generation plus a trained difference-aware LLM selector) targeting runtime efficiency of translated code, with execution time, memory and cyclomatic complexity reported alongside correctness.
extraction.title: Bridging Functional Correctness and Runtime Efficiency Gaps in LLM-Based Code Translation
extraction.venue: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), PMLR 306, 2026

techniques.technique_name: SwiftTrans: MpTranslator (parallel ICL with hierarchical-guidance fine-tuning on progressively accelerated translations) + DiffSelector (pairwise diff-aware LLM judge with ordinal-guidance training, bubble selection)
techniques.tools: Judge0 execution sandbox (each program run five times); GNU diff; compiler and platform test cases for training-data filtering
techniques.iterations: m=10 candidates per source, up to K=3 demonstrations per set; hierarchical data built with up to n=3 acceleration rounds (>=10% speedup per level); single-pass bubble selection with n-1 comparisons
techniques.metrics: efficiency: Execution Time (ms, average over efficiency-critical inputs, 5 runs) and memory usage (MB) [execution]; maintainability: cyclomatic complexity [tool-static]; correctness: Computational Accuracy (%) [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: Extended CodeNet (200 x 5 languages), extended F2SBench (1000 x 5), new SwiftBench (500 x 5, problems from Jun-Oct 2025), each with 10 efficiency-critical test cases; ClassEval-T, AlphaTrans, RepoTrans (correctness only); 20 translation directions
techniques.models: Qwen2.5-3B, open, base/instruct; Qwen2.5-7B, open; StarCoder-7B, open, code-specialized; baselines Qwen3-Next-80B, open, instruct; GPT-5, closed, reasoning; data-construction ensemble DeepSeek-Coder-V2-16B, gpt-oss-20B, Qwen3-Coder-30B, open
techniques.baselines: Correctness-Only, Correctness+Efficiency, Correctness->Efficiency prompting on Qwen3-Next-80B and GPT-5; F2STrans (ICML 2025) on Qwen2.5-3B/7B; repeated sampling; ablations (w/o Lhg, w/o Dt, tgt0-only, tgtn-only, w/o Log, w/o diff, w/o Bi-Judge, all-pair vs bubble, list-wise selection)
techniques.effect_target_headline: Average Execution Time 292 ms (SwiftTrans, Qwen2.5-7B) vs 731 ms (F2STrans, Qwen2.5-7B) and 399 ms (GPT-5 Cor.->Eff.), Table 1 Avg. column
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: applying SWIFTTRANS to Qwen2.5-7B outperforms GPT-5 by 3.8% (average Computational Accuracy)

extraction.notes: Table 1 is garbled in extraction; headline ET averages (292 vs 731, 399) were read from the reconstructed Avg. column and should be verified. Additional dims: memory 23.9 MB vs 29.1 MB (F2STrans) and cyclomatic complexity 5.7 vs 7.0 (Table 4). Inference-only (no training) variant also reported (Table 11). Incorrect translations are assigned baseline runtime in ET. Benchmark test cases were annotated by three teams of 20 professionals (not a human evaluation of outputs). No code/data URL given; no threats-to-validity section. Stage could also be considered post-generation selection; training-time chosen because both components are fine-tuned.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes a system (speculative generation forked from the reasoning prefix, early termination, elastic validation/profiling scheduling) that changes how an LLM agent produces CUDA kernels, and reports a quantitative efficiency outcome for the generated code (best kernel speedup over the KernelBench reference) in addition to system-level metrics.
extraction.title: SpecGen: Accelerating Agentic Kernel Optimization with Speculative Generation

techniques.technique_name: SpecGen: iteration-level speculative generation (non-reasoning forks conditioned on the reasoning prefix) with speedup-threshold early termination, plus ElasticScheduler (dynamic validation/profiling GPU split, LAF/FIFO priority queues, remote KV-cache for reasoning prefixes)
techniques.tools: NVIDIA Nsight Compute (NCU) 2025.1.0; nvcc with Ninja 1.13.0 (MAX_JOBS=20); PyTorch 2.10; CUDA 12.9; vLLM; Mooncake KV-transfer backend; OpenAI API v2.16.0; up to 18 H200 GPUs; regular-expression trigger parser derived from 38,745 reasoning traces
techniques.iterations: 100 iterations per task; within an iteration, K speculative forks (K = max(1, min(validation capacity, profiling capacity))) launched at trigger signals or when GPUs idle; reasoning generation terminated early when a speculative kernel exceeds the mean speedup of previously profiled kernels (alternative criteria: first-valid, historical-best, no termination)
techniques.metrics: efficiency of generated code: best kernel speedup over the KernelBench PyTorch reference, averaged over 40 timed runs after 10 warmups, aggregated by geometric mean [execution]; system-level: end-to-end execution time, profiling feedback count, validation/profiling GPU utilization, token consumption [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: KernelBench: ten Level 1 tasks (T1-T10, HingeLoss and matmul variants) and ten Level 2/3 tasks (T11-T20), 100 iterations per task; workload characterization on the same ten Level 1 tasks
techniques.models: GLM-5.1, open, reasoning, served locally with vLLM on 8 GPUs; DeepSeek-V4-Pro, closed API, reasoning, high reasoning effort; temperature 0.1, reasoning disabled for speculative forks
techniques.baselines: CudaForge (Coder-Judge multi-agent with NCU feedback); AlphaEvolve (evolutionary coding agent); KernelAgent (Meta autonomous kernel generation); CudaForge+ with doubled token budget; internal ablations (speculative generation only, + reallocation, + priority queue, + remote prefix cache) and termination-criterion variants
techniques.effect_target_headline: improving 1.24–1.91× kernel speedup under a fixed time and token budget; geomean speedup over the reference reaches 5.78× on GLM-5.1 and 3.49× on DeepSeek-V4-Pro, geomean lifts of 1.24× over CudaForge, 1.91× over AlphaEvolve, and 1.52× over KernelAgent

extraction.notes: Primarily a systems-efficiency paper (end-to-end agent runtime, profiling feedback, GPU utilization); the in-scope NF outcome is the speedup of the generated kernels (Table 6, Table 8, Table 9). Correctness is enforced by the validation gate (compile, run, numerical match) but is not reported as a comparative outcome for SpecGen vs baselines; the per-iteration success/failure distribution in Figure 3 is characterization of the baseline framework only. No threats-to-validity or limitations section, no artifact URL, no contamination discussion. Variance control is 40 timed runs after 10 warmups per kernel; no repeated whole-run seeds or statistical tests. Several tables (Tables 4, 6, 8, 9) and figures are garbled in extraction; Table 8's T18 speedup column reads 0.35 vs 55.79, which looks anomalous and should be checked against the PDF.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Exploratory single-model case study of GPT-4o refactoring an author-written Pygame codebase and adding features; prompting strategies are used but not evaluated against any no-technique or alternative baseline, so no technique is proposed or evaluated for its effect on NF quality (metrics are only before/after the LLM edit of human code).
extraction.title: An Exploratory Case Study of LLM-Assisted Refactoring and Gameplay Feature Generation in an Endless Runner Game
extraction.notes: Borderline between adjacent (LLM refactoring of human-written code, R1-R3) and context (SonarQube/MI metrics of LLM-generated features F1-F3 without an intervention comparison). Six tasks, one model, one run each.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Infrastructure/framework paper for agentic hardware/software co-design whose case studies report hardware quality-of-result (IPC speedup, clock frequency, silicon area), simulator alignment accuracy and bug-fix success, not a non-functional quality measure (readability, software runtime efficiency, security) of the LLM-generated code itself; no technique-vs-baseline comparison of code quality.
extraction.title: CHIA: An open-source framework for principled, agentic AI-driven hardware/software co-design research
extraction.notes: Borderline: the IPC-aware critical-path case study has Claude Code (Opus 4.6) edit BOOM RTL and reports 2.03x frequency / 1.97x Iron-Law speedup, and the ISA-extension case reports SPEC06 speedups (5.6% Bitmanip, 3.5% Zicond); these are hardware performance of the designed processor, not efficiency of the code as software. CIRCT issue-fixing case is LLM repair of human-written code (5 of 16 issues fixed, 3 PRs merged). Code at https://github.com/ucb-bar/chia.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes EGG, an expert-guided multi-agent (code/profile/debug) framework in which an LLM generates and iteratively optimizes Triton GPU kernels, and reports execution speedup (efficiency) of the generated kernels alongside correctness.
extraction.title: EGG: An Expert-Guided Agent Framework for Kernel Generation
extraction.venue: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026), PMLR 306

techniques.technique_name: EGG (expert-guided staged optimization: multi-seed search + algorithmic refinement + hardware-specific tuning [parallel mapping, tensor tiling, memory optimization] with stage-aware code/profile/debug multi-agent collaboration)
techniques.tools: NVIDIA Nsight Compute (NCU) metrics; CUDA 13.0, PyTorch 2.9.1, Triton 3.5.1; RTX 4090 (also RTX 5090, H20, RTX PRO 6000)
techniques.iterations: 2 seed kernels, each repaired by debug agent up to 3 times; 1 algorithmic refinement per valid seed (skipped if profile agent says not worth optimizing); then 3 sequential hardware-tuning stages, each with one repair attempt; a candidate replaces the best only if valid and faster; malformed outputs retried once
techniques.metrics: efficiency: mean speedup over PyTorch Eager, Fast1 rate (correct and faster than PyTorch Eager), latency in ms (execution); correctness: success rate (compiles and passes numerical correctness check) (execution)
techniques.benchmarks: KernelBench (250 tasks: Level 1 100, Level 2 100, Level 3 50); TritonBench real-world operators (3 tasks: Flash Attention, RoPE Embedding, INT8 Dequant MatMul); 25-task KernelBench subset for TVM Relax comparison
techniques.models: GPT-5.1, closed, general-purpose (main); Claude Opus 4.5, closed, general-purpose (KernelBench Level 2 only)
techniques.baselines: PyTorch Eager; Torch Compile (default and max-autotune); ChatGPT-5.1 and DeepSeek-V3.2 direct generation; AutoTriton (RL-fine-tuned); CudaForge (multi-agent with hardware feedback, re-evaluated under same setup); TVM Relax; handwritten TritonBench kernels; component ablations
techniques.effect_target_headline: 2.13× average speedup over PyTorch Eager on KernelBench (GPT-5.1, RTX 4090); Level 2: 2.73× vs CudaForge 2.00×
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: 100% success rate on all three KernelBench levels vs ChatGPT 5.1 60%/60%/66%

extraction.notes: Full prompts and pipeline pseudocode in appendix; no code URL given. Cost: ~20 min and ~50,000 output tokens per kernel vs CudaForge ~30 min and ~110,000. Second model (Opus 4.5) only on Level 2. No variance/repeated-run statistics. Limitations section (Appendix G) but no formal threats-to-validity. Ablation table rows garbled in extraction (full 87.6% Fast1 / 2.13×).

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes an LLM generate-verify-repair framework (compiler/test feedback, error-strategy retrieval, per-category temperature) for C-to-Rust translation and reports a quantitative memory-safety outcome (unsafe file rate and unsafe LOC rate) of the LLM-generated Rust alongside compile and solve rates.
extraction.title: AdaTrans: Automated C to Rust Transformation via Error-Adaptive Repair
extraction.venue: preprint (arXiv; manuscript submitted to ACM TOSEM)

techniques.technique_name: AdaTrans (Strategy-Driven RAG via Rust Violation-Fix Graph + Error-Stratified Transformation Strategy with per-category temperature scheduling and stagnation reset + multi-stage compile/test validation)
techniques.tools: Rust compiler (cargo build; error-code knowledge base from rustc 1.75, 517 error codes); fuzz-based differential test runner
techniques.iterations: max M = 20 iterations; stops at first iteration that compiles and passes feedback tests; RESET to fresh translation when same error category repeats more than N_L = 3 consecutive times
techniques.metrics: security (memory safety): unsafe file rate (% files with at least one unsafe block) and unsafe LOC rate [tool-static]; correctness: compilation pass rate [execution/compiler], solve rate / functional equivalence on fuzz oracle of 10-200 tests [execution], pass@k for zero-shot
techniques.benchmarks: FuzzForLeetcode (new), 104 C problems from LeetCode Weekly Contests 413-438 (22 Easy, 48 Medium, 34 Hard)
techniques.models: gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18, size undisclosed, closed, instruct
techniques.baselines: Zero-shot gpt-4o-mini (pass@1/10/20/100 over 200 samples); c2rust AST transpiler; EvoC2Rust; Tymcrat; PtrTrans; ablations w/o RAG, w/o ESTS, w/o ESTS & RAG; temperature and N_L sensitivity variants
techniques.effect_target_headline: unsafe file rate 1.19% (AdaTrans Full, three-run mean) vs 1.05% (Zero-shot LLM gpt-4o-mini) and 100.00% (c2rust); unsafe LOC rate < 0.1% vs 97.94% for c2rust
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: mean solve rate of 81.09% (± 3.09%) vs Zero-shot LLM pass@20 61.48% and Tymcrat 21.15% (improves over strongest existing LLM-based tool by 59.94 percentage points)
