extraction.notes: Security dimension is operationalised only as Rust unsafe-block usage (memory-safety proxy); the reviewer should confirm this counts as an NF security outcome. Unsafe rate vs zero-shot LLM baseline is comparable (1.19% vs 1.05%), so the NF gain is only relative to the non-LLM c2rust transpiler; the main gains are in correctness. Single backbone (gpt-4o-mini) deliberately fixed and justified. Unsafe metrics not reported for the ablations or the other LLM tools. Contamination mitigated by post-cutoff LeetCode contests. Figures with code snippets are missing from the extracted text.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Benchmark/tool paper (JETO-Mine, JETO-Bench) for execution-time improvement patches on human-written Java projects; the only LLM evaluation is an off-the-shelf agent (OpenHands with three LLMs) optimizing existing human-written code, scored by manual match to the ground-truth patch rather than measured runtime of generated code, and no NF-improving technique is proposed.
extraction.title: JETO-Bench: A Reproducible Benchmark for Execution Time Improvement Patches in Java
extraction.notes: OpenHands with GPT-5-mini correctly fixes 14.3% (13/91); GLM-5.1 and Mimo-pro-2.5 9.9% (9/91). Correct fix judged as exact AST match or semantic equivalence to the developer patch; execution-time improvement of the generated patches is not reported quantitatively. Artifact: https://github.com/khesoem/JETO-Bench.

extraction.eligibility_reason: MOA is an LLM agent pipeline that mines memory anti-patterns, synthesizes static checkers and patches existing human-written OpenHarmony C/C++ code; the NF gains (heap, PSS, binary size reductions) are measured relative to the original human code, i.e., LLM optimization/refactoring of human-written code rather than improving the quality of LLM-generated code. Borderline because the patches are LLM-edited and ablations compare NF outcomes across pipeline variants.
extraction.title: MOA: A Profiling-Guided LLM Framework for Memory-Optimization Automation at Codebase Scale
extraction.notes: Borderline EC4/adjacent vs include: LLM-generated optimization patches on human codebase with efficiency outcomes (42.2% heap reduction, 10.6% binary size reduction, 92.5% expert acceptance), compared against PatchAgent (success rate only) and ablations (w/o pattern description, w/o checker location) that do report NF metrics. Uses GPT-5.1 / GPT-5.1-Codex. arXiv preprint formatted with ACM template placeholder (J. ACM 2018). Artifact: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19248417.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes SFT plus RL (GDPO) post-training of an LLM with an explicit code-readability reward for generating executable Strudel (JavaScript-based music DSL) programs from MIDI, and quantitatively measures readability of the generated code alongside execution faithfulness. Borderline because the artifact is a domain-specific music program rather than conventional production code.
extraction.title: Decomposer: Learning to Decompile Symbolic Music to Programs

techniques.technique_name: DECOMPOSER: SFT (LoRA) on synthetic STRUDEL-SYNTH pairs followed by GDPO reinforcement learning with execution faithfulness reward (multi-instrument onset F1) and LLM-judged 12-item readability rubric reward
techniques.tools: Headless Strudel runtime (Node.js + FastAPI) for execution and MIDI rendering; mir_eval for onset F1; Qwen3.6-35B-A3B as rubric judge; Acorn JavaScript parser; AReaL training backend
techniques.metrics: readability: 12-item binary readability rubric score (Rubric) [llm-judge] and average rank from listwise LLM reranker (Rank) [llm-judge]; diversity: SelfCB (CodeBLEU self-similarity) [similarity-to-reference]; correctness/faithfulness: compile rate [execution], Onset F1, Frame F1, multi-instrument Onset F1 of rendered MIDI vs input [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: STRUDEL-SYNTH test split (1,022 pairs); LMD short fragments <30 s (~1K test); generalization: LMD 30-60 s, GigaMIDI, NES-MDB, Nottingham (200 inputs each, Best@5); ModArchive genre benchmark (4,463 inputs, 51 genres)
techniques.models: Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, 4B, open, instruct; Qwen3-8B, 8B, open, instruct/hybrid-reasoning (thinking disabled)
techniques.baselines: Vanilla Qwen3-4B/8B; SFT-only; RL without SFT; readability-weight sweep (w2 = 0 to 1.0); frontier LLMs prompted (Claude-Opus-4.6, Gemini-3.5-Flash, GPT-5.5); heuristic MIDI-to-Strudel converter
techniques.effect_target_headline: Rubric 0.74 for Qwen3-8B + SFT+RL (ours) vs 0.58 (+ SFT), 0.33 (Qwen3-8B) and 0.39 (GPT-5.5) on STRUDEL-SYNTH; 0.61 vs 0.54 (+ SFT) and 0.29 (GPT-5.5) on LMD
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: compared with the best frontier LLM, DECOMPOSER (8B) improves Onset F1 by +0.16 on STRUDEL-SYNTH and by +0.32 on LMD (Onset F1 0.73 and 0.60)

extraction.artifact_url: yewon-kim.com/decomposer (project page; STRUDEL-SYNTH stated as released)
extraction.notes: Eligibility borderline: generated artifact is a music DSL program (Strudel), not conventional production code; reviewer should confirm scope. Readability is evaluated with the same LLM judge and rubric used as the RL reward (risk of reward overfitting); no human validation or judge agreement reported. The LLM reranker Rank is mixed: for 8B on LMD, SFT+RL ranks 4.12 vs 4.01 for SFT only, and it is only comparable to frontier LLMs. Readability trades off with faithfulness (weight sweep, Fig. 4). Single run per setting, no variance. Compute only as training wall-clock (SFT about 1.5 h, RL about 8 days on 8xH100). No threats-to-validity section, only a short limitations paragraph. Tables are extracted column-wise but readable.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Hawk is a training-free retrieval/knowledge-harnessing framework that guides an LLM coding agent to generate Ascend NPU kernels, and it reports quantitative efficiency outcomes (execution speedup over a standard implementation, latency, a performance-rate score) for the generated code alongside correctness.
extraction.title: Hawk: Harnessing Hardware-Aware Knowledge for High-Performance NPU Kernel Generation

techniques.technique_name: Hawk (run-time hardware-aware knowledge synthesis with a Triple-Part Executable Knowledge Representation + bottleneck-aware 2D retrieval with reciprocal rank fusion + effect-driven LLM knowledge distillation, inside an iterative compile/execute feedback agent)
techniques.tools: Implemented as custom agent skills inside CANNBot (role-based designer/developer/evaluator orchestration, CANN tool skills, asc-devkit official documentation); Claude Code as the base agent; Ascend CANN toolchain version 8.5.1 on 8x Ascend 910B2 NPUs; BM25 for the syntactic retrieval dimension; Qwen3-Embedding-8B dense embeddings for the hardware-aligned semantic dimension; Reciprocal Rank Fusion with smoothing constant k=60; hardware profiling (e.g., MTE2-to-VEC ratios) during cold-start knowledge mining.
techniques.iterations: Maximum agent iterations capped uniformly at 30 for all compared methods; retrieval fetches Top-K=6 knowledge entries per iteration with feedback-driven query reformulation looping until the bottleneck is resolved; knowledge synthesis triggered only on four strict conditions (>=2 refinement rounds, documentation/hardware mismatch, measurable speedup above a threshold, structurally superior derivation).
techniques.metrics: efficiency: Speedup = L_std / L_opt against the CANNBench standard implementation, averaged over 20 test cases, and Performance Rate PR = (L_std - L_hw) / ((L_opt - L_hw) + (L_std - L_hw)) against the hardware theoretical lower bound, folded into an official Score = 20xCS + 30xAcc + 50xPR out of 100 [execution]; raw latency in ms [execution]. correctness: Compilation Success (CS, binary) and Acc (percentage of the 20 per-operator test cases passed) [execution]. Motivation study additionally uses Comp@1 and Pass@1 on MultiKernelBench.
techniques.benchmarks: CANNBench L1 kernels (8 operators shown: exp, foreach_addcdiv_scalar, foreach_norm, gelu, masked_scale, mish, sigmoid, swi_glu) and L2 kernels (16 complex operators), 20 test cases per Ascend C operator; motivation study uses 15 activation kernels and 17 matmul kernels from MultiKernelBench; knowledge base bootstrapped from 158 distilled entries mined from ops-nn (2,690 kernel files), strictly disjoint from the test-set categories.
techniques.languages: Ascend C (C/C++ NPU kernel language); CUDA and PyTorch used as reference points in the motivation study
techniques.models: GLM-5.1 (main backbone for Claude Code; closed/proprietary, reasoning); DeepSeek-V4-Flash (weaker backbone, generalization check); motivation study: DeepSeek-V4 Pro and GLM-4.5; Qwen3-Embedding-8B (8B, open) as the retrieval embedder.
techniques.baselines: Vanilla LLM (bare Claude Code); Few-Shot (Claude Code with a semantically retrieved reference kernel, target operator excluded from the corpus); CANNBot (base plugin with standard tools and official manuals) as the strongest/SOTA baseline; the CANNBench standard implementation as the speedup reference. Ablations: w/o Structured Representation, w/o 2D-Retrieval, w/o Distillation.
techniques.effect_target_headline: "Hawk elevates generation accuracy from 49.4% to 80.0%, while achieving up to a 2.2x execution speedup over state-of-the-art baselines" (abstract); "it achieves a higher average Acc (0.80) and a faster average execution Speedup (1.34x) across the evaluated L1 operators, significantly outperforming the strongest baseline, CANNBot (0.49 Acc and 0.86x Speedup)"; per-operator "Speedups (averaging 2.10x and 2.39x over 20 test cases, respectively)" on exp and foreach_addcdiv_scalar; L2 kernels "achieved speedups up to 3.5x"; weaker backbone DeepSeek-V4-Flash "improved the average Speedup from 0.53x to 1.35x".
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: "elevates generation accuracy from 49.4% to 80.0%" (average Acc 0.80 vs CANNBot 0.49 on L1); "100% on exp and foreach_addcdiv_scalar"; L2: "CANNBot yielded 0% Acc on 12 out of 16 operators. In contrast, Hawk delivered substantial functional improvements on 8 operators (e.g., 65% Acc on gcd)"; DeepSeek-V4-Flash "elevated the average Acc from 44.4% to 93.1%".

extraction.notes: All result figures (Figs. 6-12) are bar charts whose axis labels and values were destroyed by PDF extraction, so the per-operator numbers above come only from the prose; a human should verify them against the original PDF. Several internal inconsistencies worth checking: (a) the abstract and conclusion claim 'up to 2.2x speedup over SOTA' while the text reports average Speedup 1.34x vs CANNBot 0.86x; (b) the headline accuracy is 80.0% / 0.80 in the abstract and RQ1 but the ablation Table VI lists Hawk-Full Acc as 0.84 with Speedup normalized to 1.00x; (c) the RQ3 summary says the weaker DeepSeek backbone went from 15% to 60% Acc and 0.2x to 0.8x Speedup, while the body text of the same subsection says 44.4% to 93.1% Acc and 0.53x to 1.35x Speedup; (d) the Top-K discussion says 'K=6 yields marginal gains (+2% over K=6)', an apparent typo. CANNBench is used as the benchmark but no citation or task count for its L1 set is given beyond the 8 operators plotted. No artifact/code URL for Hawk itself is provided (only the third-party ops-nn and cannbot-skills repositories). No repeated runs or statistical tests; results appear to be single runs averaged over the 20 per-operator test cases.

extraction.eligibility_reason: ArchEval is a benchmark of LLM agents on computer-architecture design tasks; the measured outcome is the simulated performance of the designed hardware mechanism or configuration (IPC, MPKI, cycles, EDP, bandwidth vs a baseline design), not a non-functional quality (readability, runtime efficiency, security) of the generated code itself, and many deliverables are configuration files rather than production code.
extraction.title: ArchEval: Measuring AI Agents as Computer Architects
extraction.notes: Borderline: L1 (repeated simulator feedback) vs L3 (no feedback) could be read as a feedback-loop intervention, but the quality measured is architecture-design performance under a simulator, not efficiency of the code's own execution. Single-seed study, four agent configurations (GPT-5.5+Codex, Gemini 3.5 Flash, Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite, Gemma 4 31B with MiniSWE).

extraction.eligibility_reason: Empirical study of the correctness-performance gap of Triton/TileLang GPU kernels that are human-written (TritonBench) or authored by the researchers; an LLM agentic harness (AKO) is used only as an off-the-shelf tool to apply root-cause-derived optimization patterns to these human-written kernels, with no LLM technique proposed or evaluated against a baseline.
extraction.title: Correct but Slow: An Empirical Study of the GPU Kernel Evaluation Gap in Modern Domain-Specific Languages
extraction.notes: Borderline: RQ3 optimized kernels were produced with AKO (an LLM-based agentic kernel-optimization harness) under a correctness-gated protocol, and large efficiency gains are reported (e.g., TileLang LayerNorm 364 ms to 0.270 ms, 1347x on A100), but the gains are attributed to manually identified authoring patterns, AKO is not compared with any baseline, and the starting kernels are not LLM-generated. Paper motivates its study with LLM kernel generators (KernelBench) but evaluates no LLM-generated code. Artifacts at https://github.com/tingxi-li/DSLPerfGap/tree/master.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Benchmark paper that evaluates LLM coding-agent stacks (agent framework choice under a fixed LLM) and an exploratory agent-relay continuation technique on optimizing the runtime of C codebases, reporting verified speedup of the LLM-edited code. Borderline: the starting code is human-written (deliberately suboptimal), so it could be read as adjacent (LLM optimization of human-written code).
extraction.title: PERFOPT-Bench: Evaluating Coding Agents on Software Performance Optimization

techniques.technique_name: Agent framework choice under a fixed LLM (OpenCode vs Claude Code vs Codex) for autonomous profile-patch-verify performance optimization
techniques.tools: Claude Code 2.1.126, Codex CLI 0.133.0, OpenCode v1.14.31; GCC/MSVC; test.ps1/test.sh verification scripts; Intel Core i7, Windows 11
techniques.iterations: agent decides when to stop; single run per cell
techniques.metrics: efficiency: verified speedup (baseline runtime / submitted runtime) after hidden correctness tests, geometric mean over tasks [execution]; shortcut audit by automated screen plus single expert trajectory inspection [human]
techniques.benchmarks: PERFOPT-Bench (12 C tasks, ~668K LoC, 8 domains)
techniques.models: GPT-5.5 [xhigh], closed, reasoning; Claude Opus-4.7 [max], closed, reasoning; GLM-5.1, open; Kimi-K2.6, open; DeepSeek-V4 Pro [max], open, reasoning
techniques.baselines: Same LLM in a different agent framework (OpenCode vs Codex for GPT-5.5; OpenCode vs Claude Code for Opus-4.7); original suboptimal codebase as speedup baseline
techniques.effect_target_headline: oc-gpt attains a higher geometric mean on shared cells (9.2× vs. 7.8×) and wins more task-level comparisons (7 vs. 4) than codex-gpt; Opus-4.7: OpenCode 7.4× vs Claude Code 6.7×

techniques.technique_name: One-step agent relay (externalized optimization summary + fresh second session, self-relay or cross-stack)
techniques.tools: Onward terminal tool; test.ps1 verification; Claude Code, Codex CLI
techniques.iterations: 2 rounds (R1 then R2 from relay document)
techniques.metrics: efficiency: verified speedup R1 vs R2 and R2/R1 ratio [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: PERFOPT-Bench tasks T5 and T8 (2 tasks, 8 sequences)
techniques.models: GPT-5.5 [xhigh] in Codex, closed, reasoning; Claude Opus-4.7 [max] in Claude Code, closed, reasoning
techniques.baselines: First-round (R1) result of the same sequence
techniques.effect_target_headline: In all eight tested two-round sequences, R2 improves over the corresponding independent R1 score, with relative gains of 1.02–2.48×

extraction.human_eval_details: Shortcut/cheating audit by a single performance expert; no agreement reported
extraction.notes: Primarily a benchmark paper; the 'techniques' are agent-framework comparison and an exploratory, budget-confounded relay pilot without controls. Starting code is human-written suboptimal code (EC4/adjacent borderline). Correctness is a hidden-test gate, not reported as a rate. Single run per cell, no variance. Tasks are newly constructed (adapted from open-source code), partially limiting contamination. Tables garbled in extraction (Figure 2 heatmap).

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes a static graph-based detection framework and failure taxonomy for structural incoherence in LLM-generated code; it does not change the code the LLM produces. The four context-richness prompting conditions are an experimental factor, and the resulting 'structural failures' (unresolved symbols, hallucinated dependencies, undeclared config keys) are mostly correctness/integration defects rather than an NF-quality outcome of an improvement technique.
extraction.title: The Patchwork Problem in LLM-Generated Code
extraction.notes: Borderline: Table 6 reports failure counts by prompting strategy (P1 minimal 8, P2 local 17, P3 retrieved 24, P4 oracle 18) on 336 GPT-4o/Claude 3.5 Sonnet generations, which a reviewer could read as a context-retrieval technique with a code-quality outcome; categories include dead code (CFC) and missing auth guards (SSR) but both had zero findings in the controlled generations. Artifact: https://github.com/decentralizedsciencelab/PatchWork.git

extraction.eligibility_reason: Position/design-science paper that builds a reference model (SGRM) from a 44-source literature corpus and evaluates it analytically against ISO/IEC 25010; no new experimental data are collected and all quantitative figures (e.g., 73% security-defect reduction) are cited from other studies.
extraction.title: Specification-Driven Development as the Foundation of AI-Native Enterprise Software Engineering
extraction.notes: Cited primary studies worth snowballing: Marri, Constitutional Spec-Driven Development (arXiv:2602.02584, reports 73% security-defect reduction); Vilas Boas et al. (arXiv:2605.18461).

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes TRIM, a post-generation trajectory-guided minimization that edits LLM-agent-generated repair patches, and reports quantitative maintainability-related outcomes (CodeSlop/redundant patch lines removed, verbosity removed) alongside oracle correctness.
extraction.title: TRIM: Reducing AI-Generated CodeSlop via Agent Trajectory Minimization

techniques.technique_name: TRIM (Trajectory-guided Redundancy Identification and Minimization), hierarchical counterfactual patch minimization over agent repair trajectories (TRIM-G and TRIM-NG variants)
techniques.tools: task-specific test suite TF (Live-kBench crash-reproducing script / kernel jobs; SWE-Bench agent-generated tests)
techniques.iterations: Three phases (edit sequence -> file -> edit action); each candidate removal validated by execution; TRIM-G repeats each phase to a fixpoint (1-minimality), TRIM-NG single pass per granularity; at most 16 validations per bug observed
techniques.metrics: readability-maintainability: Delta Slop % = normalized reduction in patch length (modified lines), edits/hunks removed [tool-static]; verbosity removed per SlopCodeBench definition [tool-static]; correctness: Live-kBench oracle = crash-reproducing script + Gemini-3-Flash LLM judge of semantic equivalence to developer patch (9 judgments, majority vote) [execution + llm-judge]; SWE-Bench hidden fail-to-pass tests [execution]; cost = number of test-suite executions
techniques.benchmarks: Live-kBench (534 Linux kernel vulnerabilities; 433 repaired, 293 non-trivial evaluated); SWE-Bench-Verified (333 SWE-agent Claude-Sonnet-4 trajectories); 4,544 repair trajectories total
techniques.models: Gemini-3-Pro (closed); Claude-Opus-4.5 (closed); Claude-Sonnet-4 (closed); Gemini-3-Flash (closed, minimization baseline and judge); Claude Sonnet 4.6 (closed, minimization baseline)
techniques.baselines: Agentic minimization with mini-SWE-agent (Only Diff, Only Traj, Both prompts; Gemini-3-Flash and Sonnet 4.6); DD-Hunk (Delta Debugging adapted to patch hunks); original agent patch
techniques.effect_target_headline: TRIM cuts CODESLOP by 17.9%–32.9% across agentic scaffolds (Live-kBench, TRIM-G edit level); 1.6×–3.1× improvement over agentic minimization; 20.0% ∆Slop on SWE-Bench-Verified (modified files); 66% of AP-introduced verbosity removed
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: TRIM preserves oracle correctness for 327/330 (99.1%) successful repairs (SWE-Bench-Verified); Live-kBench CrashFixer 22.47% -> 23.41% (+0.94), OpenHands -1.13 under full minimization

extraction.notes: Technique is a deterministic post-processing algorithm (not an LLM call) applied to LLM-agent patches; eligibility hinges on accepting patch minimization of LLM-generated code as an NF (maintainability/redundancy) intervention. CodeSlop is a functional-redundancy (patch-length) metric defined by the authors, not an established maintainability metric; verbosity measured via SlopCodeBench definition. Live-kBench is a 'live' recent-bug benchmark (partial contamination handling). Statistical test only vs DD-Hunk (p = 0.50, 95% CI). Abstract says 17.9% while intro says 17.8%. Tables partially garbled. No artifact URL.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Benchmark paper that empirically compares LLM sampling against agentic feedback-loop scaffolds (vanilla coding agents, kernel-specialized optimization agents, traceback-driven reflection) for generating Triton kernels, reporting execution speedup (efficiency) alongside correctness on 210 operators and six hardware platforms.
extraction.title: KernelGenBench: Can LLMs and Agents Write Efficient Kernels Across Operator Sources and Hardware Platforms?

techniques.technique_name: Vanilla agentic frameworks with execution-feedback loop (Claude Code, OpenCode)
techniques.tools: verify_single.py verification CLI (combinatorial correctness tests + speedup); Triton compiler; PyTorch torch.library dispatch; three-tier anti-hack (AST scan, ghost replay, torch.profiler on NVIDIA)
techniques.iterations: Autonomous agent loop (write, verify, fix, then tune BLOCK_SIZE/num_warps/num_stages) under a 30-minute wall-clock budget per operator; no fixed iteration count
techniques.metrics: efficiency: two-level geometric-mean speedup over reference (ATen/vLLM/cuBLAS) on each method's successful set, plus fast_p (speedup > 0.8/1.0/1.5x) and matched-set speedup with paired bootstrap CIs [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: KernelGenBench-MS (210 operators: 110 PyTorch ATen, 50 vLLM v0.13.0, 50 cuBLAS 12.4) on NVIDIA A100; KernelGenBench-MC (110 ATen operators on six platforms: NVIDIA, Moore Threads, Hygon, Iluvatar CoreX, Platform A, Platform B)
techniques.models: Claude Opus-4.6, closed, reasoning/instruct; GLM-5.0, open, instruct; Qwen3.5-27B, open, instruct; MiniMax M-2.5, open, instruct
techniques.baselines: LLM sampling Pass@1 (temperature 0) and Pass@5 (temperature 0.8) with the same models and no execution feedback
techniques.effect_target_headline: Overall successful-set speedup (NVIDIA A100, 210 ops): Claude Code (Opus-4.6) 0.78x vs Pass@1 (Opus-4.6) 0.70x; Claude Code (Qwen3.5-27b) 0.70x vs Pass@1 0.85x; Claude Code (MiniMax M-2.5) 0.69x vs Pass@1 0.88x
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: Claude Code (Opus-4.6) achieves the highest overall accuracy at 87% vs Pass@1 (Opus-4.6) 41% (NVIDIA A100, 210 operators)

techniques.technique_name: Kernel-specialized optimization agents (AKO4all, AutoKernel, CUDA Optimized Skill)
techniques.tools: Method-specific profiling, skills and hardware tools retained from published workflows; benchmark verify engine; Triton compiler
techniques.iterations: Autonomous search continuing after correctness to optimize performance, bounded by a 30-minute wall-clock budget per operator
techniques.metrics: efficiency: two-level geometric-mean speedup on successful set, fast_p thresholds [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: KernelGenBench-MS (210 operators) on NVIDIA A100; KernelGenBench-MC (110 ATen operators, six platforms)
techniques.models: Claude Opus-4.6, closed (AKO4all); GLM-5.0, open; Qwen3.5-27B, open; MiniMax M-2.5, open (AutoKernel, CUDA Optimized Skill)
techniques.baselines: Pass@1/Pass@5 LLM sampling with the same models; vanilla agentic frameworks (Claude Code, OpenCode)
techniques.effect_target_headline: AKO4all (Opus-4.6) overall Spd 0.97x vs Pass@1 (Opus-4.6) 0.70x and Claude Code (Opus-4.6) 0.78x; AutoKernel (Qwen3.5-27b) reports the highest successful-set overall speedup at 1.02x (NVIDIA A100, 210 operators)
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: AKO4all (Opus-4.6) 83% vs Pass@1 (Opus-4.6) 41%; AutoKernel (GLM-5.0) 71% vs Pass@1 (GLM-5.0) 21% (overall, NVIDIA A100)

techniques.technique_name: Fixed traceback-driven reflection (Pass@5 Reflection)
techniques.tools: Benchmark verify engine tracebacks
techniques.iterations: Up to 5 rounds, stop when correct
techniques.metrics: efficiency: two-level geometric-mean speedup [execution]; cross-turn code similarity (difflib) as diagnostic
techniques.benchmarks: KernelGenBench-MS (210 operators) on NVIDIA A100
techniques.models: Claude Opus-4.6, closed
techniques.baselines: Pass@1 (temperature 0); Pass@5 independent sampling without reflection
techniques.effect_target_headline: Overall Spd 0.72x (Pass@5 Reflection) vs 0.68x (Pass@5 No-Reflect) and 0.70x (Pass@1), Opus-4.6, NVIDIA A100
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: Overall Acc 60% (Reflection) vs 57% (No-Reflect); underperforms independent sampling on vLLM (24% vs. 28%)

extraction.notes: Primarily a benchmark paper; included because it systematically compares sampling vs agentic/feedback scaffolds with an efficiency (speedup) outcome. Speedups are computed on each method's own successful set and the authors warn they are not matched-set rankings; matched-set CC vs OC comparison in Appendix O. Most agent results are single trajectories; repeated-run study uses a different model (DeepSeek-V4-Pro). Kernel-specialized agent effect is not uniform: CUDA Opt. Skill (MiniMax M-2.5) 0.80x vs Pass@1 0.88x. Cross-platform speedup degrades sharply on Platform A (0.86x to 0.18x for Claude Code Opus-4.6). Tables extracted with garbled layout; numbers read from Table 1, 4, 26. Cost: >15 billion tokens, ~$20,000; specialized agents average 4.99M tokens per success. Legacy models (Opus-4.5, GPT-5.4, GPT-5.2, GLM-4.7) evaluated only with Pass@k.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes a compiler-grounded hierarchical agent loop that rewrites LLM-produced Triton kernels and reports quantitative efficiency outcomes (kernel speedups) for the resulting code, with correctness validation.
extraction.title: Compiler-Grounded Hierarchical Diagnosis for LLM-Based Triton Kernel Optimization

techniques.technique_name: Compiler-grounded hierarchical diagnosis loop (pattern triage -> profiling diagnosis -> IR attribution -> compiler-source escalation -> evidence-backed source rewrite), with retrospective cross-operator pattern synthesis
techniques.tools: Triton; Triton-Ascend backend compiler (MLIR IR dumps, pass-level analysis); Ascend NPU profiler (AIV/AIC occupancy, hardware counters); OpenCode agent harness; CannBot skills repository
techniques.iterations: 15 optimization rounds per operator; each round validated for correctness and benchmark performance; escalation to deeper levels only when evidence is insufficient; median best-round index 10
techniques.metrics: efficiency: kernel execution speedup (initial Triton vs optimized Triton), geometric mean and median over operators, plus geometric-mean kernel time in microseconds [execution]; separate post-hoc speedup vs Torch NPU [execution]; correctness: validation/correctness test cases passed [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: NPUKernelBench-derived Ascend 950 suite (ported from KernelBench); 37 successfully converted Triton operators, 5 sampled cases each = 185 benchmark cases; Torch NPU comparison on 35 operators / 1678 cases
techniques.models: DeepSeek V4 Pro (closed/API, reasoning) driving an OpenCode agent
techniques.baselines: The initial (AI-converted) Triton kernel before optimization; separate post-optimization comparison against Torch NPU implementations
techniques.effect_target_headline: geometric-mean speedup of 4.35× and a median speedup of 2.73× from the initial to optimized Triton kernel; 22/37 exceed 2× and 13/37 exceed 5× (37 operators, NPUKernelBench-derived Ascend 950)

extraction.notes: System name is anonymized throughout ('the system'). No ablation: authors explicitly state no causal isolation of the four evidence levels, no profiling-only or always-deep control, and no token cost or wall-clock reporting. Correctness is used as a validation gate (e.g., 'passes all 50 correctness cases' for one example) but no aggregate correctness number is reported. Only one agent model evaluated, not justified. Several tables/figures garbled in PDF extraction (Figures 3-5, Table 1/2 numbers partially interleaved with text).

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes Ares, an LLM-agent loop that edits RTL code with synthesis/PPA feedback and adaptive reasoning effort; reports quantitative power-area-delay (hardware efficiency) of the LLM-edited RTL. Borderline: the input RTL is mostly existing open-source designs (LLM optimization/editing rather than generation from scratch) and efficiency is hardware PPA rather than software runtime.
extraction.title: ARES: Adaptive Reasoning-Effort Steering for PPA- and Cost-Aware RTL Optimization with LLM Agents

techniques.technique_name: Ares adaptive reasoning-effort steering (patience counter escalating medium->high effort) in an edit-synthesize-measure agent loop with long-term markdown memory
techniques.tools: Synopsys Design Compiler and PrimeTime (Nangate 45 nm library); Cadence JasperGold sequential equivalence checking; random testbench (104 vectors); Claude Code agent
techniques.iterations: iterates until cumulative cost reaches a user-set budget (e.g. ~15-20 high-calls; 25 iterations in SotA comparison); keep candidate only if FoM decreases; escalate to high effort when patience counter C >= p (p=3, w=2.8, kappa=0.05)
techniques.metrics: efficiency: FoM = normalized area x power x delay after synthesis (Synopsys DC / PrimeTime) [tool-static]; cost: normalized dollar cost in high-calls
techniques.benchmarks: 24 open-source RTL modules (19 Dr. RTL designs, 2 RTLRewriter, 3 OpenCores); 21 training, 3 held-out test (tv80, uart, controller); plus MX multiply-accumulate unit drafted by Claude Opus 4.6
techniques.models: Claude Opus 4.6 (closed, reasoning, via Claude Code)
techniques.baselines: fixed low/medium/high reasoning effort; memoryless vs baseline vs engineered long-term memory; REvolution; Dr. RTL; hand-optimized MX_fp32
techniques.effect_target_headline: the effort policy lowers the FoM by 23–27% where the best fixed effort reaches 16–23%, at equal normalized cost (three held-out test designs); controller: Ares 0.694 vs REvolution 0.943 and Dr. RTL 0.923

extraction.notes: Eligibility borderline: task is LLM optimization (editing) of existing RTL, mostly human-written open-source designs, so a reviewer may classify as adjacent (EC4); one case optimizes an LLM-drafted MAC. Efficiency = hardware PPA, not software runtime/memory. Functional equivalence is enforced as an acceptance gate (testbench + JasperGold), not reported as an outcome. Single closed model; repeated runs (3 per config, 6 on MX MAC with std). Code promised upon publication. No threats-to-validity section. Figures/Table 1 garbled in extraction.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes an agentic LLM migration loop that rewrites a mechanically transpiled Rust baseline into idiomatic Rust function by function, gated by compilation and runtime behavioural equivalence, and reports quantitative memory-safety and idiomaticity outcomes for the LLM-produced Rust (SAFE% 95, RUST% 57, counts of unsafe extern declarations, raw pointer arithmetic, deep unsafe operations, static mut globals, and unsafe blocks cut from roughly 86 to 40).
extraction.title: From C to Idiomatic Rust: A Ship-of-Theseus Agentic Translation
extraction.venue: Proceedings of the 2nd International Workshop on AI for Software Modernization (AISM '26), October 12-16, 2026, Munich, Germany; ACM

techniques.technique_name: Ship-of-Theseus agentic C-to-Rust migration: c2rust lossless baseline, leaf-first call-graph ordering, per-function LLM reimplementation, two hard gates (Gate A compilation plus idiomaticity criteria, Gate B runtime behavioural equivalence with trace-divergence feedback), split into Phase 1 (signatures and bodies) and Phase 2 (global mutable state)
techniques.tools: c2rust transpiler (Clang AST based); Clang/LLVM; the Rust compiler; static call-graph analysis for leaf-based ordering; equivalent trace instrumentation of old and new implementations for divergence diagnosis; end-to-end runtime validation with a public DNS resolver, curl download and netperf through the tunnel, plus a wire-format integration test; OpenCode-based agent infrastructure enhanced by 'rtk' and 'OAC' (neither explained); no version numbers given for any tool
techniques.iterations: Per function, the agent proposes an implementation, compiles it, runs the runtime tests and revises from compiler errors or trace divergence, repeating until Gate A and Gate B both pass, with reversion to the last verified state where needed; no maximum iteration count is stated. Phase 2 requires one global at a time with full runtime tests after each wrapping. The whole migration spanned about 45 commits (each porting one to ten functions) and 37 developer-hours over four working days
techniques.metrics: security (memory safety): SAFE% = 100(1 - (EX+NM)/(EX0+NM0)) where EX counts unsafe extern "C" fn declarations and NM counts #[no_mangle] annotations; RUST% = 100(1 - (PA+DU)/(PA0+DU0)) where PA counts raw pointer arithmetic sites and DU counts deep unsafe operations such as copy_nonoverlapping and write_bytes; also absolute counts of static mut globals wrapped and of unsafe blocks [all tool-static source counting]. readability-maintainability (idiomaticity): the five criteria C1 zero unsafe in function signatures, C2 slice-based buffer access, C3 no static mut, C4 no extern "C" on internal functions, C5 no C string or memory functions, enforced as hard errors at Gate A [tool-static]; SLOC of the resulting codebase. Correctness: compilation plus end-to-end behavioural equivalence (same output and state modification for the same input), checked after every port [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: Single case study, no benchmark suite: iodine, a production-quality DNS tunnel of approximately 12.5 kSLOC of C across 17 source files, with 168 functions ported and 37 static mut globals (16 client, 21 server). c2rust baseline counts: 178 EX, 73 NM, 319 PA, 144 DU
techniques.models: Not properly reported. The paper states translation was performed 'using subscription-based plans and the OpenCode-based infrastructure' and that 'the best result (fewest iterations) was achieved with Qwen3.6-27B'; no other model is named, no sizes or open/closed status for the others, and no per-model results are given. ChatGPT and Copilot are acknowledged only for proofreading the manuscript
techniques.baselines: The c2rust transpiler output (mechanically translated, non-idiomatic Rust) serves as the baseline against which SAFE% and RUST% are defined. No comparison against direct LLM C-to-Rust translation (the approach the paper argues against) and no comparison against other migration tools
techniques.effect_target_headline: Server porting (commits 1-31) lifts SAFE% to 72% and RUST% to 47%; client porting (commits 32-41) completes all 168 signatures at SAFE%=95%; static-mut elimination (commits 39-45, extending to the end of history) wraps the 37 static mut globals (16 client, 21 server) in atomics or mutexes, lifting RUST% to its final 57%. The final codebase is approximately 10.3 kSLOC of idiomatic Rust across 16 files, translated from an original 12.5 kSLOC C codebase, with no unsafe extern "C" function declarations and no static mut left in the evaluated code. Client porting and static-mut elimination cut the client's unsafe blocks from roughly 86 to 40. Residual gap: five signal-handler EX type aliases and six #[no_mangle] entry-point annotations, and 99 PA and 99 DU uses confined to FFI boundary adapters
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: Functional equivalence was verified end-to-end: after each of the 168 function ports and each of the 37 static mut wrappings (16 client, 21 server), Gate B ran the tunnel against the public resolver under real traffic for 30 s or more, verified curl download and netperf through the tunnel, and passed a wire-format integration test

extraction.notes: ELIGIBILITY NOTE: this is a translation/migration paper, so a reviewer could route it to the 'adjacent' side list (LLM refactoring of human-written code, EC4). It was included because the evaluated artifact is new Rust code that the LLM wrote (from a C source and a transpiled baseline), the five idiomaticity criteria and the safety counts are explicitly non-functional properties of that generated code, and the technique is an intervention (an agentic compile-plus-runtime feedback loop) designed to improve them. Other caveats. (1) The models are essentially unreported: only Qwen3.6-27B is named, as the one needing fewest iterations, and the claim that 'a particular model choice does not materially affect the outcome' is asserted without any supporting data. The agent tooling 'rtk' and 'OAC' is named but never explained or cited. (2) Single case study on one 12.5 kSLOC program; no repeated runs, no variance, no statistical test, and no comparison against the direct-LLM-translation baseline the paper argues against. (3) SAFE% and RUST% are author-defined composite metrics; they deliberately omit the raw unsafe count (justified as not penalising correct refactoring), and the headline 'no unsafe extern "C" function declarations' sits slightly in tension with SAFE% = 95% (the residual is five signal-handler EX type aliases plus six #[no_mangle] annotations). (4) Correctness is verified thoroughly but qualitatively; no pass rate or test-count figure is given, and the runtime oracle depends on a live public DNS resolver, which is not a reproducible test environment. (5) Notable negative finding worth recording: batching three Mutex wrappings produced a live deadlock that compiled and passed static checks but stalled transfers at zero bytes, and POSIX getopt() externs (optarg, optind, opterr, optopt) were found to be unwrappable and were deferred. (6) The process is explicitly human-in-the-loop: type deduplication, FFI adapter scaffolding and lock-wrapping orchestration were handled by a human as exceptions, so the 37 developer-hours figure mixes agent and human effort. (7) No artifact release; the only URL is upstream iodine (https://code.kryo.se/iodine/). (8) No contamination discussion, despite iodine being a long-standing public open-source project. (9) Figures 1, 2 and 3 extracted poorly (the three-column code listing in Figure 1 and the metric plot in Figure 3 are interleaved), but all quoted numbers come from the running text of Section 4.3 and the Validation paragraph.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Evaluates an uncertainty-aware rollback decoding technique for LLM code generation and, besides functional metrics, reports a security outcome (Patch-Aligned Safe Rate on Dsec-Python) for the generated code. Borderline: the technique targets correctness and the security metric is a coarse similarity-to-reference proxy.
extraction.title: Do Uncertainty Signals Help? A Systematic Study of Uncertainty-Aware Decoding with Rollback Mechanisms

techniques.technique_name: Uncertainty-aware rollback decoding (statement-level generation, lightweight checks with public tests, feedback/uncertainty-guided rollback, branch decay; 8 uncertainty signals compared)
techniques.tools: Syntax checking, public-test execution, repetition detection; PyTorch 2.8.0, Transformers 4.40.0
techniques.iterations: Token budget 1,536 (2x max length 768); error-line rollback for at most K=2 consecutive failures at the same location before uncertainty-guided localization; branch decay gamma=0.9; Dsec-Python at most three rollback recoveries
techniques.metrics: security: Patch-Aligned Safe Rate (PASR; line-level IoU >= 0.5 and normalized similarity >= 0.6 in modified region) on Dsec-Python [similarity-to-reference]; correctness: pass@1, AvgTestPassRate, compilation pass rate [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: HumanEval (164), MBPP, HumanEval-CPP, CodeForces2305 (90), APPS Competition subset, Dsec-Python
techniques.models: DeepSeek(-Coder) 7B, open, code-specialized; StarCoder2-7B, open, code-specialized; Qwen2.5-7B, open; Mistral-7B, open; CodeLlama-7B, open, code-specialized; SafeCoder-7B, open, code-specialized (security-tuned); CodeLlama-34B, open, code-specialized; QLoRA fine-tuned CodeLlama-7B on APPS
techniques.baselines: Equal-budget restart; vanilla decoding; feedback-only detection; feedback-guided (error-line) rollback without uncertainty; uncertainty-guided rollback without feedback; full w/o branch decay
techniques.effect_target_headline: an absolute improvement of up to 6.4% in Patch-Aligned Safe Rate on Dsec-Python (full framework vs equal-budget restart)
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: gains of up to 0.26 in pass@1 and 0.35 in AvgTestPassRate on functional code generation benchmarks (vs equal-budget restart)

extraction.notes: Security is not the target of the technique (aimed at functional correctness); the only NF outcome is PASR, a patch-alignment similarity metric that authors themselves call coarse with limited sensitivity to security improvements. dims_targeted left empty for that reason; effect_target reflects the measured security dimension. Headline 6.4% is as printed in abstract; Table II differences (e.g., 0.50 to 0.56 DeepSeek-7B) appear as up to 0.06, reviewer should check. Single run, no significance tests. Contamination only addressed by including CodeForces2305 recent problems.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes ZOMBOSS, an LLM-agent kernel-generation framework in which the agent proposes mappings inside a generated compiler boundary and is guided by measured cycle counts; compared against direct LLM agentic kernel generation (KernelCraft-style) and the compiler default on measured kernel execution cycles (efficiency) plus correctness.
extraction.title: Rethinking Agentic Kernel Generation for Emerging Accelerators

techniques.technique_name: ZOMBOSS: compiler-mediated agentic mapping search (LLM agent selects/constrains typed mapping decisions; generated ACT backend completes, legalizes and emits native code; feedback from verified correctness and measured cycles)
techniques.tools: ACT (Accelerator Compiler Toolkit) generated backend from TAIDL/TensorLift; Gemmini on Xilinx ZC706 FPGA (Chipyard GemminiRocketConfig, Vivado 2022.2, PetaLinux 2022.2) with rdcycle cycle measurement; PLENA transaction-level simulator
techniques.iterations: Same maximum number of agent iterations as the direct-generation baseline (value not stated); best verified candidate retained; incumbent replaced only when verified and strictly faster; 12 unique candidate evaluations in random-sampling comparison
techniques.metrics: efficiency: kernel cycle count measured on FPGA (Gemmini) and simulator latency (PLENA), geometric-mean speedup [execution]; correctness: full-output numerical verification against an oracle, coverage of instances with a correct kernel
techniques.benchmarks: KernelCraft benchmark definitions and input shapes: 20 Gemmini instances (BatchMatMul, GEMM, GEMV, Linear) and 36 PLENA instances (12 families incl. FFN, FlashAttn, GEMM, GEMV, GQA, MHA, MQA, SwiGLU, LayerNorm, RMSNorm, SiLU, Softmax)
techniques.languages: Accelerator ISA/assembly for Gemmini and PLENA
techniques.models: DeepSeek-V4-Flash, closed (API), instruct; DeepSeek-V4-Pro, closed (API), instruct (ablation only)
techniques.baselines: Neural: direct agentic native-kernel generation following KernelCraft; Candidate-0: compiler default mapping; random sampling over the legal catalog
techniques.effect_target_headline: geometric-mean speedups of 3.34× on Gemmini and 1.10× on PLENA relative to the compiler default; 1.79× geometric-mean speedup over Neural's best correct kernel in each of Neural's 14 successful Gemmini runs; on PLENA's 12 Neural-success instances Neural is 1.02× faster in geometric mean
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: correct verified kernel on 20/20 Gemmini and 36/36 PLENA instances; Neural succeeds on only 14/20 (70.0%) and 12/36 (33.3%)

extraction.notes: Borderline IC2: in ZOMBOSS the LLM outputs mapping decisions and the compiler backend emits the native code, so the final code is LLM-guided rather than LLM-written; the direct-generation baseline is LLM-written. The efficiency gain over the compiler default comes from LLM-guided search; vs. direct LLM generation it is mixed (better on Gemmini, slightly worse on PLENA where both succeed). PLENA results take the best of three runs. Also reports 71.2%/54.2% token reductions vs. Neural. Figures with per-instance results are garbled.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Benchmark paper (FinHardBench) that measures functional correctness and post-place-and-route timing of Verilog generated by six LLMs under fixed prompting; it does not propose or evaluate a technique to improve the non-functional quality of generated code (the feedback-driven DSE experiment selects configurations rather than generating code, and the adaptation and agentic-pilot results report correctness only).
extraction.title: FinHardBench: Can LLMs Generate Latency-Aware Hardware for Financial Computing?
extraction.notes: Measures timing quality (Fmax ratio, critical-path ratio up to 13.67x slower on VWAP) of single-shot LLM Verilog vs golden references, a context study. Exp. 2 LLM-guided design space exploration with feedback optimizes end-to-end latency but the LLM picks configurations of pre-written variants, not code. Exp. 3 (adaptation with 3 rounds of feedback) reports pass rates only, including a 'performance' (pipeline insertion) category scored by pass rate. Borderline if a reviewer treats the DSE loop as a technique on code.

extraction.eligibility_reason: AtumAI uses LLM agents with evolutionary search to generate datacenter control-plane policies, but outcomes are domain objectives of the simulated datacenter (admission success, resource cost, SLO violations, provisioned power), not non-functional quality of the generated code itself.
extraction.title: AtumAI: A Principled Framework for Agentic Generation of Datacenter Control-Plane Policies
extraction.notes: Borderline: the workload-placement score includes 'planning throughput' (scheduler's own decision throughput, improved 8%), which is partly an efficiency property of the generated policy code, but it is one term of a composite domain objective (VMScore), comparable to AlphaEvolve-style algorithm discovery. Policies are partly expressed in a formula DSL. No code/artifact URL given. Figures garbled in extraction.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Introduces a benchmark (SeGaBench) and evaluates five LLMs in a blind single-turn setting at producing performance-improving source edits of existing C/C++ programs; it measures speedup of LLM-edited code but proposes or evaluates no quality-improving technique beyond plain model comparison and repeated sampling.
extraction.title: Can Large Language Models Recover Semantic Optimization Opportunities That Compilers Miss?
extraction.notes: Benchmark paper: efficiency (speedup over -O3/LTO/PGO baseline, gap closed to oracle) of LLM-edited C/C++ is measured for five models without an intervention; could alternatively be seen as adjacent (LLM optimization of human-written code). Success@k over five samples is reported but not framed as a technique.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes RepoOMP, an LLM-agent workflow (structured dependency context + rule/agent routing + compile/check/timing verification loop) whose LLM edits repository code to insert OpenMP parallelization, and reports execution speedup (efficiency) of the LLM-edited code with correctness checks.
extraction.title: RepoOMP: Repository-Aware Hotspot OpenMP Parallelization via Dependency-Aware Context Reduction

techniques.technique_name: RepoOMP (MAP repository graph + Rule-Agent Router + Structured Transformation Context + verification/rollback loop)
techniques.tools: Bear (compilation database); tree-sitter; gprof profiling; Clang 22.0.0 -O3 with OpenMP 4.5; ThreadSanitizer (audit); Claude Code npm v1.0.8 (baseline)
techniques.iterations: Up to 3 attempts per hotspot (compile, workload-specific check, positive speedup); rollback to previous valid state on failure
techniques.metrics: efficiency: speedup over serial -O3 at 16 threads, five-run arithmetic mean, plus accepted-set median/IQR and thread/platform sweeps [execution]; cost: model-side tokens and wall-clock time; correctness: build failure / wrong answer under workload-specific oracles (MD5, PSNR, top-5 accuracy, energy drift) [execution]; ThreadSanitizer warning counts as supplementary audit
techniques.benchmarks: NPB 3.0 OpenMP C (8 kernels, Class A/B); BOTS (8 kernels); real-world repositories FFmpeg, NCNN, GROMACS (3 detailed kernels each; 951 profiled hotspots total, 330 accepted real-world hotspots)
techniques.models: GPT-5.1, size NR, closed, general/reasoning; Claude 4.5 Sonnet, size NR, closed, general; Gemini 3 Pro, size NR, closed, general/reasoning
techniques.baselines: Claude Code unstructured repository agent (same backbones, same 3-attempt budget, no MAP/STC); AutoPar (ROSE); Polly (LLVM); human-expert OpenMP versions; ablations No-Router, No-STC, Flat-Ctx, Rule-Only, Agent-Only
techniques.effect_target_headline: RepoOMP achieves average speedups of 8.23× on NPB and 8.96× on BOTS (Claude Code-based baseline 3.31× and 4.12×); nine real-world kernels: cross-backbone mean of 5.25×, improves speedup by 18–28% relative to the unstructured Claude Code baseline (4.17×)
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: RepoOMP records zero BF/WA cells in the reported task tables, whereas the ClaudeCode-based workflows incur 26 such cells

extraction.notes: Eligibility borderline on EC4/adjacent: the LLM edits existing human-written repository code (OpenMP insertion), but the LLM generates the transformation, so treated as LLM-edited code with an efficiency outcome; reviewer should confirm against the 'adjacent' side list. Stage is both pre-generation (MAP/STC context) and a post-generation verification loop; coded as pre-generation since context construction is the core contribution. Tables 6-11 garbled in extraction (columns interleaved); headline numbers taken from text. Token reduction 47-68% vs Claude Code. Released repo is a 'Simplified' version.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Controlled evaluation of a prompting intervention (a single appended sentence naming SOC 2 and data sensitivity) against a neutral prompt for LLM-generated production code, measuring security/compliance controls and insecure constructions in the generated code with hand-verified binary rubrics.

techniques.technique_name: SOC 2 directive: one generic sentence appended to the user prompt declaring the data sensitive and the artifact subject to SOC 2
techniques.tools: Custom regular-expression pattern scorer (score.py) as first pass; blind LLM semantic grader; human hand-verification as canonical
techniques.metrics: security: conformance as fraction of binary rubric items (12-15 per use case) mapped to SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria [human, with tool-static regex first pass and llm-judge second rater]; count of insecure constructions (commission items such as debug-mode RCE, broken object-level authorization) [human]
techniques.benchmarks: 4 bespoke use cases (S3 CLI with boto3, authentication service in Flask/FastAPI, RDS Terraform module, file-upload handler with personal data); 24 generations (3 models x 2 conditions x 4 cases, one generation per cell)
techniques.models: Claude Fable 5 (closed); Claude Opus 4.8 (closed); Claude Opus 5 (closed)
techniques.baselines: Neutral prompt with no security or compliance language
techniques.effect_target_headline: The single SOC 2 sentence moved every case to 86–100%, worth 23 to 50 points, and removed every insecure construction

extraction.human_eval_details: Authors hand-verified every failed item and commission flag as the canonical scores. A blinded LLM semantic grader served as a second rater: regex scorer vs LLM grader agreement 87.5%, Cohen's kappa 0.658 over 216 item judgments. No inter-human agreement is reported.
extraction.notes: Each cell is a single generation and no variance is estimated; the authors say so explicitly. Scoring is static only, and functional correctness is never executed or measured. The rubrics are the authors' own mapping of SOC 2 criteria, and the commission list was expanded after seeing the code (post hoc). All three models are from one vendor family, and the choice is justified. The paper is also a context-style measurement of unprompted defaults (47% to 88% conformance). Part of the abstract appears out of order in extraction.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes an expertise-guided, compiler-feedback agentic framework plus SFT/GRPO model adaptation for LLM translation of C/C++ into optimized HLS code, and reports quantitative efficiency outcomes (HLS-synthesis and RTL co-simulation latency cycles, speedups) of the LLM-generated code alongside functional correctness.

GM(LChatHLS /LHLSmith ) = 6.91×; Claude Sonnet 4.6: Bk /Sk is 17.46× versus Bk /Ok =6.07×; thus expertise adds 2.88× and wins 22/25 kernels against expertise off; up to 252× speedup over the reference HLS kernel

techniques.technique_name: Tool-grounded model adaptation: SFT (QLoRA) of Qwen3.6-27B on validated Sonnet 4.6 agent actions, and Vitis-grounded GRPO of Qwen2.5-Coder-7B with a correctness-gated latency/resource reward
techniques.tools: AMD Vitis HLS 2023.2 C simulation and synthesis for reward/filtering; 4-bit NF4 QLoRA rank 16, one epoch; GRPO group size 8, LoRA rank 32, 100 updates
techniques.metrics: efficiency: geometric-mean HLS-synthesis and RTL-simulation cycle gains vs base model [execution / tool-static synthesis estimate]; correctness: RTL-output passes, timing passes [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: SFT: four-kernel matched diagnostic (durbin, floyd-warshall, gemm, trmm) and five held-out kernels; GRPO: 14 Rodinia/ML4Accel training tasks, 24 PolyBench evaluation tasks
techniques.models: Qwen3.6-27B (open; SFT student); Qwen2.5-Coder-7B (open, code-specialized; GRPO); Claude Sonnet 4.6 (closed; teacher)

techniques.effect_target_headline: Fine-tuning reduces geometric-mean synthesis and RTL-simulation cycles by 1.70× and 1.60× (Qwen3.6-27B Translator, four kernels); peak per-kernel synthesis gain of 3.61× (gemm); bootstrap interval, [1.00×, 2.56×], includes one
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: RTL-output passes rise from 10 for the base model to 13 after group-relative policy optimization; SFT reaches 8 (24 tasks); timing passes change from 3/4 to 4/4 (SFT)

extraction.notes: Efficiency here is hardware latency (HLS synthesis estimates / RTL co-simulation cycles) of generated FPGA designs; reviewer should confirm this counts as runtime efficiency. Abstract headline 4.24x is the sensitivity value excluding syr2k (6.91× on all 8 common passes). Several evaluations are small (4-5 kernels) and authors flag some as preliminary; Grok/DeepSeek RTL outputs not independently replayed. Figures 6-9 heavily garbled. Evaluation kernels excluded from adaptation training data (partial contamination handling). Source code listed as 'Pending'. No threats-to-validity section. Paper says token/time overhead is specified but only model-call counts appear in the text.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes an OS-specialized multi-agent harness (specification, implementation, review, refinement agents with build/boot/test feedback) whose LLM-generated OS code is evaluated, including three performance-intent specification patches whose generated implementations are benchmarked for runtime speedup (efficiency). Borderline because the efficiency comparison is only against the unoptimized generated OS, not against an alternative technique.
extraction.title: OSFoundry: Building and Evolving Operating Systems with Specification-Guided Agents

techniques.technique_name: OSFoundry: SysSpec* (task-bounding Plan + functionality/modularity/concurrency Specification) guided multi-agent harness with implement-verify loop, OS-specific review, refinement, OS knowledge base and QEMU/GDB execution environment
techniques.tools: QEMU, GDB, xv6 build toolchain (RISC-V), Linux kernel build/selftests; OSKB with Linux-derived review prompts; Rust CLI orchestrator
techniques.iterations: Implement-verify loop until the implementation conforms to the Specification and all Plan success criteria hold; review/refinement iterations until blueprint satisfied (no fixed maximum stated)
techniques.metrics: efficiency: allocator throughput (ops/ms) under 1/2/4 CPUs, fork-exec time vs parent memory size, pipe transfer time/throughput vs chunk size (execution); correctness: xv6 functional tests (70), module-level semantic equivalence judged by GPT-5.4 (llm-judge), Linux bug-fix task success via task tests or LLM judge
techniques.benchmarks: SpecOS (xv6-riscv reimplementation, 259 modules) with 70 xv6 functional tests; 3 performance intents (per-CPU page allocator, copy-on-write fork, batched pipe I/O); GUI evolution; 11 Linux-kernel bug-fix tasks from recent commits
techniques.models: Qwen3.6-Plus, size NR, closed, instruct; GPT-5.4, size NR, closed, reasoning; Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, 35B MoE, open, instruct; GPT-5.5 (high reasoning effort), size NR, closed, reasoning (Linux tasks and Codex baseline)
techniques.baselines: Efficiency: original generated SpecOS (unoptimized) under same QEMU environment; module accuracy: Normal (natural-language description + dependency signatures) and Oracle (plus dependency source code) prompts; Linux tasks: Codex agent with GPT-5.5
techniques.effect_target_headline: Across address-space sizes from 2 MB to 32 MB, COW avoids these copies and achieves a 3.12× to 4.41× speedup over the baseline (copy-on-write fork); per-CPU allocator reaching a 19.2% improvement at 4 CPUs; batched pipe I/O At 4096 bytes, it reaches a 2.74× speedup
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: With Qwen3.6-Plus and GPT-5.4, it achieves 100% accuracy (259 modules); Qwen3.6-35B-A3B 90.3% accuracy; across 11 Linux-kernel bug-fix tasks, OSFoundry achieves 1.8× the accuracy of Codex using GPT-5.5 (9 of 11 vs 5 of 11)

extraction.notes: Eligibility borderline: efficiency outcomes are before/after measurements of three performance-intent specification patches versus the original generated SpecOS, with no comparison against a non-OSFoundry way of producing the optimization; the model used for the SpecOS evolution/performance experiments is not stated. Main comparative results concern correctness (module accuracy vs Normal/Oracle prompts; Linux bug-fix 1.8x Codex). Figure 10 and 12 values only partially in text. Linux tasks chosen to postdate model release (partial contamination handling). No code/data URL, no repeated runs, no cost reporting, no explicit threats section (failure analysis only).

extraction.title: Pseudo2CodeQA: A Benchmark for LLM-Based Structured Algorithmic Reasoning in Code Generation

techniques.technique_name: Pseudo2Code Agentic Framework (pseudocode generation agent, solution agent, test generation agent, execution-based verification)
techniques.iterations: Single pass: generated solution run against LLM-generated tests; accepted if all pass; iterative refinement left to future work
techniques.metrics: readability-maintainability: Clarity score 1-5 (readability, organization, maintainability) by GPT-5 rubric (llm-judge) and by human evaluators on 100 tasks (human); correctness: GPT-5 Correctness score and unit-test pass rate (execution)
techniques.benchmarks: Pseudo2CodeQA (300 tasks: 100 Easy, 100 Medium, 100 Hard)
techniques.models: Gemini 2.5 Pro, closed, reasoning (pipeline backbone); baselines GPT-4o Turbo, GPT-3.5 Turbo, Claude 3.5 Opus, closed; DeepSeek-Coder 1.3B/6.7B/7B, DeepSeek-LLM-7B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen 1.5B/7B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, CodeLlama-7B, Gemma 2B/7B, Phi-2, Mistral-7B, LLaMA-3.2-3B, open
techniques.baselines: Pseudo2Code (Direct) generation with the same Gemini 2.5 Pro; other commercial and open-source models with direct generation
techniques.effect_target_headline: Clarity 4.77 (Pseudo2Code Agentic Pipeline) vs 4.33 (Pseudo2Code Direct), GPT-5 rubric, 1-5 scale
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: overall score of 4.78 compared to 4.31 for the strongest baseline model (Correctness 4.75 vs 4.33)

extraction.human_eval_details: 2 evaluators, 50 tasks each (100 tasks), 1-5 rubric; no inter-rater or human-LLM agreement statistic reported despite claim of strong agreement
extraction.notes: Readability (Clarity) is measured but not targeted; the paper's aim is correctness/algorithmic faithfulness. Clarity is a GPT-5 judge score without validation statistics. Pseudo2Code (Direct) scores are identical to the Gemini 2.5 Pro row. Human evaluation appears to cover only the agentic pipeline outputs, no baseline comparison. Benchmark itself constructed with Gemini 2.5, which is also the pipeline model. No threats-to-validity section.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes Cake, where an LLM coding agent authors GPU kernels in a typed hardware-explicit IR inside an evolving compiler harness that returns localized verifier, cost-model and profiler diagnostics; reports runtime speedups of the agent-generated kernels, including a matched comparison against the same agent writing direct CUDA/PTX.
extraction.title: CAKE: Compiler-Agent Co-Design for Frontier Kernel Evolution

techniques.technique_name: Cake: agent-authored typed Cake IR with compiler-harness feedback (pre-compile verifier gates, calibrated cost model, sanitizer/profiler evidence) and co-evolution of the harness
techniques.tools: Cake IR verifier and cost model (calibrated for B200 and H100); Compute Sanitizer; CUPTI timing with L2 flush; NVIDIA CUDA toolchain
techniques.iterations: token budget (80 million tokens per clean-start run) with prespecified plateau criterion
techniques.metrics: efficiency: kernel speedup vs tuned baselines from median CUPTI GPU span, geometric-mean speedup across shapes (Gspan) [execution]; correctness: on-GPU numerical correctness gates vs reference across shapes and input distributions [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: Flash-KMeans assign kernel clean start on B200 (3 runs per arm); Kimi Delta Attention prefill (6 shapes) and decode (30 shapes); TinyGEMM (35 shapes); Alpha-MoE W8A8; 11 known-kernel reproductions (FA4, TRTLLM, DeepGEMM, CUTLASS MLA, DSv4 sparse MLA); KNN build/search and KMeans portfolios (112, 198, 124 shapes)
techniques.languages: Cake IR (Python-embedded) lowered to CUDA/PTX; control arm CUDA C++ with inline PTX
techniques.models: GPT-5.6-sol, closed, reasoning (effort xhigh)
techniques.baselines: same agent writing direct CUDA/PTX (matched clean-start arm); tuned FlashML KMeans Triton; official FlashKDA; FlashInfer; TensorRT-LLM; CUTLASS; DeepGEMM; FlashAttention-4; FlashLib
techniques.effect_target_headline: the best candidate at an 80-million-token budget reaches a median 1.144× the tuned FlashML baseline with Cake IR, versus 0.928× for direct CUDA/PTX (Flash-KMeans clean start, B200, three runs per representation); KDA reaches a 2.05× geometric-mean speedup over official FlashKDA

extraction.notes: Only the Flash-KMeans clean start is a controlled technique vs no-technique comparison (Cake IR vs direct CUDA/PTX, same model, 3 runs each, median [min,max]); other results compare against expert libraries. All reported candidates pass correctness gates, but correctness is not compared between arms. Single model held fixed by design. Low-level reference implementations hidden from agents in clean-start/frontier experiments and audited (leakage control). Cake source not released; four upstream FlashInfer PRs (#4262, #4279, #4274, #4287) given. Verifier/cost-model internals deliberately not described. LOC comparison explicitly disclaimed as not a readability metric. Figures garbled.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Evaluates LLM repair strategies (structured prompting, verification-guided iterative repair with Checkov feedback) for misconfigured IaC and reports security outcomes (target misconfiguration resolved, no new scanner findings) of the LLM-edited artifacts; borderline because the input artifacts are human-written and the task is repair.
extraction.title: IaC-Guard-V: A Verification Framework for LLM-Generated Infrastructure-as-Code Repairs

techniques.technique_name: Verification-guided iterative repair (verify-loop) with Checkov gate feedback
techniques.tools: Checkov v3.2.517 (syntax parsing, rule checks, regression detection); unified diff for minimality
techniques.iterations: Up to two retries (three total attempts); stops when all three binary gates (syntax, target-issue resolution, no regression) pass
techniques.metrics: security: verified-fix rate VFR (V2 target Checkov rule resolved and V3 no new Checkov findings) (tool-static); maintainability-proxy: patch minimality median diff ratio (tool-static diff); correctness: V1 syntactic validity via Checkov parser only
techniques.benchmarks: IaC-Guard-V benchmark: 70 misconfigured artifacts from Checkov's test suite (50 Terraform AWS, 20 Kubernetes), 70 unique rules, 8 violation classes
techniques.models: Claude Opus 4.6, size NR, closed, instruct; Claude Sonnet 4.6, size NR, closed, instruct; Llama 4 Maverick 17B active (MoE), open, instruct
techniques.baselines: Plain prompting; structured prompting
techniques.effect_target_headline: Verification-guided iterative repair statistically significantly improves verified-fix rates across all models, achieving 68–92% compared to 32–50% for baselines (Terraform; Opus 92% CI 84–98%)
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: all models achieve 100% syntactic validity (Terraform, all methods)

techniques.technique_name: Structured prompting (rule ID, description, violation class, affected resource and lines, JSON output)
techniques.tools: Checkov v3.2.517 (finding metadata and evaluation)
techniques.metrics: security: VFR, V2 resolution, V3 regression (tool-static Checkov); patch minimality diff ratio (tool-static); correctness: V1 syntax validity
techniques.benchmarks: IaC-Guard-V benchmark: 50 Terraform + 20 Kubernetes artifacts
techniques.models: Claude Opus 4.6, size NR, closed; Claude Sonnet 4.6, size NR, closed; Llama 4 Maverick 17B active (MoE), open
techniques.baselines: Plain prompting
techniques.effect_target_headline: structured prompting consistently underperforms plain prompting on Terraform (32–42% vs. 44–50%) and introduces regressions in 4–10% of cases; improves Maverick's Kubernetes performance from 45% to 95%
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: V1=95% on Kubernetes structured for Maverick; 100% otherwise

extraction.notes: Borderline EC4/adjacent: LLM repair of human-written (Checkov test-suite) misconfigured IaC; included because the LLM-edited artifact's security is measured and techniques are compared, but reviewer should confirm scope policy for LLM repair of human code. Correctness only as syntax validity. Minimality (diff ratio) mapped loosely to maintainability: structured most minimal (0.067-0.086), verify-loop mixed vs plain. Replication package URL redacted for review. Temperature 0, single run per item; bootstrap CIs and McNemar tests reported. Benchmark sourced from public Checkov tests; contamination not discussed.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes KernelArc, a multi-agent LLM framework that iteratively edits GPU kernel source under a deterministic correctness/benchmark guard, and reports quantitative efficiency outcomes (latency speedups, SOL scores, TFLOPS) for the generated code.
extraction.title: KernelArc: A Multi-Agent Framework for GPU Kernel Optimization

techniques.technique_name: KernelArc: strategy-specialized parallel agents with conclusions-only shared win/trap memory (configurable retention), deterministic cascade gate + benchmark guard, read-only cross-agent campaign leaderboard, and plateau-triggered drafting
techniques.tools: SOL-ExecBench evaluator bridge (SM clocks locked, L2 flushed, CUPTI tracing); cuBLAS/cuBLASLt, cuDNN, CUTLASS 4.4.2/CuTe DSL, Triton, CUDA/PTX; NVIDIA H100 SXM and B200 GPUs
techniques.iterations: Fixed budget of 100 candidate positions per trajectory (split evenly across agents); guard emits STOP on plateau, target reached, time budget exhausted, or candidate cap; plateau counter r triggers drafting at threshold r_draft; 5 trajectories per configuration in the ablation
techniques.metrics: efficiency: SOL score (benchmark-aggregated speed-of-light ratio across input shapes), kernel latency in ms, latency-ratio speedup vs PyTorch reference and vs optimized baseline, TFLOPS [all execution]; correctness: deterministic guard correctness predicate C(k,w) over all workload cases, pass/fail gate [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: SOL-ExecBench (235 problems; 4 categories L1/L2/Quantization/FlashInfer) - one representative task per category evaluated: L1-030 (16 shapes), L2-025 (16 shapes), L2-053, Quant-031 (16 shapes), FI-014 (30 workloads, SOL-ExecBench kernel 223); plus a 4096x4096 BF16 GEMM fixed-shape campaign
techniques.languages: CUDA C++, PTX, Triton, Python (CuTe DSL)
techniques.models: Claude Opus 5 (closed, reasoning); Claude Opus 4.6 (closed, reasoning); Kimi K3 (open); Qwen 3.8 Max; GLM 5.2; DeepSeek V4 Pro; Inkling; MiniMax M3
techniques.baselines: Single-agent private-memory configuration (the framework's own boundary case); Multi-bounded (shared memory capped at 16 entries) vs Multi-unbounded; PyTorch reference implementations; NVIDIA optimized SOL-ExecBench baselines; matched cuBLAS baseline for GEMM
techniques.effect_target_headline: At a roughly 100-candidate budget, Multi-unbounded is the strongest observed configuration: its geometric-mean speedup is 2.04x Single and 1.59x Multi-bounded, while Multi-bounded is 1.28x Single (FI-014, 5 trajectories per configuration); Single 142.6 [107.6, 190.8], Multi-bounded 182.7 [144.5, 231.0], Multi-unbounded 290.8 [197.3, 434.2]

techniques.technique_name: Guided single-agent measurement-gated optimization loop with a detailed Hopper-specific CUDA playbook (one-agent, private-memory boundary case of KernelArc)
techniques.tools: NVIDIA Nsight-style profiler targets specified by the playbook; cuBLAS (cublasGemmEx) baseline; CUDA/PTX toolchain; H100 SXM (132 SMs, HBM3 3.35 TB/s, ~989 TFLOPS BF16 peak)
techniques.iterations: Eight-hour wall-clock budget; observe-hypothesize-edit-measure loop ratcheting the accepted best only on measured improvement; 17 accepted milestones in the reported run
techniques.metrics: efficiency: BF16 throughput in TFLOPS at M=N=K=4096, percent of theoretical peak, cumulative USD cost per backbone [execution]; correctness: guard correctness harness pass/fail [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: Single fixed-shape 4096x4096 BF16 GEMM campaign on H100; L1-030 single-agent plateau comparison on B200
techniques.models: Claude Opus 5; Claude Opus 4.6; Kimi K3; Qwen 3.8 Max; GLM 5.2; DeepSeek V4 Pro; Inkling; MiniMax M3 (one trajectory per backbone)
techniques.baselines: Textbook-naive CUDA kernel seed; strongest cuBLAS end-to-end baseline measured under the same protocol (742 TFLOPS)
techniques.effect_target_headline: a single-agent automated research loop reaches 766 TFLOPS (BF16) on one fixed shape, 3.2% above the matched cuBLAS baseline measured during the campaign; progression 4.6 to 766 TFLOPS across 17 accepted techniques, reaching 77% of theoretical peak

extraction.notes: No code/data artifact URL is given (only the public NVIDIA SOL-ExecBench leaderboard link). Correctness is a hard gate rather than a reported co-outcome, so no correctness numbers are extractable. Authors are explicit that configurations change several factors together (agent count, memory scope, leaderboard access, retention horizon) so the ablation is not a per-mechanism causal estimate; permutation test p=0.0466 primary, 0.0906 excluding one non-conforming trajectory. Only 5 of 235 SOL-ExecBench tasks evaluated. Figures 2-6 garbled in PDF extraction (axis labels interleaved with text).

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes a post-generation checked-lowering runtime that rewrites LLM-generated Python tool programs (eager data loading) into bounded implementations before dispatch, and reports quantitative peak memory, hard-cap completion and latency of the resulting code against direct execution and prompting/retry baselines. Borderline: the rewrite is a deterministic audited transformation rather than an LLM step, and much of the evaluation is systems-level (checker, leases).
extraction.title: SkillEffect: Checked Lowering for Memory-Bounded Agent Tools

techniques.technique_name: SkillEffect checked lowering: recognize the LLM-generated source program, reconstruct input facts, construct and independently check a bounded target IR and live-set bound, execute in a bounded VM under a capacity lease with postcondition-gated publication
techniques.tools: CPython 3.11.15 AST-based checker and bounded VM; Linux cgroup v2 (memory.max, memory.peak, memory.events) in Docker via Colima; SQLite capacity ledger; smolagents 1.26.0 harness; vLLM serving
techniques.iterations: Single deterministic lowering per dispatch (no LLM loop); abstains on zero or multiple matching relations
techniques.metrics: efficiency: fresh-cgroup peak physical memory (MiB), task completion under externally fixed memory caps (normalized log-cap AUC, C50/C90), aggregate verified goodput, process wall time [execution]; correctness: deterministic task verifier pass and online postcondition [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: 24 task-Skill pairs over six tool families (XLSX, FlowIO/FCS, AnnData, Zarr, Polars/CSV, Biopython/FASTA); 72-plan frozen generation pool (10 tasks with verifier-valid plans); 16-task agent-harness workload; audit-log Top-k extension
techniques.models: Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct-AWQ, 14B, open, instruct; Mistral-7B, 7B, open, instruct
techniques.baselines: Direct eager execution of the generated plan; always-pinned resource-clause prompt; retry with resource/cap feedback (up to two further attempts); composition of prompt variants; reject-only profile gate and plan gate plus cgroup; deployment-owned bounded tool surface
techniques.effect_target_headline: Under the same frozen family caps, unchanged natural plans complete only the five already-safe tasks (15/30 repeated runs) ... The bounded lowerer completes all 10 tasks and 30/30 runs with no cap failure. Among the five unsafe tasks, the comparison is 0/5 versus 5/5. (Polars plan peak 338.6 MiB eager vs 69.5 MiB lowered)
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: Only after each committed container exits does the host open the exact evaluation oracle, obtaining 15/15 matches

extraction.notes: Borderline: the intervention is a deterministic audited rewrite (not an LLM) applied to LLM-generated tool programs; many results (operator characterization, cap sweep 0.950 vs 0.467 AUC) use reference eager/bounded implementations rather than model-generated code. Only 10 of 24 tasks had verifier-valid LLM plans (Qwen); Mistral produced 4 valid attempts. Prompting baselines: always-pin 9/24, retry 4/24, cap-feedback 5/24 tasks. Three repeats per cell, no statistical tests. No code URL. Abstract text partly interleaved in extraction. Limitations section present.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Benchmarks LLM-generated CUDA kernels with inline PTX and evaluates techniques (repair-conditioned SFT 'Fixit', architecture-knowledge prompt context, multi-turn execution-feedback refinement vs coding agents) with quantitative efficiency outcomes (speedup over cuBLAS/cuDNN/FlashInfer) alongside correctness.
extraction.title: PTXBench: Benchmarking and Adapting LLMs for GPU Kernel Optimization with Architecture-specific PTX

techniques.metrics: efficiency: best speedup over frontier library (cuBLAS/cuDNN/FlashInfer), target-instruction best speedup, Fast_p, measured via CUPTI median latency [execution]; target-instruction execution via Nsight Compute [execution]

techniques.models: Qwen3.6-27B, 27B, open, instruct/reasoning (adapted); Gemini 3.1 Pro, closed (repair teacher); GLM-5.2, open (reasoning teacher)
techniques.baselines: Base Qwen3.6-27B; six data recipes (s1-s6); in-context alternatives (expert guidance, BM25-retrieved repair notes with/without fixed kernel)
techniques.effect_target_headline: Qwen3.6-27B-s1 best speedup on GEMM 0.303 / 0.303 / 0.340 (≤1/≤4/≤8 turns), whereas the base model produces no correct candidates on GEMM or any MHA workload
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: s1 turn correctness on MHA-Fwd 16.7 / 16.7 / 19.8 (%) vs base '–' (no correct kernels); Triton transfer: s1 has lower turn-level correctness on every workload

techniques.technique_name: Architecture-specific knowledge pack in prompt (parameters + PTX template functions + architecture contract)
techniques.tools: nvcc; CUPTI; Nsight Compute 2025.3.1
techniques.iterations: 8 model calls per trajectory with execution feedback
techniques.metrics: efficiency: target-instruction best speedup and best speedup vs frontier library [execution]

techniques.models: Gemini 3.1 Pro, closed, reasoning
techniques.baselines: Architecture parameters only; parameters + template functions
techniques.effect_target_headline: Target inst. best speedup 0.206 / 0.375 / 0.515 with full contract vs – / 0.542 / 0.542 with template functions only and – (0.056 / 0.119 / 0.273) with parameters only
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: 38.5% of turns satisfy target instruction correctness, 18.7 points above template functions alone

techniques.technique_name: MiniPTXAgent multi-turn refinement with execution/profiling feedback (vs Antigravity and Codex coding agents)
techniques.tools: nvcc -O3; CUPTI; Nsight Compute 2025.3.1; profiling service
techniques.iterations: 8 evaluation requests per trajectory; early stop at 1.2x speedup
techniques.metrics: efficiency: median per-trajectory best instruction-qualified speedup [execution]; token cost ratio
techniques.benchmarks: PTXBench 5 primary workloads on H100, 4 trajectories each
techniques.models: Gemini 3.1 Pro, closed, reasoning; GPT-5.6 Sol, closed, reasoning
techniques.baselines: Antigravity agent (Gemini 3.1 Pro); Codex agent (GPT-5.6 Sol)

extraction.notes: Primarily a benchmark paper; main technique is Fixit SFT where base model has no correct kernels so efficiency comparison is from zero (speedups remain well below 1x of libraries). Tables extracted from PDF are garbled (column alignment of triplets uncertain). Contamination considered only via knowledge-cutoff/PTX release lag analysis. Limitations section present but no full threats-to-validity discussion. Shuffle-seed repeats and min-max across prompt variants reported.
