extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes an agentic LLM optimizer that edits recovered AMDGPU assembly of compiled kernels inside a profiling- and verification-gated search loop, and reports verified runtime speedups of the LLM-edited kernels over the original binaries.
extraction.title: AsmEvo: Agentic Assembly-Level Optimization of AMD GPU Kernels with Functional Equivalence Verification

techniques.technique_name: AsmEvo (code-object recovery + metadata-aware ABI-preserving rebuild + profiling-guided hot-window editing + correctness-gated timing + long-horizon multi-start agentic search with memory, verified composition and anti-stall supervision)
techniques.tools: ROCm on AMD Instinct MI308X/MI300X; hardware counters and instruction sampling; co2s recovery, diffverify, metadata regen, hotwindow, kerncap tools; differential oracle (cosine >= 0.9999, L_inf <= 1e-3, byte-exact integers)
techniques.iterations: 12-hour wall-clock budget per kernel with four GPU workers; stop on budget or convergence; commit only if variance-aware margin (eps=0.002, k=0.85, s_floor=1.0) met; mean 137.8 attempts and 7.0 commits per kernel on KernelBench
techniques.metrics: efficiency: verified speedup T(K0)/T(K') from median event-timed latency, geometric-mean and max speedup, number of improved kernels [execution]; functional equivalence enforced as an acceptance gate via differential replay and library/framework tests [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: KernelBench Level 1 (15 kernels) and Level 2 (15 kernels) compiled HIP objects; 4 AITer code objects; 4 vLLM/SGLang Triton JIT HSACOs
techniques.models: Claude Opus 4.8, closed, reasoning
techniques.baselines: Original unmodified compiled code object (1.00x)
techniques.effect_target_headline: On MI308X, AsmEvo improves 29 of 30 selected KernelBench kernels, reaching 1.35x geometric-mean and 3.88x maximum speedup

extraction.notes: LLM edits existing compiled kernels (not from-scratch generation). Only baseline is the original binary; no comparison to another LLM search driver or non-agentic optimizer is reported despite the paper saying search drivers are compared within the same harness. Correctness is an acceptance gate (all reported speedups are verified equivalent), not reported as a rate. Single model; timing uses median and coefficient-of-variation-based commit margin but no repeated full runs. Production results: AITer 1.09x/1.31x and Triton JIT 1.18x/1.34x geo-mean/max.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes an LLM multi-agent framework (contract-augmented specs, implementation-space planning, profiling-guided refinement) that generates CUDA kernels, evaluated on measured speedup (efficiency) with correctness as co-outcome against several baselines.
extraction.title: HIERA: Workload-Aware Planning Across Implementation Spaces for GPU Kernel Optimization

techniques.technique_name: HIERA (contract-augmented task specification + hierarchical implementation-space and optimization-direction planning with NCU profiling feedback)
techniques.tools: NVIDIA Nsight Compute (NCU); CUDA Toolkit 12.8; PyTorch 2.7.1+cu126; cuDNN 9.5.1; NVIDIA A100-PCIE-40GB
techniques.iterations: 3 refinement rounds x 6 candidates per round (budget B = 18 per task); stencil case study 5 iterations x population 10
techniques.metrics: efficiency: fast1 (fraction of tasks faster than PyTorch), fast2 (>2x speedup), speedup distribution, latency (execution, 3 warmup + 100 runs); correctness: fast0 (compile + functional validity) (execution)
techniques.benchmarks: KernelBench Levels 1-3 (250 tasks: 100/100/50); 90-task sampled subset for implementation-space comparison; 2D box stencil case study
techniques.models: DeepSeek-V3.2, open, instruct; Qwen3.6-Plus, closed, instruct; Gemini-3.6-Flash, closed, instruct
techniques.baselines: KernelBench-Caesar; CUDAForge; CUDA-L1 (training-based); fixed implementation-space variants; ablations w/o contract, w/o planning
techniques.effect_target_headline: HIERA reaches 92.4% fast0 and 60.4% fast1, exceeding KernelBench (85.2%/ 29.6%) and CUDAForge (85.6%/ 44.8%) (B = 18)
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: At B = 1, it achieves 71.6% fast0 and 32.4% fast1, outperforming KernelBench by 30.8 and 22.4 percentage points

extraction.notes: Single run per configuration (budget points from same trajectories); variance only of speedup distribution. Stencil case study: 1.53x over cuDNN. No code release stated. Paper uses AAAI template (copyright 2027) but no venue stated; treated as preprint. Figure-based results (Fig. 3, 5) not fully legible in text.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Evaluates a security-aware prompting intervention (appended OWASP security-requirements section) against a baseline prompt for LLM-generated web applications and reports quantitative security findings from SAST, DAST, SCA and manual testing.
extraction.title: Vibe Coding and Web Application Security: A Twin-Prompt Study
extraction.venue: 37th Central European Conference on Information and Intelligent Systems (CECIIS 2026)

techniques.technique_name: Security-aware prompting (application-independent OWASP Top 10 security-requirements section appended to the spec prompt), single-shot
techniques.tools: Bandit 1.9.4; ESLint 9.39.4 + eslint-plugin-security; Semgrep 1.163.0 (p/default, p/security-audit, p/owasp-top-ten, p/secrets); pip-audit 2.10.0; npm audit; OWASP ZAP (zap-stable, passive/active/API); Nikto 2.1.6; sqlmap 1.10.5; purpose-written manual test scripts
techniques.iterations: single non-iterative generation per variant
techniques.metrics: security: count and severity of confirmed (deduplicated, manually verified) findings mapped to OWASP Top 10 / CWE [tool-static + execution (DAST) + human manual testing]
techniques.benchmarks: 6 bespoke web applications (Flask, FastAPI, Express), each generated in baseline (A) and security-aware (B) variant = 12 programs
techniques.models: Claude Opus 4.8 via Claude Code (closed, agentic coding assistant)
techniques.baselines: Baseline prompt (variant A): identical spec prompt without security section
techniques.effect_target_headline: The security-aware variant produced fewer confirmed findings in every application (24 versus 51) and contained no Critical or High issues

extraction.human_eval_details: Single author performed manual security testing and assigned severity, OWASP category and confirmed/false-positive status; no second rater or agreement measure.
extraction.notes: Small preliminary study: 6 apps, 1 model, one generation per variant, descriptive only, no statistical test. Functional parity checked only at smoke-test level (not quantified). Standard tools used, but severity/confirmation labels from a single analyst without agreement. Model named 'Claude Opus 4.8' as printed.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Controlled experiment on an input-side technique (format of the architecture specification given to LLM coding agents, plus a no-architecture baseline) with quantitative maintainability-related outcomes of the generated code: LLM-judge architectural adherence, code quality and constraint compliance, and automated static constraint-violation and architecture-compliance checks.
extraction.title: Architecture as Capability Equalizer for Coding Agents

techniques.technique_name: Structured architecture specification formats in the agent prompt (Mermaid+constraints+ADRs, OpenAPI+Mermaid, C4/Structurizr DSL, TypeScript interface contracts with ArchUnit-style rules) vs prose and vs no architecture guidance
techniques.tools: TypeScript compiler (tsc --noEmit) available to the agent; custom static import analysis for constraint violations and weighted architecture compliance; API route coverage analysis
techniques.iterations: Multi-turn agent sessions, max 50 turns, agent signals done; identical across conditions
techniques.metrics: readability-maintainability: architectural adherence, code quality and constraint compliance on 1-10 scale [llm-judge, Claude Sonnet 4.6 with GPT-5 re-judging]; constraint violations via import analysis [tool-static]; weighted architecture compliance score [tool-static]; correctness proxies: completeness (judge), API route coverage [tool-static], TSC pass rate [compiler], demo run rate [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: Single bespoke Task Management API system (7 components, 25 routes, 6 constraints); 90 trials (5 formats x 6 models x 3) plus 3 no-architecture baseline trials
techniques.models: Claude Sonnet 4.6 (closed, frontier); Claude Haiku 4.5 (closed); GPT-5 (closed, reasoning); GPT-5-mini (closed); Gemini 2.5 Pro (closed); Gemini 2.5 Flash (closed)
techniques.baselines: Prose architecture specification (control); requirements-only prompt with no architecture guidance (Sonnet 4.6 only)
techniques.effect_target_headline: On the strongest models (Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5), format barely matters (quality spread 0.17–0.92). On weaker models, format produces spreads of 0.83–2.42 points; Architecture guidance raises the overall judge score by 3.34 points (5.08 → 8.42)
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: TypeScript contracts triple API route coverage for the weakest model (33% → 100%).

extraction.notes: Maintainability is operationalized as architecture conformance and judge-rated code quality, which is a looser fit to readability-maintainability than standard metrics. The judge was validated against the automated checks and a second LLM judge (Pearson r 0.47-0.60), with no human evaluation. Three trials per cell, ranges reported, no significance tests. Structured formats do not help uniformly: Gemini Pro scores 4.50 with TS contracts against 5.83 with prose, and on GPT-5 several structured formats score below prose. Correctness is only proxied by completeness, route coverage and compilation; there are no functional tests. Tables are partly garbled in extraction.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes a closed-loop agentic LLM framework that generates and iteratively refines GPU kernels (Triton) using compile, correctness and latency feedback with episodic restart, and reports execution speedups of the LLM-generated kernels and of patched models.
extraction.title: LLM4LLM: Bridging Kernel Benchmarks and Real Deployment via Closed-Loop Agentic Optimization

techniques.technique_name: LLM4LLM: real-model profiling, phase-aware task extraction, experience-guided episodic search with restart and distilled experience, deployment-time in-model acceptance
techniques.tools: Triton kernels; PyTorch profiler-based hotspot extraction; KernelBench harness; user-extensible API-correction layer (Triton, TileLang, CUDA extensions)
techniques.iterations: Candidate budget of 10 or 15 trials per task (15 used as strongest setting); episodes restart from task spec plus distilled experience record; acceptance requires normalized deployment latency <= 1 - delta
techniques.metrics: efficiency: end-to-end inference latency and speedup over eager, KernelBench Fast1/Fast2, Mean/GeoMean/P50/P75 speedup vs PyTorch eager and torch.compile [execution]; correctness: KernelBench Pass rate and in-model numerical correctness checks [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: Ten LM inference workloads (Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-32B, Llama-2-7B, Llama-2-13B, Mamba 130M/2.8B, Mamba2 130M/2.7B, RecurrentGemma-2B/9B) on A100 and H100; KernelBench Level 2 (100 tasks)
techniques.models: GPT-5.4, size undisclosed, closed; Claude Sonnet 4.6, size undisclosed, closed; GLM-5, open-weight
techniques.baselines: PyTorch eager; torch.compile; FlashAttention-2; Mamba fast paths (mamba_ssm, causal-conv1d); Sample-1, Sample-10, Iter-10 (KernelBench-style sampling and execution-feedback iteration); LLM4LLM w/o restart; prior systems CUDA-L1, KernelSkill, STARK, QiMeng-Kernel, KernelBlaster, AI CUDA Engineer (reported numbers)
techniques.effect_target_headline: achieving 3.91×/6.98× geometric-mean speedups on A100/H100 (end-to-end latency over eager); up to 2.745× GeoMean speedup on KernelBench Level 2
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: LLM4LLM (15) Pass 100 vs Sample-1 46 (GPT-5.4, KernelBench Level 2, A100)

extraction.notes: Which LLM backbone produced the end-to-end Table 1 results is not stated. Compute reported only as candidate budgets; no token/cost. Single evaluation per configuration with repeated timing but no variance. Comparison to prior systems uses their reported numbers with different aggregation conventions. Memory-safety failures discussed qualitatively (runtime validity) but not quantified as security. Limitations section present; no threats-to-validity section. Figures 5-6 garbled.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Benchmark paper that evaluates LLMs rewriting validated PyTorch query programs into CUDA/Triton kernels under an execution-guided repair loop (correctness and measured speedup fed back), with prompt-context ablations; the outcome is runtime speedup of the LLM-generated code. Borderline between benchmark and technique evaluation.
extraction.title: DataKernelBench: Can LLMs Optimize Database Queries on GPUs?

techniques.technique_name: Execution-guided multi-round repair loop with correctness mismatches, tracebacks and measured speedup as feedback (core vs full optimization scope)
techniques.tools: PyTorch 2.12.0+cu130 (torch.compile baseline), Triton 3.7.0, CUDA 13.0, cuDF 26.04, DuckDB 1.5.2 reference; NVIDIA H100 80GB
techniques.iterations: Rmax=10 rounds; stop at first candidate that is correct and has speedup >= 1.05x
techniques.metrics: efficiency: speedup vs torch.compile TorchPlan (median of 5 timed runs after 2 warmups), share of queries >=1.05x/1.20x/2x, total runtime [execution]; correctness: pass rate vs reference outputs [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: TPC-H SF10, 22 queries (plus SF100 proof of concept on 4 H100s)
techniques.languages: Python with CUDA and Triton kernels
techniques.models: GPT-5.5, closed, reasoning; Claude Opus 4.7, closed; Claude Sonnet 4.6, closed; Claude Haiku 4.5, closed; Gemini 3.1 Pro, closed; Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, open, instruct; GPT-OSS-120B, open, reasoning; DeepSeek-V4-Flash, open; MiniMax-M2.5, open; Devstral-2-123B, open, code-specialized
techniques.baselines: TorchPlan with torch.compile (primary), TorchPlan eager, Sirius (GPU DB), DuckDB (CPU); round-1 output as implicit no-repair reference; core vs full scope
techniques.effect_target_headline: the strongest full-query CUDA configuration achieves 2.11× speedup over torch.compile at full pass rate (GPT-5.5 CUDA-full, TPC-H SF10, H100); Cumulative success rises from 40% after round 1 to 57% after round 2 and 65% after round 3
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: 77.5% eventually produce a correct kernel with at least 1.05× speedup (880 trajectories)

techniques.technique_name: Workload- and hardware-context prompting (DATA and GPU prompt blocks), ablated
techniques.metrics: efficiency: change in mean speedup vs torch.compile when removing prompt blocks [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: TPC-H SF10, 22 queries
techniques.languages: Python with CUDA and Triton kernels
techniques.models: GPT-5.5, closed, reasoning
techniques.baselines: Full prompt vs prompt without GPU block vs prompt without DATA block
techniques.effect_target_headline: excluding data properties triggers a substantial performance drop of −0.40 compared to −0.27 for GPU details (CUDA, GPT-5.5 full); Triton −0.22 without workload data, −0.06 without GPU specifications

extraction.notes: Primarily a benchmark; the repair loop is the evaluation protocol and failed/slow kernels are credited at the torch.compile runtime, so speedups are not raw LLM-code speedups. Effect of the loop is reported only as cumulative success by round (correct and >=1.05x). Median over 5 timed runs but no variance across generations. Artifacts promised ('will release'). Table 1 and Table 3 are garbled; Table 2/3 values interleaved. LLM-based source audit used as additional correctness check.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes FABRICA, an agentic framework that makes an LLM translate CUDA kernels into Cerebras CSL and then optimize the generated code under a correctness gate, reporting quantitative efficiency outcomes (device-cycle speedups on simulator and WSE-3 hardware) for the LLM-written programs.
extraction.title: FABRICA: Agentic CUDA-to-CSL Translation and Optimization for Wafer-Scale Systems

techniques.technique_name: FABRICA: six-stage role-specialized agentic workflow (analyst, architect, implementer, reviewer, optimizer plus reference-isolation firewall) with retrieval from a consolidated Cerebras knowledge base, starter templates, failure-classified execution repair, and correctness-gated cycle optimization (an edit is accepted only if it stays valid and reduces median device cycles)
techniques.tools: Cerebras SDK 1.4.0 (fabric simulator) and SDK 2.10 (hardware replay); CSLC compiler; CS_Py wrapper; CTF trace parser; CS_readelf --ms for SRAM estimates; cycle/timestamp counters; WSE-3 hardware cluster
techniques.iterations: Attempt caps vary per study (translation/optimization): 1/0 for the single-attempt arm, 40/40 for the controlled and cross-model studies, 20/20 for the knowledge ablation, 10/10 for the coverage sweep, 0/10 for the optimization-only study; full arm generates three candidates before bounded repair; patience bounds unproductive optimizer search; workflows reaching a retained pass converge in a median of two evaluations
techniques.metrics: efficiency: in-kernel device cycle count and geometric-mean speedup over the same-target expert CSL reference, measured on the SDK fabric simulator and on WSE-3 hardware [execution]; correctness: bundle pass rate (compile + run + host/device contract preservation + valid timing path + numerical agreement on visible and held-out inputs), with six integrity checks against reference leakage and disabled timers [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: FABRICA-BENCH, introduced here: 49 paired CUDA/CSL tasks across four construction levels; a frozen 28-task Level 1-3 core set; an 8-task diagnostic set (5 runs each); a 15-task knowledge panel; a 12-task cross-model probe; 14 references for the optimization-only study; 35 bundles in the hardware-replay set (27 timing-comparable pairs)
techniques.languages: CUDA (source), Cerebras Software Language (CSL, target), Python (host wrappers)
techniques.models: Claude Opus 4.8 (closed, primary); Claude Sonnet 4.6 (closed); Claude Opus 4.6 (closed); gpt-oss-120b (open-weight); Gemma 4 31B (open-weight); gpt-oss-20b (open-weight); five further open-weight models on the probe; Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-14B used in the LoRA SFT pilot
techniques.baselines: Single-attempt generation with retrieval, review, repair and optimization disabled; expert-written CSL reference implementations in the benchmark bundles; ablation modes A (unguided), B (+classified execution repair), C (A + design records), D (B + design records), T (B + starting template); knowledge tiers (full knowledge / no retrieved Cerebras material / also no CSL primer)
techniques.effect_target_headline: For 27 generated/reference pairs with device-internal timing, geometric-mean speedup is 3.75x on the SDK simulator and 3.47x on WSE-3 hardware; by level on WSE-3: Level 1 7.49x, Level 2 2.56x, Level 3 2.71x, Level 4 1.24x; the optimization-only study improves all 14 measured references with a 1.44x geometric-mean speedup and seven programs improving by at least 25%
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: On a fixed 28-task Level 1-3 core comparison with Claude Opus 4.8, FABRICA raises success from 6/28 to 26/28; across the 49-task coverage evaluation, 38 tasks produce a correct program; the final three tasks are evaluated over three seeds and pass 8/9 runs; retrieved Cerebras knowledge separately raises success from 1/15 to 7/15

extraction.notes: Contamination and leakage are handled unusually carefully: a reference-isolation firewall, held-out inputs and seeds, six integrity checks, disjoint train/test splits, GEMM and GEMV held train-only because retrieved WaferLLM patterns overlap those families, and benchmark-disjoint filtering for the SFT pilot. The paper also contains a secondary training-time contribution (LoRA SFT on 6,066 harvested CUDA-to-CSL records for Qwen3-8B/14B) but reports only SDK-free structural proxy metrics (usable/contract/chrF/CSL vocabulary), not executable correctness or efficiency, so it is not recorded as a separate technique. 'Full prompts, candidates, checks, and measurements remain in the artifact' but no artifact URL is printed in the text. Attempt budgets are reported per study; no token, dollar or wall-clock cost is given. Figures 5-8 and several tables are garbled in PDF extraction (axis labels split per character); headline numbers were taken from the abstract, Section V and the conclusion.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes KOPE, an LLM agent workflow with execution feedback, Experience Graph Memory and active context injection for optimizing hardware kernels, and reports measured speedup of the LLM-generated kernels alongside pass rate, with ablations.
extraction.title: Beyond Scaling: Self-Evolving LLM Agents for Hardware Kernel Optimization via an Experience-Driven Workflow and Experience Graph Memory

techniques.technique_name: KOPE: experience-driven closed-loop kernel optimization with Experience Graph Memory (KOPE-Mem) and Active Context Management and Injection
techniques.tools: CANN Bench v0.4.0 evaluator on Ascend 910C (compile, correctness, latency); RISC-V appendix: SpacemiT K3, PyTorch 2.8.0+spacemit.0, Triton 3.6.0+spacemit.a5, FlagGems 5.3.0, triton.testing.do_bench
techniques.iterations: Iterative compile-test-profile loop per task; incumbent replaced only by a correct faster candidate; fixed 1M-token budget; max rounds not stated
techniques.metrics: efficiency: per-operator speedup vs CANN library latency, geometric mean over positive fields, paired timing ratios; benchmark composite score [execution]; correctness: case pass rate over 1,060 cases [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: CANN Bench v0.4.0, 53 operators, 1,060 cases (AscendC); appendix: FlagGems core suite on RISC-V, 21 operators, 204 cases (Triton)
techniques.models: GLM-5.2, size not stated, open, instruct; Deepseek-V4-Pro, size not stated, open, instruct
techniques.baselines: CANNBot; CUDA-Agent workflow; passive agent-led context construction (ablation); KOPE without Experience Graph Memory (ablation); cold start without memory (RISC-V appendix)
techniques.effect_target_headline: the geometric mean of KOPE's per-operator speedups is 1.54× that of CANNBot (GLM-5.2); Experience Graph Memory yields a 1.434× geometric-mean speedup (412 paired timing cases); positive-field geometric mean from 0.0382 to 0.0661 (active vs passive context)
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: Active Context Management and Injection raises pass rate from 60.0% to 84.6%; Experience Graph Memory raises full-suite pass rate from 55.2% to 84.6% (GLM-5.2, 1,060 cases)

extraction.notes: Speedup geometric means are conditional on positive fields and differ in denominators; absolute speedups vs CANN library are below 1 (e.g. 0.0661x). On the Deepseek-V4-Pro 31-operator intersection CANNBot has a slightly higher geometric mean (0.0485 vs 0.0434), so efficiency effect vs baseline is not uniform. Without-memory per-level speedups are derived, not measured. One archived run per configuration; no variance. RISC-V appendix: Ascend memory reduced fixed-case performance (0.388x to 0.145x) while K3+Ascend memory reached 0.786x. Token consumption reported (15.9B vs 1.113B). No code URL given.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes SLA-Full, a multi-agent coding scaffold that sequentially generates a portfolio of applications while extracting and migrating shared code into a Super Library, and measures maintainability of the LLM-generated portfolios (LOC, tokens, MDL, structural erosion, verbosity, patch size) alongside functionality.
extraction.title: Super Library Agent: Joint Generation and Maintenance of Multiple Applications Beyond the Single Codebase

techniques.technique_name: SLA-Full (Super Library Agent: coding agent + pre-extraction local consolidation + index-based LLM candidate extraction over NL code-chunk summaries + extraction-trace and call-graph conditioned dependency migration)
techniques.tools: mini-SWE-agent harness; cocoindex-code (AST-delimited chunk index); gpt-5.4-nano chunk summarizer; deepseek-v4-flash candidate selector; import-based file-level call graph (no LLM)
techniques.iterations: N/m rounds of generate-consolidate-extract-migrate (N=8 apps, m=2 per round, 4 rounds on WebGen-Bench; N=4 on PaperBench); one migration pass per app per round
techniques.metrics: readability-maintainability: LOC, token length (Qwen-2.5-7B tokenizer), dependency-aware MDL under Qwen-2.5-7B, Structural Erosion (share of complexity mass in functions with cyclomatic complexity >10), Verbosity (duplicated/redundant-pattern line fraction, SlopCodeBench), patch size (added LOC) under shared policy update, library utilization [tool-static]; correctness: WebGen-Bench accuracy via WebVoyager UI tests [execution], appearance score [llm-judge], PaperBench Code-Dev score [llm-judge]
techniques.benchmarks: WebGen-Bench (three 8-task suites = 24 tasks; plus 16-task low-reuse stress suite); PaperBench Code-Dev (five 4-task suites = 20 papers); post-construction shared policy updates (3 suites)
techniques.models: deepseek-v4-flash, open (size not stated), reasoning (high effort), backbone; minimax-m3, backbone robustness check; gpt-5.4-nano (closed) summarizer; gpt-5-mini (closed) judge/UI agent
techniques.baselines: Zero-Shot (independent generation, mini-SWE-agent); Librarian post-hoc library construction (K=1, K=8); SLA-Naive implicit and Ward-clustering variants; OpenHands and Claude Code zero-shot scaffolds; ablations w/o local consolidation, w/o call-graph
techniques.effect_target_headline: WebGen-Bench SLA-Full vs Zero-Shot: LOC 8552 vs 9393 (-9.0%), Tok 65633 vs 70364 (-6.7%), Verb. 0.0994 vs 0.1603 (-38.0%); PaperBench: LOC 6252 vs 6578 (-5.0%), Tok 63514 vs 68603 (-7.4%); maintenance patch size 256 vs 936 added LOC
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: WebGen-Bench Acc. 77.21 vs 76.04 (+1.5%); PaperBench Code-Dev 0.4809 vs 0.4687 (+2.6%); no functionality difference statistically significant

extraction.notes: Maintainability measured at portfolio level (all apps plus shared library). Three trials per suite, std reported, paired t-tests with bootstrap CIs (Table 6): LOC/Tok/Verb significant vs Zero-Shot on WebGen, Tok/Verb on PaperBench; MDL and Erosion not significant vs Zero-Shot. SLA-Full costs 8.3x Zero-Shot LLM spend on WebGen (3.1x PaperBench); migration turns reported. Low-reuse stress test shows functionality drop below Zero-Shot. Verbatim prompts only in released code (summarized in appendix). Some tables (3, 4, 5, 18, 19) garbled in extraction. Contamination not discussed.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Argus is a region-centric GPU profiling substrate; its main evaluation plugs Argus region reports as feedback into LLM kernel-optimization agents (AlphaEvolve, GEAK, Pragma, CUDAForge, Astra; Claude Opus 4.5/4.6) and compares the runtime speedup of the LLM-edited kernels with and without Argus, a quantitative efficiency outcome. Borderline because the paper is primarily a profiling-systems contribution and the cross-level PGO part involves no LLM.
extraction.title: Argus: Orchestrating Cross-Layer GPU Performance Measurements around Semantic Regions

techniques.technique_name: Argus region-level, interference-aware cross-layer profiling reports as feedback for LLM kernel-optimization agents (replacing end-to-end latency/NCU feedback)
techniques.tools: Argus planner/runtime over intra-kernel region tracer (Proton), NVBit, CUPTI SASS metrics, Nsight Systems, Nsight Compute (baseline); Triton TTGIR candidates, Triton compilation and numerical equivalence checks; NVIDIA H100
techniques.iterations: Fixed 25-trial budget per kernel for agent workflows; megakernel optimization trajectory of about 60 optimization steps (Figure 9)
techniques.metrics: efficiency: best-found speedup over original kernel, geometric-mean speedup, count of instances improved / >=10% speedup, best-so-far speedup vs trials, per-token decode latency (ms/token) with device-side timestamps [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: 44 Triton kernel instances from 10 kernel families (8 warp-specialized persistent GEMM configurations + 9 attention variants x 4 block sizes); one representative Triton kernel across 5 agent workflows; persistent TinyLlama-1.1B batch-1 decode megakernel; cross-level PGO on 4 GEMM shapes x 5 2/4-GPU settings (no LLM)
techniques.models: Claude Opus 4.5, size NR, closed, reasoning (agent workflows); Claude Opus 4.6, size NR, closed, reasoning (megakernel optimization)
techniques.baselines: Same agent workflow, LLM, trial budget and validation with end-to-end latency feedback plus its built-in profiler output (e.g., NCU) but without Argus; original kernels; PyTorch eager and CUDA-Graph PyTorch for megakernel context
techniques.effect_target_headline: Argus improves 39/44 cases and raises AlphaEvolve's geometric-mean speedup from 5.4% to 8.9%; megakernel: 1.65 ms/token with Argus versus 4.92 ms/token without it; across five workflows AlphaEvolve improves from 8% to 21.9%, GEAK from 12.6% to 15.1%, Pragma from 1.6% to 6.6%, CUDAForge -2.7% to 3.5%, Astra -0.1% to 2.4%

extraction.notes: Systems/profiling paper; the LLM-relevant evaluation is Section 4.1 (agentic kernel optimizers) and 4.2 (megakernel agent). Correctness is only a gate (Triton compile + numerical equivalence), no correctness rates reported. Compute reporting is a fixed 25-trial budget plus profiling overhead (not LLM tokens/cost). Single run per configuration, no variance. Cross-level PGO (7% throughput) uses an analytic model without an LLM and should not count toward the technique effect. No threats-to-validity or limitations section; no code URL. Agent workflows were reproduced by the authors, not original implementations. Figures 4-6, 8-13 partly garbled.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes a framework (milestone knowledge base + mid-state test oracle + GPU-feedback loop) that guides coding agents (Claude Code/Opus 5, Codex/GPT-5.6) to generate CUDA decode megakernels, and reports quantitative efficiency outcomes (MBU, latency speedups) of the LLM-generated kernels alongside correctness.
extraction.title: ForgeMegakernel: A General Framework for Efficient Auto-Regressive Model Decode Megakernels

techniques.technique_name: ForgeMegakernel (ten-milestone knowledge base + mid-state test oracle + fresh-context agent loop with GPU measurement and reviewer agent)
techniques.tools: NVIDIA H100 80GB HBM3; Nsight Compute (ncu) counters; %globaltimer timeline; float64 PyTorch reference; source scan/schedule audit gates
techniques.iterations: One fresh headless agent per round; campaign works on lowest unpassed milestone, advancing on gate pass plus review pass; about 48 rounds per cell (median 47, range 23-102); ablation budget 50 rounds
techniques.metrics: efficiency: model bandwidth utilization (MBU %) from host-derived byte count and two-point-slope latency, per-token latency (us/tok), speedup vs baselines [execution; profiler]; correctness: mean |delta log p| vs float64 forward pass, GSM8K answer accuracy inside SGLang, functional checks [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: 14 decode cells (model, batch, sequence length) across eight model families (Llama-3.2-1B, Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-2-13B-chat, Qwen3-0.6B/1.7B/4B/8B, Qwen2.5-3B, MiniCPM4-0.5B/1B/3B, MiniCPM5-1B, NanBeige4-3B); GSM8K 200 test questions for serving evaluation
techniques.models: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) via Claude Code, closed, reasoning/agentic; GPT-5.6-sol via codex exec, closed (single-cell check)
techniques.baselines: Coding agent with naive prompt (Observations section); SGLang 0.5.18; vLLM 0.27.1; llama.cpp; Mirage Persistent Kernel (MPK) megakernel compiler; hand-written Llama-1B megakernel; milestone ablation arms
techniques.effect_target_headline: geometric mean speedups of 1.21× over SGLang 0.5.18 and 1.54× over a megakernel compiler under identical configurations (50.5–85.9% MBU); inside SGLang on GSM8K speedups 1.03× to 1.28× with a geometric mean of 1.11×
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: On accuracy, the forged megakernels stay within 1.5 percentage points of the baseline and match or exceed it on seven configurations; ratio of their mean log-prob error to SGLang's ranges from 0.38 to 0.72, with a median of 0.66

extraction.notes: Domain is GPU kernel generation for LLM inference; the NF dimension is efficiency of agent-written CUDA. No-technique (naive-prompt agent) comparison is only in the motivating Observations on five cells (geomean 0.75x SGLang utilization); main results compare to engines/compiler. Milestone ablation is one campaign on one cell. Figures/tables (Fig. 3, Tables 2-3) are garbled in extraction. No code URL given. Only one GPU architecture; limitations section is brief.

extraction.eligibility_reason: The study evaluates LLM refinement (renaming, retyping, commenting) of existing Ghidra-decompiled code, i.e. LLM improvement of pre-existing code rather than LLM-generated code, and its contribution is an evaluation control (memorization floor) rather than a technique that improves the quality of LLM-generated code.
extraction.title: A Memorization Floor for LLM Refinement of Decompiled Code
extraction.notes: Borderline: decompiled code is machine-produced, not human-written, and the refined output is LLM-edited with readability measured (LLM judge 1-5, human calibration with one rater) and identifier similarity; but the paper proposes no NF-improving technique, it measures whether naming recovery depends on input information. A reviewer applying IC1/IC2 more loosely could treat single-pass LLM refinement as the evaluated technique.

extraction.eligibility_reason: FlashVector is an LLM agentic profile-diagnose-optimize-verify loop that generates and applies code changes (fused CUDA kernels, C++ rewrites, Cython kernels, PyTorch graph restructuring) and reports quantitative efficiency outcomes (latency speedup and throughput increase) for the resulting LLM-edited code; IC2 is met via 'edited by an LLM'. Borderline against EC4 because the starting artifact is an existing human-written production codebase, but the LLM does generate the new code, so EC4's 'no LLM generation' condition does not hold.
extraction.title: FlashVector: Agent for Hierarchical Model Serving Stack Optimization

techniques.technique_name: FlashVector (layer-agent abstraction with a knowledge base and a Profile-Diagnose-Optimize-Verify loop plus a post-run Refine stage; optimize locally, verify globally; always-on self-retriggering loop)
techniques.tools: NVIDIA Nsight Systems and Nsight Compute (nsys/ncu) for GPU profiling; eBPF for CPU/model-server profiling; PyTorch Kineto and torch.profiler mentioned; NVIDIA Triton Inference Server (C++/Python backend); PyTorch AOTInductor; Cython; CUDA/Triton kernels; production load tests and shadow-traffic canary; versions not given
techniques.iterations: Loop repeats until a maximum number of iterations is reached or an optimization criterion is satisfied (Algorithm 1); each iteration samples one layer at random; acceptance requires clearing a correctness bar, exceeding a noise floor of about plus or minus 6% end to end (improvements in the 2-6% band re-measured at up to 8x sample size, tightening to 2.1%), and passing a full-stack load test; the loop also re-triggers itself on each new model release
techniques.metrics: efficiency: latency speedup and throughput increase versus the production baseline; sustained requests per second per pod at a fixed latency SLO; p99 latency in ms; per-kernel latency in microseconds; percentage of GPU time and dispatcher overhead; per-call-site kernel speedup factors [all execution]. Correctness: element-wise output comparison against recorded baseline predictions, with class-dependent bars (bit-exact for deterministic rewrites; 1e-3 element-wise absolute deviation with at most 0.1% of elements beyond it for floating-point reordering, 1e-4 for FP32 serving; business metrics for intentional approximations; shadow-traffic canary for configuration changes) [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: No public benchmark; evaluated in situ on Unity's Vector advertising platform. Table 1 reports 6 production models (Retrieval model, Ranking models 1-4, Gamer model); Table 3 reports one preprocessor service across 3 cumulative optimization stages; Table 4 reports 4 production models (A-D) for configuration tuning; Table 2 reports 5 Cython kernel replacements
techniques.languages: CUDA, C++, Python, Cython; PyTorch model code; Golang mentioned in the stack description
techniques.models: Not reported anywhere in the paper; the underlying LLM powering the agents is never named
techniques.baselines: Existing hand-tuned production stack: for Case 2 an AOT-compiled (PyTorch AOTInductor), FP16-quantized model on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU with batch size 2000; for Case 3 a 940 RPS/pod preprocessor baseline; for Case 4 a hand-tuned configuration left at the framework default batch size with utilization-target scaling
techniques.effect_target_headline: FlashVector achieved up to 2x throughput increase and up to 1.98x latency speedup on model server, and up to 1.6x throughput increase on feature store. Case 1: speed up to 30x on the Triton input-conversion step. Case 2: attention latency cut from 996.5 microseconds to 279.8 microseconds (a 3.56x speedup); embedding changes reduce total GPU kernel time by 33.4%, cut forward-pass latency by 30.1%, and lower dispatcher overhead from 44.8% to 28.5%. Case 3: 940 requests per second at baseline, roughly 1.5k with all three in place, a 1.6x improvement
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: Because the fused kernel preserves the original operation order and accumulation precision, it generates attention weights that are bit-identical to the baseline, which we verify by element-wise comparison

extraction.notes: ELIGIBILITY IS BORDERLINE and a human reviewer should confirm the call. The system optimizes an existing, human-written production codebase (NVIDIA Triton C++, a Python feature-processing service, PyTorch model code) rather than generating programs from a specification, which looks like the 'adjacent' side list (LLM refactoring of human-written code / EC4). It was included because IC2 explicitly admits code 'edited by an LLM', EC4 requires 'no LLM generation', and the agent does write new code (a fused CUDA kernel, hand-written Cython kernels, a C++ rewrite of a deserialization path). Flip to exclude/EC4/adjacent if the review intends EC4 to cover LLM-driven optimization of existing code. Other issues: (1) The underlying LLM is NEVER named anywhere in the paper, so QA5 is 0 and reimplementation is not possible. (2) This is an industrial experience report of case studies, not a controlled evaluation: there is no ablation, no public benchmark, no artifact release, and no threats-to-validity section. (3) The agent's correctness verification is well specified (bit-exactness and tolerance bars per change class) but no aggregate correctness results are reported. (4) Measurement noise is handled rigorously (noise floor estimated from repeated no-op baseline runs, re-measurement at larger sample sizes), which is the strongest methodological element. (5) Tables 1-4 are garbled by PDF extraction: Table 1's column values are split from the model names, Table 2's left column (Python functions replaced) is separated from its speedup column, and Table 4's header row is interleaved; the mappings are recoverable but should be re-checked against the original. (6) Figures 2-6 are referenced but their content is not in the extracted text. (7) Section 5.2 text appears out of order in the extraction (Case 3 baseline setup text is interleaved into Case 2). (8) The only URL given is a GitHub issue for a contributed upstream fix (https://github.com/triton-inference-server/server/issues/8348), not a research artifact.

extraction.eligibility_reason: The study builds ten Linux utilities with a single best-practices Claude Code agentic workflow and compares their fuzz-testing reliability (crashes, hangs, memory errors) against human-written repository versions; the workflow is not evaluated as an intervention (no LLM baseline without it, no ablation), so it measures the quality of LLM-generated code rather than the effect of a technique.
extraction.title: A Study of the Reliability of Agentic AI-Generated Programs
extraction.notes: Borderline on IC1: a five-stage agentic workflow with security (SEI CERT C) and maintainability skills plus iterative security audits using static analyzers/sanitizers/Valgrind (up to 20 audits) is applied, but the comparison is AI-generated vs human-written code only. Outcome is reliability via classic black-box fuzzing and AFL++ 5.01a (crashes/hangs; many crashes are memory-safety errors): 19 failures in repository versions vs 5 in AI-generated versions across 10 utilities. Single model (Claude Opus 4.8 with Haiku subagents). Non-peer-reviewed technical report.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Compares LLM coding-agent design flows (direct RTL vs agent-written HLS C++ vs post-HLS RTL refinement, combined as AHRR) and reports quantitative efficiency (execution time from cycles x clock period, LUT/DSP/BRAM usage) of the agent-generated hardware code; borderline because the artifact is hardware description/HLS code.
extraction.title: Can Agents Design Better Chips with a Higher Level Abstraction?
extraction.venue: IEEE/ACM International Conference on Computer-Aided Design (ICCAD '26) (Invited Paper)

techniques.technique_name: AHRR: Agent-based HLS Design (agent writes HLS C++, Vitis HLS generates RTL) followed by Post-HLS RTL Refinement (agent edits generated Verilog), iterative rounds with evaluation feedback
techniques.tools: AMD Vitis 2025.2 (Vitis HLS C synthesis, Vivado RTL simulation, synthesis and place-and-route), AMD Alveo U55C; open-source coding agent pi; hidden testbench (C sim + RTL sim)
techniques.iterations: Up to 5 rounds, 60 min per round, 10 h total timeout; each round's prompt reports the previous three rounds' evaluation results
techniques.metrics: efficiency: execution time = simulated cycle count x max(post-route clock period, target), speedup relative to Direct RTL Design (execution/tool-static); resource utilization LUT/DSP/BRAM/FF (tool-static); correctness: validity = passes hidden testbench, routes, within resource ceiling (execution)
techniques.benchmarks: 11-task suite (LLM decode attention, norm+quant+linear, INT8 GEMM in 2 variants, BM25 gather, paged-KV compact, LServe page select, NMS, PointPillars encoder, stereo SAD, StreamHLS GEMM and depthwise conv)
techniques.models: Gemini 3.1 Pro (high reasoning effort), closed, reasoning; GPT-5.6-sol (extra-high effort), closed, reasoning
techniques.baselines: Direct RTL Design by the same agent; Agent-based HLS Design alone; domain-specific HLS compilers AutoSA and StreamHLS (for Post-Compiler HLS Refinement); HLS-generated RTL starting point
techniques.effect_target_headline: AHRR achieves a 2.6× geometric-mean speedup over Direct RTL Design across our benchmark suite (2.62×, n=13; Agent-based HLS alone 2.31×; Post-HLS RTL Refinement 1.17× over HLS-generated RTL)

extraction.notes: Artifact is hardware design code (HLS C++/Verilog) evaluated for latency and area; reviewers should confirm hardware code counts as production code. Each experiment run once; geometric means exclude pairs with invalid Direct RTL baselines (n=15/13). Validity (correctness) shown only as invalid markers per task, not as rates. Also evaluates Post-Compiler HLS Refinement (up to 3.3x over StreamHLS on SHL2). Compute reported only as time budgets. Authors note prompt sensitivity. Figures partially garbled.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Spotlights is an LLM agent system that discovers optimization opportunities (source locations, rationales, proposals) in existing human-written repositories; the evaluated artifact is the candidate list, not LLM-generated code. Only one case study implements a proposal (via CORAL) and measures a 10.6% runtime reduction on a single human-written pipeline, which is optimization of human code rather than evaluation of LLM-generated code quality.
extraction.title: Spotlights: Discovering Improvement Opportunities in Software Repositories
extraction.notes: Borderline: the IOCR implementation study (Sec 6.8, App D) uses an LLM program-optimization framework (CORAL) to implement a discovered change, reducing median runtime from 150.970 to 135.026 s (10.6%) with equal character accuracy 95.53%; but this is a single n=1 case study modifying human-written code, and the main evaluation is of discovery output (precision@10 0.70, recall of expert targets, run stability, cost). A reviewer may consider it adjacent (LLM optimization of human-written code).

extraction.eligibility_reason: The paper empirically evaluates a prompt-level intervention (a fixed 267-word Specification Frame preamble) applied to five LLMs generating backend Python code, and reports quantitative CWE-mapped defect counts from nine AST checkers plus Bandit security-scanner findings on that generated code.
extraction.title: Specification Before Generation: A Pre-Registered, Five-Model Paired Evaluation of a Specification Frame for LLM-Generated Code in Money, Time, Idempotency, and Access Tasks

techniques.technique_name: Specification Frame (fixed, task-agnostic 267-word specification preamble with Role/Context/Task/Constraints sections, prepended inline to every task prompt)
techniques.tools: Scoring instruments (not part of the technique): nine deterministic AST-based checkers written by the author (money_float, exact_compare, naive_datetime, sql_param, open_redirect, path_traversal, hardcoded_secret, password_hash, idempotency_key), validated with an 11-bad/11-good unit fixture gauntlet and 50 per-task fixture proofs; Bandit 1.9.4 as an instrument-blind secondary scanner; exploratory Python byte-compilation check.
techniques.iterations: None. Single-turn, one stateless call per prompt, no tools, no retrieval, no multi-turn interaction; a pre-registered one-shot rule forbade regenerating any successful output.
techniques.metrics: security: number of registered defect-class checkers that fired per output (0-5), from nine deterministic AST/regex checkers mapped to CWE-682, CWE-697, CWE-89, CWE-601, CWE-22, CWE-798, CWE-916/CWE-328 plus two domain rules with no CWE [tool-static]; Bandit 1.9.4 medium-or-high severity findings per output [tool-static]; manual adjudication of a seeded 10 percent sample of findings [human]. Exploratory, not pre-registered: Python byte-compilation success.
techniques.benchmarks: 50 author-written realistic backend tasks in four regulated domains (money MO01-MO12 = 12 tasks, idempotency ID01-ID12 = 12, date/time DA01-DA10 + DT11-DT12 = 12, authentication/access AU01-AU14 = 14), with 106 checker registrations, 11-13 per checker; 100 prompts (bare and frame arms) and 500 outputs. Not a public benchmark; all materials deposited on Zenodo.
techniques.models: claude-sonnet-5 (Anthropic, closed, flagship); gpt-5.6-sol (OpenAI, closed, flagship successor used on run day); gemini-3.1-pro-preview (Google, closed); deepseek-v4-pro (DeepSeek, open-weight lineage, hosted); qwen/qwen3.8-27b (Alibaba/Qwen, 27B, open-weight, hosted on Groq). Temperature 0 requested; two endpoints (Anthropic, OpenAI) do not accept the parameter and ran at provider default.
techniques.baselines: Paired bare arm: the identical task text with no preamble and no system message, same model and request parameters, two consecutive stateless calls per task. No length-matched neutral preamble and no reason-first control were run (acknowledged as an unexcluded confound).
techniques.effect_target_headline: "The frame reduced defects in all five models (mean reduction 0.16 to 0.70 findings per task, every Holm-adjusted sign test significant, every bootstrap confidence interval excluding zero). Where the arms differed, the frame arm won 95 of 100 times. It never made any model worse in any domain." Pooled (descriptive only): "the frame arm carried 23 findings against 148 in the bare arm, an 84 percent reduction in the named defect classes" across 250 pairs. Per model mean delta: claude-sonnet-5 0.68 [0.38, 1.02]; deepseek-v4-pro 0.40 [0.24, 0.58]; gemini-3.1-pro-preview 0.70 [0.38, 1.08]; qwen3.8-27b 0.56 [0.36, 0.76]; gpt-5.6-sol 0.16 [0.04, 0.28]. Independent scanner: "Bandit found 53 medium-or-high issues in the bare arm and 11 in the frame arm, in the same direction for every model."

extraction.human_eval_details: One annotator (the author). A pre-registered seeded 10 percent sample of 18 checker findings (seed 20260905) was adjudicated against a strict true-positive standard; all 18 were true positives. No inter-rater agreement is reported because there is only one rater.
extraction.artifact_url: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22850887 (dataset v1.1; v1.0 = 10.5281/zenodo.22598205); frame introduced in the author's book, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21584309
extraction.notes: Unusually transparent study: pre-registered with four dated addenda, a one-shot no-regeneration rule, a full deviations section, and all 500 outputs plus checkers and analysis code deposited under a DOI. Caveats a reviewer should weigh: (1) functional correctness was explicitly NOT measured (only an exploratory byte-compilation check: 247/250 bare and 236/250 frame compile, with 14 of the 14 frame failures being transport-truncated files), so a correctness/security trade-off of the kind RealSec-bench and Dai et al. report cannot be ruled out; (2) the author designed both the frame and the nine checkers and wrote the book that introduced the frame (declared as a competing interest), with Bandit as the instrument-blind corroboration; (3) 16 of 500 outputs were truncated in transport, 14 of them frame-arm, which the author notes can only bias toward the frame, and a sensitivity analysis excluding those pairs is reported and preserves every per-model conclusion; (4) one run per arm, so within-model variance is unmeasured; (5) two providers would not accept temperature 0. Dimension assignment is slightly borderline: four of the nine measured defect classes (money float arithmetic, float money equality, naive datetimes, missing idempotency) are domain-correctness rules with weak or no CWE mapping, while five are standard CWE security classes; the paper itself frames all nine as security-adjacent defect classes and Bandit corroborates only the CWE subset. Training-data contamination is never discussed (tasks are author-written and unpublished before the run, which mitigates it incidentally). Tables IV and V survived extraction mostly intact but the column-to-row alignment in Table IV is scrambled; the per-model numbers above were reconstructed from the column order given in the header and should be spot-checked.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Benchmark of LLM coding agents rewriting RTL for post-place-and-route timing closure, plus a proposed technique (TicTacSkill, an SOP-style agent skill) evaluated in a paired ablation on timing closure, WNS, energy-delay and area-delay of the LLM-edited RTL. Borderline: input designs are human-written suboptimal RTL (possible adjacent) and the NF outcome is hardware timing/PPA rather than software runtime.
extraction.title: TicTacBench: Benchmarking Timing Closure Capabilities of Coding Agents

techniques.technique_name: TicTacSkill: agent skill encoding timing-closure Standard Operating Procedures (critical-path localization, datapath/pipeline/control design checks, evidence-driven search, pre/post-PnR mismatch handling) derived from trajectory failure analysis, given to the coding agent before solving
techniques.tools: Agent tool set: compilation, SymbiYosys equivalence checking, pre-PnR STA (Yosys, OpenSTA); evaluation: LibreLane with OpenROAD and OpenSTA post-PnR STA
techniques.iterations: agent loop bounded by limited pre-STA tool calls, total execute steps and agent turns (limits not stated numerically)
techniques.metrics: efficiency: post-PnR Timing Closure Rate, Avg. delta WNS%, Avg. delta EDDP% (energy-delay-squared product), Avg. delta ADP% (area-delay product), cell count, power [tool-static, post-PnR STA]; correctness: compile, synthesizability and formal equivalence check as gate [tool-static]
techniques.benchmarks: TicTacBench (30 RTL timing-closure tasks: 25 from RTLLM 2.0 and RTL-OPT + 5 latency-changeable variants)
techniques.models: Skill ablation: GPT-5.4, closed; MiniMax M2.7, open; DeepSeek V4 Flash, open. Benchmark also: Claude Sonnet 4.6, closed; Kimi K2.6, open; DeepSeek V4 Pro, open; GLM 5.1 FP8, open; Qwen 3.5 122B, open
techniques.baselines: Same agent and task without the skill (paired); suboptimal baseline RTL design
techniques.effect_target_headline: The GPT-5.4-based agent improves from 53.3% to 56.7% Timing Closure Rate and from 48.7% to 66.4% Avg. ∆ WNS%. The MiniMax M2.7-based agent ... increasing from 23.3% to 36.7%; DeepSeek V4 Flash-based agent improves from 33.3% to 43.3%

extraction.notes: Primarily a benchmark paper; the technique (TicTacSkill) ablation is on 3 models, single run each, no statistics. Within efficiency, timing improved but area-delay product worsened for GPT-5.4 (-2.5% to -3.6%) and MiniMax (-9.6% to -10.9%), and MiniMax EDDP worsened (-0.7% to -7.2%). Table IV label 'DeepSeek' is called DeepSeek V4 Flash in text, but its w/o-skill numbers may not match the leaderboard figure (garbled); check. Failure taxonomy derived using an LLM analyst (DeepSeek V4 Flash). Correctness is only an equivalence-check gate, not reported as a rate. Input RTL is human-written suboptimal designs (EC4/adjacent borderline). Limitations section brief.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes a verification-grounded memory layer (procedural skill memory + Bayesian retry/recovery memory) for LLM EDA agents that rewrite RTL, reporting quantitative PPA (area/power/timing) improvements of LLM-edited RTL code alongside equivalence-checked correctness. Borderline domain (hardware RTL PPA as efficiency).
extraction.title: ChipMEM: Verification-Grounded Memory for EDA Agents

techniques.technique_name: ChipMEM (verification-gated procedural skill memory retrieved by RTL embedding similarity + hierarchical Beta statistical memory for tool retry/recovery advice)
techniques.tools: Yosys (synthesis and equivalence) and ABC (technology mapping) for RTL-OPT/RTLRewriter; OpenROAD/ORFS full flow for OpenTitan; Xcelium/IMC for CVDP testbenches; text-embedding-3-large and Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B for retrieval; Cadence ChipStack 2.0 EDA agent
techniques.iterations: Agent sessions bounded by tool-step/LLM-call budget (OpenTitan: at most 40 tool steps, 600 s model timeout, 7200 s session limit); five attempts per design in custom/OpenTitan studies; retrieval top-2 skills at similarity threshold 0.6; recovery advice when retry success estimate < 0.20
techniques.metrics: efficiency: mean area improvement (%), power improvement (%), timing/WNS/TNS change, cell/wire ratio after synthesis [execution/tool synthesis measurements]; correctness: functional equivalence pass rate, strict gate pass rate, CVDP hidden-test pass rate [execution/formal]
techniques.benchmarks: RTL-OPT (38 designs); RTLRewriter-Bench (59 cases: 54 short, 5 long; 54 scored); custom open-source design set (20 designs); OpenTitan (10 IP blocks x 5 attempts); held-out cohorts A (20) and B (16); CVDP CID012/CID013 (40 testbench tasks); SWE-bench Pro pilot (100 tasks)
techniques.models: GPT-5.5, size NR, closed, reasoning (medium); Qwen3.8-27B, 27B, open, NR
techniques.baselines: Same EDA agent with memory disabled; procedural-only and Bayesian-only ablations; RTL-OPT reported results for GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, DeepSeek V3, DeepSeek R1; SWE-agent baseline in pilot
techniques.effect_target_headline: on the 49-design short suite, mean area improvement is 8.69% versus 5.66%; RTL-OPT mean area improvement from 6.18% to 8.79%; OpenTitan mean area and power improvement from 0.05%/0.00% to 0.24%/2.54%
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: On RTLRewriter-Bench, ChipMEM produces equivalence-passing outputs on 39/54 scored designs versus 35/54 without memory; OpenTitan full-PPA gate passes rise from 1/10 to 4/10 with equivalence maintained at 6/10

extraction.notes: Domain is hardware RTL PPA (area/power/timing) rather than software runtime; reviewer should confirm RTL PPA counts as efficiency. CVDP testbench part is test code (EC3-type) and not used for the NF outcome. GPT-5.5 experiments run on proprietary Cadence ChipStack 2.0 agent (limits reimplementation). RTL-OPT ChipMEM result selects best valid result across three result sets (favourable selection). Custom-design Pass@k is lower with ChipMEM (80% vs 85% at Pass@5). Appendix notes the legacy OpenTitan run mined skills after every session including failures, not the PASS-only rule. Held-out transfer only on CVDP (testbench) tasks with frozen memory; held-out PPA cohorts had no memory-off comparison. Mean ± std and bootstrap CIs for cost; no significance tests on PPA. Tables garbled but recoverable. Dated year 2026 (arXiv 2609.27067).

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes CliffCompaction, a rule-based context-compaction technique for LLM coding agents, and on KernelBench Level 3 reports the runtime speedup of agent-generated CUDA/Triton kernels (an efficiency outcome of LLM-generated code) against no-compaction, alternative compaction methods and specialized kernel agents, alongside correctness.
extraction.title: CliffCompaction: Cost-Efficient Compaction for Long-Horizon Coding Agents

techniques.technique_name: CliffCompaction: threshold-triggered verbatim truncation of agent context (drop tool results >500 chars, tool-call signatures, thoughts truncated to 300 chars, keep K recent turns), discarding prior compactions
techniques.tools: OpenHands, mini-swe-agent, Terminus-2, Claude Code (via API proxy) scaffolds; KernelBench evaluation compiles kernels, checks 5 random inputs (atol=rtol=1e-2 CUDA, 5e-2 Triton), times 10 runs after 10 warmups on L40S / RTX Pro 6000 Blackwell
techniques.iterations: Compaction fires whenever context exceeds threshold B (8K-200K tokens); KernelBench agent runs to a fixed budget of 200 or 400 steps
techniques.metrics: efficiency: KernelBench geometric-mean kernel speedup vs PyTorch Eager (clamped at 10x, 0.1 for no correct kernel), % problems >1.2x and >2x [execution]; correctness: KernelBench accuracy (% problems with a correct kernel), SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench % resolved; agent cost/time also reported (not code NF)
techniques.benchmarks: KernelBench Level 3 (50 problems); SWE-bench Verified; Terminal-Bench 2.0 (89 tasks); Terminal-Bench 2.1
techniques.models: Kimi K2.7, open, instruct; Kimi K2.6, open, instruct; Kimi K2.5, open, instruct; GPT-5-mini, closed, reasoning; GLM 5.1, GLM 5, GLM 5 Turbo, GLM 5.2, GLM 5.3 Flash, GLM 4.7 Flash, open, instruct
techniques.baselines: No compaction (full context); sliding window; LLM summarization; summarization + microcompaction (Claude Code scheme); Terminus-2 native summarization; Claude Code auto-compaction; specialized kernel agents (AdaExplore, CUDA-Agent, DR.Kernel, Iterative Refinement, OpenEvolve+Memory)
techniques.effect_target_headline: KernelBench L3, Kimi K2.7 on L40S: 2.23x (CliffCompaction 128K, 200 steps) and 3.58x (400 steps) vs 1.30x (No compaction 256K); vs 2.86x sliding window, 3.47x summarization, 3.33x summarization + microcompaction at 400 steps
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: KernelBench Acc. 94% (200 steps) / 96% (400 steps) vs 86% no compaction; SWE-bench Verified Kimi K2.6 73.27% (32K) vs 73.87% full context; Terminal-Bench 2.0 Kimi K2.6 61.42% (32K/16K) vs 59.16% full context

extraction.notes: Primary aim is agent cost reduction under bounded context; the code-efficiency (NF) evidence is the KernelBench kernel-speedup experiment, where the agent is instructed to optimize speed. Most 'efficiency' numbers in the paper (cost, cache hits, wall-clock) are agent compute, not generated-code efficiency. Signal source set to 'none' because compaction is rule-based; the agent loop itself uses compile/test/timing feedback from the KernelBench environment. Specialized-agent baselines are reported from original papers on different hardware (L40S/A6000, H20). Also proposes SGV (LightGBM trajectory selector) for test-time scaling, evaluated only on correctness. Seed variance (+/-) reported for SWE-bench/Terminal-Bench but not for KernelBench. Short limitations section only.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes KernelOPT, a multi-agent LLM system (planner/executor/summarizer with NCU profiling feedback, beam search and a four-gate verification cascade) that generates and optimizes Triton kernels, and reports runtime speedup of the LLM-generated kernels vs torch.compile on KernelBench.
extraction.title: KernelOPT: Dispatch-Aware Agentic Search for GPU Kernel Optimization

techniques.technique_name: KernelOPT (Inductor-aware synthesis + profiling-guided multi-agent beam search with experience memory and four-gate verification)
techniques.tools: NVIDIA Nsight Compute 2025.1.0 (ncu --set full); Triton 3.3.0; PyTorch 2.7.0 (torch.compile Inductor max-autotune); CUDA 12.8; triton do_bench; LangGraph
techniques.iterations: T=5 iterations, N=4 plans per iteration, K=4 executor retries per plan, beam width B=4 (20 candidates per problem); early stop after 2 iterations without improvement; Gate-4 rejection gets one targeted retry
techniques.metrics: efficiency: end-to-end wall-clock speedup vs torch.compile and eager (geometric mean, optimized/matched/fallback counts), sub-kernel NCU duration, occupancy, registers [execution]; correctness: multi-seed allclose vs eager PyTorch (1e-3 per candidate, 1e-4 final) and float64 error-ratio check [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: KernelBench, all 250 problems (Level 1: 100, Level 2: 100, Level 3: 50); plus 10 Triton and 10 Helion tutorial kernels; ablations on 50-problem stratified subset
techniques.models: Claude Sonnet 4.6, size NR, closed, instruct
techniques.baselines: torch.compile (Inductor max-autotune), eager PyTorch; KernelAgent replicated on KernelBench L1 with same hardware and backend; ablations (no beam, no NCU profiling, no memory, T=1, no perf gate, no Inductor-aware filtering)
techniques.effect_target_headline: geometric mean speedups over torch.compile of 1.40× (L1), 1.15× (L2), and 1.07× (L3) across all kernels, including fallback cases; Optimized-only geomeans 2.54× (L1: 36/100), 1.84× (L2: 23/100), and 1.37× (L3: 11/50); vs KernelAgent on L1: 1.649× vs 0.966× geomean
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: KernelAgent reaches 0.966× geomean vs. torch.compile (71/100 working, 22/71 regressed), vs. KernelOPT's 1.649× (89/100 working) (KernelBench L1)

extraction.notes: Single LLM (Claude Sonnet 4.6), single run per problem; ablation differences tested with Fisher's exact test (p<0.01). Compute reported as ~1,100 H200 GPU-hours and ~60K tokens per NCU prompt; no per-run LLM call/token totals. Fallbacks preserve compiler baseline, so all-problem geomeans include 1.00x fallbacks. No dedicated threats section, but implementation limitations and unestablished claims (accepted-side rho) are discussed. Per-kernel Table 10 and several tables are garbled in extraction. KernelBench contamination not discussed.

extraction.eligibility_reason: System paper on an agent execution interface (Claude Code/Codex) for HPC job submission, recovery and policy validation; the only non-functional outcome is a single case study in which the agent parallelized a released human-written 12,693-line C solver (speed-up under bitwise identity), i.e., LLM optimization/repair of human-written code rather than a technique evaluated on LLM-generated code. Other evaluations concern policy validator decisions and submission-artifact correctness.
extraction.title: ASCEND: Personal AI Agents for Autonomous Scientific Computing Across HPC Clusters and GPU Workstations
extraction.notes: arXiv 2609.32868. Case 4.3 reports r.avaflow OpenMP speed-ups (e.g., 6.8x vs repaired serial at 16 threads; ~12 h to ~2 h) from single runs, no baseline technique comparison; agent transcripts not retained. Reviewer may consider whether an agent optimizing human-written code counts as LLM-edited code (IC2) rather than adjacent.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Gagar is a training-time RL technique (groupwise agentic grading plus sum-preserving advantage redistribution) applied to code-agent LLMs, and it reports quantitative non-functional quality outcomes for the LLM-generated patches: a rubric-weighted quality score over five maintainability-oriented criteria (4.03 versus 3.70), an average win rate of 69.8% among passing candidates, and a rise in the top quality tier from 25.4% to 34.3%, alongside correctness pass rates.
extraction.title: Groupwise Agentic Grading and Advantage Redistribution for Code Agent RL

techniques.technique_name: Gagar (Groupwise Agentic Grading for Advantage Redistribution): an SFT-trained agentic grader ranks test-passing rollouts in a shared workspace on five code-quality criteria, and the resulting quality factors drive sum-preserving rescaling of positive advantages in GRPO-style code-agent RL
techniques.tools: Executable repository tests for the binary outcome reward; Dr. GRPO mean-centered advantage estimator (no standard-deviation normalization); DAPO-style dynamic sampling to keep mixed-outcome groups; an agentic grader that reads trajectories and patches and runs targeted checks in a shared workspace; DeepSWE v1.1 and SWE-bench Pro evaluation harnesses; no tool versions given
techniques.iterations: Not an inference-time loop. Code-only RL run to step 52 (binary baseline stopped at step 28 due to degradation); batch size 128 with 16 rollouts per prompt; mixed-task runs use 1,568 prompts per update with 16 rollouts per prompt. Grading runs asynchronously with rollout collection; average end-to-end grading time approximately 600 s per group with the SFT-trained grader, versus approximately 2,000 s with the initial Claude Opus 5 grader. Quality factors: f_runner 0.9, f_min 0.4, f_max 0.85, f_low 0.2; rescaling bound lambda_max 1.5
techniques.metrics: readability-maintainability: rubric-weighted quality score W = 0.30*approach suitability + 0.25*implementation precision + 0.20*minimality of changes + 0.15*unintended side effects + 0.10*codebase consistency, each scored 1 to 5 [llm-judge]; average win rate among test-passing candidates from joint groupwise rankings [llm-judge]; share of groups ranked first with ties split equally [llm-judge]; fraction of candidates in the highest quality tier T1 [llm-judge]. Correctness: avg@3 pass rate on DeepSWE v1.1 and SWE-bench Pro [execution]. Agent process cost (not code efficiency): mean main-agent interaction turns and mean total token length [execution]. Training diagnostics: policy entropy, policy-gradient loss, mean training-rollout length
techniques.benchmarks: DeepSWE v1.1 (long-horizon software development) and SWE-bench Pro (repository-level issue resolution); avg@3 with three samples per task. The implementation-quality evaluation uses a fixed random sample of 30 DeepSWE tasks, pooling up to three rollouts per method per task with anonymized identifiers and randomized order. Task counts for the full benchmarks are not stated
techniques.languages: Not stated in the paper; the benchmarks are repository-level software engineering tasks
techniques.models: Policy models: MiMo-V2.6-Flash, 310B total / 15B active parameters, mixture-of-experts, proprietary (Xiaomi), initialized from a pre-RL SFT checkpoint; MiMo-V2.6-Pro, 1.02T total / 42B active parameters, mixture-of-experts, proprietary, likewise from a pre-RL SFT checkpoint. Online grader: the pre-RL SFT checkpoint of MiMo-V2.6-Pro (initially Claude Opus 5). Offline quality judge: Claude Opus 5, closed. External comparison models: Kimi K3 (2.8T), GPT-5.6 Sol, Claude Opus 5
techniques.baselines: Binary-outcome reward RL without online quality grading, trained under identical settings and compared at shared steps; a downweighting-only ablation that applies quality factors without restoring removed positive credit or re-centering; external frontier models K3, GPT-5.6 Sol and Claude Opus 5 for the mixed-task runs
techniques.effect_target_headline: At the final shared checkpoint, Gagar achieves a mean quality score of 4.03 versus 3.70 for the baseline, with an average win rate of 69.8% among passing candidates. It ranks first in 65.0% of groups after splitting ties. Across the audited checkpoints, improvements are most apparent in implementation precision, minimality of changes, and avoidance of unintended side effects; the fraction of candidates assigned to the highest-quality tier, T1, increases from 25.4% to 34.3%
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: At step 28, Gagar achieves 62.2% on DeepSWE v1.1, exceeding the baseline by 12.1 percentage points (the baseline fell from 58.5% at step 20 to 50.2%). With continued training, Gagar reaches a peak DeepSWE pass rate of 63.4% at step 44. On SWE-bench Pro, the baseline plateaus at approximately 59% from step 16 through step 28, whereas Gagar reaches 62.5% at step 52. After mixed-task RL, DeepSWE v1.1 avg@3 reaches 67.9 (Flash) and 71.9 (Pro), with SWE-bench Pro at 60.9 and 62.7

extraction.notes: Scope note for the reviewer: the five graded criteria (approach suitability, implementation precision, minimality of changes, unintended side effects, codebase consistency) map to the readability-maintainability dimension, and the paper frames them as producing 'maintainable, merge-ready code' that reduces developer review effort. The reported turn-count and token-length reductions (e.g. DeepSWE mean turns 132.3 to 111.6 and mean tokens 191.9k to 172.9k at step 28) are the AGENT'S process cost, not the runtime efficiency of the generated code, so they are recorded under compute_reported rather than as an efficiency outcome; a reviewer who treats agent cost as efficiency would add that dimension. Other caveats: (1) The quality evaluation is an LLM judge (Claude Opus 5) on only 30 DeepSWE tasks with up to three rollouts per method; it is blinded (anonymized identifiers, randomized order) but there is no human validation, no inter-rater agreement, and no check against the judge's own self-preference, even though Claude Opus 5 is simultaneously an external comparison model in Table 1 and was the original online grader. (2) No limitations or threats-to-validity section, no contamination discussion, no artifact release. (3) Single training run per condition and no confidence intervals or significance tests; the comparison is complicated by the baseline being stopped early at step 28 because of degradation. (4) The models (MiMo-V2.6-Flash and Pro), the grader checkpoint and the SFT data for the grader are all proprietary and undescribed, so the grading component cannot be reproduced; the advantage-redistribution mathematics and all its constants are fully specified in Section 3.3 and Appendix A. (5) Figures 2, 3 and 4 are reduced to scattered axis numbers by PDF extraction, so all numbers above were taken from the running text, which states them explicitly; Tables 1 and 2 extracted cleanly. (6) The programming language of the benchmarks is never stated.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes SAGE, an adoption-aware memory-learning agent applied to frozen LLM backbones for NPU kernel synthesis; the evaluated artifact is LLM-generated Ascend C kernel code and quantitative efficiency outcomes (speedup over torch_npu, Fast1.0, median self-speedup) are reported alongside correctness.
extraction.title: From Experience to Expertise: Adoption-Aware Memory Learning for Data-Scarce NPU Kernel Synthesis

techniques.technique_name: SAGE (Adoption-Traced Utility estimation + Utility-Gated Consolidation) persistent memory-learning kernel-synthesis agent
techniques.tools: Ascend 910C NPUs; CANN 8.5.1 with driver 25.5.1; Python 3.11.14, torch_npu 2.9.0, vllm-ascend 0.18.0rc1; OpenCode agent harness; in-kernel probes printf/DumpTensor/DumpAccChkPoint; msDebug, msSanitizer; msProf and torch_npu.profiler; hybrid sparse-dense retriever
techniques.iterations: At most T = 30 refinement rounds per operator, shared across the correctness and optimization episodes; episode terminates when the objective (correctness pass, or improved latency) is met or the interaction budget is exhausted
techniques.metrics: efficiency: Fast1.0 = fraction of solved operators whose best kernel beats the torch_npu reference latency (execution); Sself = median Tfirst/Tbest within-episode speedup (execution); per-operator speedup over torch_npu, latency measured with torch.npu.Event device-side timers, 5 warm-up + 100 timed iterations, mean per-execution latency (execution). correctness (co-outcome): Execution Rate and Compilation Rate on NPUKernelBench, correctness defined by max_abs_error <= 1e-3 and max_rel_error <= 1e-3 versus torch_npu (execution). Mechanism check: expert rating of adoption records (human).
techniques.benchmarks: NPUKernelBench, coverage-oriented 88-operator subset (20 Level-1, 50 Level-2, all 18 Level-3); transfer set of 16 xCCL operators; task-order study on 25 Level-2 source operators and 18 Level-3 targets
techniques.models: Qwen3-Coder-Next, 80B, open, code-specialized instruct; DeepSeek-V4-Flash, 284B, open, instruct; GLM-5.2, 744B, open, instruct; GLM-5.3 (used on the xCCL transfer set); all frozen backbones served locally via vllm-ascend
techniques.baselines: Refinement (iterative repair/optimization, no cross-task memory); Static RAG (same initial cold memory and retrieval pipeline, memory writes and utility updates disabled); Value Memory (EvoKernel-style value-driven cross-task memory with uniform credit assignment); ablations: Uniform Credit, w/o UGC, Random UGC; frozen-bank controls: Relevance Only, Uniform Credit, ATU
techniques.effect_target_headline: With GLM-5.2, "Relative to Value Memory, Fast1.0 increases from 75.7% to 86.9%, while median Sself improves from 3.36× to 4.47×" on the 88-operator NPUKernelBench subset; "With GLM-5.3, SAGE achieves a 43.99× speedup over the torch_npu reference on sparse flash attention"
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: "On NPUKernelBench, SAGE achieves a 95.5% execution rate versus 84.1% for the strongest controlled baseline, with 86.9% of solved operators outperforming torch_npu" (GLM-5.2, 88-operator subset); Level-3 ER 88.9% vs 61.1% for Value Memory

extraction.human_eval_details: One Ascend C expert among the authors rated 50 randomly sampled adoption records (full / partial / unrelated): 44 full (88%), 6 partial (12%), 0 unrelated; no inter-rater agreement reported (single rater). This audits adoption tracing, not the non-functional quality of the generated code.
extraction.notes: Table 1 (main results) is garbled by PDF extraction: rows and columns are interleaved, so per-cell values other than the ones quoted in the running text should be re-checked against the PDF. Figures 3-5 are reported as extracted label text only. No artifact/code URL is given (only the third-party OpenCode repository). No repeated runs, variance or statistical tests; single run per configuration, medians used because of the long-tailed speedup distribution (0.38x to 71.41x). Contamination is addressed only indirectly: cold-start differential-mining operators are stated to be disjoint from the 88 evaluation operators, and anti-hacking safeguards forbid expert-implementation leakage and semantic shortcuts, but pretraining contamination of the backbones is not discussed. Limitations appear in the conclusion rather than a dedicated threats-to-validity section. Compute reporting is limited to the 30-round interaction budget and a 10K-token resident memory budget; no token counts, wall-clock agent time, or dollar cost.

extraction.eligibility_reason: The paper proposes a measurement metric (SDLI) and applies SAST scanners to existing LLM coding-agent artifacts (SWE-bench, ProgramBench, MirrorCode) to quantify security findings; its contribution is measurement, not a technique that changes generated code. The only intervention is a single-case repair demonstration (Gemini 3.1 Pro with scanner feedback on one gowsdl state) without quantitative evaluation across tasks.
extraction.title: Trajectory-Level Security Debt in LLM Coding Agents
extraction.notes: Borderline: Section 7 (RQ4) runs four SAST-feedback repair arms (precise vs vague, 1 vs up to 5 rounds) on a single file; union scanner reading fell to 3.25 (from 14.0) for the precise arm, but this is n=1 and reported qualitatively (Table 4). Strong 'context' paper on security of LLM agent code (agree2 non-zero SDLI 3.9% SWE-bench, 26.2% ProgramBench). Artifact: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19886200. AAAI-format copyright notice suggests AAAI 2027 submission.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes an LLM agent harness (TAIC) that generates PTX from Triton kernels and iteratively optimizes it with assembly, numerical-testing and profiler feedback, reporting measured speedups (efficiency) of the LLM-generated code against autotuned Triton.
extraction.title: AI as a Compiler: Compiling Triton kernels without the Triton compiler

techniques.technique_name: Triton AI Compiler (TAIC) with Triton Compiler Environment (TCEnv): LLM AI lowering Triton-to-PTX with diagnose-plan-branch loop, subagent patches, NCU profiler feedback, randomized differential testing and optional Volta symbolic verification
techniques.tools: Nsight Compute (NCU); ptxas / PTX ISA 8.7; Triton 3.6.0 (baseline); Volta PTX verifier (extended, 42 kLoC to 60 kLoC); GPUs L40S, H100, B200
techniques.iterations: Iterative diagnose-plan-branch-evaluate cycle until API cost budget exhausted ($15 per run for complex kernels, $1 for SwiGLU in repeatability study); only safe, correct, faster candidates seed next round
techniques.metrics: efficiency: kernel latency speedup vs autotuned Triton (execution); correctness: randomized differential testing within tolerance and provable equivalence via Volta symbolic verification (tool-static)
techniques.benchmarks: 12 common kernels from TritonBench and OpenAI Triton tutorials (FP16/FP8 on Ada, Hopper, Blackwell); 10 kernels from recent ML papers (FlashAttention, FlashSinkhorn, Forgetting Attention, SageAttention, BitDelta x2, Lion, Dion, Mamba-2 x2); randomly generated integer Triton kernels for semantics test
techniques.models: GPT-6 Astra, size NR, closed, reasoning/frontier (main); GPT-5.4, GPT-5.5, GPT-5.6 Terra, GPT-5.6 Luna, GPT-5.6 Sol, size NR, closed (model comparison on FP16 GEMM)
techniques.baselines: Autotuned, hand-optimized Triton 3.6.0 compiler output; formally-verified-in-loop variant (original Volta) vs numerically verified
techniques.effect_target_headline: AI lowering achieves 0.83×-3.34× the performance of autotuned Triton (3.34× on BitDelta, 1.37× on FlashAttention, up to 2.23× on convolution); FP16 GEMM 0.83× on H100
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: Provably verified (original Volta) vs numerically verified on B200 FP16: GEMM 0.24× vs 1.03×, FlashAttention 0.78× vs 1.37×; extended Volta verifies all common kernels except reduction sum and softmax, and six of ten recent kernels

extraction.notes: Model names (GPT-6 Astra, GPT-5.6 Terra/Luna/Sol) as printed. Main grid is single run per experiment; repeatability on 4 B200 kernels x 5 runs (e.g., Convolution FP8 2.004 ± 0.197).
