Contamination addressed via random kernels and misleading cues. Prompts not given. Figure 4 Pareto plots garbled. No artifact URL. No dedicated threats section; verifier soundness limitations discussed.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Primarily a benchmark (LibraryDesignBench) but it empirically evaluates prompting interventions (agent-first explicit guidance for library designers; prescriptive implementer prompts; reasoning effort) on LLM-generated code and reports simplicity (SLOC, cyclomatic, cognitive complexity, Halstead volume) alongside test pass rate.
extraction.title: Can Agents Design Libraries for Agents?

techniques.technique_name: Explicit agent-first ('neuralese') design guidance prompt for library designers: consumer-first API sketches, runnable usage examples, testing the library with subagents
techniques.tools: tree-sitter 0.25.2; ruff format 0.16.6; prettier 3.9.6; rustfmt 1.9.0; fourmolu 0.20.1.0 (measurement); mini-SWE-agent / Codex harnesses; Harbor
techniques.iterations: Designer workflow asks subagents to write programs from sketches and fixes library until a fresh agent lands on the sketch for every sketch; 4-hour design budget
techniques.metrics: readability-maintainability: simplicity = capped reference-to-program ratio averaged over SLOC, cyclomatic complexity, cognitive complexity, Halstead volume of downstream programs [tool-static, relative to reference]; exported-name overlap with production library [tool-static]; correctness: fraction of tests passed [execution]; combined score = pass^2 x simplicity
techniques.benchmarks: LibraryDesignBench: 15 library-design tasks, 242 expert-validated downstream problems (Python 6, TypeScript 1, Rust 5, Haskell 3 tasks)
techniques.models: GPT-6 Astra (Codex, high), size NR, closed, reasoning (designer); GPT-5.6 Luna, closed, reasoning; GLM 5.3 Flash, size NR, open; DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, size NR, open (implementers)
techniques.baselines: Same designer with standard specification prompt; production (human-written) library; no library
techniques.effect_target_headline: The score rises from 44.1 to 46.4, just below production (46.6); raises the score by 2.3 points, mainly from 6.8% higher simplicity; guided libraries share fewer exported names with production, 13.4% versus 19.4%
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: the guidance prompt gains 2.5 points from simplicity and loses 0.9 from correctness

techniques.technique_name: Prescriptive implementer prompt (thin-adapter library-use rules with map/build/audit workflow) vs minimal/low/medium prescription
techniques.tools: tree-sitter 0.25.2 plus pinned formatters (measurement); Codex harness
techniques.metrics: readability-maintainability: simplicity (SLOC, cyclomatic, cognitive complexity, Halstead volume relative to reference) [tool-static]; correctness: % tests passed [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: LibraryUseBench (production libraries of the 15 LibraryDesignBench tasks, 242 problems)
techniques.models: GPT-5.6 Luna (Codex, high effort), size NR, closed, reasoning
techniques.baselines: Minimal-prescription prompt; low- and medium-prescription prompts
techniques.effect_target_headline: The default prompt instead raises simplicity from 48.7 to 60.4 over the minimal one (GPT-5.6 Luna, high effort); score 37.0 (Min.) vs 45.5 (Default)
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: % Pass 85.9 (Min.) vs 84.5 (Default High)

techniques.technique_name: Higher reasoning effort for implementer agent
techniques.tools: tree-sitter 0.25.2 plus pinned formatters (measurement); Codex harness
techniques.metrics: readability-maintainability: simplicity [tool-static]; correctness: % tests passed [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: LibraryUseBench (production libraries, 242 problems)
techniques.models: GPT-5.6 Luna (Codex), size NR, closed, reasoning
techniques.baselines: Low and medium reasoning effort
techniques.effect_target_headline: Simplicity 83.2 (Low effort) vs 72.5 (Med.) vs 60.4 (High), default prompt
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: Raising effort from low to high increases the pass rate from 51.4% to 84.5%

extraction.notes: Mainly a benchmark paper; interventions (Sec 3.3, 3.4) are secondary. Simplicity is a code-size/complexity measure of downstream programs relative to expert references, mapped here to readability-maintainability; reviewer should confirm this mapping. Explicit-guidance intervention tested with a single designer model (GPT-6 Astra, Codex) and the combined intervention only (no component ablation). Reasoning-effort simplicity drop is confounded by low-effort incomplete solutions. Figure 2/4/5/6 and Table 2/3 text extraction is garbled; Table 3 values read from flattened layout. Failure audit is by a single LLM without human labels.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes a training recipe (security-suite SFT plus GRPO RL or hint-guided on-policy self-distillation) for LLM coding agents and reports quantitative security outcomes (SecPass from security tests/exploits) of the agent-generated code alongside functional pass rates.
extraction.title: SecureVibe: Making Vibe Coding More Secure

techniques.technique_name: SecureVibe (Security Suite SFT + SecureVibe_rl GRPO / SecureVibe_hg hint-guided on-policy self-distillation)
techniques.tools: mini-swe-agent harness; Slime post-training framework; functional and security test suites of the benchmarks; SFT trajectories distilled from MiniMax M2.7; hints generated by GPT 5.6 Sol
techniques.iterations: SFT 3 epochs; RL with 8 samples per prompt (GRPO, dynamic sampling); OPSD with L4 hints
techniques.metrics: security: SecPass pass@1 (solutions passing both functional and security tests/expert exploits) [execution]; per-CWE SecPass [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: PatchEval-Gen (200 tasks, 100 held-out validation), AutoBaxBench (560 tasks, 420 validation), BaxBench (392 tasks), SusVibes (186 tasks), unseen-CWE subsets (SusVibes 78, BaxBench 140), SWE-bench Verified (500)
techniques.languages: JavaScript, Python, Go, Ruby, Rust, PHP
techniques.models: Qwen 3.5 35B (Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, open, MoE) as trained model; GPT 5.6 Sol (closed) and MiniMax M2.7 (230B, open) as reference comparisons
techniques.baselines: Qwen 3.5 35B base; Security Only SFT; Simple Mixture SFT; Security Only SFT + GRPO; GPT 5.6 Sol and MiniMax M2.7 as reference
techniques.effect_target_headline: S ECURE V IBE improves the security pass@1 by 6.9 points on BaxBench. The gains extend to unseen CWE categories, with improvements of 11.5 points on SusVibes.
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: it also improves functionality pass@1 by 13.6 points on the security coding task SusVibes and 4.1 points on the generic coding task SWE-bench Verified

extraction.notes: Only one model is trained (Qwen 3.5 35B); larger models are reference points only. Results are mean and std over 3 runs, with paired significance tests on the unseen-CWE subset. Overlap between PatchEval-Gen and SusVibes was removed and online git retrieval was blocked during SusVibes evaluation, but pretraining contamination is not discussed. Hardware (8 B200 GPUs) is reported but not training time, tokens or calls. No threats-to-validity section, only caveats in Appendix B. Table 1 is garbled in extraction.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Compares three LLMs (ChatGPT 5.5, Claude Opus 4.7, SWE 1.6) building one Streamlit app in Windsurf and rates code quality by experts; the aim is a model comparison, not proposing or evaluating a quality-improving technique.
extraction.title: Comparative analysis of the applicability of artificial intelligence models for code generation
extraction.notes: Borderline: the final scenario asks each model to refactor its own generated code, and expert-rated quality rises before/after (Claude 3.61 to 4.33, ChatGPT 3.22 to 4.00, SWE 2.17 to 3.34; 3 experts, no agreement reported). That step is part of the project scenario rather than an evaluated technique with a controlled baseline; reviewer may reconsider as a self-refinement/refactoring-prompt evaluation.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes an RL-based parametric self-evolution method (PCPO) for an LLM that generates code; in the GPU kernel design experiment the runtime speedup of the LLM-generated kernels over PyTorch Eager (an efficiency outcome) is reported. The main global-placement experiment measures task-output quality (HPWL), not code NF quality, so eligibility rests on the kernel experiment.
extraction.title: Self-Evolving Algorithm-Design Agents: Escaping In-Context Evolutionary Stagnation via Population-Curated Policy Optimization

techniques.technique_name: Population-Curated Policy Optimization (PCPO): global curated population (AST dedup, semantic-twin removal, illegal filtering, bucketed reward normalization + diversity) with hybrid on-policy GRPO and regularized off-policy updates on elite self-generated programs
techniques.tools: KernelBench timing protocol (CUDA events, warmup, repeated trials) on NVIDIA RTX 4090; DREAMPlace placer for the global placement reward
techniques.iterations: 64-rollout budget per kernel case (online/inference-time training); off-policy update every T=2 steps, top-k=4
techniques.metrics: efficiency: GPU kernel speedup = T_eager/T_kernel vs frozen PyTorch Eager baseline [execution]; (global placement: best@n HPWL of placement produced by the generated learning-rate schedule [execution], a task objective rather than code NF quality)
techniques.benchmarks: KernelBench Level-1, 4 cases (MinGPTNewGelu, SoftSign, MatmulWithDiagonalMatrices, TripletMarginLoss); global placement ISPD 2005 + ICCAD 2015, 16 chip cases (4 for training)
techniques.languages: Python (CUDA/GPU kernels; Python learning-rate schedule functions)
techniques.models: Qwen3-8B, 8B, open, instruct (thinking off) - base for PCPO; Gemma4-E4B-it, open, instruct (global placement only); GPT-5.5, closed (baseline); GPT-4o, closed (baseline); Codex with GPT-5.5, closed agent (baseline)
techniques.baselines: Qwen3-8B direct sampling, OpenEvolve, ShinkaEvolve, ThetaEvolve, GRPO, GPT-5.5, Codex (kernels); also JitRL, RePO, random replay, GPT-4o, DREAMPlace human-set parameters (placement)
techniques.effect_target_headline: PCPO achieves significant speedups on four GPU kernel designs, with an average of 8.27× speedup against the PyTorch Eager baseline (avg rank 1.50 vs 3.38 for GPT-5.5 and 6.00 for Qwen3-8B, Table 3)

extraction.notes: Eligibility borderline: the main experiment (global placement learning-rate schedules) measures HPWL of the placement, not efficiency of the code; only the extended KernelBench experiment (4 tasks, 4 independent runs, mean reported, no variance) gives a code-efficiency outcome. Correctness of kernels is a validity gate only; no correctness rate reported. Gemma4-E4B used only for placement. Compute: tokens (Fig. 11, ~4x fewer than OpenEvolve/ShinkaEvolve) and PFLOPs (Fig. 1). Tables are garbled in extraction. No threats-to-validity section, no code link.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes an agentic documentation-grounded generation plus compile/validation loop for LLM code generation and reports per-category library error counts, including unused imports (a maintainability smell the paper itself frames as reducing clarity and maintainability), alongside a correctness rate. Borderline: the main outcome is library/import correctness, and the only NF outcome is the unused-import (and arguably deprecated-API) count.
extraction.title: Understanding and Mitigating Library-Related Issues in LLM-Generated Code
extraction.venue: preprint (arXiv:2610.00622; formatted for IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering)

techniques.technique_name: Library-aware agentic code generation (Analyzer + Documentation Retrieval + Code Generator + Validator with Compilation and Dependency Management)
techniques.tools: DuckDuckGo Search API; BeautifulSoup; Python compile; pip via subprocess; importlib
techniques.iterations: Iterative Validator-to-Generator loop until validation criteria satisfied or a configured maximum number of iterations (value not stated); median 1.68-2.53 iterations
techniques.metrics: readability-maintainability: count of unused imports and deprecated library usage per model (error-category counts; instrument not clearly described for the 300-task evaluation, exploratory taxonomy built by manual annotation, kappa 0.86) [human/tool-static unclear]; correctness: code correctness rate = % files compiling and satisfying library usage requirements [execution]; total library-related errors and error reduction rate
techniques.benchmarks: New dataset of 300 code-generation tasks derived from GitHub repositories (created or maintained after June 2025) using LangChain, AutoGen, CrewAI, LlamaIndex, Agno; plus exploratory study of 100 prompt-code pairs
techniques.models: GPT-5, size NR, closed, reasoning; DeepSeek-V3, open, instruct; Qwen3, size NR, open; Mistral (Mistral 7B cited), open; Llama 3, size NR, open
techniques.baselines: Direct prompting with each LLM; ablations removing Analyzer, Validator, Documentation Retrieval, Compilation (DeepSeek-V3)
techniques.effect_target_headline: Unused Import, direct prompting vs our approach (Table II): GPT-5 27 vs 9; DeepSeek-V3 19 vs 7; Qwen-3 28 vs 14; Mistral 53 vs 18; Llama-3 44 vs 23. Overall: reducing library-related errors by 38.1%–54.6%

extraction.notes: Borderline eligibility: NF evidence limited to unused-import (and deprecated-API) counts within a library-correctness study; a reviewer may prefer EC5/correctness-only. How errors were detected in the 300-task evaluation is not described (manual vs automated). Inconsistencies: text says GPT-5 correctness +4% but Table II prints +5% (81->85); text says hallucinated errors 31->13 for GPT-5 and 48->21 for DeepSeek-V3, while Table II shows GPT-5 28->11, DeepSeek-V3 31->13, Llama-3 48->21. Max iteration count not stated; prompts not given. Compute only as median refinement iterations. Recent-repo selection (post June 2025) partially addresses contamination. Ablation only on DeepSeek-V3. No variance or statistical tests. Table I garbled in extraction.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes an agentic harness (optimization guidance plus profiling, timing and validation tools) that makes LLM coding agents edit WAM inference code, and reports latency/speedup of the agent-edited code against the same agents without the harness, with task success as a co-outcome.
extraction.title: WAMJET: A Harness for World Action Model Acceleration

techniques.technique_name: WAMJET agentic harness (optimization skill guidance, external memory, profiling/trace/timing tools, output/state checks, paired task evaluation; bottleneck-driven iterative accept/revert loop)
techniques.tools: Custom Python tools: endpoint timing, GPU trace analysis, startup analysis, deadline analysis, numerical output checker, state checks, paired task analysis with exact McNemar test; NVIDIA H100 and B200 GPUs; coding agents via Codex and Claude Code
techniques.iterations: Iterate profile-modify-validate within a user-specified search budget; two rounds (R1, R2) reported; changes reverted if slower or invalid
techniques.metrics: efficiency: warmed inference latency (ms), speedup over upstream implementation, startup time [execution]; correctness/quality: robot task success rate on RoboLab, LIBERO, LIBERO-plus, numerical drift and state checks [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: Six WAMs: Fast-WAM, Cosmos-Policy-Predict2-2B, DreamZero, LingBot-VA, Cosmos3-Nano-Policy-DROID, OpenWAM; task evaluation on RoboLab subset (20 tasks x 10 episodes), full LIBERO and LIBERO-plus
techniques.models: GPT-5.6-sol xhigh (Codex), closed, reasoning; GPT-6-astra xhigh (Codex), closed, reasoning; Claude-opus-5 xhigh (Claude Code), closed, reasoning
techniques.baselines: Official upstream implementation; same coding agent optimizing without WAMJET
techniques.effect_target_headline: WAMJET achieves up to 9.95× lossless speedup over upstream implementations (GPT-6-astra, LingBot-VA on H100: 534.9 ms w/ WAMJET R2 vs 966.7 ms w/o WAMJET vs 5323.6 ms baseline); lower reported latency than the corresponding runs without WAMJET in all 12 entries
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: OpenWAM LIBERO 98.95% baseline vs 99.10% w/ WAMJET Lossless vs 99.25% w/ WAMJET Approx.; DreamZero RoboLab 25.0% baseline vs 24.0% lossless

extraction.notes: The edited artifact is existing human-written WAM inference code optimized by LLM coding agents (edit, not from-scratch generation). Search budgets for with/without settings are said to be the same but the conclusion notes controlled comparisons under matched budgets as future work. Single run per configuration; McNemar test used only for task-success acceptance. The numerical drift checker was usually turned off. Table III/IV text garbled but recoverable. Search time shown in Fig. 3 only.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Benchmark paper that empirically evaluates an input-side technique (supplying expert three-level design guidance to LLM agents) and measures the runtime efficiency (speedup over a baseline) of the generated GPU kernels, alongside correctness.
extraction.title: D2K-Bench: Can LLM Agents Turn Expert Designs into Efficient GPU Kernels?

techniques.technique_name: Expert design guidance (L1 algorithmic insights, L2 dataflow design, L3 low-level optimization tricks) supplied to an agentic kernel-optimization loop
techniques.tools: Triton; NVIDIA Nsight Compute (ncu); CUDA Toolkit 13.0; PyTorch 2.9 prerelease (cu130); Claude Code CLI 2.1.197; Codex CLI 0.147.0; MCP tools read/write/bash/submit
techniques.iterations: 350 agent turns per task; final submission = eligible candidate with highest geometric mean speedup
techniques.metrics: efficiency: Performance Score Sperf (geometric mean speedup over first-correct Fable-5 baseline, 0.5 penalty for failed tasks) [execution]; geometric mean speedup; expert-relative performance %; fast_p thresholded speedup coverage [execution]; design/implementation completeness JSdesign/JSimpl 0-100 [llm-judge]
techniques.benchmarks: D2K-Bench (new), 26 tasks, 85 workloads, NVIDIA B200
techniques.models: GPT-6-Astra, closed; Claude-Opus-4.8, closed; GPT-5.6-Sol, closed; GLM-5.3, open; Kimi-K3, open; judge: Qwen3.8-Max-0902
techniques.baselines: Same agent runs without design guidance; PyTorch reference; expert implementations; Fable-5 first-correct submission as normalization baseline
techniques.effect_target_headline: Overall Sperf increases from 1.46 to 1.95, a 33.9% improvement (five models, 26 tasks); geometric mean speedup increases from 1.69× to 2.49× (three fully correct models)
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: correctness increases from 93.1% to 98.5% (130 model-task pairs)

extraction.notes: Primarily a benchmark paper; the evaluated intervention is human-authored expert design guidance added to the agent's input (paired with/without runs). Single run per configuration, no variance or statistical tests; no threats-to-validity section. Token/cost reported only for Claude-Opus-4.8 (US$631.56 to US$820.10). Cumulative ablation L1, L1+L2, L1+L2+L3 on three models (Figure 3). Tables partially garbled in extraction but numbers are recoverable.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Benchmark paper for LLM-generated PLC Structured Text that evaluates direct generation and four generation-and-verification workflows only by Task Success and plant-level Safety Violation (task-specified functional/interlock constraints in a simulated plant), plus generation cost; no readability, runtime efficiency or security (vulnerability) outcome of the code is measured.
extraction.title: PLCWorld: Benchmarking LLM-Generated PLC Programs in Closed-Loop Plant Simulation
extraction.notes: Borderline: Safety Violation Rate measures breaches of task-specified physical safety constraints (interlocks, collisions, conflicting outputs) during simulated plant execution; treated here as part of functional requirements rather than code security (CWE) or another NF dimension. Generation cost (calls, tokens, time) is reported but is not a property of the generated code. Frameworks (LLM4PLC, Agents4PLC, AutoPLC, SemaPLC) show no consistent gains vs matched direct GPT-5.5 (e.g., SR 61.10 direct vs 63.00 AutoPLC; SVR 19.26 vs 16.70). Code at https://yunji0516.github.io/PLCWorld/. A reviewer who counts plant-safety violations as an NF dimension may reconsider.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Benchmark paper that empirically evaluates an intervention (appending a natural-language skill distilled from a prior attempt in another DSL to an LLM agent's prompt) against matched solo attempts, measuring end-to-end runtime (efficiency) and correctness of the LLM-generated GPU kernel code.
extraction.title: MetaKernelBench: Measuring GPU Kernel Knowledge Transfer Beyond Code

techniques.technique_name: Cross-DSL skill transfer: self-distilled natural-language SKILL.md from a solo attempt in one kernel DSL (CuTe DSL or TIRx) appended verbatim to the instruction of a fresh attempt in the other DSL
techniques.tools: GPU verifier on NVIDIA B200 (5 correctness draws, 10 warmup, 50 timed calls, CUDA events); Terminus-2 scaffold via Harbor 0.20.0; PyTorch 2.13.0, CUDA 13.2, CUTLASS DSL 4.7.0, Apache TVM 0.25.0.post1; static check rejecting TIRx inline CUDA
techniques.iterations: Each attempt (solo or skill-conditioned) has a 40-minute wall-clock budget and at most 10 feedback submissions; single transfer (one round)
techniques.metrics: efficiency: end-to-end median runtime, speedup over eager PyTorch reference, paired lift (geometric mean of clipped paired runtime ratios), help/harm rates [execution]; correctness: pass rate against float64-anchored reference [execution]; skill content/uptake labels [llm-judge]
techniques.benchmarks: MetaKernelBench, 74 fused-subgraph problems (6 families: Attention 18, KV Cache 8, Linear Attention 13, MLP & Norm 17, MoE 8, Quantization 10), each in CuTe DSL and TIRx variants; problems adapted from SOL-ExecBench, FlashInfer-Bench, vLLM, flash-linear-attention
techniques.languages: Python (PyTorch) with CuTe DSL and TIRx GPU kernel DSLs
techniques.models: DeepSeek-V4-Pro, open, reasoning/instruct; GLM-5.3, open, instruct; GLM-5.3-Flash, open, instruct; Gemini 3.7 Flash, closed, instruct; GPT-5.6 Sol, closed, reasoning; Qwen3.8-Flash, open, instruct
techniques.baselines: Solo attempt by the same model on the same variant without the transferred skill, under matched per-attempt budget
techniques.effect_target_headline: paired lift over solo attempts ranges from −19% to +29% (six models, both directions); regressions occur on 16% to 45% of problems in every model and direction
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: skill-conditioned attempts passing in 62.9% of the 97 comparisons with a nonpassing source against 75.3% for solo attempts on the same variants

extraction.notes: Primarily a benchmark paper; included because it evaluates a prompting intervention (skill transfer) on runtime of generated kernels with a matched no-skill baseline. Paired lift folds correctness transitions (rescue=4, break=1/4) into the runtime metric. Single attempt per arm; permutation tests only for correlation analyses. Skill content and failure-cause labels come from LLM annotators without reported agreement. Tables 1-2 partially garbled in extraction. Openness/type of model descriptors are inferred. Project page given; code availability not explicitly stated. Limitations section present (E.1).

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes SparseCraft, a closed agentic loop in which an LLM proposer edits Chisel RTL, memory configuration and sparse-kernel schedule from measured feedback (with an LLM repairer), and reports quantitative efficiency outcomes (cycles, traffic, energy, perf/W, area) of the LLM-edited design.
extraction.title: SparseCraft: Agentic Hardware-Software Co-Optimization for Sparse Computing

techniques.technique_name: SparseCraft: closed CHIA loop with LLM proposer editing Chisel RTL/memory/schedule via MCP tools, measured-feedback work orders, gate ladder and LLM repairer
techniques.tools: Chipyard/Gemmini; sbt compile; Verilator cycle-accurate simulation (Rocket + Gemmini); bit-exact equivalence check on 32,768 outputs; yosys and OpenSTA synthesis on NanGate45; 27-rule legality checker; counter-based energy model; CHIA framework with MCP tool servers
techniques.iterations: Fixed budget of 15 iterations (counter ends the run); up to 3 repair attempts per iteration by repairer LLM, stopping on NOT ACTIONABLE or revert; Pareto non-dominance admission, rejected designs rolled back
techniques.metrics: efficiency: cycles, off-chip bytes, performance (GOPS), power, modelled energy, perf/W, perf/area, energy/op, EDP [execution: cycle-accurate simulation + modelled energy]; area via synthesis [tool-static]; correctness: bit-for-bit equivalence on all 32,768 outputs vs golden reference [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: GraphChallenge sparse-DNN layer, 512x512 upper-left block of n1024-l1.mtx times dense 512x64 INT8 (single workload)
techniques.languages: Chisel (Scala) RTL; C kernel schedule (spmm.c); configuration parameters
techniques.models: Claude Opus 5, size NR, closed, reasoning (via Claude Code agent) as proposer; repairer model not separately named
techniques.baselines: Stock Gemmini (16x16 weight-stationary array, 256 KB scratchpad, 64 KB accumulator) running block-sparse kernel (iteration 1); no alternative LLM technique or ablation
techniques.effect_target_headline: 2.1× fewer cycles, 9.8× less off-chip traffic and 22.8% less area than the block-sparse Gemmini baseline, with 5.61× higher modelled perf/W and 11.8× lower EDP (iteration 15 vs iteration 1)
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: BASELINE (ITERATION 1) AGAINST THE BEST DESIGN (ITERATION 15); NEITHER PRODUCES A WRONG OUTPUT

extraction.notes: Short workshop paper (~5 pages); single run, single workload, single model, no repeated runs or ablation (e.g., no LLM without measured-feedback work orders). Artifact is hardware RTL plus configuration and schedule, so 'efficiency' is hardware performance/energy/area of the design. Source-code link appears only as text 'sparsecraft-source-code' (no URL in extraction). Figures 2-4 garbled; Table I numbers extracted. 17 LLM sessions, 328 min active time reported.

extraction.eligibility_reason: VortexSynth uses an LLM agent (Claude Opus 5) with profiler feedback to synthesize GPU kernels for benchmark reconstruction, but the objective and outcome is matching a reference kernel's hardware-profile signature (signature distance) plus output equivalence, not improving efficiency, readability or security of the generated code.
extraction.title: VortexSynth: Profile-guided benchmark reconstruction for GPU architecture research
extraction.notes: Borderline: profile metrics (cache hit rate, coalescing, DRAM bandwidth, occupancy) are efficiency-related, but the paper explicitly optimizes for fidelity to a reference profile (sometimes deliberately reducing coalescing), not for faster or more efficient code. Single model, no runtime-speedup outcome. Figure 4 heatmap is garbled in extraction.

extraction.eligibility_reason: An AI coding agent implements 60 change requests under four interventions (cohesion prompt, quality-gated refactor, disclosed structural cost function, AI reviewer loop) versus a bare control, and the produced Java code is measured with standard maintainability/complexity/coupling/duplication tools alongside test-based correctness.
extraction.title: Conserved amount, negotiable placement. Prompting perturbs one architecture, an AI reviewer both

techniques.metrics: readability-maintainability: cyclomatic complexity (lizard), Halstead volume, CK WMC/CBO/LCOM (CK), PMD cognitive complexity, HHI/Gini/top-1 concentration of complexity and change, change entropy, propagation cost, file count, duplicated lines/density (jscpd), Maintainability Index [tool-static]; comprehension probe recall by a fresh agent [llm-judge]
techniques.benchmarks: Spring PetClinic REST, endpoint POST /api/owners, fixed plan of 60 accumulating change requests with black-box acceptance suite; two architectures (Spring @RestController, OfficeFloor pipeline); 10 runs per cell
techniques.models: claude-opus-4-8, size NR, closed, reasoning/agentic
techniques.baselines: just-solve control (bare change request)
techniques.effect_target_headline: The mutative arm's duplicated line count rose from 2,206 under the control to 2,735 under the cohesion prompt (Spring); LCOM 26.0 under the cohesion prompt vs 29.6 control (Spring)
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: strict pass rate final phase: Spring 0.108 vs control 0.267; OfficeFloor 0.050 vs control 0.325

techniques.metrics: readability-maintainability: same static complexity/coupling/concentration/duplication suite (lizard, PMD, CK, jscpd) [tool-static]; comprehension probe [llm-judge]
techniques.benchmarks: Spring PetClinic REST, POST /api/owners, 60 change requests, two architectures, 10 runs per cell
techniques.models: claude-opus-4-8, size NR, closed, reasoning/agentic
techniques.baselines: just-solve control
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: Under impact-gated the mutative arm rose, from 0.267 to 0.308 (strict pass); OfficeFloor 0.167 vs control 0.325

techniques.technique_name: formula-provided (structural cost function disclosed in the prompt as the objective)
techniques.iterations: gate available but fired on 3 of 1,200 checkpoints
techniques.metrics: readability-maintainability: static complexity/coupling/concentration/duplication suite (lizard, PMD, CK, jscpd) [tool-static]; comprehension probe [llm-judge]
techniques.benchmarks: Spring PetClinic REST, POST /api/owners, 60 change requests, two architectures, 10 runs per cell
techniques.models: claude-opus-4-8, size NR, closed, reasoning/agentic
techniques.baselines: just-solve control
techniques.effect_target_headline: cum_change_top1 Spring ctl 0.344 vs Spring formula 0.122 (OfficeFloor ctl 0.106); ck_lcom_mean falling from 29.6 to 17.3 in the mutative arm under the formula; duplication density from 0.336 to 0.378
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: formula-provided has the worst strict pass rate in the mutative arm, 0.033 against the control's 0.267; isolated pass rate 1.000

techniques.technique_name: ai-reviewed (independent reviewer agent critiques each diff for cohesion/structure; author agent resumed to act on it)
techniques.iterations: one review and one author fix turn per change request
techniques.metrics: readability-maintainability: static complexity/coupling/concentration/duplication suite (lizard, PMD, CK, jscpd) [tool-static]; comprehension probe [llm-judge]
techniques.benchmarks: Spring PetClinic REST, POST /api/owners, 60 change requests, two architectures, 10 runs per cell
techniques.models: claude-opus-4-8, size NR, closed, reasoning/agentic (author and reviewer)
techniques.baselines: just-solve control; the three other interventions
techniques.effect_target_headline: The reviewer raises the share of change landing in one file from 0.106 to 0.154, the share of complexity in one file from 0.086 to 0.135 (OfficeFloor arm); coupling, file count and per-node complexity untouched

extraction.notes: Paper's thesis is about 'placement' plasticity rather than a quality improvement; effect directions on maintainability are not framed as better/worse by the author (concentration vs distribution trade-off, duplication rose where code was pushed apart), hence 'mixed'. Single model, single application, one codebase per arm; author has declared competing interest (creator of OfficeFloor and ImpactGate). Exact prompt texts for cohesion paragraph, cost formula and reviewer are not reproduced in the paper. Tables partially garbled (Tables 1, 2, 8, 9 column alignment). Comprehension probe is an LLM-based measure.

extraction.eligibility_reason: Proposes TileCas, a pluggable extension for LLM coding-agent kernel workflows that moves generation across abstraction levels using profiling/correctness feedback, and measures execution speedup (efficiency) of the LLM-generated kernels.
extraction.title: TileCas: Cascading Kernel Development Across Programming Abstractions

techniques.technique_name: TileCas (Cross-Level Diagnosis + Abstraction Scheduling + Heterogeneous Search Tree, integrated into AKO and KDA agentic kernel workflows)
techniques.tools: TileLang (high level); Ascend C and HIP C++ (low level); Ascend 910B3 and AMD Radeon AI PRO R9700; correctness tolerance 1e-3; latency median of 5 runs after 3 warm-ups
techniques.iterations: 120-minute total budget per run (base workflow may stop earlier); five independent seeds; ~22 candidate evaluations per run on average
techniques.metrics: efficiency: speedup over KernelBench PyTorch reference latency, arithmetic mean over workloads and configurations [execution]; correctness: majority-success correctness vs reference outputs [execution]
techniques.benchmarks: KernelBench Level 3, 50 end-to-end workloads x 4 accelerator-model configurations (200 pairs)
techniques.languages: TileLang, Ascend C, HIP C++ (from PyTorch reference)
techniques.models: GPT-6 Astra, closed, low reasoning effort; DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, open, low reasoning effort
techniques.baselines: AKO-High, AKO-Low, AKO-Fixed (High then Low), AKO-Unrestricted, AKO-Random (frequency-matched routing), original KDA; ablations w/o Diagnosis, w/o Scheduling, w/o Tree
techniques.effect_target_headline: AKO with TileCas achieves an arithmetic-mean speedup of 4.84x, compared with 3.75x for the strongest evaluated baseline without TileCas, an improvement of 29.0%; KDA+TileCas improves KDA mean speedup by 69.2% (2.615x to 4.425x)
techniques.effect_correctness_headline: Correct 195/200 (AKO+TileCas) vs 191/200 (AKO-Random), 188/200 (AKO-Fixed); KDA+TileCas 195/200 vs KDA 190/200

extraction.notes: Kernel-generation efficiency paper. Compute reported as wall-clock time and candidate evaluations, not LLM tokens or cost. Prompts/agent instructions not shown in the paper (code on GitHub). Five seeds with SD and workload-level bootstrap 95% CIs; paired win/tie/loss. Random routing control derived post hoc from TileCas transition frequencies. Explicit Limitations and Threats to Validity section.
